after-major-storm-boulder-creek.title: What to Do After a Major Storm
after-major-storm-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • If you smell gas, leave the building first and call 911 from outside. A downed line or an injury is a 911 call too. None of the three waits.
  • Treat every downed or sagging power line as live, even one that looks dead. Stay far back.
  • The ground can keep sliding for days after the rain stops. Watch for fresh cracks and leaning trees, and be ready to leave.
  • Photograph damage before you clean up or make repairs, and keep receipts for emergency work, for insurance.
  • Check on older neighbors, anyone on medical power equipment, and people who live alone.

Printable version: the winter storm and outage checklist covers both halves, getting ready beforehand and checking your place afterward, on one sheet. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

The quiet after a big storm feels like the all-clear, and it isn't. A lot of the damage, and a lot of the injuries, land after the weather clears. Downed lines are still live, saturated ground keeps sliding for days, weakened trees keep falling, and hidden damage shows up when you go looking. Here's how to check your place and your neighbors safely once the worst has passed. If you smell gas, get outside first and call 911 from a safe distance. A downed line or an injury is a 911 call too.

First, the dangerous stuff

  • Downed power lines. Treat every downed or sagging line as live and dangerous, even if it looks dead. Stay far back, keep others and pets away, call 911 first, then report it to PG&E at 1-800-743-5000. Never try to move a line or a tree that's touching one.
  • Gas smell. If you smell gas, don't flip switches, use a phone, or light anything. Leave the building, then call 911 from a safe distance, and your gas provider after that.
  • Unstable trees and limbs. Storms leave "widowmakers," hanging limbs and leaning trees that come down later. Look up before you work under trees, and be cautious around any that shifted.
  • Water safety. If your power was out, well pumps and treatment may have been affected. If you lost pressure, your well flooded, or you suspect contamination, use bottled water and follow what your water provider or County Environmental Health tells you. Boil only when officials advise it for germs, because boiling does not remove chemicals.

Check your property

  • Walk the drainage again. Culverts and ditches often clog mid-storm. Re-clear them, safely and never in moving water, so the next system doesn't back up. See our culverts and drainage guide.
  • Look for erosion and slumping. Fresh cracks in the ground, tilting fences or trees, or soil pulling away from foundations are warning signs. There's more on those in winter landslide warning signs.
  • Check the roof and structure from the ground for damage, and the crawlspace or garage for water intrusion.
  • Food safety. If the fridge was off for hours, when in doubt, throw it out.

Document and report

  • Photograph damage before you clean up or make temporary repairs, for insurance. Keep receipts for emergency work.
  • Report road hazards like washouts, slides, and downed trees blocking county roads to Santa Cruz County Public Works, whose 24-hour road dispatch is (831) 477-3999. Report state-highway hazards through Caltrans or 911 if it's dangerous.
  • Report a still-out outage to PG&E so it's on their map.

Remember the risk isn't over

Ground saturated by a big storm can keep sliding for days after the rain, and back-to-back systems are common here. Keep watching the forecast, stay ready to leave if a slide threatens your home, and don't assume the danger passed with the clouds.

Check on neighbors

Mountain living runs on this. Look in on older neighbors, anyone who depends on power for medical equipment, and folks who live alone, especially after an outage. A quick knock can catch a problem before it becomes an emergency.

Frequently asked questions

What's the biggest danger after a storm?

Downed power lines are among the most dangerous, because they stay live. Stay far back, keep everyone away, and report them to PG&E and 911. Gas leaks, unstable trees, damaged structures, floodwater, and saturated ground all deserve the same caution.

Can landslides happen after the rain stops?

Yes. Saturated ground can keep moving for days after a storm. Watch for fresh cracks, tilting trees or fences, and slumping soil, and be ready to leave if your home is threatened.

How do I report storm damage to a road?

Report county-road hazards to Santa Cruz County Public Works at (831) 477-3999, and dangerous state-highway hazards via Caltrans or 911. Photograph your own property damage before cleanup for insurance.

The one thing worth repeating: if you smell gas, get outside before you call, and a downed line or an injury is a 911 call too. To report or track an outage, use PG&E. For current road, weather, and outage conditions across the valley, keep Mountain Status open, and see the Residents guide for county contacts and emergency resources in one place. Once the water has gone down, our rain tracker shows how much the storm dropped and where that leaves the season.

Last reviewed July 20, 2026. This guide points to official sources, including PG&E, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Santa Cruz County Public Works, and the National Weather Service, for anything time-sensitive.

atmospheric-rivers-santa-cruz-mountains.title: Atmospheric Rivers Explained for Santa Cruz Mountain Residents
atmospheric-rivers-santa-cruz-mountains.html:
The wind swings around to the south and turns warm, the sky drops low and gray, and by evening the gutters are running. If you've lived through a Santa Cruz Mountains winter, you've met an atmospheric river, even if you didn't call it that.

An atmospheric river, or AR, is a long, narrow band of concentrated water vapor that streams in off the Pacific and dumps enormous amounts of rain when it hits our mountains. A single strong one can deliver much of a winter's rain in a couple of days, which is exactly why they drive most of our flooding, road washouts, and debris flows. Learn to read one and you'll know when a forecast is worth taking seriously. For live forecasts, the National Weather Service is the source.

What an atmospheric river is

Picture a river in the sky, hundreds of miles long, carrying water vapor from the tropics toward the West Coast. When that moisture-laden air runs into terrain like the Santa Cruz Mountains, it's forced upward, cools, and wrings out as rain, often a lot of it, over the same watersheds again and again.

The strongest ones get called a "Pineapple Express" when the moisture tracks from near Hawaii. ARs aren't rare or exotic. They're the workhorses of California's water year, and a handful of them supply much of our annual rain.

Why they hit us so hard

Two reasons. First, our steep terrain squeezes extra rain out of every storm. Second, the San Lorenzo River and its tributaries drain a lot of that water right past our towns, so heavy, sustained rain shows up fast as high water.

Add saturated ground late in the season, and burned hillsides from the CZU fire, and an atmospheric river can mean flooding, debris flows, fallen trees, and a Highway 9 that's suddenly the weak link out of the valley.

The AR scale, from weak to exceptional

Researchers at the Scripps Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes rank atmospheric rivers on a scale of 1 to 5, from "weak" and mostly beneficial to "exceptional" and mostly hazardous. It works a lot like a hurricane category: a Cat 1 or 2 AR is usually welcome rain, while a Cat 4 or 5 is the kind that floods rivers and washes out roads.

When forecasters start talking about a strong or extreme AR aimed at the Central Coast, that's your cue to prepare in earnest. You can watch the outlooks at the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes.

How to prepare

This is the same storm prep that pays off all winter, done ahead of a named threat:

  • Clear your gutters and culverts before the season.
  • Get ready for power outages and know where to find sandbags.
  • Know your evacuation zone, especially near burn scars, and don't wait on a warning.
  • Sign up for CruzAware and PG&E alerts. The National Weather Service does not send alerts directly to the public, so watch weather.gov/mtr or a NOAA Weather Radio for watches and warnings, and Mountain Status when a storm is inbound.

With a strong El Niño forecast this winter, the odds of an active storm track are up. All the more reason to be ready before the first big AR arrives.

Frequently asked questions

What is an atmospheric river?

A long, narrow band of concentrated water vapor from the Pacific that produces heavy rain when it hits mountains like ours. A few strong ones supply much of California's yearly rain.

Why are atmospheric rivers dangerous in the Santa Cruz Mountains?

Steep terrain wrings out extra rain, the San Lorenzo River drains it fast past our towns, and saturated ground and burn scars raise the risk of flooding and debris flows. Strong ARs drive most of our winter damage.

How do I know if a storm is a big one?

Scripps ranks ARs from Category 1 (weak, beneficial) to 5 (exceptional, hazardous). When forecasters warn of a strong or extreme AR, take it seriously. Watch the NWS and CW3E.

Before the next big storm, walk through the rest of your winter checklist in the Residents guide, which pulls utilities, road status, and county contacts into one place. To see how the current season compares with the ones before it, our rain tracker charts valley rainfall against every water year back to 1937.

For live forecasts and warnings, always rely on the National Weather Service, not this page. For live local conditions, see Mountain Status. In an emergency, call 911. Last reviewed July 20, 2026.

back-to-school-boulder-creek.title: Back-to-School Dates and Resources for Boulder Creek Families
back-to-school-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • First day back is Thursday, August 6, 2026. Highway 9 gets its morning crowd back and the valley starts an hour earlier.
  • Boulder Creek kids attend San Lorenzo Valley Unified (SLVUSD). The district calendar is the authority if any date moves.
  • Get the early-out Wednesdays and back-to-school nights into your calendar now, before a 1:15 p.m. release catches you mid-meeting.
  • Handle enrollment, immunizations, supply lists, and transportation through the district and your school before the first bell.
  • Before- and after-school care runs largely through the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District.

Summer ends on a Thursday this year. The first day for 2026-27 is Thursday, August 6, 2026, which means Highway 9 gets its morning crowd back and the valley wakes up an hour earlier than it has since June.

Boulder Creek kids attend the San Lorenzo Valley Unified School District (SLVUSD), the town's recreation district fills in a lot of the before- and after-school pieces, and the district's calendar is where you confirm anything that moves. Here are the dates and the resources in one place. The official SLVUSD calendar is the authority if a date changes.

Key dates for 2026-27

From the district's board-approved 2026-27 calendar:

  • First day of school: Thursday, August 6, 2026
  • Back-to-school nights: SLV Middle School, Wednesday, August 12; SLV High School, Thursday, August 13; SLV Charter (Nature Academy), Tuesday, August 18; Boulder Creek Elementary and SLV Elementary, Thursday, August 20
  • Elementary parent/teacher conferences: October 19 to 23, 2026 (early dismissal that week)
  • Thanksgiving break: November 23 to 27, 2026
  • Winter break: December 21, 2026 to January 3, 2027, with the first semester ending December 17
  • Spring break: April 6 to 9, 2027
  • Last day of school: Thursday, June 3, 2027

Early-out Wednesdays. Boulder Creek Elementary releases at 1:15 p.m. every Wednesday except October 21, 2026. SLV Elementary releases at 1:25 p.m. Middle and high school have their own early-out days scattered through the year, so check the district calendar for those.

Get the ones that affect your week into your calendar now, before an early dismissal catches you mid-meeting. One note for searchers: our district is San Lorenzo Valley, at slvusd.org, not the similarly named San Lorenzo Unified in the East Bay.

The schools

Kids from Boulder Creek are spread across SLVUSD campuses up and down the valley: Boulder Creek Elementary, San Lorenzo Valley Elementary, San Lorenzo Valley Middle School, San Lorenzo Valley High School, and the San Lorenzo Valley Charter School.

For a fuller rundown of local schools, preschools, and daycare, see our guide to schools, preschools, and daycare in the San Lorenzo Valley.

Getting ready

A few things worth handling before the first bell:

  • Registration and enrollment. New students and returning-family updates go through the district and your school. Start on the SLVUSD site if you're new or need to update records.
  • Immunizations and records. California requires certain immunizations for school. Check with your school if you're unsure what's due.
  • Supply lists. Many classrooms post supply lists through the school, so check your school's page or office.
  • Transportation. Confirm bus routes or your drop-off plan, and remember Highway 9 traffic thickens on school mornings.

Before- and after-school care and activities

The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District runs much of the town's youth programming, and its calendar is where after-school activities, camps, and family events show up.

For broader family support, from childcare to assistance programs, see our SLV family resources guide.

Frequently asked questions

When does school start in Boulder Creek?

The first day of the 2026-27 year is Thursday, August 6, 2026. Boulder Creek students attend San Lorenzo Valley Unified (SLVUSD), and the official SLVUSD calendar is the authoritative source for that date and every break.

Which district is Boulder Creek in?

San Lorenzo Valley Unified School District (SLVUSD), based in the San Lorenzo Valley, at slvusd.org. It gets confused with San Lorenzo Unified (slzusd.org), a different district in the East Bay.

Where do I find after-school care and activities?

The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District runs much of the local youth programming. See also our SLV family resources guide. Districts and local businesses do much of their hiring in the weeks before the school year, and those openings show up on our valley job board.

Dates change, so confirm anything time-sensitive against the official SLVUSD calendar before you count on it. Spot something out of date? Tell us. Last reviewed July 21, 2026.

bcvfd-crab-feed.title: The BCVFD Crab Feed
bcvfd-crab-feed.html:
One night at the end of winter, the fire station on Central Avenue turns into a dining room, and the crew that turns out for your emergencies is carrying plates instead. The Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department's Crab Feed is the department's late-winter fundraiser: an evening of fresh crab, pasta, salad, and bread at the fire station, served by the volunteers, with tickets limited and the proceeds supporting the all-volunteer department.

It has landed in March in recent years, and it tends to sell out because the room only holds so many. If you're hoping to go, the one thing to sort out first is the date, and that hasn't been set yet.

When it happens

The department hasn't announced the next crab feed date yet. It's been held in March in recent years, so late winter is the time to start checking. When the date is set, it will appear on the Boulder Creek Fire Department website. Tickets are limited, so if you want to go, watch for the announcement and buy early rather than counting on the door.

What to expect

An indoor, sit-down evening at the fire station, 13230 Central Avenue. The department serves fresh crab with pasta, salad, and bread, and past years have had wine, beer, and non-alcoholic drinks available for purchase. It's a cracking-crab-with-your-neighbors kind of night, and the volunteers run all of it themselves.

Having been to both, here's how it compares to the summer BBQ: the crab feed is the cozy one. Everything happens inside the station, dinner only, no band and no stage, just neighbors packed shoulder to shoulder at picnic tables in the engine bay. If the BBQ is the town's big night out, this is its family dinner.

Two things to plan around:

  • Tickets are capped. The department has listed 250 tickets in a recent year, and when they're gone they're gone, so this isn't a walk-up event.
  • Price and timing move year to year. Recent tickets have run in the range of about $55 to $70 per person, and start times have varied, so go by whatever the department posts for the current year.

If you have questions, the department has listed 831-338-7222 for the crab feed.

History

The crab feed is one of a handful of fundraisers the Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department runs through the year, alongside the July 4 pancake breakfast and the summer BBQ and dance. They all serve the same purpose: keeping an all-volunteer department equipped.

That department goes back to 1892, and it started the way these things usually start, with a bad year. According to the department's own history, Boulder Creek's volunteer firefighters organized after two large fires nearly destroyed downtown Boulder Creek in 1891, and about twenty local residents trained as the town's first crew through 1891 into 1892. The fire station in the middle of downtown dates to 1939.

More than a century on, the town still funds the crew's equipment the old-fashioned way, one dinner at a time, and the crab feed is the winter one.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Boulder Creek Fire Department crab feed?

It's typically held in March, but the department sets and announces the date each year, and the next one hasn't been announced yet. Check the Boulder Creek Fire Department crab feed page in late winter.

How much are tickets, and do they sell out?

Recent prices have run about $55 to $70 per person, and yes, tickets are capped (the department has listed 250 in a recent year), so buy early once the date is announced. Go by the current-year price the department posts.

What's served?

Fresh crab with pasta, salad, and bread, at the fire station. Wine, beer, and non-alcoholic drinks have been available for purchase in past years.

Where does the money go?

It supports the all-volunteer Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department, one of the fundraisers that keeps the crew equipped alongside the July 4 pancake breakfast and the summer BBQ and dance.

Who do I contact with questions?

The department has listed 831-338-7222 for the crab feed. For the current date and tickets, the department's crab feed page is the source to watch.

See what else is happening around town on the Boulder Creek Local events page. Part of the department, or spot a detail here that needs fixing? Send it to us. For the next confirmed date and tickets, check the Boulder Creek Fire Department.

bcvfd-summer-bbq-dance.title: The BCVFD Summer BBQ & Dance
bcvfd-summer-bbq-dance.html:
One night a year the engines come out of the bay and the tables go in. That is the Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department's Summer BBQ & Dance, the department's biggest fundraiser of the year, held every August. This year it lands on Saturday, August 22, 2026, from 5:30 to 11 p.m., at the station at 13230 Central Avenue. Tri-tip and chicken cooked and served by the firefighters, three bands on a stage out back, $30 a ticket, kids under five free.

The smell gets to the sidewalk a good while before you do.

This year (2026)

  • When: Saturday, August 22, 2026, 5:30 to 11 p.m. Music starts at 5:50.
  • Where: Boulder Creek Fire Station, 13230 Central Avenue, downtown Boulder Creek
  • Tickets: $30 for dinner and dance, kids under 5 free, and a $100 four-pack online, through the department's Events.com page
  • Dinner: tri-tip, chicken, and sides, cooked and served by the firefighters in the apparatus bay
  • Music: Kentucky Mule from 5:50, Barnstormer from 7:30, Bootleg Country Band from 9:15, on a stage out back in the parking lot
  • Kids: bounce house and face painting
  • Where the money goes: new rescue and medical equipment for the crew

Anything that shifts between now and the 22nd will show up on bcfd.com or the department's Facebook page first.

What the night is like

Dinner is in the apparatus bay, the same garage the engines live in the other 364 days of the year. The rigs move out onto the apron, long tables go in, and the people who show up when you call 911 spend the evening carrying plates.

Out back, the parking lot does the rest of the work. Stage, dance floor, three bands in sequence with breaks between sets. Kentucky Mule opens at 5:50. Barnstormer takes the middle of the night at 7:30. Bootleg Country Band closes it out from 9:15. Come for the dinner and you want the early half. Come for the dancing and the back half is yours. Bringing small kids, eat early, turn them loose on the bounce house, and go home before the last band.

It stays a working fire station the whole time. Tones can drop in the middle of a song. If they do, the crew sets down whatever it is holding, the bay clears, and the engines you were eating next to go out the door with the music still playing. Nobody makes an announcement about it. That is the arrangement this town has run on since 1892, and it is the entire reason there is a barbecue.

I have been going to this one since 2006, so here is my review. The food is great. The volunteer firefighters tend bar, and they are maybe not the best bartenders, but they are certainly entertaining and they pour with a heavy hand. The stage is the part nobody warns first-timers about: every year, Boulder Creek's own Dave Dunning donates the stage, lights, and sound from his company, Legend Theatrical, and the setup rivals concerts you have paid real money for, which is a remarkable thing to find behind a small-town fire station. The bands change every year; the quality does not. By evening, half the crowd is on the dance floor and the other half is at the picnic tables, eating well, sipping their too-strong drinks, laughing and tapping along, while kids with painted faces scream and giggle through the dancers, running relays between the station and the bounce house in the rec gym. It is the town at its best, and every ticket buys rescue and medical equipment.

What your thirty dollars buys

Money from past years has gone toward new equipment: a mechanical CPR device, which delivers chest compressions to someone in cardiac arrest, and battery-powered extrication tools, the ones everybody calls the Jaws of Life. The firefighter who ran the 2023 BBQ told the Press Banner that those now ride on three Boulder Creek engines.

Here is why that has to come from a barbecue at all. Two organizations share the name. The Boulder Creek Fire Protection District is a government special district, funded by property taxes. The Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Dept is its nonprofit arm, a registered 501(c)(3), EIN 94-6106801. Fundraiser and donation money runs through the nonprofit, and it pays for the equipment the tax base does not stretch to. The department's donation page says that after processing fees, roughly 97% of what it collects goes toward new rescue and medical gear.

That gear goes to a small crew with a big footprint. The San Lorenzo Valley Post reported in 2025 that the department runs on about 40 volunteers and answers more than 1,300 calls a year across roughly 21 square miles of mountain country.

One note on taxes, because people ask. A direct donation or sponsorship to the nonprofit is generally tax-deductible. For an event ticket, only the amount you pay above the fair market value of the dinner and entertainment may qualify, so check the department's receipt or ask a tax professional for your situation.

Before you go

Park on the street, or walk down if you live close enough. The station lot is where the stage and the dance floor go, so it is not available on event night, and downtown fills in. Carpooling helps. So does planning the ride home.

Buy online in advance if you can. It tells the crew how much tri-tip to cook. The department has not posted what it is taking at the door this year, so bring some cash as a backup.

The department goes back to 1892

It started the way these things usually start, with a bad year. Two fires in 1891 came close to taking out downtown Boulder Creek. The town met within days, and by the spring of 1892 about twenty local businessmen and laborers had trained as the first crew. The fire district followed on August 17, 1923, the first in Santa Cruz County, and the station at the main intersection went up in 1939. It is the one you will be eating in. All of that is on the department's own history page.

The barbecue is younger than the department, and nobody has written down which year the first one was. If you know, or you have a photo from one of the early ones, tell us and we will put it here. The dinner sits alongside the winter crab feed and the Fourth of July pancake breakfast as the ways this town has kept its volunteers equipped, one meal at a time.

Frequently asked questions

When and where is the 2026 BCVFD Summer BBQ & Dance?

Saturday, August 22, 2026, 5:30 to 11 p.m., at the Boulder Creek Fire Station, 13230 Central Avenue, downtown. Music starts at 5:50.

How much are tickets and where do I buy them?

$30 for dinner and dance, kids under 5 free, and a $100 four-pack if you buy online. Tickets are on the department's Events.com page.

Who is playing, and when?

Kentucky Mule from 5:50 to 7:05, Barnstormer from 7:30 to 8:45, and Bootleg Country Band from 9:15 to 10:30, on a stage out back in the parking lot.

Can I bring the kids?

Yes, it is built as a family night. There is a bounce house and face painting, and kids under 5 get in free. Dinner is early and the dancing runs late, so plenty of families eat, let the kids run, and head home partway through.

Where do I park?

On the street. The station lot holds the stage and the dance floor, so it is not available that night. Downtown parking fills in, so give yourself a few extra minutes or walk if you live close.

Where does the money go?

To rescue and medical equipment for the department's volunteers, through the 501(c)(3) rather than the tax-funded fire district. Past fundraiser money has bought things like a mechanical CPR device and battery-powered extrication tools now carried on three engines.

Is this an annual event?

Yes, every August. The department also runs a crab feed in the winter.

Can I help if I cannot come?

Yes. The Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department takes card donations year-round on its donation page, and a direct donation is generally tax-deductible in full, unlike an event ticket, where only the amount above the fair market value of the dinner and entertainment may qualify. Telling a neighbor the date helps too, and more than you would think. Plenty of people in this valley find out about the barbecue the week after it happened.

See what else is happening around town on the Boulder Creek Local events page. Part of the department, or spot a detail here that needs fixing? Send it to us. For anything that changes before the 22nd, check the Boulder Creek Fire Department.

beatriz-michelena-boulder-creek.title: Beatriz Michelena: The Silent-Film Pioneer Who Brought Movie Production to Boulder Creek
beatriz-michelena-boulder-creek.html:
Boulder Creek's film history usually gets told through Mary Pickford. The real story starts a step earlier, with a Venezuelan-American opera singer who decided this valley could pass for the Gold Rush and built a town to prove it.

Beatriz Michelena was one of the first Latina women to become a star in American film, and she's a big reason movies were made in Boulder Creek at all. In early 1915 she and her husband George Middleton built a 25-building gold-rush town on family land outside town and used it as an outdoor studio. She starred in the first film shot there. By 1917 she was running her own production company, a woman with creative and financial control of her own pictures. Almost none of that work survives.

From an opera family to the screen

Michelena was born February 22, 1890, in New York City, into a household where classical music was the family business. Her father, Fernando Michelena, was a tenor born in Caracas, Venezuela. Her mother, Frances Lenord, was an operatic soprano and pianist. Fernando trained his daughters (Beatriz, Vera and Teresa Luisa) in voice himself.

She started on stage, not screen, performing under the name Beatriz Bronte in musical comedies including A Girl From Dixie in 1904 and touring in Peggy From Paris. Her 1910 return in The White Hen drew strong reviews. She was, first and for the rest of her life, a singer.

On March 3, 1907, she married George E. Middleton, a San Francisco automobile dealer. The California Motion Picture Corporation was incorporated in San Rafael on September 17, 1913, by the lawyer and mining heir Herbert Payne. Middleton came in as a partner and ran the studio, and the marriage became a working partnership.

Salomy Jane and stardom

Michelena's film debut came in 1914 with Salomy Jane, a western adapted from Bret Harte, produced by CMPC and co-directed by William Nigh and Lucius Henderson. She played the title role opposite House Peters. It was the studio's most successful picture.

UCSC's Santa Cruz Silent Cinema project puts her career in plain terms: "One of the first Hispanic women to attain stardom in the silent cinema, Beatriz Michelena appeared in at least a dozen films between 1914 and 1920." She was, the same research notes, one of very few Latina stars visible on American screens in that decade.

The project also makes a point about how she worked. Her performances favored "subtlety of naturalism" over the broad theatrical gesture typical of the period. She was working in a register closer to what film would eventually settle on than to what the stage was handing her.

Building a town outside Boulder Creek

In early 1915, CMPC needed a permanent gold-rush setting for its Bret Harte adaptations. Rather than travel to the Sierra foothills, Middleton and Michelena built one. On family land owned by the Boulder Creek lumber baron H.L. Middleton, they put up what UCSC describes as roughly 25 log cabins and frame dwellings. A period account called it "a solid, log-built village of over two dozen dwellings, stores, offices and saloons."

They named it Poverty Flat, after the setting of the film they built it for: The Lily of Poverty Flat, released in 1915, with Michelena as Lily opposite Frederick Lewis.

This is the part of her story that belongs to Boulder Creek. UCSC's research is direct about the consequence: her films were shot "in and around Boulder Creek," and that work is what made the area a desirable filming location for other companies. Cecil B. DeMille and Mary Pickford used those sets in 1917 for A Romance of the Redwoods, and the set stayed in use into the 1920s. Michelena and Middleton built the infrastructure that brought the film industry up Highway 9.

Her own company

After CMPC went bankrupt, Michelena and Middleton bought the studio and renamed it Michelena Studios. From 1917 to 1920 she headed her own production company, Beatriz Michelena Features, releasing Just Squaw (1919), Heart of Juanita (1919) and The Flame of Hellgate (1920).

It's worth stating what that meant in 1917. She was a Latina woman with her name on the studio, choosing and controlling her own pictures, at a moment when the American industry was consolidating into the Hollywood studio system that would spend the next half-century offering actresses like her almost nothing but stereotype roles.

She wrote, too. Her advice column "Talks with Screen-struck Girls" ran from 1915 to 1916, and she published articles on film history.

The films themselves haven't aged into comfort. Two of the titles listed above use language that's offensive now, and the productions traded in the Gold Rush-era racial types the source fiction supplied. We keep the original titles because that's how the films appear in archives and catalogs, and because sanding them down would misrepresent what was made.

The fire

Michelena Studios stopped producing around 1920. She and Middleton divorced in the mid-1920s. In 1927 she toured Latin America performing opera, then retired to San Rafael.

The catastrophe came later, and it was almost absurdly small in its cause. In 1931, a firecracker ignited the studio vault in San Rafael, where the nitrate negatives were stored. Everything burned. The loss was valued at roughly $200,000 at the time. UCSC's account describes children playing with fireworks near the studio; the outcome is not in dispute.

Nearly the entire filmed record of one of America's first Latina stars, and nearly every foot of film exposed at Poverty Flat, was destroyed in that vault.

Michelena died on October 10, 1942, in San Francisco, following surgery. She was 52.

What survives

One complete CMPC film is known to exist. A nitrate print of Salomy Jane turned up in Australia in 1996 and was preserved by the Library of Congress, with a new print released for limited distribution in 2008. It's the only known surviving complete work of both Michelena and the studio.

A Romance of the Redwoods, the DeMille and Pickford feature that used her Boulder Creek set, also survives; the George Eastman Museum holds a complete 35mm print, and the Mary Pickford Institute for Film Education holds a 16mm reduction print.

Recognition has been slow and partial. President George W. Bush named her in a 2002 National Hispanic Heritage Month proclamation. UCSC's researchers connect her obscurity to a broader pattern: the physical decay of silent film and the industry's abrupt pivot to sound, which erased a generation of careers wholesale.

Why she matters here

The usual Boulder Creek version is a bit of trivia: did you know Mary Pickford shot a movie up here? The fuller version gives the credit where it started. A Venezuelan-American opera singer and her business-partner husband looked at this valley, decided it could stand in for the Gold Rush, built a town to prove it, and ran a studio out of the redwoods. The Pickford picture happened because they had already built the place.

For more stories from the valley's past, browse Boulder Creek Local's Around Town history and local stories.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Beatriz Michelena live in Boulder Creek?

There's no evidence that she lived here. She was based in San Rafael and worked in Boulder Creek on productions using the Poverty Flat set. We treat any claim of local residence as unverified unless documents establish it.

What was Beatriz Michelena's connection to Boulder Creek?

She co-created and starred in films at the Poverty Flat set, a 25-building gold-rush town built in early 1915 on land outside Boulder Creek owned by her husband's uncle. Her productions are the reason other companies came to film in the area.

Can I watch a Beatriz Michelena film?

Only one of her films is known to survive complete: Salomy Jane (1914), preserved by the Library of Congress from a print discovered in Australia in 1996. It screens occasionally at archival festivals. Nearly everything else burned in a 1931 vault fire in San Rafael.

Was she the first Latina film star?

She was among the first Latina women to attain stardom in American silent cinema, appearing in at least a dozen films between 1914 and 1920. Myrtle Gonzalez was a contemporary. We avoid ranking claims like "the first" when the record doesn't support a single answer.

Who was George Middleton?

A San Francisco automobile dealer who married Michelena in 1907 and became a partner and studio manager at the California Motion Picture Corporation, which Herbert Payne incorporated in San Rafael in 1913. He co-built the Poverty Flat set. They divorced in the mid-1920s.

Last reviewed July 21, 2026. This article draws on the University of California, Santa Cruz Santa Cruz Silent Cinema project and other archival sources. Where the record is incomplete or contested, we say so rather than fill the gap.

before-first-major-rain-boulder-creek.title: What to Do Before the First Major Rain
before-first-major-rain-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Clear gutters, downspouts, and roadside culverts before the rain so the first flush doesn't back up.
  • Prep for outages now: water, lights, chargers, and a plan for anyone who depends on power.
  • If you live below or near a CZU burn scar, know your evacuation zone and leave promptly if a warning is issued. This is the one that can't wait.
  • Sign up for the county's emergency notifications and PG&E outage alerts.
  • Refresh your storm kit and keep the car at least half full through the season.

The first real storm of the season is the one that catches people out. After a dry summer, the drains are packed with needles, the ground sheds a sudden downpour instead of soaking it up, the roads run slick with the summer's oil, and on the hillsides the CZU fire burned, bare ground can send debris flows down fast. Most of the prep is cheap and takes an afternoon, and it goes a lot easier on a dry weekend than during the first downpour. Here's the Boulder Creek checklist. For live forecasts, watch the National Weather Service and our Mountain Status page.

The first real rain is also one of the best days of the year up here, if you've done the work. My own ritual once it arrives: walking the property while the redwoods drip, following the little streams that appear in the sandstone cracks, salamanders out for the moist air, the garden visibly relieved. That walk is a lot more pleasant when it isn't an inspection tour of things you forgot.

Clear the water's path

Water finds the low point, and in the mountains that's often your foundation, driveway, or road. Before the rain:

  • Gutters and downspouts: clear out summer needles and leaves, and make sure downspouts carry water away from the house.
  • Culverts and roadside drains: clear the culverts and drains around your property so the first flush doesn't back up and flood.
  • The lay of the land: look at where water will go across your property, and move anything that will wash into a drain.

Get ready for outages

The first storms bring down limbs and knock out power. Get ahead of it rather than scrambling in the dark: water, lights, chargers, and a plan for anyone who depends on power.

Our power-outage preparation guide walks through it, and you can sign up for PG&E outage alerts now.

Know the burn-scar risk

This is the serious one. Hillsides burned in the 2020 CZU fire shed water fast and can produce debris flows, fast-moving slurries of mud, rock, and trees, during intense rain.

The National Weather Service issues Flash Flood Warnings for burn areas, and those warnings often name the debris-flow risk directly. They can come with very little lead time. If you live below or near a burn scar, know your evacuation zone now, take those warnings seriously, and don't wait to leave if one is issued for your area.

Stock up and secure

  • Storm kit: refresh food, water, flashlights, batteries, and a battery or hand-crank radio.
  • Loose items: secure or store anything outdoors that blows around in wind.
  • Roof and tarps: check them while it's still dry.
  • The car: fuel up and keep it at least half full through the season.

Sign up for alerts

The single best thing you can do is make sure the warnings reach you. Register for the county's emergency notifications and PG&E alerts before the first storm, and bookmark Mountain Status for live conditions.

Frequently asked questions

Why is the first big rain such a problem here?

After a dry summer, drains are clogged, the ground sheds sudden rain instead of soaking it up, roads are slick, and burned hillsides can produce debris flows. A little prep on a dry day prevents most of the trouble.

What's the debris-flow risk in Boulder Creek?

Hillsides burned in the 2020 CZU fire can produce fast-moving debris flows during intense rain. The National Weather Service warns for these with little notice. Know your evacuation zone and leave promptly if a warning is issued.

What should I do first?

Clear your gutters and culverts, prep for a power outage, sign up for alerts, and if you're near a burn scar, know your evacuation zone. Do it on a dry weekend, not during the storm.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This is a checklist, not a forecast, and it links to official sources from the National Weather Service and PG&E. For live conditions, see Mountain Status and the National Weather Service. In an emergency, call 911.

Storm prep is one part of a longer rhythm. For the rest of the year's mountain-home upkeep, see the Boulder Creek home maintenance calendar, and the Residents guide for utilities, outage planning, and county contacts in one place. Our rain tracker shows where the season stands so far, updated daily from the Ben Lomond weather station.

big-basin-day-trip-boulder-creek.title: A Responsible Big Basin Day Trip From Boulder Creek
big-basin-day-trip-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Big Basin Redwoods State Park is open for limited day use, 8 a.m. to sunset. All campgrounds in the main park are closed.
  • The main entrance is about 9 miles up Highway 236 from downtown Boulder Creek, roughly a half-hour drive on a narrow, curvy road.
  • Parking reservations are strongly recommended: $6 per regular vehicle plus a $2 reservation fee, or $10 per vehicle without a reservation.
  • The park is still recovering from the 2020 CZU fire, so what's open changes regularly. Facilities are limited, so bring your own water, food, and layers.
  • Check the official Big Basin Redwoods State Park page before you drive up. That page, not this one, is the source of truth for current conditions, and nothing here is a guarantee of access.

Printable version: the Big Basin day-trip planner is built to travel with you, and cell service in the park is unreliable enough that paper earns its place. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

A Big Basin day trip from Boulder Creek is easy to plan and easy to get wrong right now. The park is still recovering from the 2020 CZU fire, so facilities are limited and a trail that was open last month may be closed today. None of that makes it a bad day out. It just means a little planning goes further than it used to. Here's how to put the day together.

I grew up hiking Big Basin; it was the default outing whenever family visited, and cousins from flatter places would crane their necks at trees that simply don't exist where they live. It looks different now, and it's still worth the day.

Know what you're visiting

Big Basin became California's first state park in a three-step fight (the bill signed in 1901, the land purchased in 1902, the gates opened in June 1904), and Boulder Creek has been its gateway town ever since. Then, in August 2020, the CZU Lightning Complex fire changed everything. Per CAL FIRE's incident record, the fire burned 86,509 acres across Santa Cruz and San Mateo counties. It reached Big Basin two days after igniting and, according to Friends of Santa Cruz State Parks, burned roughly 18,000 acres inside the park, over 97 percent of it, and destroyed nearly every structure, including the historic Park Headquarters.

The recovery is real, though. State Parks reports that most of the old-growth redwoods survived, new growth is coming in fast, and wildlife has returned. The park reopened for limited access in July 2022, and Sempervirens Fund notes that access has kept evolving since, shaped by both the fire and the severe storms of 2023.

You won't find the shaded, built-out Big Basin of the old photos. You'll find something rarer: an old-growth forest rebuilding itself in the open sun, with new trail mileage opening in phases. So set your expectations accordingly. Facilities are limited, shade is thinner than it used to be, and a trail that was open last month may be closed today.

Reserve your parking before you go

Day-use parking reservations are highly recommended. State Parks lists regular-sized autos at $6 plus a $2 reservation fee, or $10 per vehicle without a reservation, and parking is limited enough that showing up without one is a gamble on busy days. Book through the Big Basin parking reservation page run by Friends of Santa Cruz State Parks. Passenger vehicles use the main form; disabled parking and bus or horse trailer parking have separate reservations.

Two more parking notes. Oversized vehicles and trailers can't be accommodated for day use right now, so leave the RV at camp. And fees or rules can change, so confirm current pricing on the official park page when you book.

Getting there from Boulder Creek

From downtown Boulder Creek, turn onto Highway 236 (the Big Basin Highway) and follow it about 9 miles to the main entrance. Every road into Big Basin is curvy, and lower 236 is narrow, so give yourself 25 to 30 unhurried minutes, watch for cyclists, and use the turnouts if you're holding up locals.

If you'd rather not drive in, two alternatives are worth checking. On summer weekends between Memorial Day weekend and Labor Day weekend, State Parks has run a free pilot shuttle from the Saddle Mountain temporary parking area along Highway 236 to the main day-use area. And Santa Cruz METRO's Route 35B offers weekend bus service to the park. Both are subject to schedules and seasons, so verify each is running before you count on it.

What's open in the park

Conditions change, so treat this as a snapshot from mid-July 2026, not a promise.

The classic first stop is the Redwood Loop Trail, an easy 0.6-mile walk through the old-growth grove near the historic park core. It's flat, family-friendly, and the best place to see fire scars and new growth side by side on trees that have been alive for well over a thousand years.

The trail network keeps growing. Friends of Santa Cruz State Parks reports that a recent round of work opened about 4 more miles of trail, restoring access to Sempervirens Falls, along with segments of the Skyline to the Sea Trail from the main day-use area to China Grade Road and beyond toward Castle Rock, plus the Hihn Hammond connector along Opal Creek. At the same time, closures still happen: State Parks currently lists Hollow Tree Trail as temporarily closed from winter storm damage. Check the current trail map on the park page before you commit to a route.

Camping is the big limitation. All campgrounds in the main park are closed, and no camping reservations are available there. State Parks also lists every backcountry trail camp in Big Basin as closed from fire damage. The coastal side, Rancho del Oso, is open for day use, with no fee or reservation needed at its Nature and History Center, and the Horse Camp there has a handful of temporary walk-in campsites by reservation plus one shared bike-in site. Check the park's page for what's bookable before you plan on staying.

Expect limited services inside the park: temporary facilities rather than the old lodge-and-store setup. Bring your own water, food, and layers.

How to visit responsibly

A recovering forest asks a little more of its visitors.

  • Stay on open trails. The regrowth on either side of the tread is doing important work, and staying on the path protects both it and you.
  • Respect every closure sign. They usually mark hazard trees, unstable ground, or active restoration, even when the path beyond looks fine.
  • Pack out everything you bring in. Skip drones and speakers.
  • Don't count on cell coverage in the basin. Download maps ahead of time and tell someone your plan.

Weather deserves respect here too. Heat, wind after storms, and winter road damage all affect this park, and this site never interprets conditions for you. Check the forecast, check the park page the morning you go, and if the park says don't come, don't come.

One more way to be responsible: support the recovery. Sempervirens Fund, the land trust that helped create the park in the first place, publishes updates and supports the ongoing restoration work.

Make Boulder Creek part of the day

The most direct route into Big Basin runs straight through downtown Boulder Creek, and the town is the natural place to bookend the trip. Fuel up, grab coffee and sandwiches, and buy anything you forgot before you head up 236, because you won't find services along the way. The Boulder Creek business directory is a good place to find gas, coffee, and a bite before the climb. On the way back down, dinner or a cold drink in town lands differently when you've spent the day in the basin.

There's more to it than a nicety. Gateway towns carry the quiet costs of a beloved park, and they felt the fire as directly as the park did. Spending your money in Boulder Creek is the most direct way a day visitor helps this corner of the Santa Cruz Mountains keep rebuilding. If you want the fuller story of the fire and what it meant here, read our companion piece on the events that shaped Boulder Creek once it's live.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a reservation to visit Big Basin?

For parking, a reservation is highly recommended rather than strictly required: $6 per regular vehicle plus a $2 reservation fee, or $10 without one, per State Parks. Spaces are limited, so booking ahead through the official reservation page is the safe move. Confirm current rules on the park page before you go.

Is camping open at Big Basin?

No. All campgrounds in the main park are closed and camping reservations aren't available there, and State Parks lists Big Basin's backcountry trail camps as closed from fire damage too. Rancho del Oso, the park's coastal unit, is open for day use, with no fee or reservation at its Nature and History Center.

How far is Big Basin from Boulder Creek?

The main entrance is about 9 miles north of downtown Boulder Creek on Highway 236. The road is narrow and curvy, so plan on roughly half an hour rather than a quick hop.

Did the redwoods survive the CZU fire?

Mostly, yes. The 2020 fire affected 97 percent of the park and destroyed nearly all of its buildings, but State Parks reports that most of the old-growth redwoods survived and are regrowing. The forest looks different now, more open and sunlit, with green regrowth climbing blackened trunks.

What's the best short hike right now?

The Redwood Loop Trail, an easy 0.6-mile walk through the old-growth grove, is the reliable choice for a first visit. Longer options like the reopened stretch to Sempervirens Falls exist, but check the current trail map on the official park page, since individual trails open and close as recovery work continues.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. Details here follow official sources from California State Parks, CAL FIRE, and Friends of Santa Cruz State Parks. Current park conditions come from the official Big Basin page, not this article.

For more trails close to town, including the newly opened Miller Property County Park, see hiking in and around Boulder Creek.

Planning the rest of your day around town? Browse the Around Town guides for the San Lorenzo Valley, and see what's happening in and around Boulder Creek before you head home.

big-basin-first-state-park-history.title: How Big Basin Became California's First State Park
big-basin-first-state-park-history.html:
Big Basin became California's first state park in 1902. The fight to get there started two years earlier, in May 1900, when a group of citizens formed right in the basin to keep the last big stands of old-growth redwood away from the saw. They called themselves the Sempervirens Club. Their two-year campaign ended in a purchase that created California Redwood Park, which the Sempervirens Fund describes as "the first park established in California in the current state park system." All of it began nine miles up the road from Boulder Creek. And it began with a photographer who wouldn't hand over his negatives.

The basin before the park

People were part of this forest long before the preservation fight. California State Parks notes that humans lived in or near Big Basin for at least 10,000 years, and it identifies the Cotoni and Quiroste peoples, part of the broader Ohlone culture of the San Francisco and Monterey Bay areas, as the tribes of this landscape. They harvested seeds and acorns, wove baskets, and hunted elk and deer in these canyons.

That history isn't past tense. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band, made up of the surviving descendant families of Indigenous people taken into Mission Santa Cruz (Awaswas speakers) and Mission San Juan Bautista (Mutsun speakers), works today through the Amah Mutsun Land Trust to restore Indigenous stewardship across ancestral lands that run from Ano Nuevo through these mountains to Monterey Bay. State Parks adds that descendants of the basin's tribes are working toward federal recognition.

By the late 1800s, the same forest was coming down fast. Sawmills worked the San Lorenzo Valley below. Boulder Creek was shipping lumber out by rail. The old growth in the basin was privately owned timberland with a short life expectancy.

A photographer refuses to hand over his negatives

The usual telling starts with Andrew P. Hill, a San Jose photographer. According to State Parks' cultural history, Hill photographed redwoods at Welch's Grove in the Santa Cruz Mountains, and the grove's owner accused him of trespassing and demanded his negatives. Hill refused. He went a step further, vowing to himself to save the trees for future generations. The run-in came in 1899 or 1900, depending on the account; the Sempervirens Fund dates the start of his campaign to 1899.

Either way, Hill went home to San Jose and started organizing. A meeting at Stanford University in May 1900 pulled together journalists, politicians, artists, business owners, and scholars, and the group headed into the mountains to see the threatened forest for themselves.

Thirty-two dollars and a two-year campaign

What happened next is commemorated by a bronze plaque inside the park. California Historical Landmark 827 records that "a group of conservationists led by Andrew P. Hill camped at the base of Slippery Rock on May 15, 1900 and formed the Sempervirens Club to preserve the redwoods of Big Basin." The Sempervirens Fund's own history puts the founding gathering on May 18, along Sempervirens Creek, so accounts differ by a few days. On the substance they agree. A small group camped in the basin, decided the forest had to be saved, passed a hat, and collected 32 dollars to finance the effort.

Club member Carrie Stevens Walter put the goal plainly in 1901, writing of preserving "this magnificent domain of redwood forests," a line State Parks still quotes on the park's page. The club spent more than two years lobbying Sacramento.

The club kept the pressure local as well as legislative. In August 1901 a Sempervirens caravan rolled out of Boulder Creek for the basin with ten days of supplies and camped in the basin; that same year Father Robert Kenna gave the Boulder Creek paper his verdict after a solo inspection, calling the forest grand beyond description.

The legislature passed the enabling bill and Governor Henry Gage signed it on March 16, 1901, appropriating 250,000 dollars over five years. It was a cut-down version: the original proposal had asked for twice the money and twice the land. Then came a standoff of nearly a year and a half before the park commissioners finally voted the purchase through at San Francisco's Palace Hotel on September 20, 1902, paying 250,000 dollars for 2,500 acres, a hundred dollars an acre. The sale came with an unannounced gift: landowners Andrew Hopkins and Henry Middleton of Boulder Creek threw in a further 1,300 acres of cut-over land, which is how accounts of the founding acreage range from 2,500 to roughly 3,800. The landmark plaque dates the deeding to that September day and calls it the beginning of the California State Park System. Even then the gates stayed shut: California Redwood Park did not open to the public until June 1, 1904. The sequence comes from Traci Bliss's park history, Big Basin Redwood Forest: California's Oldest State Park (The History Press, 2021), alongside the sources above.

From California Redwood Park to Big Basin Redwoods

The new park was called California Redwood Park, and it grew from there. State Parks records that the park was renamed Big Basin Redwoods in 1927, and additional purchases (including 3,901 acres acquired from the Big Basin Lumber Company in 1906) kept expanding it. Today the park preserves more than 18,000 acres, including the largest continuous stand of ancient coast redwoods south of San Francisco, with trees between 1,000 and 1,800 years old.

The 1930s gave the park the look longtime visitors remember. Civilian Conservation Corps crews built the redwood Nature Lodge and Park Headquarters, a campfire center, a footbridge, cabins, and much of the trail network.

The club that started it all kept going too. After helping establish Castle Rock State Park in the late 1960s, the organization renamed itself the Sempervirens Fund in 1968, and it's still buying and protecting redwood forest in these mountains today.

The fire that changed everything

On August 18, 2020, the CZU Lightning Complex fire swept through 97 percent of the park's property, according to State Parks. Every historic structure was lost, including the CCC-era headquarters and lodge. The Sempervirens Fund calls the CZU fire, which burned more than 86,000 acres across the Santa Cruz Mountains, the most devastating fire ever recorded in the region.

The trees told a different story than the buildings. State Parks reports that most of the old-growth redwoods survived, and new growth has been coming back across the burned landscape ever since. Coast redwoods have lived through fire for a very long time. The visitor infrastructure hadn't.

What Big Basin looks like now

The park partially reopened in July 2022 and has been recovering in stages since. The park's official page lists day use from 8 a.m. to sunset and strongly recommends parking reservations because spaces are limited. Camping in the main park remains closed, though the Rancho del Oso campground on the coast side has reopened with five walk-in sites by reservation and one shared bike-in site.

Individual trails open and close as work continues, so check current conditions on parks.ca.gov before you drive up. This article can't promise what will be open on any given day. The Rancho del Oso side, off Highway 1 north of Santa Cruz, is open with no entrance fee.

The long-term rebuild runs through Reimagining Big Basin, State Parks' multi-year planning effort. A public visioning process wrapped up in summer 2022, and the project has since produced a Facilities Management Plan, a General Plan Amendment, and an environmental impact report, with a State Park and Recreation Commission hearing on the plans held July 2, 2026. The stated goal is to reestablish facilities that support visitors while protecting the forest that made the park worth fighting for in the first place.

Boulder Creek, the gateway then and now

Boulder Creek's own history is tangled up in this story. The town shipped the lumber that came out of these mountains, and when the logging economy faded in the early twentieth century, it leaned into visitors headed for the park instead. The Big Basin Road out of town opened in 1906, and for a while visitors kept riding the stagecoach into the park anyway, for the novelty of it. That first road was not today's Highway 236: the park's own place-names file describes it as the Old Park Road, built by a Watsonville contractor, and says it stayed the only road route into the park until the present highway opened in 1916. Rail historian Derek Whaley's Santa Cruz Trains research describes Boulder Creek transitioning "from a lumber town to a tourist town" built around attractions like Big Basin.

The geography hasn't changed. The park's official directions start here: from Highway 9 in downtown Boulder Creek, turn north onto Highway 236, and the entrance kiosk is nine miles up the road. If you're headed to the park, town is the last stop for gas, food, and supplies, the same role it's played for well over a century. Our directory of Boulder Creek businesses is a good place to see what's open before you start up Highway 236.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Big Basin open right now?

Partially. The park is open for day use from 8 a.m. to sunset, parking reservations are strongly recommended, and camping in the main park is closed while rebuilding continues, though Rancho del Oso on the coast side has a handful of walk-in and bike-in sites. Trail openings change as recovery work progresses, so check parks.ca.gov before you go.

Did the old-growth redwoods survive the 2020 fire?

Most did, according to State Parks. The CZU fire burned through 97 percent of the park and destroyed every historic building, but coast redwoods are adapted to fire, and the surviving giants have been putting out new growth since. The forest looks different than it did before 2020, and it's still recovering.

What does "California's first state park" mean?

Big Basin, established in 1902 as California Redwood Park, was the first park in what became the current California state park system. The state historical landmark at Slippery Rock marks the 1902 land transfer as the beginning of the California State Park System, and State Parks calls Big Basin its oldest park.

How do I get to Big Basin from Boulder Creek?

Take Highway 236 north from Highway 9 in downtown Boulder Creek; the park entrance kiosk is nine miles up. The road is narrow and winding, so allow more time than the mileage suggests, and confirm current access before you go.

Who lived in Big Basin before it was a park?

State Parks identifies the Cotoni and Quiroste peoples, part of the Ohlone culture, and notes that people lived in or near the basin for at least 10,000 years. The Amah Mutsun Tribal Band, descended from Indigenous people taken into the Santa Cruz and San Juan Bautista missions, stewards ancestral lands in these mountains today through the Amah Mutsun Land Trust.

Big Basin's story runs nine miles up the road, but it starts in Boulder Creek. If a redwood day is on your list, see what else is happening in town first on our Boulder Creek events calendar.

big-basin-rebuilding-plan-approved.title: Big Basin's Rebuilding Plan Is Approved: What's Coming and When
big-basin-rebuilding-plan-approved.html:
If you've been waiting to camp or wander Big Basin again, the plan that makes it possible finally has a signature on it. On July 2, 2026, California State Parks approved the Reimagining Big Basin Facilities Management Plan and a related amendment to the park's General Plan, the roadmap for rebuilding California's oldest state park after the 2020 CZU Lightning Complex fire burned through nearly all of it.

That's a milestone, not a ribbon-cutting. State Parks describes design, permitting, and phased construction stretching over several years, so the park you visit today, limited day use with much still closed, won't change overnight. The official Big Basin Redwoods State Park page and the Reimagining Big Basin site remain the source of truth as this moves forward.

What was approved

Two linked documents got the green light: an amendment to the Big Basin Redwoods State Park General Plan, and the adoption of the Facilities Management Plan that spells out how the park will be rebuilt.

The action was recorded in a Notice of Determination filed with the state on July 6, 2026, after an environmental review process that included public comment. What that means on the ground: the vision is now official, and the park can move from planning into design and construction.

Behind all of it is the 2020 CZU fire, which burned the great majority of Big Basin and destroyed nearly every building, including the historic headquarters. Most of the ancient redwoods survived. Roads, water systems, campgrounds, and visitor facilities did not, which is why rebuilding is a years-long project rather than a quick repair.

What the rebuilt park is meant to look like

State Parks has described a park that treats the old-growth core more gently than the pre-fire layout did. The main pieces:

  • A lighter-touch day-use hub. The former headquarters area is set to be rebuilt as a smaller, more ecologically sensitive day-use hub, with less paving and building footprint than before and restored forest habitat.
  • A new entrance at Saddle Mountain. The plan calls for a new park entrance at Saddle Mountain with a visitor center, café, and store, plus parking. From there, visitors would take a roughly 15-minute shuttle into the old-growth core, a system meant to run on weekends year-round and to keep car traffic out of the most sensitive groves.
  • Rebuilt campgrounds, in different places. Campgrounds are slated to return at forest-edge locations, including Huckleberry, Lower and Upper Sky Meadow, Sequoia Group Camp, and Little Basin, with a mix of car camping, cabins, walk-in sites, group sites, and trail camps. Three campgrounds that sat in sensitive old-growth stands, Blooms Creek, Sempervirens, and Wastahi, are slated to be removed and the land restored to habitat.
  • A cultural center at Little Basin. The plan includes a new cultural center at Little Basin for partnership with Indigenous groups, tied to ecological restoration and cultural activities. State Parks identifies the park as ancestral homelands of the Quiroste and Cotoni peoples.

These are the plan's intentions as approved. Exact designs, locations, and amenities can still shift through the engineering and permitting stages, so treat specifics as direction, not a finished blueprint.

What happens next

Approval starts the clock on the slow part. State Parks describes the next phases as design, permitting, and phased construction over several years, with individual pieces of the park reopening as they're built and made safe rather than all at once.

There's no single reopening date, and State Parks has not published construction start dates for the campgrounds, visitor center, or shuttle. Until those facilities are built, Big Basin continues to run on its recovery pattern of limited day use, 8 a.m. to sunset, with campgrounds in the main park closed.

So if you're waiting to camp at Big Basin again: this is the plan that makes it possible, and it will still be a while. Watch the official park page for milestone announcements.

Why this matters for Boulder Creek

Boulder Creek has been Big Basin's front door since the park was founded in 1902, and Highway 236 runs from downtown straight to the entrance. How the park rebuilds shapes traffic, tourism, and the rhythm of the season here, from a shuttle model that could change how visitors move through town to the timeline for when the campgrounds, and the visitors they bring, return.

I grew up hiking Big Basin. It was the default outing whenever family came to town, and my cousins from Indiana and San Diego would crane their necks at trees that simply do not exist where they live. I felt the pride of that early: people travel from all over the world to visit the place we get to live every day. The park looks substantially different now. But many of the largest, oldest trees survived, and today they stand surrounded by thousands of young redwoods and native regrowth taking the place of the forest that burned. Walking it now is sobering and hopeful in the same breath, which is as good a description of this valley's whole recovery as any.

For the fuller story of how the park came to be, read how Big Basin became California's first state park. To plan a visit under current conditions, see is Big Basin open.

Frequently asked questions

Was Big Basin's rebuilding plan really approved?

Yes. California State Parks approved the Reimagining Big Basin Facilities Management Plan and a General Plan Amendment on July 2, 2026, recorded in a Notice of Determination filed July 6, 2026. It's the official roadmap for rebuilding the park after the 2020 fire.

When will Big Basin be fully rebuilt and reopened?

There's no single date. State Parks describes design, permitting, and phased construction over several years, with parts of the park reopening as they're completed. No construction start or campground reopening dates have been published. Check parks.ca.gov/bigbasin for milestones.

Will camping come back to Big Basin?

That's the plan. Approved documents call for rebuilt campgrounds at forest-edge sites like Huckleberry, Sky Meadow, Sequoia Group Camp, and Little Basin, while three old-growth campgrounds are removed and restored. Until they're built, main-park campgrounds stay closed.

What is the Saddle Mountain entrance and shuttle?

The plan calls for a new entrance at Saddle Mountain with a visitor center, café, store, and parking, where visitors would board a roughly 15-minute shuttle into the old-growth core, aimed at reducing car traffic in sensitive areas. It isn't built yet.

Can I visit Big Basin right now?

Yes, for limited day use, 8 a.m. to sunset, with much of the park still closed while it recovers. See our is Big Basin open guide and confirm conditions on the official park page before you go.

We'll update this as State Parks announces rebuilding milestones. For current park conditions, the official source is always the Big Basin Redwoods State Park page. Spot something here that's out of date? Send it to us. Last reviewed August 12, 2026.

boulder-creek-4th-of-july-parade.title: The Boulder Creek 4th of July Parade
boulder-creek-4th-of-july-parade.html:
The Fourth of July in Boulder Creek runs the same way every year, in the same order: pancakes at the fire house through the morning, a parade down Highway 9 around 10 a.m., then a barbecue and live music at Junction Park that carries the afternoon. It's an all-day, all-ages tradition the Boulder Creek Business Association calls a parade the town has held "for generations." You can catch as much or as little as you like, but Highway 9 closes through downtown while the parade runs, so it helps to know the shape of the day before you drive in.

The short version

  • Pancake breakfast at the fire house, 13230 Central Avenue, from around 7 a.m. toward noon or while supplies last. There's a per-plate charge, and the department says the money raised goes toward medical and rescue equipment.
  • Parade down Highway 9 through downtown, roughly 10 a.m. to noon. Highway 9 closes through downtown while it runs, so park once and walk.
  • Barbecue and bands at Junction Park, roughly noon to 4 p.m., a block east of the highway at Middleton Avenue.
  • It's always July 4. For the coming year's confirmed times, grand marshal, and pricing, check the Boulder Creek Business Association.

This year (2026)

July 4 is a fixed date, so the parade always lands on the Fourth. In 2026 that fell on a Saturday, and the day ran to its usual shape. Good Times reported the 2026 parade aimed for about 70 entries and was grand marshaled by Dr. Kenneth Reed, a longtime community physician, with the Boulder Creek Business Association, led by president Tess Fitzgerald, organizing.

For the next Fourth of July, the specifics (grand marshal, entry count, exact breakfast pricing, and any road-closure timing) usually get confirmed closer to the date. Watch the Boulder Creek Business Association for parade sign-ups and schedule, and the Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department for the pancake breakfast.

What to expect

The day keeps a reliable rhythm, and you can join it at any point.

Morning: the pancake breakfast. The Boulder Creek Volunteer Firefighters serve breakfast at the fire house at 13230 Central Avenue, starting around 7 a.m. and running toward noon or while supplies last. Recent menus have been pancakes, eggs, sausage, and fruit. It's a fundraiser, so there's a per-plate charge, and the department says all the money raised goes toward buying medical and rescue equipment. Prices shift year to year, so check bcfd.com for the current cost.

I've been to this one every year of my life, as far back as memory goes, and the day really is the same familiar fun each time: the fire engines, the rec department's Jazzercise and Zumba crews dancing their way down the highway, local businesses marching, some years hot and some years a cool gray July, always worth it. The pancakes are delicious, plain, blueberry, or chocolate chip. And my own rite of passage came early: getting hit in the face by a piece of candy thrown from one of the parade vehicles. Watch the sky when the floats go by. It seems to happen to everyone eventually.

Mid-morning: the parade. The parade runs roughly 10 a.m. to noon through downtown Boulder Creek. Per Good Times, it typically steps off near Mountain Street and works its way to the Highway 9 and Highway 236 junction, with Highway 9 closed through downtown for the duration. Entries range from fire engines and local law enforcement to community groups, kids, and decorated everything. If you want a spot on the curb, come early. The sidewalks fill in.

Afternoon: the party at Junction Park. Once the parade clears, the Boulder Creek Recreation and Parks District hosts a barbecue and bands after-party at Junction Park, roughly noon to 4 p.m. Good Times describes gold panning for children, local vendors, food trucks, drinks, and two live bands. Junction Park sits a block east of the highway at Middleton Avenue, with the river right there, so it's an easy place to land for the rest of the afternoon.

A few practical notes. Highway 9 closes through downtown while the parade runs, so plan your driving around it or park once and walk. Bring water, sun cover, and cash for the breakfast and vendors. The whole day is built for families, and you can walk it end to end.

History

Boulder Creek has marked the Fourth with a downtown parade for a long time. The Business Association describes it as a tradition the town has kept "for generations," and Good Times reports the parade tradition spans more than a hundred years. We haven't found a verified first-year date, so we won't invent one, but the through-line is clear: a small mountain town that closes its main street once a year to walk down it together.

The pancake breakfast ties the day back to the town's oldest institution. Boulder Creek's fire department has been all-volunteer since it formed in 1892, after two large fires nearly destroyed downtown, and the breakfast is one of the ways residents still fund the equipment those volunteers carry.

One more tradition happens after the crowds thin out. If you hang around long enough after the breakfast wraps and the cleanup finishes, you may catch the annual pancake toss. The leftover batter becomes throwing stock, thick and heavy or wide and frisbee-thin depending on the cook, because every firefighter has a technique. They line up behind the station, and whoever sends one the furthest wins. There's no trophy that I know of. There doesn't need to be.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Boulder Creek 4th of July parade?

It's on July 4 every year, since it's tied to the holiday. The parade itself runs roughly 10 a.m. to noon, with the pancake breakfast before it and the Junction Park party after. For the coming year's confirmed schedule, check the Boulder Creek Business Association.

Where does the parade go, and does Highway 9 close?

The parade runs through downtown Boulder Creek. Good Times reports it starts near Mountain Street and ends at the Highway 9 and Highway 236 junction, and that Highway 9 closes through downtown while it runs. Plan to park once and walk, or route around downtown that morning.

How much is the pancake breakfast, and where does the money go?

There's a modest per-plate charge that changes year to year, so check bcfd.com for the current price. The Boulder Creek Volunteer Firefighters host it, and the department says all the money raised goes toward medical and rescue equipment.

Can I be in the parade?

Yes. The Boulder Creek Business Association handles parade registration through its July 4th parade page. Sign-ups usually open in the weeks before the Fourth.

Is there anything for kids?

Plenty. The parade itself is the main event, and the afternoon party at Junction Park has included gold panning for children, food trucks, and live music. The river at Junction Park is right there too, though it's unsupervised, so keep an eye on little ones.

See what else is on the calendar this season on the Boulder Creek Local events page. Organizing something, or spot a detail here that needs fixing? Send it to us. For this event's official source, check the Boulder Creek Business Association.

boulder-creek-emergency-contacts.title: Boulder Creek Emergency Contacts: The One-Page List
boulder-creek-emergency-contacts.html:
The short version

  • Any emergency (fire, medical, a crash with injuries, a crime in progress, a downed power line): call 911.
  • A gas smell is a 911 call too, but get outside first. Leave the building, then call from a safe distance. Don't flip a switch, use a phone, or light anything while you're still inside. Once you're safe, call your gas provider: PG&E at 1-800-743-5000, or your propane company.
  • Non-emergency Sheriff: (831) 471-1121 when you need a deputy but it isn't a 911 call.
  • Tree, slide, or flooding on a county road: county road dispatch at (831) 477-3999, answered 24/7.
  • Power out: the PG&E outage center or the 24-hour outage line, 1-800-743-5002. A downed line is 911 first, then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000.
  • Water emergency: San Lorenzo Valley Water District at (831) 338-2153, day or night.
  • Before storm season: sign up for CruzAware alerts so evacuation and weather warnings reach your phone.

Printable version: every number on this page also comes as a one-page emergency contacts card, sized for the refrigerator door, where it works during the outage that takes this site down with it. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

When a winter storm puts a redwood across the road and the power's been out since dinner, the last thing you want is to be hunting for a phone number. For any emergency in Boulder Creek, call 911. That's the whole first rule, and it covers fire, medical, crime in progress, a downed power line, or any situation where someone could get hurt.

Everything below is for the moments that aren't 911 calls: the tree across a county road, the water main bubbling up on your street, the outage that's stretched into hour six. Every number and link on this page is checked against the agency's own website, and we re-verify the list quarterly. Print it, stick it on the fridge, and you won't have to dig through a dozen sites during a storm.

When to Call 911

Call 911 for anything that threatens life or property right now:

  • Smoke or flames
  • A medical emergency
  • A crash with injuries
  • A crime happening in front of you
  • A gas smell, but get outside and call from a safe distance
  • A power line on the ground

Don't worry about whether it's "bad enough." Dispatchers would rather sort that out than have you wait. Everything else on this page is for situations that are a problem but not an emergency.

Fire: Boulder Creek Fire Protection District
