The Boulder Creek Fire Protection District is our local fire agency, based at 13230 Central Ave in the middle of town.

The district office line is (831) 338-7222. Use it for district business: questions about the department, defensible space, permits, and community programs. It is not a dispatch line. If something is burning, call 911.

For wildfire information at the regional level, CAL FIRE covers our area through its San Mateo-Santa Cruz Unit (CZU), headquartered at 6059 Highway 9 in Felton. The unit office number is (831) 335-5353, again for administrative questions rather than reporting fires.

Law Enforcement: Santa Cruz County Sheriff

Boulder Creek is unincorporated, so law enforcement is the Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office.

For a deputy when it's not an emergency (a cold burglary, ongoing noise, suspicious activity that's already over), call non-emergency dispatch at (831) 471-1121. The main Sheriff's Office line is (831) 454-7600 for records and general business. The full list of division numbers is on the Sheriff's phone directory.

There's also a Boulder Creek Sheriff's Service Center right in town at 13210 Central Avenue, reachable at (831) 454-7440. It's a satellite office, not a dispatch center, so hours vary. Call before you drive over.

One number here is easy to get wrong. The countywide phone directory doesn't carry a Boulder Creek line; it lists the San Lorenzo Valley service center separately at (831) 454-7400. Those are two different numbers, one digit apart, and 454-7440 is the Boulder Creek one.

Roads: County Public Works and Caltrans

Road problems split two ways in Boulder Creek, and knowing which agency owns the road saves you a transfer.

County-maintained roads (most of the neighborhood roads off the highway) belong to Santa Cruz County Public Works, part of the county's Community Development and Infrastructure department. Their road dispatch line, (831) 477-3999, is answered 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and it's the number for a tree down across a county road, a slide, a flooded section, or a failing culvert. The department's main line is (831) 454-2160, weekdays 8 to noon and 1 to 5.

Current closures are posted on the county's road closure dashboard. One heads-up: on the county's Transportation and Roads page, that dashboard is now labeled "Road Advisories," not "Road Closures," so scan for that wording.

Highway 9 and Highway 236 are state highways, so they're Caltrans territory. For current highway conditions, check the Caltrans road information page or call 1-800-427-7623 and enter the route number.

If a downed tree involves power lines, treat it as an emergency: call 911 and stay well away.

Power and Gas: PG&E

For outages, start at the PG&E outage center, where you can report an outage and check the outage map, or call the 24-hour outage line at 1-800-743-5002. PG&E's customer service line is 1-877-660-6789.

For a downed power line, PG&E's own guidance is blunt and worth repeating: call 911 first, then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000. Keep people and pets far away, and assume every line is live.

If you smell gas, get outside and away from the building first, then call 911. Once you are safe, call your gas provider. That's PG&E at 1-800-743-5000 for natural gas, or your propane company if your house runs on propane, as many in the valley do. Their outage and safety support page covers other reporting options.

PG&E also offers outage updates by text, email, or phone if you sign up through your PG&E online account. It's worth doing before storm season, since those alerts are tied to your service address.

Water: San Lorenzo Valley Water District

Most Boulder Creek homes get water from the San Lorenzo Valley Water District, headquartered at 13060 Highway 9 in Boulder Creek.

One number covers everything: (831) 338-2153. During office hours (weekdays 8:30 to noon and 1 to 5, phones until 4:30) you'll reach staff directly. For a water emergency after hours, a main break, or a big leak, call the same number; the district says calls forward to an answering service that reaches their on-call staff. Details are on their customer service page.

If you're on a different system (some streets are served by small mutual water companies), your bill has the right number. Add it to your copy of this list.

Alerts: Sign Up for CruzAware

CruzAware is the county's emergency and non-emergency alert system, operated by the County of Santa Cruz with Santa Cruz Regional 9-1-1. It sends evacuation notices, severe weather warnings, and other public safety alerts by text, phone call, and email. Signing up takes a few minutes at cruzaware.org, and the county's alert information page explains the system. No alert system can promise delivery in every situation, so registering more than one contact method is smart. We have a full walkthrough in our CruzAware setup guide.

Back yourself up with channels that don't depend on CruzAware: Nixle is a separate service you can join by texting your ZIP code to 888777, and Wireless Emergency Alerts and the Emergency Alert System reach your phone and radio with no signup at all.

Keep This List Where You Can Find It

Phones die in outages and cell service up here gets thin in a storm. A paper copy in a kitchen drawer costs you nothing. We re-check every number on this page against the agencies' own sites each quarter; if you ever find one that's changed before we do, tell us and we'll fix it.

For the fuller picture of who serves what, utilities, permits, and county contacts all in one place, see the Residents guide. When the lights go out, our power outage plan walks through what to do next.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who do I call about a tree down across my road?

If lines are involved or it's blocking an evacuation route during an active emergency, call 911. Otherwise: county road dispatch at (831) 477-3999 for county-maintained roads, any hour. If it's on Highway 9 or 236, it's Caltrans; check conditions or call 1-800-427-7623. On a private road, clearing it is generally the road association's job.

What's the non-emergency number for the Sheriff in Boulder Creek?

Call (831) 471-1121 for non-emergency dispatch when you need a deputy. The Boulder Creek Sheriff's Service Center on Central Avenue is (831) 454-7440 for local, non-urgent matters.

Who do I call when the power goes out?

Report it and track it through the PG&E outage center, or call the 24-hour outage line at 1-800-743-5002. If you see a downed line, that's a 911 call first, then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000.

Is there one number for water problems?

For San Lorenzo Valley Water District customers, yes: (831) 338-2153, day or night. After hours it forwards to an answering service that contacts on-call crews.

How current is this list?

Every contact is checked against the agency's own website, and we review the page quarterly. If an agency's information isn't listed here, go straight to that agency's site rather than guessing.

Last reviewed July 21, 2026. Every number and link on this page was checked against the responsible agency's own website. For anything time-sensitive, the official source is linked inline.

boulder-creek-fire-1891.title: The Night Boulder Creek Burned: July 16, 1891
boulder-creek-fire-1891.html:
At half past one on the morning of Thursday, July 16, 1891, a telephone rang in Santa Cruz with news from up the valley. The Santa Cruz Surf printed it a few hours later, before anyone knew how bad it was:

BOULDER ON FIRE. A Late Message Tells of a Big Conflagration. At 1:30 o'clock this morning a telephone message was received which said that Boulder Creek was all on fire. The Central House was burning, and the flames were raging in all the buildings in its proximity on both sides of the street.

By daylight the business district of Boulder Creek had stopped existing. Every building in the town's two central blocks was gone except one, and the town had nothing to fight the fire with. It is the largest single event in the town's history that almost nobody talks about now, and the contemporary record of it is unusually complete.

What burned

The Surf's full account the next day called it "the most destructive fire that ever visited this county." The fire ran between one and three in the morning. The one building left standing was the store originally put up by Cunningham & Co., by then owned by Dougherty & Middleton.

The loss list reads like an inventory of what a lumber town needed:

  • a large hotel
  • six saloons
  • a jewelry store
  • a restaurant, a candy store and a fruit store
  • a livery stable and a blacksmith shop
  • several dwellings

All of them frame buildings. Thirteen families were left without a home. Behind the east-side block, fronting the railroad, seven cottages burned as well.

The Surf put the aggregate loss at $40,000, with the individual figures computed by Supervisor W. D. Rodgers. The largest single loss was M. Sarmento's, at $4,000 in building and stock. McAbee Bros. lost a $2,500 stable and a $500 residence.

Papers around the state ran it on the front page the next morning with bigger numbers. The San Jose Mercury-news headed it "BOULDER BURNED... Every Building But One in the Business Portion of Town Destroyed." A Morning Press headline put the loss at $80,000. Both figures were early estimates made within a day, and neither is better evidenced than the other, so we report the range rather than picking.

How it started

The fire was first seen at twenty minutes before one by Mrs. Bigley, who lived on a street overlooking the business district and raised the alarm.

It began in the kitchen behind S. S. Johnson's Enterprise saloon, in a room used as a residence by his bartender, I. O. Fish. Fish said no fire had been lit in that room all day, because the family had eaten a cold supper. On that basis the Surf concluded the blaze "undoubtedly was of incendiary origin."

That is a nineteenth-century newspaper's judgment, not a finding. No arrest or inquest has turned up in the record so far. What can be said is that the paper closest to the event, reporting the day after, believed the fire was set.

Why the town could only watch

One sentence in the Surf's account explains the whole night, and it is the reason this fire shaped everything that came after:

Boulder is well supplied with water for domestic use, but lacking in power for fire purposes. Without any organized fire company and practically without water, there was nothing possible to do but to let the fire take its course.

Boulder Creek in July 1891 had roughly 800 people, a railroad terminus, a freight yard, a $4,000 schoolhouse built the year before, two churches, and no fire department at all.

Two days later the Surf ran an editorial headed "Forty Thousand Dollars", which is the clearest statement of the lesson anyone drew at the time:

...the tuition fee the town of Boulder has paid to learn the lesson that there is no safety for a town or city without water supply for fire protection... a high hill just in the rear of the town from whence any required "head" of water could be secured. All that was required... was to excavate storage cisterns at a cost not to exceed $3,000 and it would have been impossible for Boulder to burn.

The town built what the editorial described, slowly. The Sanborn insurance map of 1892 still records no fire engines, no hose carts, and water facilities rated "not good." By June 1897 the map shows a volunteer company of thirty men with a hose cart and 400 feet of hose, plus nine hydrants. By 1908 there are two concrete reservoirs on the hill west of town, 285 feet above Main Street, delivering 125 pounds of gravity pressure. That is the 1891 editorial, built.

The people who paid the tuition are the same people who built it. Articles of incorporation for the Boulder Creek Hose Company Building Association were filed with the Secretary of State in December 1894. Four of its seven directors, Sarmento, McAbee, Middleton and Hollenbeck, are names on the 1891 loss list. The full story of that is in how Boulder Creek got its fire department.

What happened next, immediately

Rebuilding started before the ashes were cold. The barber, Luke Dennison, had a tent pitched on the site of his shop before noon the following day. A builder had orders to start a new building for John Levick and expected it ready for business by Saturday night. Howard West and M. Sarmento both ordered lumber that same day, for a new hotel and a new store.

They were, after all, standing in the middle of one of the largest lumber-shipping points in the United States. Redwood was the one thing nobody had to wait for.

And it was not the only fire that year

1891 was a bad year in the valley generally.

  • July 16: the town fire.
  • August 26: fire above Boulder Creek destroyed roughly 800 cords of wood and two bridges. The Surf described the Boulder valley as "a perfect furnace for three days."
  • October 26: Dougherty's Mill, near Boulder Creek, burned, at a reported loss of $50,000.

Three major fires in four months, in a town whose entire economy was cut wood.

Where the town stood afterward

The census the town reported to its own insurance mapmakers tells the rest. Around 800 people in the Surf's 1891 estimate; 500 on the Sanborn map of 1892; 500 again in 1897; 700 by 1908. The town lost roughly a third of its population in the decade after the fire, and the redwood trade was slumping at the same time. The Surf itself called 1891 "a dull year for Boulder."

Boulder Creek got it back, and then some. But the downtown that burned in 1891 is not the downtown that stands now, and that is the practical reason so few buildings here are older than the 1890s.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Boulder Creek really burn down?

The business district did. On July 16, 1891, fire destroyed every building in the two central blocks except one store, including a hotel and six saloons, and left thirteen families homeless. Houses outside those blocks survived, so the town was not wiped off the map, but its commercial core was.

What caused the 1891 Boulder Creek fire?

It began in a kitchen behind the Enterprise saloon, in a room where the occupant said no fire had been lit that day. The Santa Cruz Surf concluded it was "undoubtedly of incendiary origin," meaning arson was suspected. No prosecution has been found in the record.

How much damage did the fire do?

The Santa Cruz Surf put the loss at $40,000. Statewide papers the same week reported up to $80,000. Both were estimates made within a day or two of the fire.

Why was there no fire department?

There simply wasn't one yet. The Surf states directly that the town was "without any organized fire company and practically without water." The department came into being after this fire, and the Hose Company Building Association was incorporated in December 1894.

Is this the same as the 1897 fire people mention?

No. The fire of April 14, 1897 destroyed the neighboring village of Lorenzo, a mile south, and is a separate and much smaller event. The two are easy to confuse, partly because some out-of-county papers filed the Lorenzo fire under a Boulder Creek headline.

Sources for this article are the Santa Cruz Daily Surf of July 16, 17 and 18, 1891, held by the California Digital Newspaper Collection, together with the Sanborn fire insurance maps of 1892, 1897 and 1908. If your family was here for it, or you have papers from the rebuild, we would like to hear from you.

boulder-creek-fire-department-history.title: How Boulder Creek Got Its Fire Department, and Why Nobody Agrees How Old It Is
boulder-creek-fire-department-history.html:
Ask when the Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department was founded and you can get three answers, all from serious sources. The department says 1892. The earliest paperwork anyone has found is dated December 1894. And the department's own 1940 anniversary coverage says the present organization dates from 1931.

None of those is wrong. They describe different things, and once you lay the record end to end, the disagreement stops being confusing and starts being the story.

Start with what is certain: there was nothing in July 1891

The single most useful sentence in the whole file is in the Santa Cruz Surf's report on the fire that destroyed the town's business district on July 16, 1891:

Boulder is well supplied with water for domestic use, but lacking in power for fire purposes. Without any organized fire company and practically without water, there was nothing possible to do but to let the fire take its course.

That is contemporary, printed the day after, in the paper that had a local agent in town. As of July 16, 1891, Boulder Creek had no fire company. Any founding date earlier than that is ruled out.

Then the 1940 account says why one appeared

At the dedication of the new fire house in May 1940, the Santa Cruz Sentinel looked back at how the department began:

But it was fire, the uncontrolled outburst of 1891, which burned off a solid block of buildings and threatened the whole village, which brought about the fire department. Yesterday the first fire-fighting equipment, an old hose cart donated by R. C. Kirby of Santa Cruz, was exhibited along with the modern La France and old Ford outfit of the present department.

So the department was formed in response to the 1891 fire, and its first piece of apparatus was a secondhand hose cart given by a man in Santa Cruz. That is a recollection published 49 years later, so treat the framing as recollection. But it fits everything else.

The earliest hard document is December 1894

On December 11, 1894 the Sacramento Daily Union reported articles of incorporation filed with the California Secretary of State for the Boulder Creek Hose Company Building Association, with a principal place of business at Boulder Creek and capital stock of $5,000. Its seven directors were B. G. Hollenbeck, Frank Waters, M. C. Sarmento, O. L. McAbee, F. A. Middleton, Hartman and W. Allen.

Read that list next to the 1891 fire's loss list and something jumps out. Sarmento lost $4,000, the largest single loss of the night. McAbee Bros. lost a stable and a residence. Dougherty & Middleton lost a blacksmith shop and took damage to the one store that survived. Hollenbeck lost furniture. That surviving store also fixes the geography: the railroad depot stood just behind the Dougherty and Middleton store, and the store's site is where the fire department stands today, per local historian Lisa Robinson's The San Lorenzo Valley (Arcadia Publishing, 2012), p. 40.

Four of the seven men who incorporated the fire company had been burned out three years earlier. That is the causal link stated in personnel rather than rhetoric.

Note what incorporated, though. It is a building association, a body formed to own and finance a building to house a company. That structure implies a company already existed to be housed. So December 1894 is the earliest paper, not necessarily the earliest company.

Which is why 1892 holds up

The window is therefore July 1891 to December 1894, and the department's own date of 1892 sits inside it.

The insurance maps bracket it from both sides without closing it:

Source Date What it records
Santa Cruz Surf July 1891 "without any organized fire company"
Sanborn map June 1892 "No Steam & No Hand Engines. No Independent Hose Carts." Water facilities "Not Good"
Secretary of State December 1894 Hose Company Building Association incorporated, $5,000
Evening Sentinel March 1897 "the Boulder Creek fire boys will have a new 700 pound fire bell"
Sanborn map June 1897 "Volunteer Co., 30 men. 1 Hose Cart. 400' Cotton, rubber-lined Hose," nine hydrants

The 1892 map is worth reading carefully, because it is the one that looks like a contradiction and isn't. It records no apparatus. A volunteer company organized in 1892 that had not yet bought a cart would produce exactly that map. So 1892 is not merely unrefuted, it is inside the evidenced window and consistent with everything on either side of it.

For a while this site treated the department's "since 1892" as unsupported and pulled it from an article. That was too cautious, and we are saying so here. The defensible line is that the department was organized between the fire of July 1891 and the end of 1894, and its own date of 1892 falls squarely inside that.

What is still missing is a founding notice. There isn't one in the digitized papers, and there is a structural reason: Boulder Creek had no newspaper of its own until the Mountain Echo began on October 24, 1896. A company organized in 1892 or 1893 would have been announced locally, in a paper that did not yet exist. The Santa Cruz dailies carried Boulder Creek only in short column items. The remaining places to look are the state corporation file behind the 1894 filing and the department's own records, which in 1940 still included a list of past presidents.

The bell a president rang

By 1895 the outfit is being called Boulder Creek Hose Company No. 1, and in June of that year it held an entertainment at Middleton's Hall. In 1898 a kitchen fire is reported in a residence "adjoining the Boulder Creek hose company, known as the Swamp House." On July 4, 1899 the company marched in the town's Independence Day parade alongside the Ben Lomond brass band, a Boys' Brigade, a Girls' Drill Corps and both baseball teams.

Somewhere in there the town acquired the strangest object in its history.

The Evening News of May 17, 1940 explains the name of the McKinley Bell: it was called that because President William McKinley set it ringing electrically, from Washington, D.C., to open the Golden Jubilee Fair at the Mechanics' Pavilion in San Francisco. The paper thought that was probably the first time electricity was ever used to ring a bell to open a fair.

On the authority of a letter from the late J. H. Aram to R. Leslie Hall, written at Mountain View on April 21, 1929, the bell was bought at the close of the fair by a San Francisco firm and purchased from them by the old Boulder Creek Hose Company in August 1898. It hung over the old firemen's hall for years, calling the town to fires and announcing special occasions. By 1940 it was sitting in a shed behind the new fire house, waiting for a campanile.

Three notes on that story, because it is a good one and worth getting right.

The fair was January 1898, not 1897. The 1940 article says "the winter of 1897," but California's Golden Jubilee and Mining Fair ran at the Mechanics' Pavilion from January into March 1898, its mining fair opening the last Saturday in January. The corrected year makes the rest of the account fit better, since the bell is said to have been bought at the close of the fair and sold on to the Hose Company in August 1898.

Contemporary descriptions of that opening credit a golden key, electric lights and a curtain, and do not mention a bell. Remotely opening a fair was something McKinley did more than once in 1898, so the practice is well established, but the bell itself rests on a 1929 letter recalling events of thirty years earlier, printed by a newspaper another eleven years after that. We are repeating what the department was told in 1940, not something independently confirmed.

The San Francisco firm's name needs a fresh look at the page. The 1940 text reads "W. T. Cahall and Company." San Francisco's well-known bell founder in that era was W. T. Garrett & Company, whose initials match, and this project has already caught the same scan turning Ralston into "Kalmon" and Peery into "Peory." Until someone re-reads the page image, we are leaving the firm unnamed rather than printing a name that may not exist.

Keep the McKinley Bell separate from the 700-pound bell the fire boys took delivery of in March 1897. Those are two different bells, and the sources are easy to conflate.

1923, 1931, 1935, 1940

The rest of the line is easier to follow.

January 1923. The fire committees of the Boulder Creek Improvement Club and the Ben Lomond Improvement Club met jointly and designated the territory to be protected as the San Lorenzo Valley Fire District, covering Boulder Creek and its neighborhoods, Brookdale, Ben Lomond, Felton and Mount Hermon. The 1894 building association was still going at that point, 29 years old.

1931. This is the year that explains the whole disagreement. The Evening News of May 17, 1940 states it plainly:

The Present Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department resulted from re-organization which took place in 1931.

It then quotes the minutes. The meeting was called to order by temporary chairman F. O. Moody and elected Frank Clement president, R. Bonetti vice-president, Ernest Locatelli treasurer, Phil Hartman secretary, and Arthur Waters fire chief.

The word doing the work there is re-organization. The 1940 paper itself distinguished the present body, dating from 1931, from the earlier fire organizations in town. So 1892 and 1931 are both true, of different things, and any published claim should say which one it means.

1935. The town siren is in use, summoning members of the volunteer fire department.

May 18, 1940. The $13,000 fire house is dedicated before a reported crowd of 4,000.

The short version

  • No fire company existed on the night of July 16, 1891. Confirmed, contemporary.
  • The 1891 fire is what caused one to be formed. Reported in 1940, consistent with everything else.
  • A company existed by 1894 at the latest, when its building association incorporated, and four of the seven directors were 1891 fire victims.
  • 1892 is inside the evidenced window and positively supported.
  • The department as it exists today dates its own present organization to a 1931 reorganization.
  • The exact founding date is probably not recoverable from newspapers, because the town had no paper until October 1896.
  • The district itself says the same thing: BCFD's own site gives 1892 for the department and 1923 for the Boulder Creek Fire Protection District, which matches the window in the record and the January 1923 meeting that designated the San Lorenzo Valley Fire District.

Frequently Asked Questions

When was the Boulder Creek Volunteer Fire Department founded?

Between July 1891 and December 1894. The Santa Cruz Surf states there was no organized fire company on the night of the July 1891 fire, and the Hose Company Building Association incorporated in December 1894. The department's own date of 1892 falls inside that window and is supported by the record.

Why do some sources say 1931?

Because the present organization dates from a reorganization that year. The Evening News of May 17, 1940 says so directly and quotes the minutes of the meeting. Both 1892 and 1931 are accurate about different bodies.

What was the department's first fire engine?

A secondhand hose cart, donated by R. C. Kirby of Santa Cruz. It was still around in 1940 and was displayed at the fire house dedication alongside the department's American LaFrance engine.

What is the McKinley Bell?

Boulder Creek's old fire bell, bought by the Hose Company in August 1898. It got its name because President William McKinley was said to have set it ringing electrically from Washington, D.C. to open California's Golden Jubilee fair in San Francisco in January 1898, before the bell ever came to Boulder Creek. That account comes from a 1929 letter quoted in 1940 and is not independently confirmed.

Where can I support the fire department now?

The department's two big community fundraisers are the crab feed in late winter and the summer BBQ and dance.

Sources: Santa Cruz Daily Surf, July 17, 1891; Sacramento Daily Union, December 11, 1894; Evening Sentinel, March 24, 1897; Sanborn fire insurance maps, 1892, 1897 and 1908; Santa Cruz Evening News, January 19, 1923 and May 17, 1940; Santa Cruz Sentinel, May 19, 1940. If the department holds minute books, rosters or a past-presidents list, those records would close the founding question for good, and we would be glad to help transcribe them.

boulder-creek-fire-house-1940.title: The 1940 Fire House: The Building the Whole Valley Turned Out For
boulder-creek-fire-house-1940.html:
On the evening of Saturday, May 18, 1940, a reported four thousand people came to Boulder Creek to watch a building get dedicated.

For a town of a few hundred, that is worth sitting with. The valley emptied into Boulder Creek for a fire house.

The day

The Santa Cruz Sentinel led its Monday paper with it: "Crowd Of 4000 Sees Boulder Creek Fire House Dedicated."

There was a parade of fifty floats and vehicles, led by grand marshal Santos Ornes, a descendant of one of the valley's pioneer Spanish families, followed by the Boulder Creek high school band and the Veterans of Foreign Wars. Celebrants turned out in logger and frontier outfits, some of them wearing several weeks of beard for the occasion. The route ran down Central Avenue to Redwood Rest.

Then a potluck dinner, a boxing program, and dancing at Locatelli's.

Dr. G. L. Fleming was general chairman. Clyde Larsen chaired the dedication program itself. Reuben Ralston was president of the fire department.

The building

The fire house cost $13,000 and was built to double as a community center, which is most of why the turnout made sense. A town that had been meeting in whatever hall was available was getting a room of its own.

The Evening News special section of May 17 describes it as a "dignified grey stucco building," designed by architect Lynn Duckering of 27 Front Street, Santa Cruz.

It was built under the supervision of O. P. Berthelsen, described in that same section as a man "who has at one time or another, either constructed or worked on nearly every structure in Boulder Creek."

That sentence deserves a second read. If it is even approximately true, Berthelsen is a single named builder connecting a large share of the town's standing fabric, and almost nothing else about him has been written down. He is at the top of our list of people to research.

The fittings the paper thought worth mentioning say a lot about 1940:

  • a reversible furnace that doubled as an air conditioner
  • modern spring track doors
  • an outdoor alarm box that triggered the siren
  • a siren that could also be set off by telephone
  • an American LaFrance engine in the bay

And the donations say a lot about the town:

  • landscaping given by Ray Hartman of Leonard Coats Nursery, Santa Cruz
  • Venetian blinds by the Boulder Creek Improvement Club
  • the flagpole by H. B. Spencer and Dr. W. E. Stires

Duckering turns up once more the following year, advertising himself in the Sentinel as "Architect for new Boulder Creek fire house and reconstruction of Boulder Elementary School, making it earthquake proof." That dates a seismic reconstruction of the school to roughly 1940 or 1941, very likely under the Field Act, California's school safety law passed after the 1933 Long Beach earthquake. Worth confirming before anyone states the Field Act connection outright.

What was on display

The department brought out its history. Alongside the new American LaFrance and an old Ford outfit sat the first fire-fighting equipment the town ever had: a secondhand hose cart donated decades earlier by R. C. Kirby of Santa Cruz.

The Sentinel used the occasion to explain where the department came from:

But it was fire, the uncontrolled outburst of 1891, which burned off a solid block of buildings and threatened the whole village, which brought about the fire department.

Somewhere behind the new building, in a shed, sat the McKinley Bell, waiting for a campanile that would hold it. It had hung over the old firemen's hall for years. Its name comes from President William McKinley, who rang it electrically from Washington, D.C. to open a San Francisco fair in the winter of 1897, before the Hose Company bought it in August 1898. The full account is in the fire department's history.

The oldest man in town said something worth keeping

The dedication is also the occasion on which Boulder Creek's origins got recorded, more or less by accident.

W. S. Rodgers, then 87, community leader, historian, and one of the town's first school trustees, still holding that position after roughly seventy years, told the crowd he had arrived in Boulder Creek on May 11, 1870. And he settled a naming question:

Some say that this used to be called Dogtown. I deny that. But it did have the name of Stumptown until we got busy and cleared out the stumps, built houses and made a real community out of it. Then we got a new name, Boulder Creek.

He described settlers building a little redwood schoolhouse with donated lumber and labor, and one settler's wife teaching for six months without pay so the community could qualify for state aid. He said the first cash money in the valley came from tanbark sold to the Santa Cruz tanneries.

Both of those check out against records found separately and much later. A county apportionment table from November 1872 shows a funded Boulder Creek school district drawing state and county money, which is exactly the aid that unpaid stint was aimed at. And an 1879 report on tanbark peelers in the valley documents the trade he remembered.

Two of the town's first pupils were still alive to be named that day: Fred Brimblecom and George Notley. Alongside Rodgers, Santos Ornes and Mrs. Catherine Cahill were honored as the oldest surviving pioneers.

Rodgers is also the source of a mistake worth flagging, because it shows how these recollections work. He put the railroad's arrival in 1884. The contemporary record has construction under way in March 1885 and passenger service being advertised at the end of that April. He was a year out, which is about what you would expect from a memory seventy years deep, and it is a good reason to check the charming parts of his account against paper wherever possible.

What we still do not know

The database does not establish whether the 1940 building is the structure now standing on Central Avenue or was later replaced or rebuilt. The 1931 Sanborn sheet, which would help, was never digitized. This is a question the fire district itself can almost certainly answer, and it is worth asking before anyone points at a building.

Frequently Asked Questions

When was the Boulder Creek fire station built?

The fire house was dedicated on Saturday, May 18, 1940, at a cost of $13,000. It was designed as a combined fire station and community center.

Who built the Boulder Creek fire house?

Architect Lynn Duckering of Santa Cruz designed it. Construction was supervised by O. P. Berthelsen, who the 1940 papers say had worked on nearly every structure in Boulder Creek.

How many people came to the dedication?

The Santa Cruz Sentinel reported a crowd of 4,000, with a fifty-float parade, a potluck, a boxing program, and dancing at Locatelli's.

Was Boulder Creek once called Stumptown?

According to W. S. Rodgers, who arrived in 1870 and spoke at this dedication, yes. He also specifically denied that it was ever called Dogtown. More on the town's names in how Boulder Creek got its name.

Sources: Santa Cruz Sentinel, May 19, 1940 and May 17, 1941; Santa Cruz Evening News, May 17, 1940, all held by the California Digital Newspaper Collection. If your family knows what became of the McKinley Bell, please get in touch.

boulder-creek-golf-country-club.title: Boulder Creek Golf & Country Club: What to Know Before You Play
boulder-creek-golf-country-club.html:
The redwoods stand close enough to the fairways here that a bad slice disappears into shade and redwood duff, and you stop looking. That's the round at Boulder Creek Golf & Country Club, open to the public and playing nine holes at 16901 Big Basin Highway.

If your last memory of the place is an 18-hole round, that part has changed. The property lost its full 18-hole layout to the 2020 CZU fires and reopened after rebuilding the front nine. Alongside the golf there's an 18-hole disc golf course and a restaurant and bar on site.

You can book tee times up to seven days out, and the Pro Shop answers at (831) 338-2111. Rates and course status change, so treat the club's own pages as the last word and call before you make the drive.

The course today: nine holes in the redwoods

The club has been here since 1961. It started as a nine-hole course, added a second nine in 1966 for a full 18, and was laid out by golf architect Jack Fleming. Then the 2020 CZU Lightning Complex fires burned through the property.

What came back is a restored nine holes threaded among redwoods and small lakes. The club describes it as fresh air and quiet fairways, which is a fair description of a short mountain round rather than a championship marathon.

The club's scorecard is not currently posted on its rebuilt website, so ask at the Pro Shop. Because the current 9-hole par and yardage aren't listed in plain text on the site, this guide doesn't print a number that might be stale. Check the posted scorecard, or ask the Pro Shop when you book, so you know exactly what you're walking.

What it costs and how to book

Green fees are posted on the club's golf page, which as of August 2026 says rates are temporarily unavailable while the club rebuilds its website. Call the Pro Shop for current pricing, or confirm when you book.

Book online through the club's EZLinks tee sheet, where tee times open up to seven days in advance, or call the Pro Shop at (831) 338-2111. The course itself runs 6:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. every day, and disc golf check-in at the clubhouse is 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Disc golf on the back of the property

If you throw discs instead of swinging clubs, the club runs an 18-hole disc golf course called Redwood Run, with an option to play 27, open to the public at $12 per player from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily. Check in at the clubhouse before you play.

A few house rules are worth knowing on the drive over:

  • Dress code: shirts and shoes are required, and tank tops aren't allowed.
  • No dogs on the course.
  • Errant discs: private homes border several holes, so if a disc sails onto someone's property, get the homeowner's okay before you go looking for it.

The restaurant and bar

There's a full bar and restaurant on site, and the hours shift by day, so they're worth reading before you count on a meal.

Golf: every day, 6:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.

Bar: Monday to Thursday 1:00 to 9:00 p.m., Friday 11:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., Saturday and Sunday 7:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m.

Restaurant: Monday to Wednesday 11:30 a.m. to 8:30 p.m., Thursday and Friday 11:30 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., Saturday 10:30 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., Sunday 10:30 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

The club notes the bar reserves the right to close earlier or later, so a call to (831) 338-2111 saves a wasted drive on a slow day.

Where to stay if you're making a weekend of it

There's no lodging at the club itself. The club has pointed visitors to the Brookdale Lodge, a historic redwood inn a few minutes down Highway 9 in Brookdale. If you'd rather be closer to downtown Boulder Creek, our guide to where to stay covers the local options.

Getting there

The club sits at 16901 Big Basin Highway, on the Big Basin Way side of town heading toward the state park. It's a short drive from downtown Boulder Creek, and the last stretch is classic mountain road: give yourself a few extra minutes and watch for cyclists and one-lane pinch points. If you're new to driving these roads, our mountain roads guide is worth a read.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Boulder Creek Golf & Country Club open to the public?

Yes. It's a public course, and anyone can book a tee time online through the club's EZLinks page up to seven days ahead or by calling the Pro Shop at (831) 338-2111. The disc golf course is public too.

How many holes is the golf course now?

Nine. The property was an 18-hole course before the 2020 CZU fires, and it reopened after rebuilding the front nine. The separate disc golf course is 18 holes with an option to play 27.

How much does it cost to play nine holes?

The club's rates are temporarily unavailable online while it rebuilds its website, so call the Pro Shop at (831) 338-2111 for the current fee when you book.

Does the golf club have a restaurant?

Yes, there's a full bar and restaurant on site, but the kitchen and bar keep different hours that have changed since the club rebuilt its website. Check the club's restaurant page or call (831) 338-2111 before you rely on a meal.

Making a day of it? Our Boulder Creek business directory covers more places to eat and shop near Big Basin Highway, and the Around Town guide rounds up other ways to spend an afternoon in the valley. Before you head out, call the Pro Shop at (831) 338-2111 to confirm the day's hours and rates.

boulder-creek-history-timeline.title: Boulder Creek History Timeline: From Ancient Redwoods to Today
boulder-creek-history-timeline.html:
Boulder Creek doesn't have a single founding date, and many of the dates people repeat about the town don't hold up once you go looking for the paper behind them. So every entry below is tied to a source. Where accounts disagree, this page says so rather than smoothing it over, and a few of the most-repeated Boulder Creek dates turn out to be the shakiest ones.

For the story behind the dates, start with our short history of Boulder Creek. This page is the skeleton it hangs on.

Before 1850: the valley's first people

When What
10,000+ years ago People are living in the Santa Cruz region. The Indigenous people of this area speak Awaswas, one of at least eight languages in the Ohlone family.
1769–1834 The mission period disrupts Indigenous communities across the region. Descendants of people taken into Mission Santa Cruz (Awaswas speakers) and Mission San Juan Bautista (Mutsun speakers) form today's Amah Mutsun Tribal Band.
Present The Amah Mutsun steward ancestral lands they know as Popeloutchom through the Amah Mutsun Land Trust. This is current work, not history.

Written records for the upper San Lorenzo Valley specifically are thin, and this timeline doesn't name the exact village communities that lived along this stretch of river.

1860s–1870s: mills, mail, and a rival town

When What
Early 1860s Joseph Wilbur Peery builds a small sawmill across from Bear Creek. A settlement called Boulder grows around it. Edward Martin's 1911 county history dates his arrival to 1868.
February 8, 1868 The county Board of Supervisors grants a petition for a road up the San Lorenzo from Priest's place to the mouth of Boulder Creek, and orders T. W. Wright to survey it.
April 11, 1868 The Board accepts the survey, declares the road a public highway, and appropriates $500 toward its first mile. This is the earliest hard date we hold for anything at Boulder Creek. The San Lorenzo Valley Museum separately uses 1868 as the town's founding year, on the grounds that the first school was built then.
1871 The Saratoga Toll Road is completed, improving travel over the mountains.
December 28, 1872 The Santa Cruz Weekly Sentinel prints the official notice of a new post office at "Boulder Creek, Santa Cruz Co., Cal. Joseph Peerey, P. M." The federal name sticks. A county apportionment table the previous month shows a funded Boulder Creek school district already in existence.
September 1873 A branch flume or feeder is reported planned for extension up Boulder Creek and Bear Creek, earlier than the flume's usual 1875 start date.
August 1874 The San Lorenzo Valley Flume & Transportation Company incorporates.
January 1875 Peery founds Lorenzo, a rival town on the county road a mile south, between today's Boulder Creek and Brookdale.
October 1875 The V-shaped flume opens, floating rough lumber roughly twelve miles down to Felton. It leaks, jams, and runs dry every summer.
1879 The South Pacific Coast Railroad buys the flume company outright.

1880s–1915: the boom

When What
1880 The South Pacific Coast's narrow-gauge mainline through the Santa Cruz Mountains opens.
June 21, 1883 The Felton & Pescadero Railroad incorporates: stage one up the valley, stage two meant to continue toward Pescadero. Stage two never happens.
April 1885 The first train reaches Boulder Creek. The town becomes the end of the line and the shipping point for the upper valley's mills. The flume is demolished along the new route.
1885–1915 Boulder Creek ranks among the largest lumber exporters in the United States, the fifth largest in the country by Whaley's account, around the turn of the century (Santa Cruz Trains, pp. 249 and 257). Year-round population passes 800 at the peak, but does not hold there: the Sanborn insurance maps record 500 in 1892, 500 again in 1897, and 700 in 1908.
1886 The Moody and Cress livery stable begins hauling visitors from the rail terminus toward Big Basin, the start of the gateway role.
1887 Southern Pacific leases the system (July 1). The Lorenzo station is renamed Filbert. Construction begins on the Dougherty Extension.
July 16, 1891 Fire destroys every building in the town's two central blocks but one, including a hotel and six saloons, leaving thirteen families homeless. The Santa Cruz Surf puts the loss at $40,000 and reports the town had "no organized fire company." An editorial two days later demands a gravity water supply. See Fires, Floods, and Storms.
December 11, 1894 Articles of incorporation for the Boulder Creek Hose Company Building Association are filed with the Secretary of State. Four of its seven directors were burned out in 1891. The fire department's founding sits somewhere between July 1891 and this date, so its own "1892" is inside the evidenced window.
March 1897 The Evening Sentinel reports "the Boulder Creek fire boys" are about to take delivery of a new 700-pound fire bell. The McKinley bell follows in August 1898.
April 14, 1897 A kitchen fire destroys Lorenzo's two major hotels and its town hall. The San Francisco Call and the local Evening Sentinel put the loss at $12,000; the Sacramento Daily Union and Los Angeles Herald ran $15,000. The town survives it: the June 1897 Sanborn map shows Lorenzo standing two months later, and the 1908 survey shows it had grown, so whatever finally ended Lorenzo came after 1908. The Sacramento Daily Union ran the same wire story under the headline "FIRE AT BOULDER CREEK"; it is a separate event from the 1891 fire.
June 1897 The Sanborn map records a volunteer fire company of 30 men with a hose cart and 400 feet of hose, where the 1892 map had recorded none. The town is lit by "Coal Oil & Electric."
1899 The Dougherty Extension reaches roughly eight miles up the San Lorenzo, below Castle Rock Ridge.
May 1900 Conservationists led by photographer Andrew P. Hill camp in Big Basin and form the Sempervirens Club. Landmark 827 dates the camp to May 15; the Sempervirens Fund says May 18.
September 20, 1902 The state takes title to the heart of Big Basin, creating California Redwood Park, the first park in what became California's state park system.
February 15, 1902 Boulder Creek votes to incorporate as a city, 107 to 45, and elects its first trustees. The Santa Cruz Morning Sentinel carried the result the next morning; the Supervisors certified the proceedings on the seventeenth. This rules out the 1905 date that circulates online. See Why Isn't Boulder Creek a City?
1905 Southern Pacific surveys toward Pescadero Creek with a Big Basin branch in mind. The 1906 earthquake shelves it. Rail access to the park never comes.
1906 The earthquake does little damage in Boulder Creek. The branch is later converted from narrow to standard gauge. The town's saloons back an initiative to disincorporate, aimed at a council that had raised their licence fee. It fails, the fee doubles again, and the number of saloons falls from sixteen to eight.
1912 A second attempt to disincorporate fails to reach the required two-thirds majority.
May 19, 1909 The Dougherty line's little locomotive, the Dinkey, begins hauling prospective lot buyers to the Wildwood subdivision. The excursions run five seasons.
December 1904 Surveyors complete a successful route survey for a rail tunnel connecting Boulder Creek with Pescadero. The 1906 earthquake and the financial panic that follows kill the plan, and the town stays the end of the line.
1907 Southern Pacific finishes converting the Felton–Boulder Creek branch to standard gauge; the line over the mountains follows by 1909.

1915–1934: the pivot

When What
Early 1915 The California Motion Picture Corporation builds Poverty Flat outside town, roughly 25 log and frame buildings representing a gold-rush camp. At least eight films are shot there.
1915 Residents vote to disincorporate, 173 to 72, in the first Boulder Creek election in which women take part. The argument that carries it is that the county will maintain the roads, sewers and street lights and build the town a library. Boulder Creek returns to county rule and has stayed unincorporated ever since. (Tally per Ross Eric Gibson, Santa Cruz Sentinel, October 22, 2023; the certified returns are still being sought.)
~1915 Regular service on the Dougherty Extension ends.
1917 Cecil B. DeMille and Mary Pickford shoot exteriors for A Romance of the Redwoods on the Poverty Flat set. Neighboring Felton disincorporates. On April 4, the Dougherty rails are sold for scrap.
1921 Regularly scheduled evening freight service on the branch ends.
1923 Soul of the Beast films in Boulder Creek in the spring, with the elephant Anna May. It was released in 1923.
1927 California Redwood Park is renamed Big Basin Redwoods State Park.
1931 A vault fire at the California Motion Picture Corporation's San Rafael studio destroys the nitrate negatives. Most of the film shot at Poverty Flat is lost. In March, Southern Pacific replaces the branch's passenger trains with Pacific Greyhound buses. The volunteer fire department reorganizes, electing Frank Clement president and Arthur Waters chief. The 1940 papers describe this as the origin of "the present" department, which is why 1892 and 1931 are both cited as founding dates.
January 26, 1934 The last freight train leaves Boulder Creek, hauling the sidetracked boxcars down to Santa Cruz and closing the town's railroad era after 49 years. Whaley (Santa Cruz Trains, p. 251) and Robinson (The San Lorenzo Valley, p. 48) agree on the date.

1930s–1990s: resort town, disaster town

When What
1930s Civilian Conservation Corps crews build Big Basin's redwood Nature Lodge, headquarters, campfire center and much of the trail network.
February 26, 1940 A severe storm wrecks the mountain mainline between Santa Cruz and Los Gatos. Abandonment follows in November, ending the valley's rail link.
May 18, 1940 The $13,000 fire house is dedicated before a reported crowd of 4,000, with a 50-float parade and dancing at Locatelli's. The Sentinel had put the cost at $15,000 three months earlier, while it was still building. Architect Lynn Duckering; built under O. P. Berthelsen, said to have worked on nearly every structure in Boulder Creek. At the ceremony W. S. Rodgers, 87, recalls arriving on May 11, 1870 and says the place was once called Stumptown.
December 1955 The Christmas flood hits the San Lorenzo Valley.
1957 Alfred Hitchcock films Vertigo's redwood sequence at Big Basin, not Muir Woods, despite what the film's story says. Released 1958.
1968 The Sempervirens Club, after helping establish Castle Rock State Park, renames itself the Sempervirens Fund.
March 1976 The Boulder Creek Historical Society is founded, later renamed the San Lorenzo Valley Historical Society.
1980 Boulder Creek is recognized as a census-designated place in the U.S. Census.
January 1982 A major storm triggers the Love Creek landslide, one of the valley's worst disasters.
1992 Downtown Boulder Creek plays the fictional town of Buzzsaw in the Universal feature Out on a Limb.
December 1999 The museum opens in the former Grace Episcopal Church at 12547 Highway 9, a building that originally stood in the town of Lorenzo.

2000–today

When What
2006 The Tripper films at Big Basin in February. In December, Steve Wozniak visits the DigiBarn computer museum in Boulder Creek.
August 16, 2020 The CZU Lightning Complex fire ignites. It burns more than 86,000 acres across the Santa Cruz Mountains, destroys homes throughout the valley, and sweeps through 97 percent of Big Basin, taking every historic structure in the park. Most old-growth redwoods survive.
July 2022 Big Basin partially reopens for day use.
January 2023 Atmospheric rivers hit the CZU burn scar, bringing debris flows and road damage.
2024 The Santa Cruz County Grand Jury reports on CZU recovery under the title Four Years Later The Flame Still Burns.
July 2, 2026 The State Park and Recreation Commission hears the Reimagining Big Basin planning documents. Rebuilding continues in stages.

Dates we are still chasing

These are the gaps we haven't closed yet, listed so you know what this timeline doesn't cover:

  • The 1902 incorporation paperwork. Closed on the vote itself, which the Sentinel reported on February 16, 1902. We would still like the county or state filing behind it.
  • Contemporary returns for the 1906, 1912 and 1915 votes. Gibson gives 1915 as 173 to 72, but all three tallies still rest on a 2023 column rather than on the papers of the day, and we would like the Mountain Echo's coverage of the campaigns.
  • The fire department's exact founding date. Bracketed to July 1891 through December 1894 and probably not recoverable from newspapers, since the town had no paper of its own until the Mountain Echo began in October 1896. The next places to look are the state corporation file and the department's own records.
  • The Fourth of July parade's founding year. Widely celebrated, not yet documented. Hose Company No. 1 marched in a full parade in 1899, so it was already established by then.
  • KBCZ's founding and first broadcast dates. To be confirmed with station and FCC records.
  • When the Poverty Flat buildings came down. No documented end date exists.
  • The "Dodge City of California" phrase. Repeated constantly, not sourced to an original newspaper yet. The saloon count is largely answered: six burned in 1891, sixteen were trading at incorporation in 1902, and eight were left after the licence fee rose.
  • Lumberjack Days and the Art, Wine and Music Festival: start, pause and end years.

If you can close one of these, we'd love to hear from you. Family papers, programs, and old newspaper clippings are exactly what fills these holes.

Frequently Asked Questions

When was Boulder Creek founded?

There's no single founding date. A sawmill went up in the early 1860s, the post office opened under the name Boulder Creek in 1872, and the town took its lasting shape when the railroad arrived in April 1885.

What is the most important date in Boulder Creek history?

April 1885, when the first train arrived. The railroad terminus concentrated the town's commercial core where it still sits, drove the lumber boom, and set up the tourism economy that replaced it.

When did Boulder Creek stop being a city?

1915, when residents voted to disincorporate. Felton did the same in 1917.

When did the trains stop running to Boulder Creek?

Passenger service ended in March 1931, replaced by buses. The last freight train left in January 1934, ending 49 years of rail service.

How old is Big Basin?

It became California Redwood Park in 1902 and was renamed Big Basin Redwoods State Park in 1927. Some of its redwoods are estimated at 1,000 to 1,800 years old.

What happened in Boulder Creek in 2020?

The CZU Lightning Complex fire ignited on August 16, 2020, burning more than 86,000 acres, destroying homes across the valley, and burning through 97 percent of Big Basin. Recovery is ongoing.

Want the story behind the dates rather than the bare timeline? Start with our short history of Boulder Creek, then read about the Poverty Flat movie set outside town and why Boulder Creek isn't a city.

boulder-creek-holiday-events.title: Boulder Creek Holiday Events Guide
boulder-creek-holiday-events.html:
Come December, the town Christmas tree lights up in the middle of downtown while a crowd of neighbors watches Santa flip the switch. That's the shape of the holidays here: downtown, together, and a little homemade.

The centerpiece is the Downtown Boulder Creek Winter Festival, the town's tree-lighting and "Santa comes to town" celebration, with music, a food court, and a full slate of family activities filling the middle of town. This year it runs Saturday, December 5, 2026, from 2 to 6 p.m., on Forest Street downtown. For the activity schedule, check the Boulder Creek Business Association (BCBA) and the Recreation and Park District (BCRPD).

The Winter Festival (tree lighting and Santa)

The Winter Festival is free to attend, hosted by the Boulder Creek Business Association together with the Recreation and Park District and the local Odd Fellows (IOOF). Everything turns on one moment: Santa arriving to light the town Christmas tree. Around it runs an afternoon that stretches into evening:

  • Music and shopping: live music from local bands and holiday shopping with artisan vendors
  • Food and drink: a food court, plus s'mores, and beverages for the grown-ups
  • Free from BCRPD: a snow-play area, a holiday hay ride, and community crafting
  • Ticketed extras: photos with Santa (typically in set windows), a petting zoo, and DIY crafts

Walking in is free, but a few things run on tickets: Santa photos, the petting zoo, and some of the crafts. Bring a little cash, or check the organizer for details. The date, time, and activity list get set fresh each year, so confirm this year's with BCBA before you go.

Two notes from a family that never misses it. The tree itself got a refresh of its lights not long ago, and it shows; the lighting brightens up our little town and brings the season in beautifully. And the winter market is where I do a real share of my Christmas shopping, handmade and unique gifts for family and friends that nobody else will be giving.

First Friday in December

Downtown's monthly First Friday picks up a holiday feel in December, with shops open late and the whole street festive. It's a quieter way to shop local and take in the season if you'd rather skip the crowds of the big festival.

Shop local for the holidays

The holidays are a good time to keep your dollars in town. Our shop-local Boulder Creek holiday gift guide walks through what you'll find downtown, and the directory lists what's open.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Boulder Creek Winter Festival?

This year it's Saturday, December 5, 2026, from 2 to 6 p.m., on Forest Street downtown. The date is set fresh each year, so check BCBA's Winter Festival page for the schedule.

Is the Winter Festival free?

It's free to attend. Some activities, like photos with Santa, the petting zoo, and certain crafts, are ticketed. BCRPD also runs free activities like a snow-play area and hay ride.

What holiday events does Boulder Creek have besides the festival?

The December First Friday downtown takes on a holiday feel with shops open late. Watch BCBA and BCRPD for additional seasonal happenings.

Dates and details are set by the organizers, so confirm with BCBA and BCRPD before you go, and tell us once this year's date is posted.

Planning the rest of your December? Browse the Boulder Creek events calendar for what else is happening downtown this season.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026.

boulder-creek-logging-history.title: The Logging Boom: When Boulder Creek Ran on Timber
boulder-creek-logging-history.html:
For about half a century, the town had one job: cut the redwood and get it down out of the mountains. Rail historian Derek Whaley, whose Santa Cruz Trains project is the best-documented account of this era, writes that Boulder Creek was one of the largest exporters of lumber in the United States from 1885 to 1915. That's not small-town boosterism about a small town. It's the reason the town is here at all, and the near-loss of the forest around it is the reason Big Basin exists.

Here's how a valley of thousand-year-old trees became a lumber capital, and what the boom left standing when it was over.

The forest before the saws

Start with what the loggers found. The Santa Cruz Mountains held roughly 300 square miles of ancient redwood forest, and the Sempervirens Fund doesn't soften it: in the late 1800s, most of it was "logged down to bald hills." Trees a thousand years old and older came down in a few decades.

That forest wasn't wilderness in the empty sense. People have lived in this region for more than 10,000 years, according to the Santa Cruz Museum of Natural History, and the Awaswas-speaking peoples here tended the landscape rather than simply occupying it. Their descendants in the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band steward ancestral lands in these mountains today through the Amah Mutsun Land Trust. The logging era wasn't the beginning of human history in this valley. It was a violent interruption of a much longer one.

First mills on the upper river

Commercial logging reached the upper San Lorenzo Valley in the early 1860s, when Joseph Wilbur Peery put up a small sawmill across from Bear Creek. A settlement called Boulder grew up around the milling work, got a post office named Boulder Creek in 1872, and kept the name.

The early operations stayed small and local because they had to. A mill in the 1860s could cut lumber all day, but hauling it down a rough mountain road to Santa Cruz was slow, costly work. That one bottleneck kept the upper valley quiet through its first decade.

The flume years, 1875 to 1885

The first real attempt to break the bottleneck was a wooden trough. A flume company incorporated in August 1874 (Whaley's pages render the name as both the San Lorenzo Valley Flume & Lumber Company and the Flume & Transportation Company) began construction in early 1875, and by that October a V-shaped flume was carrying rough-cut lumber roughly twelve miles from the upper San Lorenzo down to Felton, where it met the railroad to Santa Cruz. The company built a large mill near the confluence of Kings Creek and the San Lorenzo River, upstream of town, and Whaley's company history records that the flume turned the little settlement of Boulder into a much more substantial Boulder Creek.

It also records the flume's problems, and they showed up almost at once. The 40-inch trough couldn't keep up with the valley's lumber output, it leaked, and its water supply ran dangerously low every summer. A severe winter storm in early 1876 damaged it badly. Seventy years later W. S. Rodgers, who had watched it work, put the failure in one line for the Santa Cruz Sentinel of May 19, 1940: the flume was never a success, for lack of swift running water.

The contemporary papers push the system earlier than the usual 1875 date and show it running better than its reputation suggests. A branch flume up Boulder Creek and Bear Creek was already being reported in September 1873. By June 1876 the Santa Cruz Weekly Sentinel had it "working like a charm" with about twenty-five men employed on it. And on one Friday in June 1881 the flume moved 116,400 feet of lumber in under nine hours, which the paper called the most work ever done in a single day, noting the flume's capacity had more than doubled in six months.

So the railroad took over. In 1879 the South Pacific Coast Railroad bought the flume company, and in June 1883 it incorporated a subsidiary, the Felton & Pescadero Railroad, to replace the trough with rails. When the narrow-gauge line reached Boulder Creek in April 1885, crews tore out the flume along the route. The trough era lasted ten years.

The boom, 1885 to 1915

The railroad changed the scale of everything. With the first train in April 1885, Boulder Creek became the end of the line and the shipping point for every mill working the upper valley, and Whaley records more than 800 people arriving to support the local industries, many of them living in town year-round. Lumber went out by the trainload for thirty years, the stretch when Whaley ranks Boulder Creek among the largest lumber exporters in the country.

The clearest picture of how industrial it got is the railroad the loggers built for themselves. After the Santa Clara Valley Mill & Lumber Company's mill burned in 1886, brothers James and William P. Dougherty didn't wait for Southern Pacific to extend the branch. In the late winter of 1887 they started building their own narrow-gauge line, the Dougherty Extension Railroad, running north from the Boulder Creek freight yard along the San Lorenzo River.

By 1899 it reached its furthest point upriver, a bend of the San Lorenzo in the shadow of Castle Rock Ridge. Spurs served a string of operations: Ephraim Bradbury Morrell's mill at Two Bar Creek, Cunningham & Company, and the S. H. Chase Lumber Company among them.

The number that conveys the scale best comes from a 1940 retrospective in the Santa Cruz Evening News, written when men who had worked the boom were still alive to be interviewed. In the 1880s and 1890s, it said, the trade supported "no fewer than 25 sawmills within a five-mile radius of the town of Boulder Creek alone," part of more than 300 saw and shingle mills operating in the Santa Cruz Mountains since the 1840s. By 1940 three principal sawmills were left in the region. Treat those figures as an informed estimate from an old logger rather than a survey, but the shape is right: this was not a town with a mill, it was a town inside a mill district.

The same account dates the technical shift. By 1876 most water-powered mills had given way to steam mills running high-speed circular saws that could turn out 25,000 to 30,000 feet a day, while bull teams were still dragging the logs to them into the early 1900s.

Demand rarely let up. The San Lorenzo Valley Chamber of Commerce notes that the whole valley ran as a logging center in these years, and that San Francisco's rebuilding after the 1906 earthquake pushed demand for local lumber even higher. The quake and fire that devastated the city barely touched Boulder Creek, and the town spent the next several years shipping the redwood that rebuilt it.

Running out of trees

The boom ended the way every cut-out-and-get-out boom ends. By the early 1900s the big timber within reach of the rails was going fast, and mills began closing as the accessible stands ran out. The Dougherty line's regular service wound down around 1915, and on April 4, 1917, its rails were sold for scrap, feeding the steel demand of the First World War.

Downriver, the Southern Pacific branch hung on with resort passengers and lighter freight, but the direction was set. Passenger trains gave way to buses in 1931, and in January 1934 the last freight train left Boulder Creek.

Whaley's one-line summary of what followed is the fairest one: the town "transitioned begrudgingly from a lumber town to a tourist town." The mills and the freight yard gave way to summer cabins and resort traffic, and the town settled into the quieter shape it still has. Our short history of Boulder Creek follows that longer arc.

The trees that were saved

The logging story has a second ending, nine miles up the road. By 1900, most of Big Basin's old growth was privately owned, and Boulder Creek businessman Henry L. Middleton was the public face of the company that held it. Most of the basin land, though, belonged to his quieter partner, the Palo Alto financier Timothy Hopkins, as Traci Bliss lays out in her park history Big Basin Redwood Forest: California's Oldest State Park (The History Press, 2021). Either way, the plan was harvest. That May, a group led by San Jose photographer Andrew P. Hill camped in the basin, formed the Sempervirens Club, and passed a hat that collected 32 dollars to start the campaign. Two years of lobbying produced a state bill in 1901, and in 1902 California bought 3,800 acres of ancient forest, which the Sempervirens Fund calls the first park established in the current state park system.

Big Basin Redwoods State Park now preserves more than 18,000 acres, including the largest continuous stand of ancient coast redwoods south of San Francisco. The 2020 CZU fire burned through 97 percent of the park, but most of the old growth survived, which says something about what those trees have already lived through. The full preservation story is in our article on how Big Basin became California's first state park.

What you can still see today

The logging era hides in plain sight around town. The San Lorenzo Valley Museum at 12547 Highway 9 keeps the photographs, tools, and records of the mill years, and it's the right first stop if this article leaves you wanting more.

Along the river between Ben Lomond and Boulder Creek, concrete piers and sawed-off pilings from the railroad still stand in and beside the water, though most of the old right-of-way now runs through private property, so look from public road crossings rather than wandering the grade.

And the second-growth redwoods on every ridge around town are the boom's most visible legacy. Nearly all of them sprouted from the stumps the loggers left, which means the forest you drive through on Highway 9 is itself an artifact of the timber years, still quietly repairing the damage.

Frequently Asked Questions

When was Boulder Creek's logging era?

Commercial milling started in the early 1860s with Joseph Wilbur Peery's small sawmill, but the industrial boom ran from the railroad's arrival in April 1885 until about 1915, when the accessible big timber was largely gone. The last freight train left town in January 1934.

How did lumber get out of the valley before the railroad?

From 1875 to 1885, a twelve-mile V-shaped flume floated rough-cut lumber from the upper San Lorenzo Valley down to Felton. It leaked, ran short of water in summer, and couldn't handle the valley's output, so the South Pacific Coast Railroad replaced it with the rail line that reached Boulder Creek in 1885.

Was all the old-growth forest around Boulder Creek cut down?

Most of it. The Sempervirens Fund estimates roughly 300 square miles of ancient redwood in the Santa Cruz Mountains were logged in the late 1800s. The major surviving old growth near Boulder Creek is in Big Basin, which the state began protecting with a 3,800-acre purchase in 1902.

What was the Dougherty Extension Railroad?

A private narrow-gauge logging railroad the Dougherty brothers built north from Boulder Creek starting in 1887 for the Santa Clara Valley Mill & Lumber Company. It grew several miles up the canyon and served a string of mills. Service ended around 1915 and the rails were sold for scrap in 1917.

Where can I see remnants of the logging era?

The San Lorenzo Valley Museum in Boulder Creek covers the period in depth, and concrete piers and cut-off pilings from the rail line are still visible along the San Lorenzo River, mostly viewable from public crossings since much of the old route is private property. Big Basin's old growth shows what the whole range once looked like.

Once you start noticing the mill-era bones, the town gets harder to drive through without stopping. Trace the rest of the arc, from resort cabins to today, in our short history of Boulder Creek, or plan an afternoon around the photographs and tools at the San Lorenzo Valley Museum on Highway 9.

boulder-creek-main-street-1891.title: Boulder Creek's Main Street in 1891, Building by Building
boulder-creek-main-street-1891.html:
Nobody ever wrote a directory of Boulder Creek's business district in the 1880s. What exists instead is a list of what burned.

When fire destroyed the town's two central blocks on July 16, 1891, the Santa Cruz Surf printed a building-by-building inventory of the loss, in order, walking down one side of the street and back up the other. It is an odd way to acquire a streetscape, and it is the most detailed picture of downtown Boulder Creek available for any date before the insurance maps start in 1892.

Here it is, in the order the paper gave it.

The west side

Starting at the corner opposite the Cunningham store, which was the one building in either block that survived the night:

  1. George H. Holloway, saloon
  2. A vacant store room
  3. J. A. Bernheim, jewelry store
  4. W. G. Sawin, fruit store. Sawin was the local agent for the Santa Cruz Surf and other papers, which is very likely why this list is as good as it is.
  5. A vacant lot, 20 feet wide
  6. The Central Hotel, owned by Howard West, occupied by Lew Weber. This is the "Central House" named in the first telephoned bulletin at 1:30 that morning.
  7. The Enterprise Saloon, S. S. Johnson, with the residence of his bartender I. O. Fish behind it, a barn, and a disused shooting gallery. The fire started in the kitchen behind this building.
  8. John Levick, saloon and club rooms
  9. Andy Baldwin, restaurant and lodging house
  10. Levick's residence

The east side, fronting Main Street

  1. Herring & Daveley, butchers
  2. Wm. Walker, saloon
  3. A barber shop. The barber was Luke Dennison, who had a tent pitched on this spot before noon the next day.
  4. A shoe shop, with rooms behind
  5. M. Sarmento, saloon, club house and residence. Sarmento's was the largest single loss of the fire at $4,000.
  6. Dougherty & Middleton, hay barn
  7. McAbee's residence and livery stable

Behind that block, fronting the railroad, stood seven cottages, all destroyed.

The streets named in the report are Main, Oak and Railroad.

What the list tells you about the town

Count the saloons. Holloway, the Enterprise, Levick's, Walker's, Sarmento's, and the paper's summary elsewhere puts the total at six. In two blocks.

That is a lumber town at the end of a railroad line, with a floating population of mill and woods workers coming into town with pay. It is also the practical background to a thing people repeat about early Boulder Creek without a source: the "Dodge City of California" nickname. We have not found that phrase in an original newspaper, and we are not going to assert it. But six saloons in the two blocks that burned is a documented number, and it sits alongside another one: after the town incorporated in 1902 and its council raised the saloon license fee twice, the count came down to eight.

Notice also what is not on the list. There is no drug store, no bank, no church, no school. Those existed or arrived, but not in these two blocks. The town's $4,000 schoolhouse had been built the year before, and the Methodist and Presbyterian churches were elsewhere. The absence of a drug store turns out to matter, and we come back to it below.

And notice the mix. A jewelry store and a candy store sat between saloons and a livery stable. This was not a camp. It was a town with 800 people in it that expected to keep growing.

The map picks up where the list stops

The first Sanborn fire insurance map of Boulder Creek was surveyed in June 1892, eleven months after the fire, and the town is caught mid-rebuild. Four storefronts on prime Main Street frontage of block 29 are labeled "Vac. S." for vacant store. By the 1897 survey, all four are occupied.

The 1892 map also carries the best single annotation in the whole series. The general store at the north end of block 30 is marked with 100 fire buckets distributed on the roof, two roof hydrants, a roof ladder, and three lengths of hose. A merchant was running a private fire brigade on his own roof, one year after the fire, in a town whose own map cover said it had no fire appliances at all.

Two other continuities are worth having:

  • The hotel was renamed, not rebuilt. "Morgan Ho." on the 1892 map occupies the same footprint as "Alpine Ho." in 1897 and 1908.
  • A Chinese laundry stands on the same block south of Lomond in 1892, 1897 and 1908, which pushes the documented Chinese business presence in Boulder Creek back sixteen years from where we previously had it.

The corner the fire did not touch

One absence on the loss list turns out to matter. There is no drug store among the burned buildings, and there is a good reason: it was a block away, and it stayed put for the next sixty years.

A drug store holds the same footprint at the southeast corner of Main and Forest on the 1892, 1897 and 1908 maps, with saloons opposite it in every one of those years. The 1892 sheet stacks three labels into that one building: Drugs. / Dr's. Off. / White Laundry T.C., with a wash room behind. By 1897 it is down to the single word Drugs.

The name follows in the papers without a break. J. H. Armistead purchased the Boulder Creek Pharmacy on July 28, 1896, and a purchase means the business was already older than that. The same Armistead becomes the town's first treasurer when Boulder Creek incorporates six years later. From there the chain runs to new owners in July 1931, Victor Zahlout that August, the Elgins selling in June 1937, a modernization that November, and Jep and Pat Anderson in May 1941.

The detail worth keeping is from November 4, 1931: "Dr. Johannes will keep office hours at the Boulder Creek pharmacy Monday and Wednesday mornings." The town had no resident physician, so the drug store was where you saw a doctor, two mornings a week. And the 1892 map shows that was not an improvisation. There had been a doctor's office in that building forty years earlier.

So this corner is a story about continuity, not turnover, which makes it the exact opposite of the two blocks that burned. One caution before anyone calls the standing building Victorian: the store was rebuilt in the autumn of 1937, and a one-storey building went up adjoining it in April 1938. Whatever is there now has that seam in it.

One trap worth naming for anyone trying this at home. Do not align by street number. The numbering in these eras is nothing like today's five-digit addresses, and the "Main St" of the 1908 map is the street now signed as Central Avenue and Highway 9. Align by footprint, corner and neighbor, or you will confidently place a building a block from where it stood.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many saloons did Boulder Creek have?

Six burned in the two central blocks in the July 1891 fire. After incorporation in 1902 the town council raised the saloon license fee twice, and the number in town fell to eight. Those are the two documented counts we have.

Was Boulder Creek really called the "Dodge City of California"?

The phrase gets repeated locally, but we have not traced it to an original newspaper, so we do not state it as fact. If you have seen it in print somewhere with a date, please tell us.

Did the pharmacy downtown used to be a saloon?

The record says no, at least for the corner of Main and Forest. A drug store occupies that footprint on the 1892, 1897 and 1908 insurance maps, and the Boulder Creek Pharmacy name runs continuously in the newspapers from 1896 onward, so there is no gap in which a saloon stood there and was later replaced by a druggist. Saloons were across the street, not on that corner.

What is the oldest building in downtown Boulder Creek?

Uncertain, and contested. The historical marker at Grace Episcopal, built 1906, calls it the oldest surviving building in town, but other markers from the same body date buildings to the 1890s. What is clear is that the 1891 fire is the reason so little downtown fabric predates the 1890s.

Where can I see these maps?

The Sanborn fire insurance maps of Boulder Creek for 1892, 1897 and 1908 are digitized and free at the Library of Congress. The 1931 sheet was never digitized.

Source: Santa Cruz Daily Surf, July 17, 1891, held by the California Digital Newspaper Collection, and the Sanborn fire insurance maps of Boulder Creek for 1892, 1897 and 1908 at the Library of Congress.
