For the night itself, see the 1891 fire. If you know which present-day storefront sits on any of these footprints, that is exactly the knowledge the maps cannot supply, and we would like to hear it.

boulder-creek-notable-disasters-history.title: Fires, Floods, and Storms: The Events That Shaped Boulder Creek
boulder-creek-notable-disasters-history.html:
Around here, people talk about go-bags, generator plans, and river levels the way other towns talk about traffic. There's a reason, and it's on the record.

The San Lorenzo Valley has come through a documented run of hard events: the fire that burned down the business district in 1891, damaging floods in 1940, 1955, and 1958, the deadly storm and landslides of January 1982, the CZU Lightning Complex fire in 2020, and the atmospheric river storms of January 2023. Here's what happened in each, drawn from contemporary newspapers, flood reports, USGS studies, and CAL FIRE records, along with the official alert systems that exist because of this history.

Why this valley sees big water and big fire

Boulder Creek sits near the top of the San Lorenzo River watershed, in a steep, forested canyon that catches enormous amounts of rain. The numbers say so.

During the December 1955 storm, the Boulder Creek Locatelli Ranch station recorded 9.11 inches of rain in a single 24-hour period, and 20.11 inches over about two weeks, according to a US Army Corps of Engineers flood report digitized by Santa Cruz Public Libraries. In January 1982, the US Geological Survey documented a storm that dropped as much as half the region's average annual precipitation in about 32 hours.

Steep slopes. Saturated soil. A fast river, and a forest that evolved with fire. That combination has shaped the valley's biggest days, and it's why the events below still come up in conversation here.

July 16, 1891: the night the town burned down

The oldest disaster on this list is the one that rearranged Boulder Creek permanently, and almost nobody talks about it now.

At 1:30 on the morning of Thursday, July 16, 1891, a telephone message reached Santa Cruz saying Boulder Creek was on fire. The Santa Cruz Daily Surf ran it that same morning: the Central House was burning and the flames were "raging in all the buildings in its proximity on both sides of the street."

By the time it stopped, every building in the town's two central blocks was gone except one, the store originally put up by Cunningham & Co. The Surf's inventory of the losses reads like a portrait of a lumber town: a large hotel, six saloons, a jewelry store, a restaurant, a candy store, a fruit store, a livery stable, a blacksmith shop, and a row of dwellings, all of them frame buildings. Thirteen families lost their homes. The paper put the loss at $40,000 and called it "the most destructive fire that ever visited this county." Front pages around the state the next morning ran higher numbers, up to $80,000, and headlines like "Every Building But One in the Business Portion of Town Destroyed."

The fire started in the kitchen behind S. S. Johnson's Enterprise saloon. Mrs. Bigley, who lived on a street above the business district, saw it first, at twenty minutes to one, and raised the alarm. The bartender who lived in that room said no fire had been lit there all day because the family had eaten a cold supper, and the Surf concluded the blaze "undoubtedly was of incendiary origin." Nobody was ever charged.

Why it burned: no water, and nobody to fight it

The single most important sentence in the whole account is the one explaining why the town could only stand and watch:

Boulder is well supplied with water for domestic use, but lacking in power for fire purposes. Without any organized fire company and practically without water, there was nothing possible to do but to let the fire take its course.

Two days later the Surf ran an editorial headed "Forty Thousand Dollars," calling that sum "the tuition fee the town of Boulder has paid to learn the lesson that there is no safety for a town or city without water supply for fire protection." It pointed at the hill directly behind town, from which any needed head of water could be had, and calculated that storage cisterns costing no more than $3,000 would have made it "impossible for Boulder to burn."

The town did what the editorial said. The Sanborn insurance map of 1892 still shows no fire engines, no hose carts, and water facilities rated "not good." By June 1897 the map records a volunteer company of thirty men with a hose cart and 400 feet of hose, and by 1908 two concrete reservoirs on the hill west of town, 285 feet above Main Street, feeding ten hydrants at 125 pounds of pressure. That is the system the 1891 editorial drew up, built out over seventeen years.

It also explains something you can still see. Articles of incorporation for the Boulder Creek Hose Company Building Association were filed with the Secretary of State in December 1894, and four of the seven men who signed them, Sarmento, McAbee, Middleton and Hollenbeck, are names on the 1891 loss list. The men who lost the most built the fire department.

Rebuilding started before the ashes cooled. The barber, Luke Dennison, had a tent pitched on the site of his shop before noon the next day.

And 1891 was not one fire but three. In August, 800 cords of wood and two bridges burned above town, with the valley described as "a perfect furnace for three days." In October, Dougherty's Mill burned, at a loss of $50,000.

September 1904: the fires that ringed the county

Two years after Big Basin became a park, and three months after it finally opened its gates, the mountains nearly took it back. In the first week of September 1904, after days of record heat, a fire that started at the Waterman Mill on Pescadero Creek pushed toward the new park. The contemporary accounts differ from the version usually retold. The San Francisco Call reported that it was the women at the Governor's Camp who got the first warning, at two o'clock on the Tuesday morning, September 6, rather than Warden Humphrey Pilkington being woken and riding out. The Santa Cruz Surf counted the party as Mrs. Pilkington and six other women. By noon, lumbermen from Bloom's Mill forced the camp's evacuation, and the women walked out over rough mountain country to Boulder Creek, a mile and three quarters to the mill and about nine more from there, where they learned that fires were burning across the whole county. Estimates ran from six to twenty separate fires in the Santa Cruz Mountains at once, and the fact that none of them merged is given as the reason the region escaped catastrophe. Accounts of the fire's scale vary; a later academic history describes a single, smaller fire, so the numbers here are Traci Bliss's.

How hard it was to raise a crew is contested: Bliss describes a wage offer that few took up, while Yaryan's history has Warden Pilkington protecting the central park with a crew of a hundred men. Within forty-eight hours the fire was being fought by the private crews who knew the ground, Bloom's Mill lumbermen and Southern Pacific track crews, joined by a twelve-man relief expedition of Stanford students under Professor Dudley, who carried in food and were credited with stopping the fire from crossing the Pescadero ridge. Dudley reported the fire practically under control on September 12, and the ancient redwoods at the heart of the park were intact. Two park bridges burned; the park reopened the following July. The account comes from Bliss's park history, Big Basin Redwood Forest: California's Oldest State Park (The History Press, 2021).

The Christmas flood of December 1955

The flood old-timers still measure everything against arrived on the evening of December 22, 1955. A Santa Cruz Public Libraries factsheet calls it the highest flooding in Santa Cruz history. On the upper river near Boulder Creek, the water ran roughly 3 to 3.5 feet higher than the previous flood of record from 1940, according to the Corps report.

The damage ran the length of the valley. Heavy rain scoured out large trees, which floated downstream and jammed at narrow points in the channel, backing up water and shoving the river out of its normal alignment. Bridges, road fills, and small channel dams were undercut and washed out.

A Santa Cruz Sentinel-News account from December 25, 1955, quoted in the Corps report, put it plainly: nearly 100 homes along the river were destroyed, and Highway 9 was blocked by slides and downed trees. The road to Big Basin closed too.

Seven people lost their lives in the San Lorenzo River Basin during the flood, five in the city of Santa Cruz and two near Mount Hermon, and an estimated 2,830 people were displaced. Boulder Creek itself came through lighter than downstream: mostly scoured channel banks, damaged cabin camps, and undercut bridge approaches.

The lesson the Corps drew is worth keeping. Many people had heard the warnings on local radio and didn't believe the water could rise that far.

A smaller flood followed in April 1958. Minor by comparison, but it still forced about 250 people in the northern part of the county from their homes and caused an estimated $170,000 in damage.

January 1982: the storm and the Love Creek slide

The storm of January 3 through 5, 1982, was a different kind of event. Rain fell so hard and so fast that hillsides across the region gave way. The USGS documented more than 18,000 slides that turned into debris flows across the San Francisco Bay region, and landslides accounted for 25 of the storm's 33 deaths.

The worst of it happened just down the valley from Boulder Creek. Above the community of Love Creek, near Ben Lomond, more than 459,000 cubic meters of earth and rock slid off a mountainside and buried ten people in their homes.

Countywide, the Santa Cruz Public Libraries factsheet records 22 dead, 50 injured, 135 homes destroyed, 300 damaged, and more than $106 million in combined public and private losses. Unlike 1955, when most of the damage hit the city of Santa Cruz, about 90 percent of the 1982 damage fell outside city limits, in the mountains and valley.

That storm is why debris flow risk gets treated as seriously as river flooding here, especially on slopes that have burned.

August 2020: the CZU Lightning Complex fire

The CZU Lightning Complex began with lightning strikes on August 16, 2020, and became the event that most directly shaped the Boulder Creek of today. According to CAL FIRE's incident record, the fire burned 86,509 acres across Santa Cruz and San Mateo counties and was declared contained on September 22, 2020, after 37 days. It destroyed 1,490 structures, damaged 140 more, and took one civilian life.

Within Santa Cruz County, the losses centered on the San Lorenzo Valley and the ridges around it. Lookout Santa Cruz has reported the county's tally of 911 homes destroyed, a number this community knows without looking it up. Boulder Creek's own fire department served in the unified command that fought the fire, alongside CAL FIRE and neighboring districts.

The fire also burned 97 percent of Big Basin Redwoods State Park, the park this town has been the gateway to since 1902. Most of the old-growth redwoods survived, and the park has been reopening in stages since July 2022.

Years later, the rebuilding is still under way, and many neighbors are still working through permits, insurance, and construction. That's part of daily life here, not a closed chapter, and it's the main reason this site treats preparedness as a permanent topic rather than a seasonal one.

January 2023: atmospheric rivers on a burn scar

The winter of 2023 tested the valley again. A series of atmospheric river storms delivered unusually large amounts of rain in January 2023, enough that the USGS deployed temporary rain gauges in the county, including one in Boulder Creek along Hilton Drive, specifically to support emergency response and track how the landscape was holding up after the fire.

Roads and trails in and around Big Basin that had been reopening after the fire took new damage, and Sempervirens Fund notes that park access has continued to evolve because of both the fire and those storms.

The 2023 storms made the modern pattern clear. In this valley, fire and flood aren't separate stories. A burned slope sheds water differently for years, so a wet winter after a fire year deserves extra respect.

What this history means for living here now

The practical takeaway isn't fear. It's the habits this town already keeps: know your evacuation routes, keep the truck fueled and a power outage plan ready for storm season, and sign up for official alerts before you need them.

Santa Cruz County's alert system is CruzAware, and you can register through the county's alert notification page to get warnings by text, phone call, email, or the CruzAware app. For weather itself, the National Weather Service San Francisco Bay Area/Monterey office issues the forecasts, watches, and warnings that cover Santa Cruz County.

In any immediate emergency, call 911. This site shares history and pointers, but it never interprets live emergency conditions, and neither should any website. Official alerts and dispatchers do that job. If you want the alert sign-ups and county emergency contacts gathered in one place, start with our Residents guide.

And if the history itself pulls you in, the San Lorenzo Valley Museum keeps a gallery right in Boulder Creek at 12547 Highway 9. It's the natural next stop for photographs and records of the valley's floods, fires, and the people who rebuilt after each one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Boulder Creek ever burn down?

Effectively, yes. On the night of July 16, 1891, fire destroyed every building in the town's two central blocks except one, including a hotel and six saloons, and left thirteen families homeless. The Santa Cruz Surf called it the most destructive fire the county had seen and put the loss at $40,000. The town had no organized fire company and no water pressure to fight it with, which is what prompted the fire department and the reservoirs that followed.

When did Boulder Creek get a fire department?

Between July 1891 and December 1894, and the record can't yet narrow it further. The Surf's report on the 1891 fire states plainly that the town had no organized fire company that night, and articles of incorporation for the Boulder Creek Hose Company Building Association were filed with the Secretary of State in December 1894. The department's own date of 1892 falls inside that window. Separately, the present department dates from a reorganization in 1931, which is why sources seem to disagree: both dates are right, about different bodies.

What was the worst flood in Boulder Creek history?

The December 1955 flood is the flood of record for the San Lorenzo River. Per the Army Corps of Engineers report, it exceeded the previous record flood of 1940 by roughly 3 to 3.5 feet near Boulder Creek, killed seven people in the river basin, and displaced an estimated 2,830 residents.

How big was the CZU fire, and how did it affect Boulder Creek?

Per CAL FIRE, the CZU Lightning Complex started August 16, 2020, burned 86,509 acres in Santa Cruz and San Mateo counties, destroyed 1,490 structures, and caused one civilian death. The losses in Santa Cruz County were concentrated in and around the San Lorenzo Valley, including hundreds of homes in the Boulder Creek area.

How do I sign up for local emergency alerts?

Register for CruzAware through the county's alert notification page. You can receive alerts by text, call, email, or the mobile app. Pair that with forecasts from the National Weather Service Monterey office, and call 911 in any immediate emergency.

Why does a fire make future floods worse?

Burned slopes absorb less water and shed soil and debris more easily, which raises the risk of flooding and debris flows for years afterward. That's why the USGS put rain gauges in Boulder Creek during the January 2023 storms, and why post-fire winters get extra attention here.

Did Big Basin survive the fire?

The fire burned 97 percent of the park and nearly all of its buildings, but most of the old-growth redwoods survived and the park has been reopening in stages since July 2022. Check the official state parks page before visiting, since access is still limited and changes.

boulder-creek-power-outage-plan.title: Power Outage Plan for Mountain Households
boulder-creek-power-outage-plan.html:
The short version

  • Sign up for alerts now, not during the storm. Get outage notifications from PG&E and emergency alerts from CruzAware, and save PG&E's 24-hour outage line, 1-800-743-5002, in your phone.
  • Treat every downed line as live. Stay back, call 911, then call PG&E's emergency line at 1-800-743-5000. That's a different number from the outage line.
  • Run a generator outside only, more than 20 feet from windows, doors, and vents, never inside a home or garage. Put a carbon monoxide detector near every sleeping area.
  • On a well? Store water. No power means no pump. A common rule is one gallon per person per day, and more when outages can run for days.
  • Know who needs a check-in. Trade phone numbers before storm season with neighbors who are older, live alone, are on wells, or depend on medical equipment.

The first big storm of the season usually announces itself the same way up here: the wind funnels up the canyon, a fir comes down across a line somewhere along Highway 9, and the lights blink once and quit. Anyone who's spent a winter in Boulder Creek knows outages come with the territory, and a little planning turns a three-day one from a crisis into an inconvenience.

A solid outage plan for a Boulder Creek household comes down to five things you set up before the wind picks up: alerts from PG&E and the county, a safe way to run backup power, stored water if you're on a well, a plan for food and medicine, and a habit of checking on the neighbors. Most of it takes one weekend afternoon. If you only do one thing today, sign up for outage alerts and save PG&E's 24-hour outage line, 1-800-743-5002, in your phone. When the lights go out, PG&E's outage map and alerts are the source of truth for what's happening and when power might come back, and even their estimates can change as crews find the actual damage.

After a lifetime of these, our house treats a routine outage as something between a chore and a holiday: lanterns on, easy food, reading by candlelight, early bedtime, a little like camping at home. We only bought our first generator last year. The trick is that the calm is downstream of the boring preparation below, and the difference between an adventure and a miserable week is mostly whether you did the preparation in September.

If You See a Downed Line

Assume every downed line is live.

  1. Stay back and keep everyone away from it, including pets. Don't touch it, and don't touch anything it's touching, like a fence, a puddle, or a branch.
  2. Don't drive over it.
  3. Call 911. Then call PG&E at 1-800-743-5000, the 24-hour emergency line.

That is a different number from the outage-reporting line further down this page. For a line on the ground, use 911 and 1-800-743-5000.

Know the Three Kinds of Outages

Most of our outages are storm outages: wind, falling trees and limbs, or equipment trouble. They arrive with little warning, and restoration in steep, wooded terrain can take longer than it does in town because crews have to find the damage before they can fix it.

The second kind is a Public Safety Power Shutoff, or PSPS. That's a planned shutoff PG&E calls during dry, windy, high fire-risk weather so its lines can't spark a wildfire. PG&E says it does its best to alert customers ahead of time by email, phone call, and text, but the company also notes that in some cases the first alert may not come until the same day the power goes off. The California Public Utilities Commission oversees these events and describes them as a measure of last resort. Either way, the practical lesson is the same: don't count on long notice. Have your plan ready before fire season, not during it.

The third kind is the one most people here have felt without knowing its name: Enhanced Powerline Safety Settings, or EPSS. In high fire-risk areas, PG&E sets its lines to trip instantly on any contact. A branch, an animal, anything. The power then stays off until crews patrol the entire line, which in this terrain is not quick. PG&E turns the settings on based on daily wildfire risk, most likely May through November. That's why fire-season outages in the San Lorenzo Valley are sudden, frequent, and long, and why they can happen on a clear day with no PSPS announced.

Set Up Alerts Before You Need Them

Start with PG&E. If the account is in your name, you automatically get outage notifications for your service address, and you can fine-tune how you're contacted through your online account. If you rent, or you want updates on a parent's place or a second property, use PG&E's address-level alerts: search any address on the outage map, select "Get outage updates," and enter your phone or email. You don't need an online account for that, and PSPS address alerts are available by call and text too.

Then add the county layer. CruzAware is Santa Cruz County's alert and warning system, and it's how you'll hear about evacuations, road closures, and other emergencies that often travel with big outages. Sign up at cruzaware.org and pick how you want to be reached. The county also lists a quick option to text your ZIP code to 888777 for basic text alerts. That 888777 number is Nixle, a separate service the county also uses. Signing up for one does not sign you up for the other, so if you want both, do both.

Finally, report what you see. If your power's been out a while and nothing shows on the map, report it through the PG&E Outage Center or call 1-800-743-5002. Outages in the far reaches of the district sometimes need a phone call before anyone knows a tap line is dead.

Generator Safety Comes First

A generator is the difference between a rough week and a manageable one, but it's also the most dangerous thing in this plan, so be direct with yourself about it.

  1. Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open.
  2. Run it outside only, more than 20 feet from any windows, doors, and vents.
  3. Put a battery-powered or battery-backup carbon monoxide detector near every sleeping area, and check it when you check your smoke alarms.

Those rules come from the CDC. Carbon monoxide is odorless and colorless, it kills more than 400 Americans a year, and people who are asleep can die before they ever feel sick. Ready.gov gives the same 20-foot rule and adds a few worth keeping: keep the generator dry and out of the rain, let it cool before refueling, and use heavy-duty extension cords rated for the load.

The generator isn't the only source of carbon monoxide in a cold house. A few things belong outside, away from windows, doors, and vents, no matter how cold it gets:

  • Your gas stove or oven. Never use it to heat the house.
  • A charcoal grill or camp stove. Never bring one indoors or into a garage, not even to cook.
  • Anything else that burns fuel. If it makes a flame, it makes carbon monoxide, and it belongs outside.

The second rule is about your wiring. Never plug a generator into a wall outlet or connect it directly to your panel without proper equipment. PG&E's backup power safety page is blunt about this: power that backfeeds from your generator into the lines can injure the crews working to restore your neighborhood. If you want the generator to run household circuits rather than extension cords, have an electrician install a transfer switch or equivalent equipment that isolates your home from the grid. And store fuel outside the house, never indoors.

If you're considering a battery system instead, the same isolation rules apply, and an electrician or installer should handle the interconnection. Batteries avoid the carbon monoxide risk, which is a real advantage in a house full of people waiting out a storm.

PG&E Programs That Help Pay for Backup Power

Two PG&E programs are worth checking before you buy anything.

The Portable Battery Program offers no-cost pre-qualification to Medical Baseline or Self-Identified Vulnerable customers who rely on a medical device, assistive technology, or durable medical equipment, and who have had at least one PSPS since 2024 or three or more EPSS outages since 2024. If you pre-qualify, PG&E's program partners reach out to assess your household and your equipment.

The Generator and Battery Rebate Program pays a $300 base rebate, with up to $200 more for customers on CARE or FERA. It covers addresses in high fire-threat districts or on an EPSS circuit. Eligible equipment is a portable battery between 290Wh and 1,000Wh, or a CARB-compliant portable generator. One rebate per household. You have to apply within 12 months of purchase or by December 31, 2026, whichever comes first. If you bought equipment a while ago, that end-of-2026 date is the one to watch.

Water When the Well Pump Is Down

If you're on a private well, no electricity means no pump, which means no water. Plan for stored water as a matter of course: a common rule of thumb is one gallon per person per day, and more is better when outages can run multiple days. Cases of bottled water work, and so do food-grade containers you fill and rotate a couple of times a year. Keep separate buckets or jugs for flushing toilets, since that's where household water use quietly adds up. A pressure tank buys you a little water after the power drops, but don't count on much.

Running the well off a generator is not a plug-in job. A submersible well pump is typically 240 volts and hardwired, which means a properly installed transfer switch and a generator sized by an electrician, not an extension cord run out from the porch. Sort that out before storm season if you want it, because nobody is coming to wire it during one.

Septic Systems

If your septic system has a pump or an alarm panel, it stops working when the power does. Treat wastewater as limited for the duration: minimize water use, skip the laundry, and go easy on flushing. Gravity-fed systems generally keep draining without power, so the useful thing is to know which kind you have before storm season rather than during one. If you're not sure, a septic contractor can tell you.

If you're on San Lorenzo Valley Water District water, your situation is different from a well household, but storing some water is still smart. Treatment and pumping infrastructure need power too, and storms that cause outages can also cause line breaks. If you have questions about how the district handles outages in your neighborhood, call them at 831-338-2153 and ask. No system can promise uninterrupted service in a storm, so a few stored gallons is cheap insurance either way.

Food, Refrigeration, and Medicine

The rules here are simpler than most people think, and they come straight from foodsafety.gov. An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours, and a half-full one for about 24. So the strategy is: don't open the doors unless you have to, and eat from the pantry first. Perishables like meat, poultry, fish, eggs, and leftovers that spend more than 2 hours above 40 degrees should be tossed. Frozen food that still has ice crystals, or that reads 40 degrees or below, can be safely refrozen. Never taste something to decide whether it's safe. When in doubt, throw it out.

An appliance thermometer in the fridge and one in the freezer take the guesswork out of all of this, and a cooler with ice extends your window if the outage stretches on.

Refrigerated medication has its own clock. Ready.gov advises discarding refrigerated medicine after a day without power unless the label says otherwise, and calling your doctor or pharmacist right away for a replacement. If your household depends on any medication that's temperature-sensitive, ask your pharmacist ahead of time exactly how long it lasts warm, and write the answer on the box.

One more habit that pays off: when an outage starts, unplug electronics and appliances. Power sometimes comes back with surges that can damage what's plugged in. Leave one lamp on so you know when service returns.

If Someone Depends on Powered Medical Equipment

If anyone in your home relies on electricity for medical needs, get them enrolled in PG&E's Medical Baseline Program now. Eligibility is based on medical need, not income. Enrollees get extra electricity at the lowest rate tier, and, more importantly for us, extra advance notifications before a PSPS. PG&E sends Medical Baseline customers additional alerts at 48 hours, at 24 hours, and again just before the power goes off.

A medical practitioner certifies the application, and you can start it online. Two details trip people up. The application has to be submitted within 90 days of the practitioner's signature, so don't let a signed form sit in a drawer. And enrollment has to be renewed: permanent conditions self-recertify every four years, while non-permanent conditions recertify every two years with a practitioner. PG&E's Medical Baseline line is 1-877-660-6789 if you have questions about either.

Enrollment is not a backup power plan by itself, though. Talk with the medical provider about how long each device runs on battery, what the fallback is, and at what point you'd relocate to somewhere with power. Write that threshold down before you need it.

Check on the Neighbors

This is the part of the plan Boulder Creek already does well. Know which of your neighbors are older, live alone, are on wells, or depend on medical equipment, and trade phone numbers before storm season. A text thread for your road costs nothing and works as long as someone has signal. When an outage hits, a quick knock on the right door can matter more than everything else on this page.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I find out when my power will be back on?

Check the PG&E Outage Center map or call the 24-hour outage line at 1-800-743-5002. PG&E posts estimated restoration times once crews assess the damage, and those estimates can change. Nobody else, including this site, can promise a restoration time, so treat PG&E's latest update as the answer.

Will PG&E warn me before a Public Safety Power Shutoff?

PG&E says it tries to notify customers ahead of a PSPS by email, phone, and text, but it also says the first alert may sometimes come the same day power is turned off. Keep your contact info current on your PG&E account, sign up for address alerts if you're not the account holder, and have your supplies ready before fire weather arrives.

How far from the house does a generator need to be?

More than 20 feet from any windows, doors, and vents, per the CDC, and never inside a home or garage, even with everything open. Pair it with a battery-powered carbon monoxide detector near every sleeping area. If you want it wired to the house, have an electrician install a transfer switch so it can't backfeed into the lines.

How long is food safe when the power's out?

About 4 hours in an unopened refrigerator, about 48 hours in a full freezer, and about 24 in a half-full one, according to foodsafety.gov. Toss perishables that spend more than 2 hours above 40 degrees, and never taste food to test it.

What if someone in my house uses an oxygen machine or other powered medical device?

Enroll them in PG&E's Medical Baseline Program for extra notifications before planned shutoffs, and work out a written backup plan with their medical provider: battery runtimes, a charging plan, and the point at which you'd move them somewhere with power.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This article links to official sources from PG&E, the California Public Utilities Commission, the CDC, Ready.gov, foodsafety.gov, and Santa Cruz County. When the power is out, PG&E's outage map and official alerts are the current source of truth for restoration times.

An outage plan is one piece of getting a mountain home ready for winter. Fold it into the seasonal rhythm with the Boulder Creek home maintenance calendar, sort out who serves your address in the utilities guide, and keep the Residents guide handy for county contacts and emergency resources in one place.

boulder-creek-public-transportation.title: Getting Around Without a Car: Transit Options From Boulder Creek
boulder-creek-public-transportation.html:
The short version

  • The everyday ride: Santa Cruz METRO's Route 35 runs seven days a week down Highway 9 to downtown Santa Cruz. A local ride is $2 cash.
  • The weekday express: Route 35X leaves Santa Cruz every 30 minutes from 6:30am to 5:30pm and carries most of the daytime service to town.
  • Students ride free: K-12 students and college students with a valid ID pay nothing.
  • Over the hill: Take Route 35 to downtown Santa Cruz, then transfer to the Highway 17 Express for San Jose and Diridon Station.
  • Can't use a regular bus? METRO ParaCruz and Lift Line both run door-to-door rides.
  • One habit: Schedules change with each service update, so check the linked timetables for exact times at your stop.

You don't need a car to get out of Boulder Creek. You can ride a bus to Santa Cruz seven days a week, catch a weekday express to the coast, or connect over the hill to San Jose with a single transfer. The catch is the evening timetable and the weather, so it pays to know how the pieces fit before you leave the driveway. Here's the map.

Route 35 is the backbone

Route 35, the Highway 9/Scotts Valley line, is how Boulder Creek connects to the rest of the county without a car. It runs between the RiverFront transit stops on Front Street in downtown Santa Cruz and the Country Club end of Big Basin Way, passing through Ben Lomond, Felton and Scotts Valley on the way.

In and around town, the schedule's timepoints include Highway 9 at Middleton Avenue in the middle of downtown, Pool Drive at Highway 9 by the Mountain Store, and Big Basin Way out toward the Country Club neighborhood. Heading toward Santa Cruz, buses stop at Highway 9 and Main in Ben Lomond, then at Highlands Park or Glen Arbor Road at Quail Hollow depending on the trip, then San Lorenzo Valley High School before reaching the Cavallaro Transit Center in Scotts Valley.

The pattern differs by day. On weekends there's no express, and Route 35 covers the valley on its own about every 30 minutes, leaving downtown Santa Cruz from 7:30am to 10:30pm, with the last inbound bus pulling out of Country Club at 10:47pm. On weekdays Route 35 handles the early morning and the evening while the 35X express covers the middle of the day, and the last Route 35 trip leaves Santa Cruz at 11:00pm. Pull up the Route 35 timetable for the exact times at your stop, because first and last trips differ by direction and day of week.

If you're new in town and still setting up the rest of your life here, our new resident quick-start guide covers the non-bus logistics.

Route 35X, the weekday workhorse

On weekdays only, METRO runs Route 35X, the Santa Cruz/Boulder Creek Express, and it carries most of the daytime service to town. Buses leave the RiverFront stops in Santa Cruz every 30 minutes from 6:30am to 5:30pm, 23 trips in all, with 21 trips running the other way and the last of those leaving the Mountain Store at 5:33pm. The express skips Scotts Valley Drive at Granite Creek, which trims seven to ten minutes off the Route 35 running time.

In town the trips alternate, one out to the Mountain Store and the next out to Country Club, so downtown Boulder Creek gets a bus about every 30 minutes while each of those two ends sees one about every hour.

If you go to Santa Cruz on any kind of regular clock, the 35X is the one to learn. Check the Route 35X schedule for the exact departures at your stop, since express trips are the first thing to shift when METRO adjusts service.

What it costs

Fares are the easy part, and they're posted on METRO's Fares & Passes page. A single local ride is $2.00 cash for adults, or $1.00 for riders 65 and older and riders with disabilities. A day pass runs $6, and a 31-day pass is $65, with discount versions at $3 and $32. If you pay by tapping a contactless card or phone, Tap2Cruz caps an adult at $5 of local fares in a day, or $2.50 at the discount rate, which beats the $6 day pass.

The best deal in the system goes to students. K-12 riders travel free through the Youth Cruz Free program, which makes Route 35 a real option for SLV High and middle school students heading up and down the valley. College students with a valid student ID also ride free, and so do riders who are legally blind.

Getting to San Jose and over the hill

There's no direct bus from Boulder Creek over Highway 17, but the connection is straightforward. Ride Route 35 to its downtown Santa Cruz end at the RiverFront stops on Front Street. The Highway 17 Express boards a short walk away in the same RiverFront area, at Front Street near Trader Joe's, and runs weekdays and weekends to Diridon Station in San Jose, where Caltrain, Amtrak, and light rail all connect.

The Highway 17 Express uses its own fare: $7.00 for a single ride, $3.50 discount, or a $14 day pass. A 31-day Highway 17 pass is $145. If you're commuting to the South Bay a few days a week, do the math on passes before you settle into paying cash each way.

Weekend bus to Big Basin

On weekends, Route 35B runs from the Cavallaro Transit Center in Scotts Valley up Highway 9 and out to Big Basin Redwoods State Park, with five trips in each direction. It picks up in Boulder Creek on the way, in the middle of downtown and again out at Country Club, so you don't have to start from Scotts Valley. The Big Basin leg is seasonal and doesn't run in winter, so check the route page before you build a day around it. If you're headed that way, our Big Basin day trip guide covers what to expect once you're there, including the park's parking-reservation advice, which makes the bus a smarter play than it might sound.

Door-to-door rides: ParaCruz and Lift Line

Two services cover trips a fixed-route bus can't.

METRO ParaCruz is METRO's ADA paratransit: accessible, shared door-to-door rides for people who can't use regular buses because of a disability. It serves destinations within three-quarters of a mile of an operating bus route, which in our corner of the county means the Highway 9 corridor. You apply through ADAride, online at adaride.com or by phone at 877-232-7433, and a decision comes within 21 days. Once you're eligible, rides are booked one to three days ahead at 831-425-4664, and the base fare is $4 per trip.

Lift Line is run by Community Bridges, a local nonprofit, and provides door-to-door rides for seniors 60 and older and people with disabilities across Santa Cruz County, with a focus on medical trips, meal-site rides, and essential errands. Some of its programs carry income qualifications, and rides need to be scheduled in advance. Start with the application on its site or call 831-688-9663 on a weekday to sort out which program fits.

If a ride is about a medical appointment, ask both services what applies to you. The eligibility rules differ, and plenty of valley residents qualify for one and not the other.

School buses for SLVUSD students

San Lorenzo Valley Unified runs its own home-to-school buses, separate from METRO, and posts route sheets by bus name on its Transportation Department bus information page. Ridership is fee-based: as posted for the current cycle, an annual pass is $220 round trip or $116 one way, a semester pass is $116 or $58, and ticket books run $20 for 20 tickets. Students with qualifying IEPs are exempt from fees, and there's a hardship application for families receiving county assistance. The transportation office in Ben Lomond answers questions at 831-336-2223. Confirm prices and routes with the district before the school year starts, since both get updated over the summer.

Remember the free alternative for older kids: K-12 students ride METRO at no cost, and Route 35 stops at SLV High.

A few caveats to plan around

The bus works well here, with two limits worth knowing before you give up a car entirely.

  • Early and late: midday buses come about every 30 minutes, but once the last 35X has run the gaps stretch toward an hour, and the final bus toward Santa Cruz leaves Boulder Creek at 11:14pm on weekdays.
  • Storm season: when Highway 9 closes for trees or slides, buses reroute or hold just like everyone else. Sign up for alerts through CruzAware and check METRO's rider alerts on the route pages before heading out in bad weather.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a bus from Boulder Creek to Santa Cruz?

Yes. METRO Route 35 runs seven days a week along Highway 9 from Boulder Creek through Ben Lomond, Felton and Scotts Valley to downtown Santa Cruz, and on weekdays the Route 35X express covers the same trip every 30 minutes from 6:30am to 5:30pm.

How much does the bus cost from Boulder Creek?

A local single ride is $2.00 cash, with a $1.00 fare for riders 65 and older and riders with disabilities. Day passes are $6 and 31-day passes are $65. K-12 students, college students with ID, and riders who are legally blind ride free.

Can I get from Boulder Creek to San Jose by bus?

Yes, with one transfer. Take Route 35 to the RiverFront stops in downtown Santa Cruz, then board the Highway 17 Express to Diridon Station in San Jose. The express runs weekdays and weekends and costs $7.00 for a single ride.

What if I can't ride a regular bus?

Two door-to-door options serve Boulder Creek. METRO ParaCruz covers riders whose disability prevents using fixed-route buses, with an application through ADAride and $4 base fares. Lift Line, run by Community Bridges, serves seniors 60 and older and people with disabilities, with some income-qualified programs.

Do school kids ride METRO free?

Yes. The Youth Cruz Free program lets K-12 students ride any METRO route at no cost, no pass purchase required. SLVUSD's own yellow-bus service is separate and fee-based, with passes sold through the district's transportation office.

Planning to lean on the bus for a while? Save the Route 35 timetable to your phone, then browse the Residents guide for the rest of the valley's utilities, services, and county contacts in one place. And if a shorter commute would settle the question altogether, our valley job board lists what is hiring close to home.

boulder-creek-roads-parking-notes.title: Mountain Roads, Parking, and When Highway 9 Gets Complicated
boulder-creek-roads-parking-notes.html:
The short version

  • Check conditions before you leave. Caltrans QuickMap or our Mountain Status page for what's happening now; call 1-800-427-7623 for the state highways, (831) 477-3999 for county roads.
  • Highway 9 is a curvy 30-minute redwood drive. If five or more cars stack up behind you, use the next turnout. It's the law, and it's the neighborly thing to do.
  • Give cyclists at least three feet when you pass, and on this many blind curves that mostly means waiting for a straight stretch.
  • Downtown parking is street-scale. Arrive early on weekends and event days, and don't block driveways, hydrants, or the width of the road.
  • Don't count on your phone. Coverage drops out in the canyon, so download offline maps before you go.
  • Big Basin is about 9 miles up Highway 236: no RVs or trailers for day use, and reservations are highly recommended.

A few miles out of Santa Cruz, Highway 9 slips under the redwoods and stays there. The road narrows, the curves keep coming, and the trees hold the light down all the way to Boulder Creek. It's a genuine mountain road, and it asks for more patience than speed. Expect cyclists on every curve, plan for small-town parking rather than big-lot parking, and don't count on cell signal the whole way up. None of that should scare you off. It's a beautiful drive. It just goes better for everyone, visitors and locals alike, when you know what kind of road you're on before you're on it.

What follows are the durable patterns, the things that are true most days. For what's happening right now, always go to the live sources linked throughout, because we can't promise you an open road or an empty parking spot, and neither can anyone else.

Know Whose Road You're On

Two highways define driving here, and both are state routes maintained by Caltrans. Highway 9 runs the length of the San Lorenzo Valley, connecting Santa Cruz to Felton, Ben Lomond, Brookdale, and Boulder Creek before climbing over the ridge toward Saratoga. Highway 236 splits off from downtown Boulder Creek and loops through Big Basin Redwoods State Park.

For either route, you can check current conditions by entering the route number at Caltrans' road information page, calling 1-800-427-7623, or opening QuickMap, which shows closures and incidents in real time.

Nearly everything else, the smaller roads that branch off the highway, is maintained by Santa Cruz County, and those closures show up on the county's Road Closure Dashboard instead. If you come across a tree down or a flooded stretch on a county road, the county's 24-hour road dispatch is (831) 477-3999. Knowing which agency owns the road you're on saves you a phone transfer, and our emergency contacts page keeps all of these numbers in one place. For anything dangerous happening right now, call 911.

What Driving Highway 9 Is Like

Highway 9 between Santa Cruz and Boulder Creek is about thirty minutes of continuous curves through redwood shade. The trees make it darker than you expect at midday and slick with needles and moisture long after rain has stopped. Sight lines are short, shoulders are thin or missing, and passing opportunities are rare, so the pace of the whole road is set by its slowest vehicle. Build that into your schedule and the drive is a pleasure instead of a frustration.

If that slowest vehicle is you, that's fine, but use the turnouts. California law, Vehicle Code 21656, requires a slow-moving vehicle on a two-lane road to pull into the next turnout or safe area whenever five or more vehicles stack up behind it. Locals use the turnouts reflexively and notice, kindly or otherwise, who doesn't. Pulling over for ten seconds is the single most neighborly thing a visitor can do on this road.

A few other habits that fit the road:

  • Don't stop in the travel lane for photos, even briefly, since the next driver comes around the curve blind.
  • Use your headlights in the redwood shade.
  • Leave the map-app shortcuts alone in bad weather, because those side roads are narrower, steeper, and slower than the highway they're avoiding.

Sharing the Curves with Cyclists

Highway 9 is one of the classic road cycling climbs in the Bay Area, and you'll meet riders on it, especially on weekend mornings. The law here is specific. California's Three Feet for Safety Act, Vehicle Code 21760, requires drivers to give at least three feet of clearance when passing a bicycle, and when three feet isn't possible, to slow down and pass only when it won't endanger the rider.

On a road with this many blind curves, that mostly means waiting. Hang back at a comfortable distance, wait for a straight stretch or a turnout, then pass with room to spare. The wait is rarely more than a minute, and it beats meeting an oncoming car mid-pass with a cyclist on your right. Riders, for their part, tend to use the turnouts too when a line forms. The road works because most people extend each other that courtesy.

Parking in Boulder Creek

Boulder Creek's downtown is a few blocks of Highway 9, and parking is small-town scale: street parking along the highway and side streets, plus modest lots serving individual businesses. On an ordinary weekday you'll likely find a spot within a short walk. On sunny summer weekends, holiday events, and festival days, the easy spots go early, so arrive on the early side or be ready to park a few blocks out and walk.

A few requests from the people who live here:

  • Watch the posted signs, and don't block driveways, fire hydrants, or the fire station's approach on Central Avenue.
  • Don't park in business lots you're not patronizing.
  • Leave room at trailheads and turnouts for residents whose driveways share them.
  • Never park where your car narrows the road itself, because fire engines and delivery trucks need every foot of width these roads have.

If a spot feels questionable, it probably is.

Highway 236 and the Big Basin Run

The drive from downtown Boulder Creek to Big Basin Redwoods State Park is about 9 miles up Highway 236, and the park's own guidance says it plainly: all roads into Big Basin are curvy. Sections of 236 are effectively single-lane threading between old-growth trunks, so take it slow and expect to yield.

Two things to know before you commit to the drive. First, the park currently can't accommodate oversized vehicles or trailers for day-use parking, so leave the RV at camp. Second, day-use parking is limited and the park highly recommends reservations. Check the park page for current reservation details before you go, since post-fire recovery means conditions there keep evolving. When 236 has a problem, it shows up in the same Caltrans tools as Highway 9: QuickMap, the route lookup, or 1-800-427-7623.

Don't Bet on Your Phone

Cell coverage in the San Lorenzo Valley is real but patchy, and it drops out in stretches of the canyon along both highways, with dead pockets that vary by carrier. Plan around that. Download offline maps before you leave, screenshot your destination and any reservation, and tell someone where you're headed if you're hiking. If your plans depend on calling ahead, make the call from town rather than the road. Coverage can also degrade in storms and outages, which is one more reason the paper-map habit never really died up here.

When Storms Change Everything

In winter, atmospheric river storms can close sections of Highway 9, Highway 236, and the county roads with little warning, through flooding, slides, or downed trees and lines. The durable advice is to check before you drive: the NWS Bay Area forecast for what's coming, QuickMap and the county Road Closure Dashboard for what's closed, and our Mountain Status page, which gathers the official links.

If you reach water across the road, turn around. The National Weather Service warns that twelve inches of moving water can carry away most cars and that the road under floodwater may already be gone. Never drive around closure barriers; they're there because someone confirmed the road isn't safe.

Storm days are not the days to visit. But if you're already here when weather rolls in, businesses in town stay friendly, and waiting out a squall with coffee beats testing a flooded dip in the road every time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Highway 9 open right now?

We never answer that from a static page, and you shouldn't trust any page that does. Check Caltrans QuickMap, enter route 9 at the Caltrans road information page, or call 1-800-427-7623. Our Mountain Status page links all of the live sources in one place.

Can I drive an RV or trailer to Big Basin?

Not for day use right now. The park's official page says no oversized vehicles or trailers can be accommodated for day-use parking, and stretches of Highway 236 are narrow enough that big rigs struggle regardless. Park the RV elsewhere and drive in with a passenger vehicle, ideally with a parking reservation.

Where should I park for a day in downtown Boulder Creek?

Street parking on and just off Highway 9 is the main supply, with small business lots for customers. Come early on weekends and event days, obey posted signs, and don't block driveways, hydrants, or road width. There's no big central lot, so expect a short walk and treat it as part of the visit.

Will I have cell service on the drive up?

Sometimes, and you shouldn't plan around it. Coverage drops in stretches of the canyon on both highways and varies by carrier, so download offline maps, save what you need before leaving Santa Cruz or Saratoga, and let someone know your plans if you're heading into the parks.

What do I do if a tree is down across the road?

If wires are involved or it's blocking traffic dangerously, call 911 and keep your distance. Otherwise report it: (831) 477-3999 reaches Santa Cruz County's 24-hour road dispatch for county roads, and Caltrans handles Highways 9 and 236, reachable via roads.dot.ca.gov or 1-800-427-7623. Our emergency contacts list has the full set of numbers.

Heading up soon? Check the live sources first on our Mountain Status page, keep the Boulder Creek emergency contacts handy for a tree down or a closure, and see the Residents guide for utilities, permits, and county contacts in one place.

boulder-creek-tree-work-questions.title: Tree Work in Boulder Creek: Questions to Ask Before Anyone Touches a Redwood
boulder-creek-tree-work-questions.html:
The short version

  • Permits are parcel-specific. Some tree work in Boulder Creek needs a county permit, depending on your overlays (Coastal Zone, riparian corridor, sensitive habitat). Check your parcel in the county GIS tool and confirm with county planning before cutting. Never rely on a contractor's "no permit needed up here."
  • Hire licensed and insured. Tree work above $1,000 is licensed contracting; the classification is C-49 Tree and Palm. Tree contractors must carry workers' compensation insurance even if they work alone. Verify both at CSLB before anyone climbs.
  • Defensible space is not a clear-cut. The state's guidance is about spacing, limbing, and fuel reduction across zones out to 100 feet, not blanket removal. Ask any bidder for a zone-by-zone plan.
  • An arborist tells you whether the tree needs the work at all; a contractor license only says a business can legally do it.
  • After a storm, slow down. Urgency is the sales tactic. Take a day to check the license, verify insurance, and get a second bid.

The redwood is probably the reason you bought the place. So before anyone puts a saw to a tree on your Boulder Creek property, get three things straight: whether the job needs a permit, whether the outfit doing it is licensed and insured for tree work specifically, and whether the plan serves your fire safety or just someone's invoice.

Tree work is the most consequential home service in this town. Done right, it protects your house. Done wrong, it can cost you a code enforcement case, a lawsuit, or the tree itself. None of this is legal advice. It's the list of questions that keeps neighbors out of trouble.

First Question: Does This Tree Need a Permit?

Don't let anyone, a tree company included, tell you flatly that "you don't need a permit up here." Sometimes you do, and it depends entirely on where the tree stands.

Santa Cruz County's tree protection and removal rules require a county permit when a tree sits in the county's Coastal Zone and meets the "significant tree" definition, and also when a tree stands in designated sensitive habitat. The Significant Trees Protection chapter of the county code spells out the definitions. Inside urban and rural service lines the trigger starts at 20 inches diameter at breast height, and in the Coastal Zone the rules cover not just removal but trimming more than one third of a tree's green foliage. Whether any of that applies to your parcel is a map question, and the county points people to its GIS tool to check.

Then there are creeks, which is closer to home for most of us. The county's riparian corridor ordinance protects a band along every stream, 50 feet out from each side of a perennial stream and 30 feet from an intermittent one, and it defines tree and shrub removal, meaning topping or felling anything taller than 8 feet, as a regulated development activity inside that corridor. In a town threaded with creeks that feed the San Lorenzo River, many backyards include riparian corridor. Cutting there without county sign-off is how well-meaning people end up in enforcement.

Two more wrinkles. Commercial timber operations are a separate world, regulated through CAL FIRE under the state Forest Practice Act, and the county's tree page notes that some removals need a CAL FIRE permit rather than a county one. And for genuine emergencies, the code does allow immediate action when a hazardous tree threatens life or property, with a report to the county afterward. That's for real emergencies, not for the tree that's looked sketchy for three years.

The short version: permits can be required in Boulder Creek depending on your parcel's overlays, and the only reliable answers come from the county's Environmental Planning pages or a call to the Unified Permit Center. A good local tree company will know this and say so. Treat "no permit needed, trust me" as a red flag, and get the answer in writing either way.

Defensible Space Is Not a Blank Check

Fire safety is the reason for most tree work here, and the state's actual guidance is more surgical than a clear-cut. CAL FIRE's defensible space program requires 100 feet of defensible space around structures under Public Resources Code 4291, organized in zones:

  • Zone 0 is the first 5 feet from the house, kept ember-resistant.
  • Zone 1 runs to 30 feet, kept "lean, clean and green."
  • Zone 2 continues to 100 feet or your property line, where the goal is reducing fuel, not eliminating trees.

Notice what the guidance asks for: spacing between trees that widens with the slope, limbs removed within 10 feet of chimneys and stovepipes, lower branches limbed up at least 6 feet from the ground, dead material out. The spacing numbers matter up here, because they're written for terrain like ours. CAL FIRE asks for:

  • 10 feet between trees on flat or mild ground under a 20 percent slope
  • 20 feet on a 20 to 40 percent slope
  • 30 feet on anything steeper

Healthy, well-spaced, limbed-up trees are compatible with defensible space. So when a bidder's fire-safety plan is "take them all down," ask them to walk you through it zone by zone against CAL FIRE's own standards.

Defensible space work also doesn't override the permit rules above. Fire safety and habitat protection can apply to the same tree, which is exactly why the county wants eyes on removals in protected areas. Your local fire agency can weigh in too, and CAL FIRE notes local standards are sometimes stricter than the state minimum.

Licenses, Insurance, and Why Tree Work Is Special

Tree work above $1,000 is licensed contracting in California, and the classification to look for is C-49 Tree and Palm, which replaced the old D-49 designation. Check any company in the CSLB license lookup before they climb anything.

Here's the part too few homeowners know. Because the work is so dangerous, CSLB requires tree service contractors to carry workers' compensation insurance whether or not they have employees. Most trades can claim an exemption if they work alone. Tree contractors can't.

The license lookup shows the workers' comp status, so verify it there rather than taking a business card's word. Ask separately for a certificate of general liability insurance sent directly from the insurer. If a climber gets hurt or your neighbor's roof gets a new skylight, the difference between an insured and uninsured outfit is the difference between a claim and a catastrophe.

For the broader hiring mechanics, including the down payment cap and the three-bid habit, see our guide to hiring a contractor in the Santa Cruz Mountains. All of it applies doubly to tree work.

What an ISA Certified Arborist Adds

A contractor license says a business can legally do the work. It says nothing about whether the tree needs the work. That's where an International Society of Arboriculture credential comes in, and you can find and verify credentialed professionals through the ISA's Find an Arborist tool. One caveat: listing is voluntary, so a legitimate arborist might not appear, but a credential claim you can't verify there is worth questioning.

For anything involving a permit, expect an arborist's report to be part of the application. The county's tree pages spell out what its reviewers want to see. And for a healthy tree you merely worry about, an arborist consult is cheap insurance against removing something that just needed pruning.

After the Storm: Slow Down

Every big winter blow shakes loose a wave of door-knockers with chainsaws, and the patterns reported after storms in many communities are consistent enough to name. Be careful with anyone who:

  • Shows up uninvited and says your tree is about to fall.
  • Pushes you to decide on the spot.
  • Wants cash or a big deposit up front.
  • Has no license number on the truck or the paperwork.
  • Can't produce insurance certificates.

Urgency is the tool. The pitch works because you're rattled and the driveway is blocked.

The counter-moves are boring and effective. If a tree is genuinely dangerous right now, on a structure or blocking your only way out, that can justify emergency action; document everything with photos first. If it's into power lines, that's PG&E's problem to make safe, not a job for anyone's chainsaw, yours included. For everything else, take a day. Check the license, verify workers' comp, call a second company for a competing bid. A tree that has stood for eighty years will almost always stand through your due diligence.

Questions to Ask Before You Sign

Ask every tree bidder these, and note who answers cleanly:

  • What's your C-49 license number?
  • Does this job need a county permit or CAL FIRE involvement, and who confirms that?
  • Can your insurer send me certificates for liability and workers' comp?
  • Is removal necessary, or would pruning meet the fire-safety goal?
  • What happens to the wood and slash, and is hauling included in the bid?
  • Who's responsible if the neighbor's fence takes a hit?

Local companies that work Boulder Creek every week answer these without flinching. Our directory lists local tree services as a starting point; being listed isn't an endorsement, so run the checks regardless.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a permit to remove a tree on my own property in Boulder Creek?

Sometimes. It depends on whether the tree stands in the Coastal Zone, a riparian corridor along a creek, sensitive habitat, or another protected overlay, and that's parcel-specific. Check your parcel in the county GIS tool and confirm with county planning before cutting. Never rely on a contractor's verbal assurance that no permit is needed.

Does trimming count, or just removal?

In protected situations it can count. In the Coastal Zone, the county's significant tree rules cover trimming more than one third of a tree's green foliage, and the riparian ordinance regulates topping as well as felling. Light pruning for health and clearance is a different animal from major canopy reduction, so describe the actual scope when you ask the county.

What if a tree is about to come down on my house right now?

True emergencies are treated differently; the county code allows immediate action when a hazardous tree requires it for safety of life or property, with a report to the Planning Director afterward, within 10 working days under the significant tree chapter. Photograph the situation before and after, and if power lines are involved, stay clear and call PG&E first.

How do I verify a tree company is legitimate?

Three lookups: their license and workers' comp status at CSLB, any arborist credential at Trees Are Good, and insurance certificates sent directly from their insurer. Remember that tree contractors must carry workers' comp even as one-person operations.

Will clearing trees satisfy my defensible space requirements?

Not necessarily, and it may be more than the standard asks. CAL FIRE's guidance is built on spacing, limbing, and fuel reduction across three zones out to 100 feet, not blanket removal. Get a zone-by-zone plan, and check whether your local fire agency applies stricter standards before committing to removals you can't undo.

Last reviewed July 16, 2026. This article links to official sources from Santa Cruz County, CAL FIRE, and the California Contractors State License Board. Permit requirements and parcel-specific rules come from the responsible county agency, not from a general article like this one, and none of this is legal advice.

Tree work is one piece of owning a home in the redwoods. For the rest of the year's upkeep, see the Boulder Creek home maintenance calendar, and the Residents guide for utilities, permits, and county contacts in one place.

boulder-creek-utilities-guide.title: Utilities, Water, and Waste in Boulder Creek: Who Serves What
boulder-creek-utilities-guide.html:
The short version

  • Electricity: PG&E. Report an outage at 1-800-743-5002. For a downed line, get clear, call 911, then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000.
  • Water: most homes are on the San Lorenzo Valley Water District (831-338-2153); outlying parcels run on private wells.
  • Sewer or septic: mostly septic, overseen by Santa Cruz County Environmental Health (831-454-2022). A slice of town near the core is on the CSA 7 county sewer.
  • Trash, recycling, and organics: GreenWaste Recovery (831-426-2711), and it's now mandatory countywide.
  • Propane and internet: you choose your own provider, so check what actually reaches your address before you commit.

When the power drops and the well pump goes quiet, there's no city hall up here to sort it out for you. Boulder Creek is unincorporated county, so each service has its own provider, and knowing who to call is half the job.

Electricity comes from PG&E. Water for most homes comes from the San Lorenzo Valley Water District, though plenty of properties run on private wells. Most homes treat waste on septic systems overseen by Santa Cruz County Environmental Health, while a slice of town near the core is on a county-run sewer. Trash, recycling, and organics pickup is GreenWaste Recovery, the county's franchised hauler, and it's not optional anymore. Many households heat with delivered propane from private suppliers you pick yourself, and internet depends on your exact address, so look it up rather than trusting a list.

One standing caveat for the whole page: service territories and providers change, and boundaries here are parcel-specific. When a decision matters, confirm with the provider directly.

Electricity: PG&E

PG&E is the electric utility for Boulder Creek and the rest of the San Lorenzo Valley. For outages, the PG&E Outage Center has the live outage map, reporting tools, and alert signups, and the 24-hour outage line is 1-800-743-5002.

A downed line is a different call. Get well away from it, dial 911 first, then PG&E's emergency line at 1-800-743-5000. General customer service, including starting or stopping service when you move, is 1-877-660-6789, around the clock.

Two things are worth knowing as a mountain customer. PG&E is regulated by the California Public Utilities Commission, which also oversees Public Safety Power Shutoffs, the planned outages PG&E can call during high fire-risk weather. Outages are enough of a fact of life here that they deserve their own plan; our power outage plan for mountain households covers alerts, generators, and food safety.

On the gas side, don't assume. Some addresses have PG&E natural gas service and many mountain properties don't, relying on delivered propane instead. Check with PG&E about what's actually connected at your address before you buy appliances that expect one or the other.

Water: SLV Water District or Your Own Well

The San Lorenzo Valley Water District has supplied water in the valley since 1941 and serves Boulder Creek, Brookdale, Ben Lomond, Lompico, Zayante, Scotts Valley, Manana Woods, and Felton through more than 7,900 connections. The district office is right in town at 13060 Highway 9, and the phone number is 831-338-2153. Starting or stopping service, billing questions, and leak reports all go through the district; the website has a start and stop service section, and for anything urgent, call.

Not every Boulder Creek property is a district customer, though. Outlying parcels and some older neighborhoods run on private wells or small shared systems, and the only reliable way to know a specific property's status is to ask the district or look at what the seller discloses in escrow.

If you're on a well, you're your own water utility: testing, treatment, and the pump are on you, and Santa Cruz County Environmental Health is the local agency that regulates individual water systems. Keep in mind that a well pump needs electricity, which is exactly why well households should read the power outage plan.

Sewer or Septic: Probably Septic

Most Boulder Creek homes treat wastewater on-site with a septic system. The oversight agency is Santa Cruz County Environmental Health, which permits new systems, repairs, and upgrades, and handles maintenance requirements. If you're buying, building, or your drainfield is acting up, they're the call: 831-454-2022, or EnvironmentalHealth@santacruzcountyca.gov. Septic in the San Lorenzo Valley is its own subject, with small lots, steep slopes, and creeks nearby, so involve the county early rather than after a contractor has started digging.

There are two exceptions to the septic rule. A portion of the Boulder Creek community is connected to a sanitary sewer run by the county as County Service Area 7, Boulder Creek Sanitation, which operates its own treatment facility; connected properties pay an annual sewer charge on the property tax bill, and the county's number for the district is 831-454-2160.

Separately, the water district owns and operates a small wastewater system serving roughly 56 homes in Bear Creek Estates. If you're not sure which category your property falls into, check your property tax bill for a sewer service charge, or call the county.

Trash, Recycling, and Organics: GreenWaste Recovery

Curbside collection in unincorporated Santa Cruz County, which includes all of Boulder Creek, is franchised to GreenWaste Recovery. Single-family homes get weekly pickup of garbage, recycling, and organics, with garbage carts from 20 to 96 gallons and recycling and organics carts included at no extra charge. To sign up or ask about service on a private road, call 831-426-2711 or email SantaCruzCS@GreenWaste.com.

Here's the part that catches people: service is now mandatory. Under the county's universal service requirement, every developed property in the unincorporated county must either subscribe with GreenWaste or register with the county as a self-hauler, and the county has set a compliance deadline of November 1, 2026, with fines that start at $100 and escalate from there. If you've been quietly trunk-hauling your own bags for years, this is the year to get legal, one way or the other.

For everything the truck won't take, the nearest facility is the Ben Lomond Transfer Station at 9835 Newell Creek Road in Ben Lomond. It also hosts a household hazardous waste drop-off on Thursdays from 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., which is where old paint, batteries, pesticides, and motor oil should go; bring proof of residency, and call 831-454-2606 with questions. Check the county Public Works site for the station's current general hours before you load the truck.

Propane and Heating Fuel

If your home heats or cooks with propane, you're dealing with a private, competitive market rather than a utility with an assigned territory. That has a real upside: you can shop. Suppliers differ on per-gallon price, tank rental versus ownership, delivery schedules, and minimums, so it pays to call two or three, ask neighbors who they use, and request current pricing in writing before you commit.

If you're new to a propane house, find the tank, learn to read the percentage gauge, and don't let it run low heading into a stretch of winter storms, when delivery schedules get tight for everyone. We're deliberately not naming suppliers here because companies and coverage change; your neighbors' current recommendations will be fresher than any list we could publish.

Internet and Phone

Anyone who promises you a tidy list of Boulder Creek internet providers is guessing, because availability varies street by street in the San Lorenzo Valley. The reliable method takes five minutes: put your exact address into the FCC National Broadband Map, which shows every provider that reports service at your location and what speeds they claim.

Treat those listings as claims to verify, not guarantees, then confirm with each provider's own address checker before you schedule anything, and ask the closest neighbors what they actually use and how it holds up in winter. That last step is the one that saves you, because a provider that's fine in town can be a different experience at the end of a long canyon road.

Whatever you choose, remember that home internet and cordless phones die with the power. If you work from home, think through your outage fallback, whether that's a cell plan with hotspot data or knowing which nearby spots have power and signal.

Who to Call: The Short List

Keep this somewhere findable.

  • Downed line: stay far away, call 911 first, then PG&E's emergency line at 1-800-743-5000.
  • Power outage with no downed line: PG&E's 24-hour outage line, 1-800-743-5002.
  • Water service, leaks, or billing on district water: San Lorenzo Valley Water District, 831-338-2153.
  • Septic permits and problems: County Environmental Health, 831-454-2022.
  • Sewer questions in the CSA 7 area: 831-454-2160.
  • Trash, recycling, and organics: GreenWaste Recovery, 831-426-2711.
  • Household hazardous waste: 831-454-2606.
  • County emergency alerts: sign up for CruzAware at cruzaware.org so road closures and evacuation notices reach you directly.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I know if my house is on SLVWD water or a well?

Check your mail for a water bill from the San Lorenzo Valley Water District, or call the district at 831-338-2153 with your address and ask. If you're buying a home, the disclosures should say, but verify with the district anyway, because boundaries are parcel-specific and small shared systems exist too.

Is garbage service really required in Boulder Creek?

Yes. The county's universal service requirement says every developed property in the unincorporated county must subscribe with GreenWaste Recovery or register as a self-hauler, with a compliance deadline of November 1, 2026 and escalating fines after that. Call GreenWaste at 831-426-2711 to get set up.

Is Boulder Creek on sewer or septic?

Mostly septic, overseen by County Environmental Health. The exceptions are properties connected to the CSA 7 Boulder Creek Sanitation sewer in part of town, which show a sewer charge on the property tax bill, and about 56 homes in Bear Creek Estates on a small district-run system.

What internet providers serve Boulder Creek?

It depends on your exact address, so look yours up on the FCC National Broadband Map and then confirm with each provider directly. Coverage changes street by street in the valley, and neighbors on your own road are the best source for how a connection really performs.

Where do I take paint, batteries, and other hazardous waste?

To the household hazardous waste drop-off at the Ben Lomond Transfer Station, 9835 Newell Creek Road, on Thursdays from 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., per the county's HHW page. Bring proof of residency, and call 831-454-2606 if you're not sure an item is accepted.

Last reviewed June 25, 2026. Service territories, rates, and county rules change, so confirm anything decision-critical with the provider or agency directly.

Keep this page handy, and for the rest of what a mountain household needs to run, see the Residents guide for utilities, permits, and county contacts in one place.

boulder-creek-weekend-itinerary.title: A Boulder Creek Weekend: The Locally Supportive Itinerary
boulder-creek-weekend-itinerary.html:
The short version

  • Make two reservations first: Big Basin day-use parking, which takes no same-day bookings, and, if you want it, Sunday wine tasting at Big Basin Vineyards.
  • Book lodging early. The town keeps only a few options, and the redwood campground on Grove Street is the one built for a weekend like this.
  • Provision in town. Johnnie's and Wild Roots outfit a park day, and there are no services on the road into Big Basin.
  • Saturday is Big Basin, downtown shops, and dinner. Sunday is a sandstone ridge or a river beach, then the museum and a glass.
  • Season matters. This plan is built for spring through fall. In winter, the parks and the river play by different rules.

Sleep under the redwoods at the campground on Grove Street, provision at the town's two markets, spend Saturday in Big Basin, and give Sunday to a sandstone ridge or a river beach. That's the shape of a two-day Boulder Creek weekend that keeps your money in town, with the museum, the shops, and a mountain-grown wine tasting filling the edges. Two things to settle before anything else: reserve your Big Basin parking, since same-day reservations aren't available, and book your lodging, because the town keeps only a few options and is upfront about it. This plan assumes the spring-through-fall window. In winter, the parks and the river play by different rules.

And for calibration, here's the local's version: my own ideal Saturday is a walk into town, breakfast at Bella's, a coffee at Jenna Sue's after, a slow lap of the shops with the mandatory hello to the kittens in the corner window, sandwiches from the Wild Roots deli, and the walk home to eat them in the garden. Most of this itinerary is that day with reservations attached.

First, the real lodging picture

Boulder Creek isn't a hotel town, and there's no use pretending otherwise. Our verified directory currently lists two lodging operations.

Redwood Resort at 150 Grove Street is the one built for a weekend like this: a seasonal campground with tent and RV sites among the redwoods, a pool, dogs welcome, and online booking, all within an easy walk of downtown. Stay there and your lodging dollars stay in town while your car mostly stays parked.

The other listing, Redwood Christian Park, is a retreat center that hosts groups rather than individual weekenders, so it's the answer for a reunion or retreat, not a couple's getaway.

If canvas isn't your style, short-term rentals turn up around town on the usual platforms, though we don't list or vouch for individual rentals. And if you end up basing down the valley instead, the rest of this itinerary still works as two day trips.

Before the weekend: two reservations

Book your Big Basin day-use parking through the Friends of Santa Cruz State Parks form. Per California State Parks, reservations are highly recommended because spaces are limited: $6 for a regular vehicle plus a $2 reservation fee, versus $10 without one. The form doesn't take same-day bookings, so what's left on the morning of is first come, first served. Oversized vehicles and trailers can't be accommodated right now.

Planning Sunday wine tasting? Reserve at Big Basin Vineyards too. The estate tasting room on Memory Lane pours Saturdays and Sundays from noon to 5, by reservation through its site.

Saturday morning: provision in town

Start downtown. Grab coffee and breakfast at one of the town's cafes, but lean on our current food guide and its phone numbers rather than a search result, since hours shift seasonally at small operations.
