Then build a picnic. Johnnie's Super Market, the town grocery since 1938, opens at 8 every morning and makes deli sandwiches from family recipes. Wild Roots Market, locally owned since 1991, opens at 9 with a deli counter and shelves stocked heavily from nearby farms.

Either one outfits a day in the park better than anything you'd have packed from home, and there are no services on the road into Big Basin, so buy your water and snacks here.

Saturday: Big Basin, thoughtfully

Big Basin Redwoods State Park, California's oldest state park, is about 9 miles up Highway 236 from downtown, a curvy, unhurried 25 to 30 minutes. The park is open 8 a.m. to sunset for limited day use while it recovers from the 2020 CZU fire, and what's open changes, so check the official park page the morning you go.

Walk the Redwood Loop through the old-growth grove first, then pick a longer route from the current trail map if you want more miles. Expect limited facilities, thinner shade than the old photos suggest, and a forest doing something you won't see many other places: rebuilding itself in the open sun.

We've written a full companion piece on doing this day well, shuttle and bus options included, in our Big Basin day trip guide. One planning note shapes the whole weekend: all campgrounds in the main park remain closed, which is why staying in Boulder Creek and day-tripping in is the practical move.

Come down the mountain by late afternoon and give the town's shops an hour before they close.

Air & Fire at 13150 Highway 9 stays open until 6:30 most days, with crystals, incense, jewelry, and work from more than 50 regional artists. SWAG at 13026 Highway 9 deals in restored mid-century stereos, vinyl, and vintage and local apparel, in an 1893 building the shop notes was the first in the country owned and operated by women; call 831-295-9191 for the day's hours.

For dinner, Scopazzi's at 13300 Big Basin Way is the town's historic landmark dining room, serving dinner from 4 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. If you'd rather end the day outdoors, The Sawmill north of downtown does American fare and craft beer with a big outdoor area and a music stage, though it's expected to close temporarily for renovations after August 14, 2026, so call 831-610-8196 before counting on it. If a show or gathering lands on your weekend, our events calendar is the place to check. The food guide has the full spread if you want other speeds.

Sunday morning: ridge or river

Two good options, depending on your legs.

The hike: Castle Rock State Park sits at the top of Highway 9 on Skyline Boulevard, a slower mountain drive from town. Per State Parks, it's open for day use from 6 a.m. to sunset, the Kirkwood entrance station runs 8 to 5, and vehicle day use is $10. You get sculpted sandstone, big views toward the ocean, and 34 miles of trails, plus open rock climbing if that's your thing. Know before you go: no dogs on trails, and no cell reception in the park, so download your map first.

The slow morning: sleep in and walk to Junction Park at Middleton and Railroad Avenues, where a small beach meets the San Lorenzo River beside a lawn and picnic tables. In summer the river here is the town's swimming hole. Bring the coffee you bought downtown and call it recovery.

Either way, lunch is easy: River Dogs, the outdoor stand at 123 Forest Street behind Joe's Bar, serves Chicago-style Vienna Beef dogs with a fire pit for cool days and an acoustic stage when there's music. Its posted schedule runs weekend hours from 11:30 to 5, and it closes for bad weather, which is fair for a place with no roof.

Sunday afternoon: history, then a glass

The San Lorenzo Valley Museum's Grace Episcopal Gallery at 12547 Highway 9 opens Wednesday through Sunday from 1 to 4, admission free, donations welcome. The museum is marking 50 years in 2026, and the current Retrospect exhibit looks back across all of them. An hour here reframes everything you drove past this weekend, from the logging years to the fire.

Then, if you reserved, finish at Big Basin Vineyards' estate tasting room at 830 Memory Lane, pouring until 5 on Sundays. It's a short drive up a narrow lane from town, so sort out a designated driver before the first pour, not after. If wine's not your thing, a last unhurried lap of downtown with an early dinner does the same job of ending the weekend in town rather than in traffic.

If your weekend stretches to Monday

Monday is Boulder Creek's quiet day. Several restaurants, Scopazzi's among them, close Monday and Tuesday, and the museum galleries stay dark until Wednesday. The markets carry the day: Johnnie's and Wild Roots are open daily. Check the food guide before assuming anything else is open.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need reservations for this weekend?

Two are worth making ahead: Big Basin day-use parking, since the reservation form doesn't take same-day bookings and walk-up spaces are first come, first served, and the Big Basin Vineyards tasting room if you want Sunday wine. Lodging at Redwood Resort books online, and summer weekends are its season, so don't sleep on that one either.

Can I camp inside Big Basin instead of staying in town?

No. All campgrounds in the main park are closed while recovery work continues, per State Parks. The campground at Redwood Resort in town is the closest way to sleep under the redwoods and still walk to dinner, which is not a bad consolation.

Is this itinerary doable without hiking?

Yes. Swap Castle Rock for the river morning, keep the Redwood Loop at Big Basin, which is a flat 0.6-mile walk rather than a hike, and the rest of the weekend is markets, shops, museum, meals, and wine.

What about winter?

This plan is built for spring through fall. In winter the river runs high, River Dogs closes in bad weather, park trails close after storms, and Highway 9 itself sometimes has opinions. The bones still work on a clear winter weekend, but check the park pages and call ahead everywhere.

Why aren't there any lodging recommendations beyond the campground?

Because we only name what we can verify, and town lodging is limited: the directory lists the campground and a group retreat center, period. Short-term rentals exist on the usual platforms, but we don't list private rentals or pretend to have vetted them. When that changes, this page will change.

That's a full weekend without leaving the San Lorenzo Valley. Lock in your Big Basin parking and a campsite first, then use our verified directory to fill in shops and services and the events calendar to catch anything happening while you're in town. For utilities, road conditions, and county contacts, our Residents guide keeps the practical stuff in one place.

boulder-creek-winter-storm-checklist.title: Winter Storm Checklist for Boulder Creek Homes
boulder-creek-winter-storm-checklist.html:
The short version

  • Sign up for CruzAware and PG&E outage alerts before the season starts.
  • Clean gutters, downspouts, ditches, and culverts, and check them again after the first storm.
  • On a clear day, flag dead limbs and leaning trees, and book tree work early.
  • Stock a week of supplies: the ready.gov kit plus mountain extras, especially stored water if you're on a well.
  • Run any generator outside only, more than 20 feet from windows and doors, with a CO detector inside.
  • Save road dispatch, (831) 477-3999, and bookmark the closure dashboard and Mountain Status before you need them.
  • In any emergency, call 911 first.

Printable version: the winter storm and outage checklist is the print version, readable by flashlight when the power has been out since dinner. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

The first big atmospheric river of the season tends to find whatever you didn't get to: the clogged culvert, the dead limb over the driveway, the flashlight with dead batteries. Getting a Boulder Creek home ready is really five jobs, and you can knock them out in one good October afternoon. Below, each one is in the order that tends to matter most, with a link to the official source so you can go deeper where your property needs it. And one rule stands over the whole page: in any emergency, call 911 first.

Every item on this list has bitten my own household at least once: the propane refilled after the gauge dropped low instead of before, the firewood bought during the first cold week at everyone-else-wants-it prices. What newcomers get wrong about winter here isn't toughness, it's planning. A multi-day outage, up to a week in a bad year, is normal and survivable, and with a plan it's closer to an adventure than an emergency.

Why Storms Hit Harder Up Here

The big winter storms that soak the Santa Cruz Mountains are usually atmospheric rivers, long corridors of moisture that NOAA describes as rivers in the sky. Most are harmless rain-makers, but the strong ones can stall over a watershed and, in NOAA's words, create extreme rainfall and floods, disrupt travel, and set off mudslides. Our steep canyons, tall trees, and one main highway mean the same storm that's a gray Tuesday in Santa Cruz can be downed lines, a closed road, and a three-day outage in Boulder Creek.

That's not a reason to dread winter. It's a reason to spend one afternoon getting ahead of it.

First: Set Up Your Alerts

Everything else on this list works better when you hear about weather early.

Sign up for CruzAware, Santa Cruz County's alert and warning system, at cruzaware.org. It's how the county sends evacuation notices, severe weather warnings, and other public safety alerts by text, call, and email. Register more than one contact method, since no alert system can promise delivery every time.

Bookmark the National Weather Service Bay Area office, which writes the forecasts and warnings for our mountains. When a storm is coming, their watches and warnings are the source of truth, not a weather app's blue icon.

Then set up outage alerts with PG&E. Account holders get them automatically for their service address, and anyone can sign up for updates on any address through the outage map. Our full walkthrough of outage prep, including generators, food safety, and the Medical Baseline program, is in the power outage plan.

Clear the Water's Path

Most storm damage to homes in these mountains starts with water going where it shouldn't. Before the first big rain, walk your property in work gloves and look at where water flows and pools.

Clean the gutters and downspouts, and make sure downspouts carry water away from the foundation instead of dumping it against the house. Clear leaves and redwood duff out of any ditches, culverts, and drains on your property, and check them again mid-season, because one storm can refill them. If your driveway has a culvert, look through it; a plugged culvert is how driveways wash out. The county's storm preparedness page has a downloadable checklist and property-specific guidance worth reading before the season.

If water on your parcel is a recurring problem, the Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz County works with rural homeowners on erosion and drainage, and you can request services through their site.

For flood-prone spots, sandbags help more than people expect. In Boulder Creek, the fire district keeps two self-serve sand bunkers through the winter season, with sand and bags at both:

  • Boulder Creek Golf Course, Highway 236 and E Hilton
  • Redwood Elementary School, 16900 Highway 9, north of town

Bring your own shovel. Locations can change season to season, so call Boulder Creek Fire at (831) 338-7222 before you drive out. The county also posts a countywide list on its storm preparedness page, with a limit of 15 bags and no contractors. A county tip worth repeating: only fill bags halfway, because half-full bags stacked up hold water back better than bags filled to the top. Our sandbags and road closures guide has the wider valley list.

Look Up at Your Trees

Do this on a clear day, not when the wind's already blowing. Walk around the house and look for dead limbs over the roof, driveway, and parking spots, and for trees that lean harder than they used to. You don't need to be an arborist to spot an obviously dead top or a big broken limb hanging in the canopy, and it's worth having a professional look at anything that worries you before the ground gets saturated. Winter tree work gets booked out fast once the first storm hits.

Two hard rules:

  • Tangled in power lines: don't touch it, don't cut near it, and call 911, then PG&E.
  • Down across a county road: that's road dispatch at (831) 477-3999, any hour; our emergency contacts list has every number on one page.

Storm-season tree work overlaps with fire-season work. CAL FIRE's defensible space guidance calls for removing dead and dying vegetation, keeping the first five feet around the house clear of combustible material, and maintaining 100 feet of defensible space, which state law requires. Limbs you remove in October are limbs that can't land on your roof in January or carry fire in August.

Stock Supplies for a Week of Weird

Boulder Creek's version of storm supplies assumes the power might be out and the road might be closed for a few days. Ready.gov's kit guidance is the baseline: one gallon of water per person per day for several days, several days of food that doesn't need cooking, a flashlight, a battery-powered or hand-crank radio, phone chargers with a backup battery, and your prescription medications, plus basics like pain relievers.

Then add the mountain extras: extra water if you're on a well, since no power means no pump, a full tank of gas or charge in at least one vehicle, cash in small bills, pet food, and anything a baby or an elder in your house can't go without. If you heat with propane, check the tank gauge going into winter rather than during the first cold snap; our utilities guide covers who to call about propane, water, and everything else.

The Generator Rule That Saves Lives

If your storm plan includes a generator, this is the part of the checklist you memorize. Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. The CDC says to operate generators only outdoors, more than 20 feet from windows, doors, and vents. Carbon monoxide is odorless and colorless, it kills more than 400 Americans a year, and sleeping people can die without ever waking up. Put a battery-powered carbon monoxide detector near every sleeping area and test it when you test your smoke alarms.

Never plug a generator into a wall outlet or your panel without a transfer switch installed by an electrician; backfed power can hurt the line crews working to get your neighborhood back on. The full setup details are in the power outage plan.

Know Your Roads Before the Storm

The middle of a storm is a bad time to learn where road information lives. Save these now.

For county-maintained roads, the county's Road Closure Dashboard shows current closures, and road dispatch at (831) 477-3999 answers around the clock. For Highway 9 and Highway 236, which are state routes, check Caltrans road conditions or call 1-800-427-7623. Our Mountain Status page pulls the official links together in one place.

And one rule from the National Weather Service that's absolute: never drive into water on a road. Six inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult down, twelve inches can float most cars, and the road under that water may not be there anymore. Turn around. No shortcut in the valley is worth it.

The One-Afternoon Version

Here's the whole checklist, compressed. Sign up for CruzAware and PG&E alerts. Clean gutters, downspouts, ditches, and culverts. Walk the property and flag dead limbs and leaning trees, and book tree work early if you need it. Build the ready.gov kit plus mountain extras, especially stored water if you're on a well. Confirm the generator lives outside, 20 feet from openings, with a CO detector inside. Save the road dispatch number and bookmark the closure dashboard, Caltrans, and Mountain Status. Then check the drainage again after the first storm, because the first storm always finds something.

None of this guarantees an easy winter, and nobody can promise you one. But a prepared house turns most storms into stories instead of emergencies.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should I start storm prep in Boulder Creek?

Aim to finish by mid-October. The big atmospheric river storms typically arrive between late fall and early spring, and tree crews, roofers, and gutter cleaners book up once the first system is in the forecast. The NWS Bay Area office is the place to watch for what's coming.

Where do I get sandbags near Boulder Creek?

Boulder Creek Fire keeps two self-serve sand bunkers through the winter season: the Boulder Creek Golf Course at Highway 236 and E Hilton, and Redwood Elementary School at 16900 Highway 9. Sand and bags are at both; bring your own shovel. Call (831) 338-7222 to confirm before you drive out, since locations can change. Santa Cruz County also posts a countywide list on its storm preparedness page, with a limit of 15 bags and no contractors.

Who do I call when a tree falls across the road?

If power lines are involved or anyone's in danger, call 911. Otherwise, for county-maintained roads, call road dispatch at (831) 477-3999, answered 24 hours a day. If it's on Highway 9 or 236, that's Caltrans territory, 1-800-427-7623. On a private road, clearing it is generally up to the road association or the neighbors.

How much water should we store?

Start with ready.gov's rule of one gallon per person per day for several days, then add more if you're on a well, since your pump stops when the power does. Separate jugs for flushing toilets stretch your drinking water further. A multi-day outage after a storm is common enough here that erring on the high side is cheap insurance.

Is it ever safe to drive through a flooded stretch of Highway 9?

No. The National Weather Service is blunt: it's never safe to drive into floodwater, twelve inches can carry away most cars, and the pavement underneath may have collapsed. Turn around, check the Road Closure Dashboard or Mountain Status, and wait it out.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This checklist links to official sources from the National Weather Service, Santa Cruz County, CAL FIRE, the CDC, and Ready.gov. Conditions on your parcel and during an active storm come from the responsible agencies and the official sources linked above.

Storm prep is one afternoon in a year of mountain-home upkeep. For the deeper outage-and-generator walkthrough, see the Boulder Creek power outage plan, and keep the Residents guide handy for utilities, permits, and county contacts in one place. For how wet the season has been so far, see the rain tracker.

buying-local-boulder-creek.title: Why Buying Local Hits Different in a Mountain Town
buying-local-boulder-creek.html:
There used to be a feed store in town. Boulder Creek Feed and Pet Supply was the one stop: chicken feed, dog food, crickets for the reptiles, treatments for the pond, a true, extensive store, all in one trip on Highway 9. It closed the way businesses close here, quietly, and nothing replaced it. Now the same errand is split across multiple stops: some from Scarborough Home & Garden, some from Mountain Feed down in Ben Lomond, the rest from a pet store in Santa Cruz, a full trip down the valley for what used to be ten minutes in town.

That's the whole argument for buying local in Boulder Creek, and it fits in one sentence: we have one main street, and every storefront on it is load-bearing. No lecture coming, and nobody's asking you to cancel your Prime account. But I've lived here my whole life, and I've learned the difference between a town that spends at home and one that pieces its errands together from three other towns.

A town this size doesn't have spare storefronts

In a city, when a shop closes, three more like it are a short drive away. Boulder Creek doesn't work that way. Here, one business often is the category. One pharmacy. One lumber yard. A couple of markets. When a storefront goes dark on Highway 9, the thing it sold doesn't get slightly less convenient. It usually leaves town entirely, and the replacement is a drive down the valley.

That drive is the real price of a closure. It's not only your time, though winter road conditions and summer weekend traffic stretch the round trip past what the map promises.

It's that every errand leaving the valley makes the next closure a little more likely, because the businesses that remain are splitting a smaller pie. Small towns lose services in a slow spiral, not all at once. The spiral stays quiet until suddenly it isn't.

The flip side is just as real. Every business that holds on keeps the town more complete: more reasons to walk downtown, more jobs that don't require a commute over the hill, more lit windows on a rainy January evening. To see what's here right now, the directory is the current, verified inventory, and our guide to eating in town covers the food side in detail.

The fire made the stakes plain

Boulder Creek doesn't need a hypothetical to understand fragility. In August 2020, the CZU fire put this town under evacuation orders, my family included. I ended up in a one bedroom studio in Moss Landing for a month with the dogs, the cats, a parrot, and our chickens and ducks living out back. My partner stayed behind. He took vacation time from his career fire job to work as a Boulder Creek volunteer firefighter, one of the crew that stayed to protect the town. According to Cal OES, the fire leveled 1,490 structures across Santa Cruz and San Mateo counties. Boulder Creek itself held.

Here's what I remember about coming home. After a day spent emptying a fridge that had sat rancid for a month, I drove into town and filled a cart at Wild Roots, and that night I cooked a real meal for the first time since August. It sounds like nothing. It was everything. That's the part of local buying that never shows up in an economics chart. The market that knows its regulars. The hardware store with generator parts in October. You can't spin those up on demand. You keep them by using them in the ordinary years.

What the numbers support, and what they don't

You've probably seen big claims about local spending, like "a dollar spent locally circulates three times longer." We're not going to hang the argument on those numbers, because the most-quoted versions come from studies commissioned by local-business advocacy groups, and the figures vary a lot depending on who ran the study and how. If we can't verify a number to a source we trust, we don't print it.

Here's what does hold up. The SBA Office of Advocacy counts 36.2 million small businesses in the United States, which is 99.9 percent of all businesses. They employ 62.3 million people, 45.9 percent of the private-sector workforce, and their activity makes up 43.5 percent of GDP. Small business isn't a niche. It's roughly half the working economy, and in a town like this one, it's nearly all of it.

The circulation argument works fine without an exact multiplier. When you buy from a Boulder Creek business, the money you spend has a decent chance of paying a local wage, covering rent on a local building, hiring a local tradesperson, or backing the kind of small community sponsorship that never makes headlines. Spend that same money with a distant retailer and essentially none of it comes back up Highway 9. You don't need a precise ratio to see which direction helps the town you live in.

What local-first looks like in practice

The habit that matters most: make town your first stop, not your fallback. Before defaulting to a drive or a browser tab, take thirty seconds to check whether someone in Boulder Creek sells the thing or does the thing. The directory exists for that question, and every listing in it has been verified against a first-party source.

Some of it is easy, because the local options are good. The town has two full grocery stores: Johnnie's Super Market, which has been feeding Boulder Creek since 1938 and makes its deli sandwiches from family recipes, and Wild Roots Market, locally owned since 1991 and stocked heavily from local farms. Between them, most weekly shopping never needs to leave town.

In our house the habit looks like a fresh fruit run to Wild Roots once a week, sometimes twice. The baby's vote is blackberries, loudly.

A few other low-effort shifts, take them or leave them:

  • Eat in town once more per month than you do now. The current food guide lists everything verified open, from sit-down dinners to a hot dog stand with a fire pit.
  • Think local for gifts. Downtown's shops and studios cover more ground than people expect, and a gift bought in town is two gifts, one for the recipient and one for the street.
  • Hire local for services when the option exists. Trades, repairs, lessons, care. Service dollars are some of the stickiest local dollars there are.
  • Tell people. A recommendation to a neighbor costs nothing and is worth more to a small business than most advertising.

The no-guilt clause

Everyone in this town buys things online, and everyone drives over the hill sometimes for selection or price. That's fine. A local-first habit isn't a purity test, and a household budget is a real constraint that no one gets to lecture you about.

The goal is only this: when the local option exists and roughly works, give it the first look. If the town's businesses get the first look from the people who live here, most of them will still be here the next time the road closes, the power drops, or the smoke rolls in. That's the whole trade, and it's a good one.

cruzaware-setup-guide.title: How to Set Up CruzAware Alerts (and What They Cover)
cruzaware-setup-guide.html:
The short version

  • Sign up at cruzaware.org. The county publishes no fee for registration, standard carrier rates apply, and it takes about ten minutes. It's how the county sends evacuation notices and other urgent alerts by text, phone call, email, and a mobile app.
  • Have an email address, your phone number, and your street address ready. The address is what ties you to the alerts for your specific area.
  • Weather alerts are a separate opt-in. Registering doesn't turn them on; you switch them on in your account's Notifications area afterward.
  • Register more than one contact method. No alert system can guarantee delivery.
  • CruzAware is for receiving information. In an actual emergency, call 911.

Up here, a fire or a flood can move faster than word of mouth, and the phone tree that used to warn a canyon town doesn't outrun either one. So if you do one preparedness task this month, make it this: sign up for CruzAware, Santa Cruz County's alert system, at cruzaware.org.

It's how the county sends evacuation notices and other urgent alerts by text, phone call, email, and a mobile app, and it's about the single highest-value ten minutes of preparedness on offer for a Boulder Creek address. One thing to be clear about first: CruzAware is for receiving information. In an actual emergency, call 911.

What CruzAware Is

CruzAware is the official emergency and non-emergency alert system for Santa Cruz County, operated by the County of Santa Cruz together with Santa Cruz Regional 9-1-1, the agency that dispatches for communities across Santa Cruz and San Benito counties.

The county's alert information page describes what it carries: critical information during natural disasters, severe weather events, and public safety incidents, plus non-emergency notices like roadwork and community-level impacts. The county lists four ways those messages reach you: text message, phone call, email, and a mobile app.

The non-emergency messages are for residents of unincorporated areas of the county. Boulder Creek is unincorporated, so that part of the system applies here: road work, utility work, and other community-level impacts on our side of the county line.

The signup site lives at cruzaware.org, which takes you to a registration portal hosted by Genasys, the county's alert platform vendor. The portal describes itself as "the emergency and non-emergency alert and warning system for the residents of Santa Cruz County." It's available in English, Spanish, and Portuguese, and per the county's CruzAware FAQ, your information is used only for alerts and isn't sold or shared outside the system.

Anyone with a stake in the county can register: people who live here, work here, own property here, or just want to keep an eye on conditions for family who do.

What the Alerts Cover

The county's FAQ lists the range: earthquakes, floods, gas leaks, power outages, fires, and other situations that affect safety. Alerts can be geo-targeted, meaning they go to people who registered an address in the affected area.

That's the detail that matters most for San Lorenzo Valley residents. An evacuation warning for a specific slice of Boulder Creek reaches the accounts that put an address in that slice, which is why the address step below isn't optional busywork.

Topic-based alerts, including weather, are a separate opt-in. Registering does not turn them on. You select them in your account's Notifications area after you sign up, and step 4 below walks through it.

There's a limit worth knowing, straight from the county's own FAQ: no system can guarantee delivery. Phones get turned off, texts fail, emails land in spam. The county's advice is to register more than one contact method, and it's good advice.

How to Sign Up, Step by Step

Here's what the registration form asks for. You'll need an email address, your phone number, and your street address.

  1. Go to cruzaware.org. You'll land on the registration portal. Under the Login box, find "Don't have an account?" and select "Click here to register."
  2. Enter your email address. The form marks this required, and it's used for alerts and account recovery.
  3. Enter your cell phone number and leave the "Receive text messages on this phone" box checked if the phone can get texts. The form lets you register with phone, email, or both, and recommends both so alerts reach you in more situations. If your phone can't receive texts, an email is required.
  4. Enter your full street address and pick the match from the dropdown list as you type. This is required, and it's what ties you to location-specific alerts. The form's own tip: if your address doesn't appear, add your zip code, or click your location on the little map. Rural addresses in the valley sometimes need that nudge.
  5. Create a password, confirm it, and select Register. The password must be at least 12 characters and include at least one number, one capital letter, and one lowercase letter, with no spaces. Special characters are not required. The form runs a reCAPTCHA check as part of submission.

That's the core signup. If anything on the form looks different when you get there, follow what the portal says; the form is the source of truth and it does get updated.

After You Register: Five Minutes of Fine-Tuning

Once you're in, the account menu lets you strengthen your setup. The county FAQ walks through each item.

  1. Add more locations. You can register multiple addresses: home, work, a kid's school, an aging parent's place in the valley. Each one extends your geo-targeted coverage.
  2. Add more contact methods. Additional emails and phone numbers, including a landline or a family member's cell, can all receive your alerts.
  3. Save the senders in your phone. The portal lists exactly how alerts arrive: phone calls from +1 (831) 453-0048, texts from short code 65513, and email from CruzAware. The portal gives the email sender as noreply@genasys.com and the county FAQ gives it as cruzaware@genasys.com, so safelist both addresses, or safelist the genasys.com domain. Create a contact called "Santa Cruz County Alerts" with that phone number so a 2 a.m. call gets answered instead of ignored.
  4. Turn on weather alerts. This is a separate opt-in. Registering does not give you CruzAware weather alerts. The portal's own warning: to receive weather alerts you must select the weather categories in the Notifications area of your account and have an address on file. Do both. In a canyon that floods, this is the step to not skip.
  5. Check the prescribed-burn box. In the same Notifications area, the county directs residents to check "Prescribed burn" to get prescribed-fire notices from the County, CAL FIRE, and State Parks. Useful here, where smoke in the air is a question worth answering fast.

If you have questions the portal doesn't answer, the county's contact for the system is CruzAware@santacruzcountyca.gov, listed right on the portal.

If It Says You're Already Registered

Common situation: you try to sign up and get a pop-up saying your email or number is already registered. That's usually not an error. When the county moved from its old CodeRED system to CruzAware, existing contact information was transferred over.

The portal's instruction is to go back to the login screen, choose "Forgot your Password?", and enter your email or cell number to reset access. Once you're in, check that your addresses and contact methods are current, because a migrated account may be carrying old information.

How CruzAware Differs from NWS and PG&E Alerts

These three systems overlap less than people assume, and the safest setup is all three.

CruzAware is county-operated and opt-in. It's the channel for local emergency instructions, including evacuation warnings and orders, and it only knows the contact methods and addresses you give it.

National Weather Service products come from the federal forecast office for the San Francisco Bay Area (based in Monterey), which covers Santa Cruz County. The NWS issues the underlying weather watches and warnings. The most severe ones can also reach your phone automatically through Wireless Emergency Alerts, the federal push system that needs no signup, which the county lists as a separate channel alongside NOAA Weather Radio and the Emergency Alert System. NWS tells you a dangerous storm is coming; CruzAware is where local agencies tell you what to do about it here.

PG&E notifications are separate again. PG&E offers outage updates by text, email, or phone when you sign up through your PG&E online account, and those alerts are about electric service tied to your account. They won't carry evacuation information, and CruzAware won't give you outage restoration estimates. PG&E's own rule for a downed line applies no matter what alerts you have: call 911 first, then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000. For the rest of your outage prep, see our Boulder Creek power outage plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does CruzAware cost anything?

The county publishes no fee for registration, and standard text and call rates from your carrier apply. Registration asks only for contact details, an address, and a password.

Do I need to give my address?

The live form requires an address at signup, and it's central to how the system works: geo-targeted alerts, including evacuation notices for your specific area, depend on it. An address alone isn't enough for weather alerts, though. Those also require selecting the weather categories in your account's Notifications area. You can add more addresses after registering.

Will I get alerts if I never sign up?

Some, maybe. The most severe warnings can arrive through Wireless Emergency Alerts, which are automatic. But WEA is a blunt instrument, and county alerts targeted to your neighborhood go only to registered CruzAware contacts. Don't count on being covered without signing up.

Is signing up a guarantee I'll be warned in time?

No, and the county says as much. Delivery can fail if your phone is off, your contact info is stale, or a message lands in spam. Register multiple contact methods, keep them current, and treat alerts as one layer alongside your own awareness of conditions.

How do I update my info or unsubscribe?

Log in at cruzaware.org and use the account menu to edit contacts, addresses, and notification settings. There's an Unsubscribe option that the county FAQ says deletes your contact data from the system.

Last reviewed July 3, 2026. Details here follow official sources from Santa Cruz County, the county's CruzAware FAQ, and the Genasys registration portal. Program details and requirements come from the responsible county agencies, not from a general article like this one.

Signing up takes about ten minutes and it's the foundation the rest of your preparedness sits on. When it's done, put the other emergency contacts and utility details in one place with the Boulder Creek Residents guide.

culverts-drainage-boulder-creek.title: How to Prepare Your Culverts and Drainage Before Winter
culverts-drainage-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Before the first storms, clear every culvert inlet and outlet of the summer's needles, leaves, branches, and silt. A blocked outlet is as bad as a blocked inlet.
  • Clean the roadside and yard ditches that feed the culverts, or the water never reaches the pipe.
  • Point gutters and downspouts away from the foundation, and watch for soil eroding around a culvert or a sagging road edge.
  • Do it on a dry day, wear gloves, and never work in flowing storm water.
  • Culverts on your own property and driveway are yours. County-maintained roads are the county's; report a blocked one to Santa Cruz County Public Works at (831) 477-3999. Private shared roads usually fall to the owners.

The first real storm finds every culvert you forgot about. One clogs, the water backs up, and by morning your driveway is running like a creek or a piece of your road has slid downhill. The culprit is almost always the same: a blocked culvert or overwhelmed drainage. Culverts are the pipes that carry water under driveways and roads, and in a redwood canyon they clog fast with needles, leaves, and silt over a dry summer.

Clearing them before the rains is some of the highest-value storm prep you can do, and it's mostly a shovel-and-gloves job. Here's how to think about it, and who's responsible for what.

Why culverts matter so much here

Mountain storms drop a lot of water fast, and that water has to go somewhere. When a culvert is blocked, the water backs up, jumps the road or driveway, and carves a new path, often straight through the dirt holding your road up.

A single plugged culvert can wash out a driveway, flood a garage, or cut off access. Keeping them clear is the difference between water passing under your road and water taking your road with it.

What to do before the rains

  • Find your culverts and drains. Walk your property and driveway and locate every culvert inlet and outlet, plus roadside ditches and any drains around the house. They're easy to forget until they fail.
  • Clear the inlets and outlets. Remove the summer's needles, leaves, branches, and built-up silt from both ends so water can flow through. A blocked outlet is as bad as a blocked inlet.
  • Clean the ditches that feed them. Roadside and yard ditches that carry water to the culvert need to be clear too, or the water never reaches the pipe.
  • Check the roof-to-ground path. Make sure gutters and downspouts carry water away from the house and toward a drain, not against the foundation.
  • Watch for undermining. If you see soil eroding around a culvert or the road edge sagging, that's a warning sign to address before a storm makes it worse.

Do this on a dry day, wear gloves, and never work in flowing storm water. If a culvert is collapsed or badly undermined, that's a job for a professional or, on a county road, for the county.

Who's responsible for what

This is where people get tripped up. In general, culverts and drainage on your own property and private driveway are yours to maintain. Culverts under county-maintained roads are the county's responsibility, and you can report a blocked or failing one to Santa Cruz County Public Works, whose 24-hour road dispatch is (831) 477-3999.

Many roads up here are private, though, shared by the neighbors on them, and on those the maintenance, including drainage, usually falls to the property owners. If you're not sure whether your road is county-maintained, the county can tell you.

During and after storms

If you can safely see that a culvert is starting to back up during a storm, clearing the debris at the inlet can prevent a washout, but only if you can do it without stepping into moving water or a flooded ditch.

After a big storm, check your culverts again; they often clog mid-storm and stay blocked. For the bigger post-storm walk-through, see what to do after a major storm.

Frequently asked questions

What is a culvert and why does it clog?

A culvert is a pipe that carries water under a driveway or road. In the redwoods they fill with needles, leaves, and silt over the dry season, and a blocked culvert backs water up and causes washouts and flooding.

When should I clear my culverts?

Before the first major storms, ideally in early fall, and again after big storms, since they often clog mid-storm. Do it on a dry day and never work in flowing water.

Who's responsible for the culvert on my road?

Culverts on your own property and private driveway are yours. County-maintained roads are the county's (report issues to Public Works at (831) 477-3999). Private shared roads are usually the owners' responsibility. Confirm with the county if unsure.

Last reviewed July 20, 2026. Details here follow official sources from Santa Cruz County Public Works.

Storm prep, not storm response. Report blocked culverts on county roads to Santa Cruz County Public Works at (831) 477-3999. For live conditions, see Mountain Status, and for the rest of the season's checklist, the Residents guide pulls utilities, permits, and county contacts into one place. For where the season stands so far, see our rain tracker. In an emergency, call 911.

day-with-kids-boulder-creek.title: A Day in Boulder Creek with Kids
day-with-kids-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Morning: free library programs (storytime Wednesdays at 11 a.m., playgroup Fridays at 11 a.m.), or summer Water Park Wednesdays at Junction Park.
  • Treat and lunch: downtown bakeries and quick counter spots, nearly all within a short walk of the river.
  • Afternoon: the river beach at Junction Park (no lifeguard, watch your kids) or play structures at Garrahan Park.
  • Hot or rainy day: the library, one of the rec center's indoor youth classes if the schedule lines up, or a drive down to Haven Play Lounge in Scotts Valley.
  • Cost: most of the best parts are free. Hours and schedules shift by season, so call ahead when a plan hinges on one stop.

By eleven on a Wednesday morning, the story room at the Boulder Creek library fills up with toddlers and the grownups who carried them in. That's the shape of a good day here: you can fill one with young kids without leaving the valley, and most of the best parts cost nothing.

This guide is field-tested from stroller level: ours is at the age where the library story room, the kitten window, and a river beach constitute a full and excellent day.

Start at the library or a playgroup in the morning, grab a treat and an easy lunch downtown, spend the afternoon at the river or a park, and keep an indoor backup in your pocket for hot afternoons or rainy days. Hours and program schedules shift by season, so treat each link as the source of truth and call ahead when a plan hinges on one stop.

Morning: library programs and free playgroups

The Boulder Creek Branch Library at 13390 West Park Avenue runs the free kids' programming you can plan a week around:

  • Toddler and Preschool Storytime: every Wednesday at 11 a.m., with stories and songs for little ones and their grownups.
  • Discovery Zone Playgroup: a drop-in free-play hour for young kids and a caregiver, Friday mornings at 11.
  • Make and Explore: a STEAM building program for the six-and-up crowd on Wednesday afternoons at 1:30, with a new project most weeks.

Branch hours are Monday through Thursday 10 to 6, Friday 11 to 5, and Saturday 10 to 5, and the events calendar is where seasonal one-off performances show up too.

In summer, the rec district adds Water Park Wednesdays at Junction Park, a free outdoor playgroup with water play, sand building, and river exploration, Wednesdays from noon to 3 p.m., June through August. It's run by the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District, and it's an easy way to fill a summer Wednesday for the under-eight set.

A treat break downtown

For something sweet mid-outing, three counters downtown will hand you a treat on the spot.

  • Jenna Sue's Cafe, 13090 Highway 9, keeps Dessert First Bakery's cupcakes, cookies, and pastries in its case, since the bakery works out of the kitchen there.
  • The Tree House Cafe, 13266 Highway 9, has pastries alongside the coffee, open from 6 a.m. on weekdays and 7 a.m. on weekends, closing at 2:30 p.m.
  • Red Pearl does fried bananas, almond cookies, and sticky red bean buns, all quick and worth the stop.

The town's other bakers, Wildstone and Butter Late Than Never, work by market stall and custom order rather than a walk-in counter, so they're a plan-ahead treat rather than a mid-afternoon one. Our bakery guide covers how to buy from each.

If you're downtown on a Thursday afternoon, the Boulder Creek Farmers Market at Junction Park (1:30 to 5:30 p.m.) is its own treat, with local vendors and music.

Lunch that works with a stroller

Downtown lunch is short, casual, and close to the river. Taqueria Los Gallos is a sit-down taqueria on the main drag, and El Rey Leon is a food truck parked downtown with outdoor seating. The Sawmill Restaurant and Alehouse has burgers, pub fare, and outdoor seating, though it's a short drive up Highway 9 rather than a downtown walk.

For grab-and-go, Johnnie's Super Market and Liquor makes fresh deli sandwiches daily, and Wild Roots Market has a deli and prepared foods you can carry to a picnic table. When it's open, River Dogs of Boulder Creek, the outdoor hot dog stand on Forest Street, is about as kid-friendly as lunch gets, with vegetarian options and occasional live music.

Full hours and phone numbers are on our food and drink page. Call ahead if you're set on a particular spot, since small kitchens keep limited days.

Afternoon: river and parks

The classic Boulder Creek afternoon is the river. Junction Park, a block off the main street at Middleton and Railroad Avenues, has a small beach, San Lorenzo River access, a lawn, and picnic tables.

The river is a popular summer swim spot, and it is swim at your own risk. There's no lifeguard, the current and depth change with the season, and you keep your own eyes on your kids near moving water. Bring water shoes for the rocks.

If you want play structures and room to run, Garrahan Park at 15555 Highway 9 has a walking track, a soccer field, play structures, a gazebo, benches, and a barbecue area, open sunrise to sunset. It's the better pick for a picnic-and-playground afternoon or a birthday gathering.

Around town you'll also catch pop-up messy-play and water-play events run by Messy Play Kits, a Boulder Creek maker of handcrafted sensory and STEAM kits for ages 3 to 8 that partners with the rec district on park events like Water Park Wednesdays and the September Splashfest at Garrahan Park.

Indoor and rainy-day backup

Boulder Creek doesn't have a drop-in indoor play space of its own, so a hot or rainy afternoon comes down to three moves: the library, which is a legitimate indoor plan with books and programs; an indoor class at the rec center if the timing lines up; or a drive.

The rec center is the underrated one. The Recreation and Park District runs a rotating slate of indoor youth classes through the school year, movement and gymnastics for the youngest, ninja warrior and tumbling for the ones who need to burn it off, plus art and enrichment sessions, and the lineup changes each season. Registration opens ahead of each session and popular classes fill, so the move is to check the schedule before the rain starts rather than during it.

The nearest dedicated indoor option is Haven Play Lounge and Cafe at 108 Whispering Pines Drive, Suite 125, in Scotts Valley, an indoor play lounge and cafe with open-play sessions for ages 0 to 10. It's roughly a 25 to 35 minute drive down the valley, so it's a plan-ahead outing rather than a spur-of-the-moment stop, and its posted hours are limited: open Monday through Wednesday and Friday 9 to 5, Saturday 10 to 4, closed Thursday and Sunday. Check before you drive.

For the toddler-and-under crowd

The youngest kids have their own small scene here. Miss Brooke's Mini and Me Music Classes, led by Boulder Creek early-childhood educator Brooke Powell, are mommy-and-me music and movement sessions for infants, toddlers, and preschoolers, with reach-out and scheduling through her Instagram.

The rec district's Enchanted Little Forest Friends program serves ages 3 to 7 with a play-based outdoor morning, and the library's Friday Discovery Zone Playgroup is built exactly for this age.

Once a year the town also throws The Great Summer Playdate, a free playdate for kids up to age 5 that Miss Brooke's and Messy Play Kits co-host. The next one is Saturday, July 25 at 10:30 a.m., with the location shared through the signup.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there an indoor play place in Boulder Creek?

Not in town. The library is the best indoor option locally, especially on program days. The nearest dedicated indoor play lounge is Haven Play Lounge and Cafe in Scotts Valley, about a 25 to 35 minute drive, with open play for ages 0 to 10 and limited posted hours, so confirm before heading over.

Can kids swim in the river at Junction Park?

The river beach at Junction Park is a popular summer swim spot, but it's swim at your own risk. There's no lifeguard, water conditions change through the season, and young kids need close, constant supervision near moving water. Water shoes help on the rocks.

What free kids' programs run each week?

The library hosts Toddler and Preschool Storytime on Wednesdays at 11 a.m., Discovery Zone Playgroup on Fridays at 11 a.m., and Make and Explore STEAM on Wednesday afternoons. The rec district runs free Water Park Wednesdays at Junction Park, noon to 3 p.m., June through August. Check the library and BCRPD calendars for the current schedule.

Where can I take a toddler on a rainy day?

Start with the Boulder Creek library and its storytime and playgroup, check the rec district's current indoor class schedule, then keep Haven Play Lounge in Scotts Valley as a drive-worthy backup. Miss Brooke's Mini and Me music classes are another indoor option for the youngest kids; reach out through her Instagram for the current schedule.

Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, only a starting point. See the full directory and events calendar for hours and details, and if a program or listing has changed, tell us at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact so the next family gets it right.

does-it-snow-boulder-creek.title: Does It Snow in Boulder Creek? Mountain Weather Through the Year
does-it-snow-boulder-creek.html:
Once every few winters, someone spots a thin line of white on the redwoods, grabs a photo, and the whole valley is talking about it before the coffee's cold. That's about the measure of it: snow here is rare enough to be news.

Boulder Creek sits at about 500 feet, low enough that snow at town level is a once-in-a-few-years event that usually melts by lunch, though the higher ridges above the valley catch a dusting more often. What the town gets instead is a lot of rain in winter, dry warm summers, and a microclimate that runs warmer and sunnier than the foggy coast down the highway. Here's what the weather really asks of you through the year.

The one-line climate

Boulder Creek has what climatologists call a warm-summer Mediterranean climate: cool, wet winters and warm, dry summers, with almost all the year's precipitation falling between roughly November and April. Summers are close to rainless. Town-center temperatures run to an August high around 80 degrees and a December low in the high 30s, so hard freezes and heat waves both happen, but neither is the norm.

The thing to understand about weather up here is that elevation does most of the work. The town center sits near 500 feet, but the surrounding hills climb toward 2,700 feet on the ridges, and every thousand feet changes the rain, the temperature, and the odds of snow. Your road can be clear while a friend a few hundred feet higher is socked in.

Rain is the real story

Boulder Creek is one of the wetter spots in the greater Bay Area, and that's the number that matters here. Estimates of average annual rainfall vary a lot depending on the source and exactly where it's measured, generally landing somewhere in the 40-to-55-inch range for the town, well above the roughly 30 inches that falls on the Santa Cruz coast. The ridges above town collect even more. And the year-to-year swing is enormous: local records have run from under 20 inches in a dry year to over 100 inches in a wet one.

That rain is why winter, not snow, is the season that tests a mountain house. The big storms are usually atmospheric rivers, long plumes of moisture that can stall over the watershed and drop rain for days. What that leaves behind tends to be downed trees, saturated ground, and road closures rather than snowbanks. Our winter storm checklist walks through getting a Boulder Creek home ready for both.

So when does it snow?

Rarely, and mostly up high. Snow turns up on the higher ridges of the Santa Cruz Mountains most winters, usually as a dusting on the highest peaks rather than a real accumulation. It very rarely reaches as low as Boulder Creek at around 500 feet, and even more rarely sticks to the ground. So a dusting on the ridges or up toward the Highway 236 and Highway 9 high points a few times each winter is normal. Snow that reaches downtown and stays is the rare event people remember and photograph.

It does happen. In February 2023, a cold storm dropped snow across the Santa Cruz Mountains, including the Boulder Creek area, with up to about 8 inches piling up at the highest peaks. It followed the region's first winter storm watch in more than a decade, which tells you how unusual a real snow event is here.

Our place caught that kind of storm a few years back, and the snow stuck around for days. The best part wasn't the snow. It was the dogs, who had never seen it: a Doberman and a cane corso running, prancing, sliding, and jumping to catch snowflakes in their mouths, two very large dogs playing like little goofballs. Rare isn't the same as never, and when it lands, the whole valley turns into that.

Go back to February 2001 and there's a documented morning when heavy, wet snow fell on downtown Boulder Creek before dawn and built up until late morning, then melted off. Those are the events that punctuate the record. We won't put a frequency on town-level snow, because the answer is that it's rare and irregular, not something you can set a calendar by.

What it means for the roads

When snow and ice do show up, they mainly complicate the higher mountain highways, not downtown. In that February 2023 storm, both directions of Highway 17 over the summit shut down for a mix of downed trees, a jackknifed truck, and snow at the top. On Highways 9 and 236 the more common cold-weather hazard is ice on the shaded high stretches rather than accumulation, and in a cold enough storm Caltrans can post chain controls on the mountain routes.

Chains are a rare need here, but not an impossible one. If a cold system is in the forecast, check Caltrans road conditions or the Caltrans QuickMap before you drive, and carry chains if you're heading over a summit. Our Mountain Status page pulls the official road and weather sources together, and driving mountain roads covers the habits that keep you out of trouble in fog, rain, and the occasional ice.

Fog, heat, and the coastal difference

What newcomers notice is how different Boulder Creek feels from Santa Cruz, 15 miles away. The town sits inland of the coastal fog belt, so summer days here often burn off sunny and warm while the coast stays gray and cool under the marine layer.

That's the tradeoff people move here for: more sun in summer, at the cost of colder winter nights, since the valley can pool cold air and hold morning fog once the rains come. Under the redwoods it's shadier and cooler than open ground any time of year, its own kind of air conditioning in August.

The practical takeaways are simple:

  • Dress in layers you can shed as the day warms.
  • Expect cooler and wetter than the Santa Cruz forecast. Most apps pull from the coast or from San Jose over the hill, and neither one is your weather.
  • Watch the local forecaster. For what's coming, follow the National Weather Service Bay Area office, which writes the forecasts and warnings for these mountains, rather than a generic weather icon.

Frequently asked questions

Does it snow in Boulder Creek?

Very rarely at town level. At about 500 feet, Boulder Creek sees snow that reaches the ground only once in a few years, and it usually melts fast. The higher ridges above the valley catch a light snow a few times most winters. Real town-level snow, like February 2023, is uncommon enough to make the local news.

How much rain does Boulder Creek get?

A lot by Bay Area standards. Estimates vary by source and location, generally in the 40-to-55-inch range a year for the town, versus about 30 inches on the Santa Cruz coast, with even more on the ridges. Wet and dry years swing hugely, from under 20 inches to over 100.

Do I need snow chains for Highway 9?

Almost never, but occasionally yes. Snow and ice are rare down in town, but the shaded high stretches of Highways 9 and 236 can ice up in a cold storm, and Caltrans can post chain controls on the mountain routes. Check Caltrans before a cold-weather drive and carry chains if you're crossing a summit.

Why is Boulder Creek warmer than Santa Cruz in summer?

Because it sits inland of the coastal fog. The marine layer that keeps the coast gray and cool often burns off, or never reaches, up the valley, so summer afternoons here run warmer and sunnier. The flip side is colder winter nights and morning fog in the valley.

What months are the rainy season?

Roughly November through April, with the wettest stretch in the heart of winter around January. Summers are nearly rainless. If you're planning outdoor projects or a visit, the dry window runs late spring through early fall.

Getting a mountain home ready for winter? Start with the winter storm checklist and the power outage plan. For live conditions any day of the year, check Mountain Status. For the numbers behind those seasons, our rain tracker charts valley rainfall year by year back to 1937. Spot something here that needs updating? Send it to us.

downtown-boulder-creek-guide.title: Downtown Boulder Creek in an Afternoon
downtown-boulder-creek-guide.html:
I learned Junction Park the way most Boulder Creek kids do. My younger sister and I spent summer afternoons on the sandy beach hunting salamanders along the river bank and lizards under the rocks, while our older brother and his friends swam across to jump off the boulders into the deep, cold water. Decades later the arrangement hasn't changed: little kids on the sand, big kids on the rocks, cold water for everyone. If you only do one thing downtown on a warm day, put your feet in that river.

An afternoon is the right amount of time for the rest of downtown, and here's how I'd spend it: browse the shops along Central Avenue, catch the free San Lorenzo Valley Museum between 1 and 4, and eat before you head home. Here's what's open, laid out in the order an afternoon tends to take it.

One thing to know before you come up the hill. Boulder Creek is a working mountain town of homes, hardware, and groceries, not a resort built for visitors. That's a good part of why it's worth the trip, and it's also why hours shift with the seasons and staffing. If one particular stop matters to you, check its site or call before you drive.

Getting oriented

Downtown runs along Central Avenue, which is also State Route 9, so some addresses in this guide read "Highway 9" and others "Central Avenue." Same street. Everything sits between roughly 12550 and 13300, so once you've parked you can walk the whole strip. Plan to park once and stay on foot.

Visit Santa Cruz County describes the row as "boomtown architecture that gives you the feeling that you've stepped back in time," which is a fair account of the view from the sidewalk.

The shops

Air & Fire, A Mystical Bazaar at 13150 Highway 9 is the shop people remember after they've gone home: handcrafted soaps and candles, incense, crystals, tarot decks, books, and jewelry, with work from more than 50 local artists. It also keeps the most generous hours on the strip, Tuesday through Sunday 11 to 6:30 and Monday 11 to 4, with seasonal variation.

SWAG at 13026 Highway 9 calls itself "the eclectic collective," and the inventory backs that up: restored midcentury stereos, vinyl, vintage and local apparel, jewelry, art, consignment pieces, and the occasional music event. It doesn't post hours online, so treat it as a happy discovery rather than a scheduled stop, or check before you go.

Viscosity at 13158 Central Avenue is a working blown-glass studio with a gallery of locally made pieces, plus classes if you want to try the torch yourself. It doesn't post public hours, so contact the studio to schedule a visit if the glass is your main event.

lille aeske arthouse at 13160 Highway 9 is a small gallery, performance venue, and gathering space with a real 2026 calendar of shows and workshops. Its regular hours are short, Saturday and Sunday 11 to 3, but if your visit lines up with an evening performance, that's the most memorable way to spend time in town after dark.

Beck's Shoes at 12550 Highway 9, near the south end of the strip, is the outpost of a family shoe company that's been fitting feet since 1919. It runs a short week, currently Thursday through Sunday, so check the store page if you're coming early in the week.

Scarborough Home & Garden at 13110 Highway 9 is the Ace Hardware affiliate that keeps the town running, open daily. A hardware store might seem like an odd visitor stop, but it's the fastest way to read what kind of town this is, and it's where you'll find the forgotten flashlight, rain shell, or barbecue tool.

Two smaller stops round out a browse. Ginia's Gems sells memory-wire jewelry with semiprecious stones alongside herbal remedies and local honey; its web presence is thin, so check the site for current details. And Hennig Studios & Gallery at 211 Grove Street, a ceramics studio and gallery, opens to the public the first Sunday of every month from noon to 5, by appointment otherwise. If your afternoon happens to fall on a first Sunday, take it.

The museum hour

Time your walk so you pass 12547 Highway 9, at the south end of town, between 1 and 4 on a Wednesday through Sunday. The San Lorenzo Valley Museum keeps its main gallery in a 1906 former church listed on the National Register of Historic Places, admission is free, and 2026 is its 50th anniversary year, with a retrospective exhibit up through late 2026.

The museum is also the reason this site has a history section. I grew up here and knew almost none of our town's history until I started spending time in that little building. The town has lived through more lives than its size suggests, and the museum is the door into all of them.

It's the best hour of context you can get on everything else you'll see. Our full museum guide covers the exhibits, the archives, and the second gallery in Felton.

The river

Boulder Creek's park district keeps Junction Park at the intersection of Middleton and Railroad Avenues, a block east of the highway, with a beach, river access, grass, and picnic tables. The district's own page calls the river here "a favorite swimming hole" in summer, and on a hot July day you'll see why.

Use judgment, though: it's an unsupervised mountain river, conditions change, and there's no lifeguard. Dogs are welcome on leash. A couple hundred feet downstream, Barbara Day Park (locals say Dam Park) is getting improvements, and north of town Garrahan Park adds a walking track and play structures, sunrise to sunset.

The park sits on ground worth a second look while you're standing on it. This was Boulder Creek's railroad yard until 1934, which is why the streets around you are named Railroad, Junction, and Middleton.

Eating without a plan

You won't go hungry, and you don't need reservations anywhere downtown. The full picture is in our where to eat in Boulder Creek guide, but for an afternoon's purposes:

  • Johnnie's Super Market at 13225 Highway 9, the town grocery since 1938, makes deli sandwiches from family recipes and is open daily from 8 a.m.
  • Wild Roots Market at 13159 Central Avenue is the natural grocery, open daily 9 to 9, with a deli kitchen for prepared food. Either one outfits a picnic for Junction Park.
  • River Dogs does Chicago-style hot dogs from its stand on Forest Street, weather permitting, if you'd rather eat something cooked outdoors.

Sit-down options run from sushi to Italian; again, the eating guide has hours and the fine print.

If you have more time: Big Basin

The road to Big Basin Redwoods State Park leaves Highway 9 right downtown; turn onto Highway 236 and the entrance kiosk is nine miles up. A few things to know before you go:

  • Hours: the park is open 8 a.m. to sunset for day use only.
  • Camping: all campgrounds are currently closed.
  • Parking: spaces are limited, so State Parks recommends reserving a spot ($6 plus a $2 reservation fee, or $10 without a reservation, when space exists).
  • Dogs: leashed dogs are allowed in paved areas only, not on any trail or fire road.

The CZU Fire changed how the park looks, but most of the old-growth redwoods survived and the forest is visibly coming back. Check parks.ca.gov for current conditions before making the drive.

Closer to town, Big Basin Vineyards pours its mountain-grown wines at the estate on Memory Lane on Saturday and Sunday afternoons, noon to 5, with reservations through its site.

Visiting a small town well

A few habits make you the kind of visitor Boulder Creek is glad to see:

  • Buy something where you browse. These are single-location businesses, not chains.
  • Park without blocking anyone. Keep driveways and the highway shoulder clear.
  • Leave the river as you found it. Pack out what you bring, and keep dogs leashed in the parks.
  • Treat the hours here as snapshots from July 2026, not promises. The town's businesses are small enough that one sick employee changes the day. When in doubt, call.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which day is most of downtown open?

Saturday gives you the widest overlap: the museum (1 to 4), Air & Fire, Beck's, Scarborough, both markets, plus the weekend-only spots like lille aeske, Viscosity's posted gallery hours, and the Big Basin Vineyards tasting room. Monday and Tuesday are the quiet days, with the museum closed and several shops dark.

Do I need a reservation for Big Basin?

For day-use parking, State Parks recommends one because spaces are limited, and camping isn't an option at all right now since the campgrounds are closed. Check parks.ca.gov for current conditions and reservation links before you drive up Highway 236.

Can you swim in the river downtown?

Junction Park has river and beach access, and the park district itself calls it a favorite summer swimming hole. There's no lifeguard and conditions vary with the season, so treat it like the wild river it is, watch kids closely, and keep dogs on leash.

How much time should I plan?

Three to four hours covers a browse of the shops, the museum hour, and food, without rushing. Add a half day if you're continuing to Big Basin, and check the park's reservation situation first.

Is downtown walkable?

Yes. The businesses in this guide sit between roughly 12550 and 13300 on Highway 9, which is Central Avenue through downtown (the same road), so it's a park-once town. The compact center is the reason an afternoon works.

Planning the visit around a particular weekend? Check what's on the Boulder Creek events calendar before you drive up, and browse the full business directory for anything this afternoon didn't cover.

driving-mountain-roads.title: How to Drive Mountain Roads: Deer, Fog, Downed Lines, and the Turnout Habit
driving-mountain-roads.html:
The short version

  • Deer are the everyday hazard. They're most active at dawn and dusk. If one steps out, brake firmly, stay in your lane, and don't swerve. Where there's one deer, expect more.
  • Use the turnouts. When cars stack up behind you, pull into a turnout and let them by. California law requires it once five or more are lined up; good neighbors do it sooner.
  • Treat every downed line as live. If one lands on or near your car, stay inside, honk, call 911, and wait for a responder to tell you it's safe. Get out only if fire or another immediate danger forces you.
  • Slow way down for fog. Low beams, never high beams, and leave extra following distance.
  • Carry chains for cold-snap summit drives, and watch for ice on shaded curves and bridge decks long after the sunny stretches have thawed.

There's a bend on Highway 9 where the redwoods lean in and the light goes green, and if a deer steps out at dusk, that's the spot. Driving these roads well up here isn't luck; it's a short list of habits you can learn before you need them, which is the difference between a routine commute and a bad night. For the roads themselves, who maintains what, parking, cyclists, and the Big Basin run, see our roads and parking notes, and for storm-season prep, the winter storm checklist. Live conditions always come from the official sources gathered on our Mountain Status page, never from a static article, and anything dangerous happening right now is a 911 call.

Deer: The Everyday Hazard

Forget the dramatic stuff. The animal most likely to dent your week is a deer at 6 a.m. on Highway 9. Caltrans' deer safety guidance leads with timing: "deer are most active at dusk and dawn: periods when your vision is most compromised." Around here that's the commute, both directions. Build the expectation into those drives, especially the stretches where forest runs right to the pavement, which is most of them.

The technique matters more than the worry. Caltrans' advice, condensed:

  • Slow down when you see a deer, because it's unpredictable.
  • Expect company. Deer rarely travel alone, so one crossing means more are likely behind it. Wait a beat before rolling on.
  • If one steps out, "brake firmly and calmly, and stay in your lane." Swerving is how a deer strike becomes a tree strike or a head-on; Caltrans warns it can make you lose control and turn a bad situation much worse.

A long blast of the horn, they note, can scare deer off the road. Your headlights, your speed, and your willingness to just brake are the whole toolkit.

The Turnout Habit

If you drive these roads slower than the traffic behind you, and everyone does sometimes, towing, sightseeing, new to the curves, the turnouts are yours to use, and not just as a courtesy. California Vehicle Code 21656 requires a slow-moving vehicle on a two-lane road where passing is unsafe, with five or more vehicles lined up behind, to pull into the nearest designated turnout or any safe turnout area and let them by.

Five is when the law kicks in; good neighbors do it at two or three. Ten seconds in a turnout resets everyone's day, defuses the tailgater problem, and marks you as someone who gets it. Our roads and parking notes cover the turnout etiquette in more detail, along with the three-foot law for passing the cyclists you'll share every climb with.

Downed Lines: Stay in the Car

Storms drop trees, trees drop lines, and this is the piece of storm driving that isn't intuitive, so it gets its own section. PG&E's rule is absolute: always assume a fallen power line is live. Never touch one, never drive over one, and keep people and pets away.

If a line comes down on or near your car, the counterintuitive part begins: stay inside. The ground around the car may be energized, and stepping out can put your body between two voltages. PG&E's instructions:

  • Sound the horn, roll down your window, and call 911. After 911, PG&E's line is 1-800-743-5000.
  • Warn anyone approaching to stay back, then wait until a firefighter, police officer, or PG&E worker tells you it's safe to exit.
  • Leave only if fire or another immediate danger forces you out. If you have to, remove loose clothing, jump clear so you're never touching the car and the ground at the same time, land with your feet together, and shuffle away keeping both feet close together on the ground.

That's worth rehearsing mentally precisely because every instinct says get out. When a line is down on your car and nothing inside is forcing you out, staying put is the safer choice.

Fog: Low Beams and Humility

Fog rolls up the valley and pools in the canyon dips, sometimes in bands a few hundred yards long, so you can drive from clear to blind in seconds. The National Weather Service's fog guidance starts simple: slow down, allow extra time, and put your low beams on, which also lights your taillights for the driver behind you. High beams are the classic mistake; the NWS notes they cause glare that makes it harder to see ahead, not easier. Leave generous following distance, since the car ahead may stop for something you can't see yet.

If it gets bad enough that you can't safely continue, don't creep along blind. The NWS procedure: hazard lights on, pull into a safe spot or well off the road, and once stopped, turn off all lights except the hazard flashers, set the emergency brake, and take your foot off the brake pedal so your brake lights don't lure a following driver into your bumper. That last detail is the one nobody knows and the one that prevents the chain collision.

Chains, Traction, and the Occasional White Morning

Snow is a rare visitor at Boulder Creek's elevation, more common up on Skyline and the Highway 9 summit, but when Caltrans posts chain controls anywhere you're driving, they're law, not advice. The definitions from Caltrans' chain control page:

  • R-1 requires chains on all vehicles except passenger vehicles and light trucks under 6,000 pounds with snow tires on at least two drive wheels.
  • R-2 requires chains or traction devices on everything except four-wheel or all-wheel drives with snow-tread tires on all four wheels.

Even exempt vehicles must carry chains or traction devices in the control area, and the speed limit when chains are required is 25 or 30 mph.

Two practical notes. Install chains only where you can pull completely off the roadway to the right; Caltrans is explicit that stopping in a traffic lane endangers you and blocks everyone. And check conditions before a cold-snap drive over the hill via Caltrans road information or 1-800-427-7623. Ice is the sneakier local threat: shaded curves and bridge decks stay frozen long after sunny stretches thaw, so a clear blue morning after a cold night deserves gentle inputs in the shade.

Storms, Water, and the Shortcut Trap

The storm-driving fundamentals live in two companion pieces, so here they are by reference rather than repetition. Never drive into water across the road, period; the reasoning and the numbers are in the winter storm checklist, along with how to check closures before you leave.

That water rule is the one I'll personally vouch for. In a big storm you have no idea how deep a sheet of brown water across the road runs, or what the road still looks like underneath it. Drive in and the best case is getting stuck; the worse cases involve your floor pan, your engine, or the creek. Turn around, take the long way, arrive late.

And when Highway 9 does close, resist the map app's creative alternative. The side roads it offers are narrower and steeper than the highway, often single-lane, sometimes private or dead-end, and they shed the same trees and rocks with less room to escape and worse cell coverage when it goes wrong, as covered in our roads and parking notes. If the main road is closed in a storm, the move is usually coffee in town, not adventure routing. When conditions are changing, check Mountain Status for the live official sources before you commit to the drive.

No page can promise you a safe trip, and we won't. But these mountains reward drivers who are patient, lit, and predictable, and the habits above are what that looks like at the wheel.

Frequently Asked Questions

When am I legally required to pull over and let cars pass?

On a two-lane road where passing is unsafe, CVC 21656 requires you to use the nearest turnout or safe pull-off once five or more vehicles are lined up behind you. Local practice is to do it sooner. It takes seconds and it's the single most appreciated habit on Highway 9.

What do I do if a deer jumps out?

Brake firmly, stay in your lane, and don't swerve, per Caltrans; swerving trades a survivable impact for an unpredictable one. Then remember deer travel in groups, so proceed slowly. If people are hurt or the car is disabled in the roadway, call 911.

A power line is down across the road. Can I drive over it if it looks dead?

No. PG&E says to always assume a fallen line is live and never drive over one. Stop well back, call 911, then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000. If a line contacts your car, stay inside, honk, and wait for responders; exit only if fire or another immediate danger forces you out, jumping clear with feet together.

Do I really need chains in Boulder Creek?

Rarely in town, but carry them for cold-snap drives over Highway 9's summit or Skyline, because when chain controls are posted they apply to you, and even exempt 4WD vehicles must carry traction devices in the control area. Check Caltrans or 1-800-427-7623 before you go; icy shaded curves are the more common local reality.

What's the right way to drive fog on Highway 9?

Slow down, low beams on (never high beams), and leave extra following distance, per the National Weather Service. If visibility collapses, pull well off, hazards on, all other lights off, parking brake set, foot off the brake pedal. Fog pools in the canyon dips, so expect it to come and go along the same drive.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This article links to official sources from Caltrans, PG&E, the National Weather Service, and the California Vehicle Code. Live road and weather conditions come from those official sources, not from a static article.

Before your next drive over the hill, check the official conditions gathered on our Mountain Status page, and see the roads and parking notes for turnout etiquette, cyclists, and the Big Basin run. If the drive over the hill is the part you would rather not keep doing, the valley job board is worth a look first.

earthquakes-santa-cruz-mountains.title: Earthquakes in the Santa Cruz Mountains: A Boulder Creek Preparedness Guide
earthquakes-santa-cruz-mountains.html:
The short version

  • Secure the heavy stuff. Strap the water heater, anchor tall bookcases and dressers, and take down heavy mirrors and art hanging over beds and couches. A Saturday with straps and museum putty is the highest-value hour here.
