  • Store water and supplies. One gallon of water per person per day, and more up here, because roads and utilities can stay down for days. Add food, a hand-crank radio, a first-aid kit, medications, and sturdy shoes and gloves by each bed.
  • Learn Drop, Cover, and Hold On, and practice it once with the household so the motion is automatic.
  • Sign up for alerts. Install MyShake for a few seconds of warning before shaking, and register for CruzAware to get evacuation orders after a quake.
  • Older raised-foundation home? Check Earthquake Brace + Bolt eligibility, then have a licensed contractor or structural engineer look at your crawl space.

Ask anyone who was here for Loma Prieta and they'll tell you where they were standing. One of the most famous faults on Earth runs through these mountains, and the 1989 quake started about 15 miles east of here, across the ridge. No one, including the U.S. Geological Survey, can tell you when the next big one will hit, so the useful work isn't worrying about timing. It's the handful of things that make your household safer whenever it comes: secure the heavy stuff, store water and supplies, learn Drop, Cover, and Hold On, and sign up for alerts.

Most of it takes a weekend, and none of it requires you to become a seismologist. We live in earthquake country. That's not a reason to be scared. It's a reason to be ready, the same way we get ready for winter storms and fire season.

The most recent reminder came in April 2026, a quick jolt centered right here in the mountains. I was holding our sleeping baby when it hit, and it felt like a freight train running under the house: sudden, jolting, heart racing, and over before it really began. My partner ran in to check on us; the baby never even woke up. That's most earthquakes here, a few seconds that reset your respect. The preparation below is for the one that runs longer.

The San Andreas Fault Runs Through These Mountains

The San Andreas is not a distant California abstraction up here. The USGS describes the San Andreas Fault Zone as "the main part of the boundary between the Pacific tectonic plate on the west side and the North American plate on the east side." Those two plates grind past each other at a rate the USGS puts at "50 mm/yr (about 2 inches/yr)." That steady motion loads the fault with the strain that earthquakes eventually release.

The stretch nearest us has a name. The USGS calls it the Santa Cruz Mountains section, and says it "stretches 62 km (39 mi) from Los Gatos (near San Jose) to San Juan Bautista, CA and was last ruptured in the famous 1906 San Francisco earthquake." Boulder Creek sits in the mountains just west of that stretch of the fault.

Other mapped faults are closer to home than the well-known Bay Area names. The San Gregorio fault runs offshore, following the coast, and the Zayante-Vergeles fault zone crosses the Santa Cruz Mountains. The Hayward and Calaveras faults run through the wider Bay Area too, which is part of why this region is studied as closely as it is.

One point is worth holding onto: proximity to a fault tells you an earthquake is possible, not that one is imminent. Nobody can predict earthquakes. For the specific hazard at your parcel, the authority is the USGS, not a blog and not a neighbor's hunch. Their earthquake hazards program publishes the maps and forecasts that professionals rely on, and it's the right place to send any question that starts with "how likely is."

What the 1989 Loma Prieta Earthquake Tells Us

Loma Prieta is local history, not ancient history, and it's the clearest picture we have of what a major quake does to this terrain. According to the USGS, "On October 17, 1989, at 5:04 PM (PDT), a magnitude 6.9 earthquake" struck the region. The USGS places the epicenter "near Loma Prieta peak in the Santa Cruz Mountains, approximately 9 miles northeast of Santa Cruz and 60 miles southeast of San Francisco." That peak is in our mountains, roughly 15 miles east of Boulder Creek, across the ridge.

The toll was serious. The USGS records "63 deaths, 3757 injuries, and an estimated $6 billion in property damage," and calls it "the strongest earthquake to hit the San Francisco Bay region since the M 7.9 Great San Francisco earthquake of 1906." Longtime residents remember the collapsed section of the Bay Bridge and the Cypress Street Viaduct in Oakland, but the shaking was felt hardest right here in the mountains, where roads cracked, chimneys came down, and homes shifted on their foundations.

The damage patterns were predictable, and most of them are the kind you can plan around: things falling, water and power cut off, roads blocked, and older houses moving because they weren't bolted down. Every step below addresses one of those.

Secure Your Space and Store Supplies

The Earthquake Country Alliance, a public-private partnership that includes the USGS and California's emergency management agencies, organizes what to do before, during, and after a quake into Seven Steps to Earthquake Safety. The first is "Secure your space." Walk your house and picture it shaking hard for fifteen seconds. What falls?

A water heater that isn't strapped can topple, break a gas line, and cut off a big reservoir of drinkable water all at once. Tall bookcases and dressers can tip onto a bed or a doorway. Heavy mirrors and framed art over the couch become projectiles. Straps, flexible fasteners, and museum putty are cheap, and a Saturday spent anchoring the worst offenders is the highest-value hour in this whole guide.

The third step is to organize disaster supplies, and up here that starts with water. Ready.gov's standard is one gallon per person per day, and because mountain roads and utilities can stay down for days after a big quake, more is better. If you're on a well, the pump won't run without power, so stored water isn't optional.

Keep a few days of non-perishable food, a manual can opener, flashlights, a battery or hand-crank radio, spare batteries, a first-aid kit, any critical medications, and sturdy shoes and work gloves next to each bed for the walk across broken glass in the dark. Our power outage plan for mountain households covers the water, food, and backup-power side in more depth, and most of it applies directly here.

Retrofit and Bracing: Route This to a Pro

Loma Prieta was hard on older houses that weren't fastened to their foundations, and a lot of Boulder Creek's housing stock predates modern seismic standards. A well-established fix exists. The California Residential Mitigation Program, a joint effort of the California Earthquake Authority and state emergency management, runs the Earthquake Brace + Bolt (EBB) program. It describes the retrofit plainly: "the foundation is 'bolted' to the frame of the house, and when there are walls called 'cripple walls' in the crawl space under the house, they are 'braced' with plywood," which helps "prevent the house from sliding or toppling off of its foundation during an earthquake."

The program is limited to "wood-framed, pre-1980 homes with a raised foundation," and when funds are available it offers "up to $3,000 toward a code-compliant seismic retrofit." Households with a yearly income of $94,480 or less may qualify for up to $7,000 more on top of that, through the program's supplemental grant.

Two conditions the program's summary pages tend to bury:

  • Your ZIP Code has to be eligible. Good news for us: Boulder Creek's 95006 appears on CRMP's current eligible-ZIP list, which is posted with a December 2024 date, and Ben Lomond's 95005 is on it too.
  • Registration isn't open year-round. It opens for a limited period each year, and the program doesn't announce the next window far ahead. The reliable move is to get on the notification list at earthquakebracebolt.com or call CRMP at (877) 232-4300, rather than checking back and hoping to catch it.

Whether your specific house is a candidate, and how the work should be done, is a question for a licensed contractor or a structural engineer, not a DIY weekend and not this article. Check your eligibility with the program first, then get a professional's eyes on your crawl space. This is one of the few home projects that can change whether your house is livable after a major quake.

Learn Drop, Cover, and Hold On

When the ground moves, the goal is to avoid being knocked down and avoid being hit by what's falling. The Great ShakeOut, run by the same earthquake-safety partnership, gives the three steps:

  • Drop where you are, onto your hands and knees. As the ShakeOut puts it, this "protects you from being knocked down and reduces your chances of being hit by falling or flying objects."
  • Cover your head and neck with one arm and hand, crawling under a sturdy table if one is close or next to an interior wall if not.
  • Hold on until the shaking stops, gripping your shelter if you're under one and protecting your head and neck if you're not.

If you are in bed when it starts, stay there. Turn face down and cover your head and neck with a pillow.

Skip the old advice about doorways and running outside. Most injuries come from moving during the shaking. If you use a wheelchair, the guidance is to "LOCK your wheels (if applicable)," then cover your head and neck with your arms, a book, or a pillow, and hold on. Practice it once with the kids so the motion is automatic, because a real quake is not the moment to think it through.

After the Shaking Stops

The minutes after a quake are when a lot of the injuries happen. Work through these in order.

  • Expect aftershocks. They can come within seconds and can be strong enough to bring down what the first shock loosened. When one starts, Drop, Cover, and Hold On again.
  • Check for injuries. Yourself first, then the people with you. Put on the shoes and gloves you staged by the bed before you walk anywhere, because broken glass is the most common post-quake injury.
  • Gas and propane. If you smell gas or propane, get everyone out of the building, then call 911 from outside. Do not flip light switches, use a phone, or start a vehicle inside or next to the building. Most of the San Lorenzo Valley runs on propane rather than PG&E natural gas, so the standard "shut off the gas at the meter" advice does not fit many homes here. If you are on propane, the shutoff is the valve on the tank itself, not a meter at the house. Find that valve now, while nothing is wrong, and know which system your house is on. If you do shut off gas or propane, leave it off and have the utility or your propane supplier turn it back on. On PG&E natural gas, call 911 first and then PG&E at 1-800-743-5000.
  • Don't tie up 911. Do not call for information, to ask what happened, or to report a power outage. Keep the line open for people who are hurt or trapped. Report an outage to PG&E at 1-800-743-5002 instead.
  • Check on neighbors once you are safe, especially older residents and anyone living alone. On these roads, a neighbor is going to reach you before a crew does.
  • Watch for CruzAware messages. Evacuation orders after a quake can follow from landslides, damaged roads, or fire, and the county sends them through that system. If the county tells you to leave, leave.

Sign Up for Earthquake and Emergency Alerts

Two different systems are worth setting up, and they do different jobs.

The first is earthquake early warning. MyShake is a free app built by UC Berkeley's Seismology Lab in partnership with "USGS ShakeAlert and the California Governor's Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES)." It delivers ShakeAlert-powered notifications and is available in the Apple App Store and on Google Play. The point of ShakeAlert is to give you a few seconds of warning before strong shaking arrives, enough time to Drop, Cover, and Hold On.

Be clear about what it is and isn't. The USGS states plainly that ShakeAlert "is not earthquake prediction." It detects a quake that has already started and races the alert ahead of the shaking. Alerts can also arrive through your phone's Wireless Emergency Alerts and, on many Android phones, through the built-in Android Earthquake Alerts system.

The second is your county's emergency notifications. CruzAware is Santa Cruz County's alert and warning system, and it's how you'll hear about evacuations, road closures, and other emergencies that often follow a major quake. Register at CruzAware.org and choose how you want to be reached: text, phone, email, or app. While you're on the county's Plan and Prepare pages, learn your evacuation zone and grab the household safety checklist, since the same plan serves earthquakes, fires, and storms.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which faults are near Boulder Creek?

The San Andreas is the big one. The USGS identifies a "Santa Cruz Mountains section" running "62 km (39 mi) from Los Gatos (near San Jose) to San Juan Bautista," and Boulder Creek sits in the mountains just west of that stretch. The fault marks the boundary between the Pacific and North American plates. Other mapped faults nearby include the San Gregorio, offshore along the coast, and the Zayante-Vergeles fault zone. We are not going to quote you a distance from your driveway to a fault trace, because that depends on which mapped strand you measure to. For parcel-level answers, use the USGS Quaternary Fault and Fold Database and the California Geological Survey's EQ Zapp mapping tool, which show mapped faults and state-designated fault zones by address.

Was the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake near here?

Yes. The USGS places the magnitude 6.9 quake's epicenter "near Loma Prieta peak in the Santa Cruz Mountains, approximately 9 miles northeast of Santa Cruz," on October 17, 1989. It caused 63 deaths, thousands of injuries, and about $6 billion in damage, and the shaking hit the mountains hard.

Can anyone predict when the next big earthquake will happen?

No. The USGS is direct that its ShakeAlert system "is not earthquake prediction." No credible source can tell you the date of a future quake. Warning systems like ShakeAlert detect a quake that has already begun and send an alert seconds ahead of the shaking. That's why preparation, not prediction, is where your effort belongs.

What's the single most important thing to do first?

Two things, and both take minutes. Install MyShake and sign up for CruzAware so you get warnings and evacuation notices, then strap your water heater and anchor the tallest furniture in your house. After that, work on water storage and a family Drop, Cover, and Hold On practice.

Is my older Boulder Creek house safe in an earthquake?

That depends on your specific house, and it's a question for a professional. Many older homes on raised foundations can be strengthened by bolting the house to the foundation and bracing the cripple walls, work supported by the Earthquake Brace + Bolt program for qualifying pre-1980 homes. Eligibility is also tied to ZIP Code, and 95006 is on the program's current eligible list, dated December 2024. Registration opens only for a limited period each year, so join the notification list at earthquakebracebolt.com or call CRMP at (877) 232-4300. Then have a licensed contractor or structural engineer assess your crawl space.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This guide links to official sources from the U.S. Geological Survey, the Earthquake Country Alliance, the California Residential Mitigation Program, and Santa Cruz County. Parcel-level hazard and property-specific advice come from the USGS, the responsible county agency, and qualified professionals.

Preparedness is one line in a bigger rhythm up here. When the power goes out after a quake, our power outage plan for mountain households takes over, and the Residents guide pulls together utilities, emergency contacts, and county resources in one place. The single best next step: install MyShake and register for CruzAware before you close this page.

el-nino-winter-boulder-creek.title: El Niño Is Here: What a Strengthening 2026-27 Winter Could Mean for Boulder Creek
el-nino-winter-boulder-creek.html:
Ask anyone who's wintered up here and they'll tell you how it goes: the San Lorenzo comes up, a tree comes down across Highway 9, the power blinks out for a day or two, some years worse than others. So when word gets around that a strong El Niño is on the way this winter, it's worth knowing what that does and doesn't tell us. The word-of-mouth part checks out: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center has an El Niño Advisory in effect and gives it high odds of strengthening into a big event. What that means for Boulder Creek specifically is the murkier question. A strong El Niño tilts the odds toward a wetter winter across California, but the signal is strongest in Southern California and much shakier up here in the Santa Cruz Mountains. So the move isn't to panic, and it isn't to bank on a soaking. It's to get storm-ready now, because our winters bring floods, outages, and road trouble in plenty of years, El Niño or not.

The mountain's own barometer in our house isn't the forecast anyway, it's the first deep rain. After a long fire season there's a morning when the petrichor rolls up off the redwoods and the whole valley exhales. Whether this winter turns out soaked or ordinary, that morning is coming, and the prep below is what makes it feel like relief instead of a starting gun.

What NOAA is forecasting

Per the Climate Prediction Center's discussion issued July 9, 2026, El Niño conditions are present now, there's about a 97 percent chance they persist through early spring 2027, and there's roughly an 81 percent chance of a very strong El Niño during October through December, an event that would rank among the largest on record since 1950. El Niño is a natural warming of the tropical Pacific that shifts weather patterns worldwide; a strong one tends to nudge the winter storm track in ways that raise the odds of wet weather across the southern United States.

Two caveats worth holding onto. First, this is a forecast, and forecasts change; the CPC updates it monthly. Second, El Niño describes odds, not certainty, and it says more about the season as a whole than about any single storm or date.

What a strong El Niño could, and couldn't, mean here

This is the part that gets oversold. El Niño's clearest, most reliable effect in California is on Southern California, where strong events raise the chance of a wet winter. For the Bay Area and Santa Cruz Mountains, the connection is real but weaker and less consistent. Strong El Niño winters here have run the gamut from very wet to fairly ordinary. So no one, us included, can tell you this winter will be a big one for Boulder Creek.

What we can say is that a stronger, more active storm track raises the odds of the kinds of winters our terrain handles badly: saturated ground, swollen creeks and the San Lorenzo River, power outages, fallen trees and limbs across roads, and stretches where Highway 9 is the weak link in and out of the valley. Those risks show up in ordinary winters too. A strong El Niño just makes it a worse year to be caught unready.

What to do now, while it's dry and calm

Spread the work across the fall instead of scrambling when the first big system shows up. Start here:

  • Prepare for outages before you need to. Water, lights, a way to charge phones, and a plan for anyone who depends on power. See our power-outage preparation guide.
  • Get your winter-storm basics in order. Supplies, defensible drainage, an evacuation-ready mindset. See the winter storm checklist.
  • Know your roads. Understand how Highway 9 and mountain roads behave in storms, and where to check conditions.
  • Sign up for alerts now. Register for PG&E outage alerts and county emergency notifications before the season, not during a storm.

We'll be publishing more focused fall and winter guides, on getting your culverts and drainage ready, understanding atmospheric rivers, and where to find sandbags and closures, and linking them here as they go up.

How to watch it through the fall

Don't chase every headline. A few trustworthy sources beat a stack of scary ones:

  • NOAA Climate Prediction Center, the monthly ENSO update
  • National Weather Service, Bay Area, local forecasts, watches, and warnings
  • PG&E outages and safety, outage map and alert sign-up
  • Our Mountain Status page, which pulls the live local sources together

Frequently asked questions

Is a strong El Niño really coming this winter?

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center has an El Niño Advisory in effect, with about a 97 percent chance it lasts through early spring 2027 and roughly an 81 percent chance of a very strong event in October through December. It's a forecast, and it updates monthly.

Does that mean Boulder Creek will have a wet, stormy winter?

Not necessarily. El Niño's strongest California signal is in the south; for the Santa Cruz Mountains the connection is weaker and less consistent. It raises the odds of an active winter but doesn't guarantee one. Prepare either way.

What should I do to get ready?

Spread the prep across the fall: get ready for power outages, work through the winter storm checklist, understand mountain roads in storms, and sign up for PG&E and county alerts now.

Where should I watch for updates?

The NOAA Climate Prediction Center for the seasonal outlook and the National Weather Service for actual forecasts. For live local conditions, use Mountain Status. To watch how the season turns out against that forecast, our rain tracker follows valley rainfall through the water year.

This page reflects the NOAA forecast as of the reviewed date and is not a substitute for official forecasts and alerts. For live conditions, see Mountain Status. In an emergency, call 911. Last reviewed: 2026-07-20.

essential-shops-boulder-creek.title: The Essential Shops: What You Can Buy in Town
essential-shops-boulder-creek.html:
You can run a full Saturday of errands in Boulder Creek and get further than most towns this size let you. Hardware and lumber, two full grocery stores, an independent pharmacy that delivers across the valley for free, a full-service vet, and more gift and specialty shops than a drive-through suggests, nearly all inside about a mile of Highway 9.

What follows is a needs-based tour, sorted by the errand rather than the address. Hours shift with the seasons and with who's staffing up here, so check before you make a special trip. For everything in town beyond the essentials, the full directory is the master list.

Hardware, lumber, and the endless mountain-house fix

Two related stores split the work. Scarborough Home & Garden at 13110 Highway 9 takes the home-and-garden side: pet food, gardening supplies, canning gear, cleaning supplies, and the everyday household stuff. It's open seven days, Monday through Saturday 8 to 5 and Sunday 9 to 5.

For building projects, Scarborough Building Supply runs the yard at 12990 Highway 9 and stocks the building standards: lumber, paint, tools, and hardware. It's open weekdays 7:30 to 6 with shorter weekend hours. Between the two, most repair-and-project runs never need to leave the valley.

Here's what these stores mean in practice. Last week I ran out of chicken feed, drove into town, and picked up a bag of King 16% Layer Crumble, the ladies' favorite, before the hens noticed anything was awry. Then down the way to the hardware store for a jug of strong, industrial strength vinegar for a safe weed spray along the front of the house, part fire safety, part weed suppression. Two errands, twenty minutes, zero trips over the hill. That's the whole case for these stores in one morning.

Groceries: two real markets, different personalities

Boulder Creek keeps two full grocery stores a couple of blocks apart, which is its own kind of small-town luxury.

Johnnie's Super Market at 13225 Highway 9 has anchored the north end of downtown since 1938, and it's a complete market: produce sourced locally where possible, a meat and seafood counter, a deli making sandwiches daily, a bakery case, and a deep wine, spirits, and beer selection. It opens at 8 a.m. every day, running to 9 p.m. most nights and 10 on Friday and Saturday.

Wild Roots Market at 13159 Central Avenue is the natural-foods counterpart, locally owned since 1991, with organic produce, a deli and kitchen, and baked goods from its Sunflour Bakehouse. It's open daily 9 to 9. There's a second Wild Roots down the valley in Felton, but the Boulder Creek store is its own full market.

Between them, the grocery question in town isn't "can I get it here" so much as "which store carries my version of it."

Pharmacy: independent, and it delivers

Boulder Creek Pharmacy at 13081 Central Avenue has served the town for over 40 years as a locally owned, family-operated pharmacy, and it covers more ground than newcomers expect. Prescriptions get filled quickly and by a friendly neighbor, and it offers free delivery throughout the San Lorenzo Valley, which counts for a lot when a car is in the shop or a storm has the roads a mess, though popping down into town is half the point of living here. The shelves go far beyond medications: toiletries, cleaning supplies, local gifts like Boulder Creek swag, local candles, and huckleberry candy and syrup, plus a real baby section. When our baby needed gas relief drops urgently, we were home with them in fifteen minutes, with relief shortly after. Try that with a drive down the valley. It's also, for what it's worth, our baby's favorite shop in town, with the toy shelf to thank, edged out only by the kitten rescue.

Hours are Monday through Friday 9 to 6 and Saturday 10 to 4, closed Sunday. The phone is 831-338-2144.

Pets and gardens

There's no standalone pet store in town, but Boulder Creek Veterinary Clinic at 12870 Highway 9 covers the animal side thoroughly: a full-service clinic with surgery, dental, boarding, exotic pet care, and an online pharmacy, open six days a week including two evenings. The phone is 831-338-7205.

For pet food and garden needs, Scarborough Home & Garden carries pet food, gardening, and outdoor supplies, and Good Vibes, covered below, leans into houseplants.

Gifts, style, and the specialty row

Downtown's specialty shops cluster along a few blocks of Highway 9, and they run more varied than a first drive-through suggests.

  • Air & Fire, the "mystical bazaar" at 13150 Highway 9, stocks handmade soaps, candles, incense, crystals, jewelry, tarot decks, books, and local art, and hosts classes and readings. It's open daily with seasonal hours posted on its site.
  • SWAG at 13026 Highway 9 mixes restored mid-century stereos, vinyl, vintage apparel, and local art and jewelry inside an 1893 building the shop describes as the first US building owned and operated by women. The business association lists it open Tuesday through Saturday afternoons. SWAG also carries select items from Stumptown Supply, a Boulder Creek-born online brand making apparel and gifts around San Lorenzo Valley history, so you can see the goods in person even though the brand itself has no storefront.
  • Ginia's Gems at 13133 Highway 9 sells handmade memory-wire jewelry with semi-precious stones plus herbal remedies and local honey. Call ahead for current hours.
  • Boulder Creek Antiques at Mac's Place, at 13164 Highway 9, deals in furniture, collectibles, and vintage finds, and it's open daily, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m..
  • Wild Lilith, an independent boutique at 13120 Highway 9, keeps limited weekday hours, per that same listing.
  • Good Vibes at 13124 Highway 9 is a newer shop carrying plants, clothing, and locally made goods.

And in a genuine small-town plot twist, there's a shoe store: Beck's Shoes runs a discount showroom at 12550 Highway 9 at the south end of town, open Thursday through Sunday, 10 to 6, selling premium work, outdoor, and casual footwear at reduced prices, in-store only.

Secondhand and vintage: the hunt side of the street

Boulder Creek's secondhand shopping starts at one door. Springygirl at 13130 Central Avenue is the town's secondhand boutique: gently used women's clothing and accessories, hand-picked piece by piece. It's open Friday through Sunday, noon to 5, and since everything in the room is one of a kind, the shop is different every few weeks. Phone 831-704-2994. The vintage overlap is already on this list: SWAG for vintage apparel, vinyl, and restored stereos, and Mac's Place for furniture, collectibles, and vintage finds. What the town doesn't have is a thrift store; the nearest is The Abbot's Thrift at 6164 Highway 9 in downtown Felton, open Monday through Saturday 9 to 7 and Sunday noon to 5.

Herrick Games and Hobbies at 13111 Pine Street covers the tabletop people on your list: Warhammer and the wider Games Workshop range, board games, and a deep paint wall. The shop takes special orders and hosts painting classes.

Gifts made in the building

Three doors in town sell art made here. Viscosity Art Glass at 13158 Central Avenue sells blown glass out of the working studio, Fridays 1 to 3 and Saturdays 1 to 5. Lille Aeske Arthouse at 13160 Highway 9 hangs a rotating monthly show with work for sale during weekend gallery hours. And Hennig Studios at 211 Grove Street opens its ceramics gallery the first Sunday of each month, noon to 5, and by appointment at 831-338-2098. First Friday evenings put all of it out together, 5 to 8 p.m. downtown.

Cannabis, for adults 21 and over

Boulder Creek also has a licensed adult-use dispensary. Creekside Wellness at 12603 Highway 9 has operated since 2018 under state license C10-0000008-LIC, open Monday through Saturday 10 to 7 and Sunday noon to 6. It's a 21-and-over business, ID required.

What this list is, and isn't

This is the errand-running core: the places that keep a household fed, medicated, repaired, and now and then gift-wrapped without a drive down the valley. It's a working list, not the whole town.

Boulder Creek's cafes, restaurants, and bars get their own guide in where to eat in Boulder Creek, services from plumbers to salons live in the directory, and if you've just moved here, the new resident quick-start guide puts these stops in week-one order. For utilities, permits, and county contacts in one place, see the Residents guide.

Missed a shop, or spotted a detail that's changed? The directory page is the place to tell us.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a hardware store in Boulder Creek?

Yes, two related ones. Scarborough Home & Garden at 13110 Highway 9 covers home, garden, pet, and household goods, open seven days a week, and Scarborough Building Supply at 12990 Highway 9 handles lumber, building supplies, paint, and tools.

Does Boulder Creek have a real grocery store?

It has two. Johnnie's Super Market, a full-line independent grocery in business since 1938, and Wild Roots Market, a natural-foods grocery with a deli and bakery, sit within a few blocks of each other downtown, both open daily.

Is there a pharmacy in town?

Yes. Boulder Creek Pharmacy at 13081 Central Avenue is independent and family-operated, open weekdays and Saturdays, with free prescription delivery throughout the San Lorenzo Valley.

Where can I buy gifts locally?

The downtown blocks hold most of it: Air & Fire for candles and artisan goods, SWAG for vinyl and vintage, Ginia's Gems for handmade jewelry, Mac's Place for antiques, Wild Lilith and Good Vibes for boutique goods, Springygirl for secondhand fashion, and Herrick Games and Hobbies for games and miniatures. Hours vary by shop, so check before a special trip.

Is there a thrift store in Boulder Creek?

Not in town, currently. Springygirl on Central Avenue is a secondhand boutique rather than a thrift store, and SWAG and Mac's Place cover vintage. The nearest true thrift is The Abbot's Thrift in downtown Felton, open seven days a week.

Where can I buy local art?

From the people who made it: Viscosity Art Glass on Central Avenue, Lille Aeske Arthouse on Highway 9 during weekend gallery hours, and Hennig Studios on Grove Street on first Sundays. First Friday, the monthly evening art walk, is the easiest single window onto all three.

What will I still need to drive down the valley for?

Big-box selection, mostly. The town covers hardware, groceries, pharmacy, shoes, gifts, and pet care through the vet, but department-store shopping and specialty chains mean a run to Scotts Valley or Santa Cruz. The full local list lives in our directory.

every-home-service-boulder-creek.title: Every Home Service You Need in the Mountains
every-home-service-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Check the license first. Before you pay anyone, look up the contractor at the CSLB license lookup and confirm it's active, matches the work, and carries a current bond.
  • Deep benches: plumbers, electricians, general contractors, and tree crews all have several Boulder Creek options.
  • Thin spots: roofing, flooring, handyman work, and chimney sweeps are harder to find, and a few of those come from outside the valley.
  • Need someone fast? Several local crews list 24-hour emergency service, including for wells, electrical, and septic.
  • Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, just verified facts to plan around. Missing your go-to person? Tell us and we'll check them out.

When the water heater quits on a Sunday morning, the mountains ask you a question the flatlands don't: who do you call? The hardware store, the plumber, and the tree crew aren't around every corner the way they are in Scotts Valley or Santa Cruz. Owning a home up here means keeping a short list of people you can reach when something goes wrong, and this is that list, organized by the problem you're trying to solve rather than by trade name.

Inclusion isn't an endorsement. Where we could confirm a state contractor license, we've noted the number, which points to the one habit worth building first.

Check the license before you hire

California wants the contractor licensed for any job that needs a building permit, uses employee labor, or runs to $1,000 or more in combined labor and materials. That covers most structural, electrical, plumbing, and roofing work.

You can look up any license in about two minutes at the CSLB license lookup, which shows whether it's active, what classification it covers, and whether the bond and workers' comp are current. We verify licenses when we add a contractor, but statuses change, so confirm it yourself before money changes hands. For the bigger picture on vetting a contractor in the Santa Cruz Mountains, see our guide on hiring a contractor in the Santa Cruz Mountains.

Water: plumbing, wells, and septic

Everyday plumbing has depth right in town. Apollo Plumbing (Boulder Creek) handles drains, pipes, fixtures, and water heaters. Travis Martin Plumbing (Boulder Creek, CSLB #1048423, C-36), which also does business as San Lorenzo Valley Water Heaters, covers drains, fixtures, water heaters, and filtration. Hwy 9 Plumbing (Boulder Creek, CSLB #1045811, C-36) does residential repairs, water heaters, and leak diagnosis; find its number in our directory.

Down valley, Collins Coastal Plumbing (Ben Lomond, CSLB #1004212, C-36), Wade's, Inc. (Ben Lomond, CSLB #1087260), and J Fisher Plumbing (Felton, CSLB #985600) round out the options.

Wells and pumps are their own specialty. Tavares Plumbing and Pumps serves Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, and Felton with pump installation, tanks, and 24-hour emergency service. Maggiora Bros. Drilling (Watsonville) has drilled and serviced county wells since 1962; confirm mountain coverage for your specific job.

For septic, Affordable Septic & Excavating Services (Boulder Creek) advertises pumping, inspections, repairs, installations, and 24-hour service. If you're new to owning a septic system, read our septic basics primer before your first pump-out.

Power: electricians

Boulder Creek has a solid bench of licensed electricians. SE Electric (Boulder Creek) does residential and commercial installation, repair, and lighting. Big Basin Electric (Boulder Creek), Wilson Electric (Boulder Creek, CSLB #1058620, C-10), and PCIS (Boulder Creek, electrical and low-voltage, with 24/7 emergency service) are all in the directory.

Down valley you'll find Jessi Phillips Electric (Ben Lomond, CSLB #980978, C-10) and SLV Electric Inc (Felton, CSLB #881810, C-10). Adding solar? Farinsky Energy Solutions (Ben Lomond, CSLB #1118587, C-46 and C-10) installs photovoltaic systems.

Build and remodel: general contractors

For a build, an addition, or a remodel, the valley's roster of licensed general contractors runs deep. In Boulder Creek: Geist Builders Group, Meadows Custom Builders, LK Construction and Management, Markey Construction (home builds, remodels, decks, fences, retaining walls, and concrete), Kevin Foster Construction, JRG Construction, GNN Construction, Aaron Chase Construction, and Platinum Contracting Services. In Ben Lomond: Eric Martin Construction and Lotz Construction. In Felton: Dixon Construction and Oliveira & Sons. For cabinets and finish carpentry, Gary Fox Cabinets (Boulder Creek, CSLB #697984, B) is a licensed option.

Phone numbers for the ones without a linked site are in the directory, and we have a dedicated roundup of valley-based general contractors coming as the hub series fills out.

A note on handymen. There are people doing this work in and around town, but handyman work generally doesn't require a contractor's license, which means there's no register for us to check them against the way we check a licensed trade. Rather than pick names we can't verify, we've left this one to you: ask a neighbor, or ask at the counter at Scarborough Building Supply. For anything beyond a small job, the licensed builders above will often take on minor work.

Surfaces: paint, concrete, roofing, and floors

Painters are well covered. In Boulder Creek: Jeff Vedder Painting, Machado Bros. Painting (CSLB #1012390, C-33), and California Custom Painting and Design (CSLB #1019283, C-33), which also handles cabinetry and tile. In Felton, Fine Edge Painting (CSLB #1110102, C-33).

For concrete, Boulder Creek Concrete (Boulder Creek, CSLB #1142895, C-8) does flatwork, foundations, and retaining walls, and Terry Miller Concrete (Ben Lomond, CSLB #755895, C-8) is a long-established option.

Roofing is thinner. The one verified roofer serving the valley is Christopher A New Roofing (Ben Lomond, CSLB #668255, C-39); its number is in the directory.

Flooring is thinner still. Briones Built (Boulder Creek, CSLB #1115996, B) is a licensed general contractor based in town that advertises flooring installation, though its posted flooring service area names Felton and Ben Lomond rather than Boulder Creek, so ask. There's no flooring-only specialist based in the valley. If you install floors in the San Lorenzo Valley, please tell us.

Outside: landscaping, tree work, and gutters

For landscape design and installation, Baxter Landscaping, Inc. (Scotts Valley, CSLB #829811, C-27), Angus Hill Landscapes (Boulder Creek, CSLB #1127823, C-27), and Good Earth Landscape & Design (Ben Lomond, CSLB #874175, C-27) are licensed C-27 contractors.

One thing to know going in: these are design-and-install firms. For ongoing mow-weed-and-haul work you want a maintenance gardener instead, and several serve the valley; we list them in our gardeners and yard help guide.

Tree work is the one trade Boulder Creek has in real depth, which makes sense in a redwood forest. Christianson Tree Experts, Stellar Tree Care, Sunderland Tree Service, and Travis Tree Professionals are all Boulder Creek based and cover pruning, removal, and defensible-space work. Before anyone climbs, read our questions to ask in tree work in Boulder Creek, including the county permit thresholds for large trees.

For gutters, Daniel's Cleaning Services (Seaside) cleans rain gutters, chimneys, and dryer vents across the county, including the San Lorenzo Valley; its number is in the directory.

Heat: HVAC, chimney, firewood, and propane

Two licensed HVAC contractors serve the area: Herranen Heating & Air (Ben Lomond, CSLB #814852, C-20) and Zephyr Climate Solutions (Felton, CSLB #1072237, C-20), which specializes in ducted and ductless mini-splits.

If you burn wood, get the chimney swept yearly. No chimney sweep is based inside the valley, so both options come from outside it: Safeguard Chimney Sweep Company (Watsonville, operating since 1979) and Daniel's Cleaning Services (Seaside).

For the wood itself, Cozy Firewood (Felton) delivers and stacks seasoned oak, almond, and eucalyptus. On propane, Mountain Propane Service (Felton) is the locally owned choice, and both Ferrellgas and AmeriGas cover the 95006 area as national providers.

Clean: house cleaners

Three cleaning services are based right in Boulder Creek: San Lorenzo Valley Housekeeping (operating since 2012), SCM Custom Cleaning, and Clean Mountain House Cleaning. Soap Bubble Cleaning Service works the valley from Brookdale at 831-252-0720. Further out you'll find Clean Impressions LLC (Felton), Christi's Green Cleaning, and Santa Cruz Maids. Our full house cleaners guide has the details.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which home services don't exist locally?

We don't list a chimney sweep based inside the San Lorenzo Valley; the ones serving the area come from Watsonville and Seaside. Maintenance gardeners are on a separate page. Handymen we've left off deliberately, since the work usually isn't licensed and we can't verify them the way we verify a licensed trade. Licensed builders often take on the small jobs a handyman would. If you know of someone we've missed, tell us.

How do I check that a contractor is licensed?

Use the CSLB license lookup at cslb.ca.gov. Enter the license number or business name and confirm the license is active, matches the classification for your work, and carries a current bond.

Do these companies come up the hill?

The ones listed as Boulder Creek based do, and each entry notes its home town and service area. For businesses based down valley or over the hill, especially wells and specialty trades, call and confirm they cover your exact address before scheduling. Access and road conditions are part of every mountain job.

Why isn't my go-to person on here?

Probably because we haven't verified them yet, not because anything is wrong. We only list businesses we can confirm directly, and the directory grows every week. Send us a name through the submit page and we'll check it out.

Last reviewed July 24, 2026. License numbers here come from the California Contractors State License Board. Statuses change, so confirm any license yourself at the CSLB before you hire.

Inclusion isn't an endorsement, just verified facts to plan around. Full contact details for every trade above live in the business directory, current happenings are on the events calendar, and if a listing has changed or we're missing someone you'd call, tell us through the submit page.

family-day-trips-boulder-creek.title: Family Day Trips From Boulder Creek
family-day-trips-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Easiest with little kids: Roaring Camp trains and Henry Cowell's flat redwood loop, both in Felton, roughly 15 to 20 minutes south on Highway 9.
  • Beach day: figure 35 to 50 minutes down Highway 9 to the Santa Cruz waterfront. Save your directions first, because cell service drops out along the way.
  • Bigger hikes: Castle Rock for ridge-top views ($10 parking), or Big Basin, which is open again but still recovering from the 2020 fire. Check access before you drive up.
  • Older kids and teens: the Mount Hermon Adventures zipline in Felton, with age, height, and weight rules and reservations you'll want to book ahead.
  • Before you load the car: confirm hours, fees, and closures on each destination's official site, and check Caltrans QuickMap and our Mountain Status page for road conditions.

Point the car south from Boulder Creek and the day opens up fast. Redwood trains in Felton, state parks in every direction, a zipline strung through the treetops, and the beach waiting at the bottom of Highway 9. The gentlest, most kid-friendly stops cluster down the valley toward Felton, while the state parks each reward a phone call or a look at the website before you commit.

One caveat runs through everything below: every drive time here is an approximation, because mountain roads, roadwork, and weather keep changing the math. Treat each destination's official site as the source of truth for hours, fees, and closures.

Roaring Camp Railroads (Felton)

Roaring Camp Railroads in Felton runs heritage steam and diesel trains through the redwoods and down to the Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk, and the whole place is built around families: a kids' club, birthday packages, and seasonal event trains. Plan for roughly a 15 to 20 minute drive south on Highway 9, keeping in mind that's an estimate.

Ticketing, ride times, and event schedules shift through the year and sell out on busy weekends, so book and confirm on Roaring Camp's own site before you go. We don't publish its prices or times here because they move; the official page is where to check.

Big Basin Redwoods State Park: check first

Big Basin Redwoods State Park is California's oldest state park and Boulder Creek's backyard, but it's still recovering from the 2020 CZU fire, and much of it remains closed. It's open for limited day use only, parking is first come, first served, and reservations are encouraged rather than required.

State Parks lists day-use fees of $6 plus a $2 reservation fee, or $10 without a reservation, and no fee to arrive on foot, by bike, or by bus. There's no drinking water on site except at the kiosk, so pack your own.

This is a real destination again, though a different one than the old photos show, with thinner shade and trails that reopen in phases. Confirm current access before you drive up. For the full planning picture, see our responsible Big Basin day trip guide.

Henry Cowell and Fall Creek (Felton)

Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park in Felton is the gentler redwood walk for families. A flat, stroller-friendly loop threads through old-growth trees near the main entrance, and a quieter Fall Creek day-use unit sits a little further on, with about twenty miles of trails and historic lime kilns.

The Fall Creek trailhead and free parking are on Felton Empire Road, and that unit has no facilities and no dogs, bikes, or fires. State Parks runs seasonal junior ranger and interpretive programs at Henry Cowell, but the times shift by season, so check the park's site or call ahead for the current schedule. Figure on about a 15 to 20 minute drive down Highway 9, roads permitting.

A beach day down Highway 9

The Santa Cruz beaches sit at the bottom of the valley, and the drive down Highway 9 through Felton and Ben Lomond is the part to plan around. It's a winding, mostly two-lane mountain road, so give yourself a comfortable buffer rather than a tight door-to-door estimate.

Plan for something like 35 to 50 minutes to the Santa Cruz waterfront depending on traffic and where you're headed, and expect summer weekend congestion both on the road and at beach parking. Save your directions before you drive, since cell service drops out along stretches of Highway 9.

The Beach Boardwalk is also the end of the line on a Roaring Camp beach train, which turns the drive-and-park problem into part of the fun.

Mount Hermon Adventures zipline (Felton)

For older kids and teens with a taste for heights, Mount Hermon Adventures in Felton runs a redwood zipline and aerial adventure course. Courses carry age, height, and weight requirements, reservations are typically needed, and availability is seasonal and weather-dependent, so this is one to book and confirm directly on their site rather than show up for.

It's a short drive down the valley, in the same Felton cluster as Roaring Camp and Henry Cowell, which makes it easy to pair with another stop.

Castle Rock, for a bigger hike

If your family hikes and wants ridge-top views, Castle Rock State Park sits up on Highway 35 about two and a half miles southeast of the Highway 9 junction, with sandstone formations along Skyline. Parking is $10 a day at a self-serve kiosk, and the gate locks at sunset, so it's a daytime trip. Weekdays are quieter for parking. This one suits kids who can handle real trail miles more than a toddler stop.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the best family day trip that isn't weather-dependent?

Roaring Camp Railroads in Felton is the most weather-proof and family-oriented option nearby, since the train rides run rain or shine on a set schedule and the site is built around kids. Confirm ride times and book on Roaring Camp's own site, because schedules and availability change seasonally.

Is Big Basin open for a family visit right now?

Big Basin is open for limited day use as it recovers from the 2020 fire, with much of the park still closed, first-come parking, and encouraged reservations. Facilities and water are limited. Always check the official State Parks access page before you drive up, because what's open changes.

How long is the drive to the beach from Boulder Creek?

Plan for roughly 35 to 50 minutes down Highway 9 to the Santa Cruz waterfront, but treat that as an approximation. Highway 9 is a winding two-lane mountain road, summer weekends get congested, and cell service is patchy, so save directions ahead and check QuickMap and Mountain Status before you go.

Are there redwood walks easy enough for little kids?

Yes. Henry Cowell in Felton has a flat, stroller-friendly loop through old-growth redwoods near the main entrance, which is gentler than most of Big Basin's current trails. Check the park site for seasonal junior ranger programs, and note the Fall Creek unit has no facilities and no dogs.

These are starting points, not guarantees. Conditions and hours change, so each destination's official site rules. For more local ideas and seasonal outings, browse our Visit and Around Town pages, and if something here is out of date, let us know at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact.

famous-people-boulder-creek.title: Famous People Who Lived in, Grew Up in or Visited Boulder Creek
famous-people-boulder-creek.html:
Search "famous people from Boulder Creek" and you'll mostly find the same uncited Wikipedia paragraph, copied from one list to the next and never checked. This page is built the other way around. Every person here carries an explicit label for what their actual connection to town is, and anyone whose connection didn't survive checking simply isn't on the page.

Two ground rules run underneath all of it:

  • No addresses. We don't publish anyone's home address, parcel, directions, or current routine. A public connection to this town isn't a license to point at someone's house.
  • Boulder Creek is not the whole valley. We keep it distinct from Felton, Ben Lomond, Brookdale, Big Basin, and Santa Cruz, because conflating them is exactly how these lists go wrong.

How the labels work

Label Meaning
Born / Raised in Boulder Creek Documented childhood here
Former resident Lived here for a documented period
Publicly documented resident Currently or recently based here per their own public professional material
Worked / Filmed in Boulder Creek Came here for professional work, did not live here
Founded a Boulder Creek institution Built something that existed here
Documented visitor A specific, dated visit
Awaiting verification Plausible, not yet proven: do not repeat as fact

Raised here

Pat Burrell: Raised in Boulder Creek

Born in 1976 in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, Burrell grew up in Boulder Creek and played San Lorenzo Valley Little League. He was the first overall pick in the 1998 MLB draft, taken by the Philadelphia Phillies, and won World Series championships with Philadelphia in 2008 and San Francisco in 2010.

One detail gets mangled constantly: there is no Boulder Creek high school. Burrell attended San Lorenzo Valley High School (which is in Felton, the valley's shared high school) for his freshman year, then transferred to Bellarmine College Prep in San Jose, where he graduated. So it's "raised in Boulder Creek," not "went to Boulder Creek High."

Evidence: confirmed. SABR biography

Paul Locatelli, S.J.: Born and raised in Boulder Creek

Born September 16, 1938, Locatelli grew up on the family ranch in Boulder Creek. Obituaries differ on the birthplace itself, some giving Boulder Creek and at least one giving Santa Cruz. His father ran Locatelli Brothers Lumber, and the family also grew walnuts and grapes, an upbringing that sits right at the intersection of this town's timber and agricultural history.

He became a Jesuit priest and an accountant, and served as the 27th president of Santa Clara University from 1988 to 2008, then as its chancellor and as Secretary for Higher Education for the Jesuits worldwide. He died July 12, 2010, in Los Gatos.

One frequently repeated detail needs care. The family's lumber land is reported to lie within what is now Big Basin Redwoods State Park. That's Big Basin, nine miles up Highway 236, not the town, and the parcel history is a research lead we haven't confirmed.

Evidence: confirmed for upbringing and career; the birthplace and the Big Basin land claim are research leads.

Former residents

Cora Evans: Former Boulder Creek resident

A Catholic convert from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Evans was a reported mystic and stigmatist who promoted a devotion she called the Mystical Humanity of Christ. She moved to Boulder Creek in the summer of 1956 and died here on March 30, 1957, at age 52. She completed her final manuscript, I Was a Pilgrim in History, in Boulder Creek.

Her canonization cause is active, and its status is frequently overstated. The Diocese of Monterey opened formal proceedings in 2010, and the diocesan phase closed with canonical rites at San Carlos Cathedral in Monterey on January 22, 2023, sending the documentation to Rome. Her title is Servant of God, the first stage of the process.

She is not Venerable, not Blessed, and not a saint. Anyone writing otherwise, in either direction, is getting ahead of the Church's own record.

Evidence: confirmed. Archdiocese of San Francisco

Christopher Hills: Founded a Boulder Creek institution; former resident

Hills (1926–1997) settled in Boulder Creek in the early 1970s and founded University of the Trees, a non-profit school and communal residence built around consciousness research, which granted its own degrees. University of the Trees Press, founded in 1976, published his books and resident students' research. The institution closed in 1994 for financial reasons, and Hills died in Boulder Creek on January 31, 1997.

He was also, improbably, a major figure in the global spirulina industry, sometimes called "the father of spirulina," with ventures in Santa Cruz, Israel, Taiwan, and Mexico, and donations of the algae to Afghanistan, Vietnam, Ethiopia, and Sri Lanka.

The dates need care. The Stanford finding aid says the Hillses founded University of the Trees Press in 1976 and that the school was accredited by the State of California in 1977; it gives no founding year for the school itself. Secondary sources put that at 1973, which the finding aid neither confirms nor contradicts.

His papers are held at Stanford as the Christopher Hills papers, M2705, in Special Collections. Note the collection title: it's not a joint collection.

Norah Hills, his wife from 1950 until her death in 1995, is widely described as co-founder of University of the Trees. That billing is thinly sourced, and we label it awaiting verification. Not because it's implausible, but because the pattern of erasing women from institutions they helped build is common enough that it deserves real evidence rather than a repeated line.

Evidence: well documented; founding year and Norah's role are research leads. Stanford finding aid

Jonathan Franzen: Awaiting verification

The novelist (The Corrections, which won the 2001 National Book Award, plus Freedom, Purity, and Crossroads) is a documented Santa Cruz resident. Published interviews describe him leaving New York for Santa Cruz full time in the 2010s without fixing a year. The Boulder Creek connection is separate and much weaker: a local-press account that he and his partner Kathy Chetkovich "first lived together in Boulder Creek," beginning around the time he started spending time in these mountains in October 1998.

No published source gives years for a Boulder Creek residence. Until one does, we're not claiming a period, and we're not treating "lives in the Santa Cruz Mountains" as equivalent to "lived in Boulder Creek."

Evidence: research lead.

Publicly documented residents

Nick Herbert: Publicly documented resident

A physicist and author based in Boulder Creek from at least the early 1980s, Herbert wrote Quantum Reality (1985), Faster Than Light (1988), and Elemental Mind (1993) here. He was part of the Fundamental Fysiks Group, the Berkeley-area circle of the late 1970s that pushed on the philosophical foundations of quantum mechanics, and later served as Fringe Science editor at Mondo 2000. He was also a figure in a Boulder Creek poetry scene known locally as the Bistroscene.

His most consequential idea is also the one most often described wrongly. Herbert's FLASH proposal (First Laser-Amplified Superluminal Hookup) suggested amplifying one photon of an entangled pair so its polarization could be read without collapsing the state, which would have allowed faster-than-light signalling.

It does not work. It was published in 1982 in Foundations of Physics on the recommendation of referee Asher Peres, who knew it was flawed and argued the flaw would be instructive. He was right. Rebuttals by Wootters and Zurek, and independently by Dieks, showed the required perfect copying is impossible, and those 1982 papers are what established and named the no-cloning theorem, now foundational to quantum information science. A 1970 paper by James Park had already proved the same impossibility and gone unnoticed.

So the accurate framing isn't "Boulder Creek physicist invented FTL communication." It's that a productive, publicly refuted error from a Boulder Creek desk helped produce one of quantum mechanics' load-bearing theorems. Sources disagree on whether he was a core or peripheral member of the Fundamental Fysiks Group.

Evidence: well documented; FLASH history confirmed. Scientific American

Jordan Hubbard: Publicly documented resident

A co-founder of FreeBSD in 1993, Hubbard wrote the Ports collection, the package tools, and sysinstall, later served as Apple's Director of Unix Technologies, was CTO at iXsystems, and now works at Nvidia. The Boulder Creek connection comes from his own self-listed professional location.

That's genuine but not independent. We list him as a documented resident and flag the sourcing, and we'd like an interview or a published profile that establishes it directly.

Evidence: well documented, self-reported.

Martan Mann: Publicly documented resident; works in Boulder Creek

A jazz pianist and educator with a master's from San Jose State, Mann is a past Improvisation Chairman of the Music Teachers' Association of California and the author of Jazz Improvisation for the Classical Pianist, New Age Improvisation for the Classical Pianist, and Improvising Blues Piano. He teaches privately from Boulder Creek and has served as house pianist for the Jazz Society of Santa Cruz jam, the latter in Santa Cruz, not here.

Evidence: well documented via his own professional material.

Institutions and the people who came to them

DigiBarn Computer Museum: Founded a Boulder Creek institution

Founded by curator Dr. Bruce Damer and Allan Lundell, DigiBarn housed a personal-computing collection inside a 90-year-old old-growth redwood barn at Ancient Oaks Farm in Boulder Creek. The collection ran from a 1962 LINC through the homebrew era to 1990s networked computing, and included a Cray-1, a Xerox Alto, and Apple and Atari machines, many kept in working order.

It survived the CZU fire. DigiBarn's own site puts it plainly: "The DigiBarn survived the 2020 CZU fire inferno!", and adds that "the fire was stopped a mile from here." That near miss changed the project's direction. Damer credits the Internet Archive for storing the museum's Apple documents collection during the emergency, and the museum has since turned toward digital preservation, "starting with an initiative to scan and preserve the rarest documents, all to be provided to you online."

A Boulder Creek barn full of irreplaceable computing history, saved by a mile of fire line, is one of the better CZU near-miss stories, and one you rarely hear.

Two things to be clear about, because most write-ups aren't:

  1. It never kept regular walk-in hours. DigiBarn ran scheduled public open houses that anyone could sign up for, and outside those, access was by arrangement with the curator: scholars, computing figures, serious press.
  2. The physical collection is on long-term loan to the Computer Museum at System Source in Hunt Valley, Maryland. That's DigiBarn's own statement, current as of its 2022 site update rather than confirmed for this year. The virtual museum at digibarn.com remains online.

So this article doesn't tell you that you can visit. If you want to see the collection, it's in Maryland.

On the founding date. DigiBarn's own about page dates the museum to May 7, 2001, when Bruce Damer, JM Valera, and Allan Lundell bought the first pieces of the collection. The barn itself was bought in August 1998, which is what the site's "our 25th year" line for 2022 counts from.

Evidence: CZU survival, the Maryland loan, the May 2001 founding date, and Damer's role are confirmed by DigiBarn directly. Note the site's front page still presents itself as current for 2022, so it confirms status as of then, not today.

Steve Wozniak: Documented visitor, December 14, 2006

The Apple co-founder visited Ancient Oaks Farm and DigiBarn on December 14, 2006, for a Discovery Channel interview shoot and his first tour of the collection. Present were the Discovery crew, curator Bruce Damer, Allan Lundell (who had worked with Wozniak on the 1982 US Festival), and Sellam Ismail of the Vintage Computer Festival. Filming took place among the redwoods and inside the barn, around the Cray-1, the Xerox Alto, and the Mac collection. He signed a newly delivered 24-inch iMac on his way out.

It's the best-documented celebrity visit in modern Boulder Creek history, because the host published a dated, photographed account of it.

Evidence: confirmed by primary source. DigiBarn's own record

Worked and filmed here

Beatriz Michelena: Worked and filmed in Boulder Creek

One of the first Latina stars of American silent film, and co-creator of the Poverty Flat movie set built outside town in 1915. She headed her own production company from 1917 to 1920. Full profile.

Mary Pickford: Filmed in Boulder Creek

The biggest star in the world in 1917, when she shot exteriors for Cecil B. DeMille's A Romance of the Redwoods on the Poverty Flat set. She did not live here. Full profile.

Historical figures

Joseph Wilbur Peery: Early settler; founded a Boulder Creek institution

Built a small sawmill across from Bear Creek in the early 1860s, around which the settlement of Boulder grew. He became the first postmaster when the Boulder Creek post office opened in 1872, the act that fixed the town's name. In January 1875 he founded Lorenzo, the rival town a mile south that the railroad ultimately doomed. See how the name was settled.

Still to verify

  • Aric Cushing, actor and director
  • Samuel H. Rambo, California State Senator
  • Winfield Scott Rodgers
  • Henry L. Middleton, the landowner behind the Poverty Flat set
  • Josephine Clifford McCracken, writer and conservationist

Help us get this right

If you're on this list and want your entry corrected, expanded, or removed, contact us and we'll handle it. If you know of someone missing, tell us what the actual connection is and how you know: firsthand, family knowledge, or something you read. All three are useful, and each one gets labeled for what it is.

For more on the people and places behind these names, read how Boulder Creek got its name and the story of the Poverty Flat movie set that drew Hollywood into the redwoods.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the most famous person from Boulder Creek?

Pat Burrell is the most widely known person raised here: first overall pick in the 1998 MLB draft and a two-time World Series champion. Paul Locatelli, S.J., who grew up here on the family ranch, led Santa Clara University for twenty years.

Did Steve Wozniak visit Boulder Creek?

Yes, on December 14, 2006, for a Discovery Channel shoot and a tour of the DigiBarn computer museum. The visit is documented with dated photographs by DigiBarn itself.

Can I visit the DigiBarn museum?

No. It never kept regular walk-in hours; visits came through scheduled open houses or by arrangement with the curator. DigiBarn states that the collection is on long-term loan to the Computer Museum at System Source in Hunt Valley, Maryland. The virtual museum remains online at digibarn.com. The barn itself survived the 2020 CZU fire, which stopped about a mile away.

Is Cora Evans a saint?

No. Her title is Servant of God, the first stage of the canonization process. The diocesan phase of her cause closed in January 2023 and the documentation went to Rome. She has not been declared Venerable, Blessed, or a saint.

Did Jonathan Franzen live in Boulder Creek?

Possibly, briefly, in the late 1990s, but no source gives dates, and he is a documented Santa Cruz resident. We list it as an unverified claim rather than a fact.

Why does this list have so many caveats?

Because the alternative is repeating other people's mistakes. Small-town notable-people lists get copied without checking, and a claim survives for decades on nothing but repetition. That's why every entry here is labeled by the strength of its evidence.

fire-insurance-santa-cruz-mountains.title: Fire Insurance in the Santa Cruz Mountains: How It Works and Where to Get Help
fire-insurance-santa-cruz-mountains.html:
The short version

  • Don't let coverage lapse. If you were non-renewed, keep your current policy in force while you sort it out, and ask your insurer for the reason in writing.
  • Re-shop the admitted market every year before you settle for the FAIR Plan. Carriers that had nothing for your address last year are filing to write again in high-fire areas, and nobody will call to tell you.
  • The FAIR Plan is fire-only and temporary. Pair it with a Difference in Conditions (DIC) policy for water damage, theft, and liability. It caps the dwelling at $3 million and does not sell the DIC itself.
  • Home hardening can lower your bill. Every action under the state's Safer from Wildfires program qualifies for a discount, though no one can promise a specific number.
  • Know your rights. The California Department of Insurance explains coverage rules, checks moratoriums, and takes complaints at 800-927-4357.

The envelope from the insurance company is the one nobody up here wants to open, and plenty of neighbors have opened it. If you were non-renewed, or your premium jumped to a number that made you sit down, that experience is common in high-fire country, and it isn't a verdict on how you keep your property.

Here's how the system works, so you can walk into the phone calls knowing the terms. Read it as general information, not insurance advice. It can't tell you what to buy or what your policy should cost. For that, talk to a licensed insurance agent or broker and to the California Department of Insurance, whose consumer hotline is 800-927-4357.

Why Insurers Are Pulling Back in High-Fire Areas

Santa Cruz County is officially in the high-fire conversation. In its January 2025 fact sheet Summary on Residential Insurance Policies and the FAIR Plan, the California Department of Insurance lists Santa Cruz among the counties "at or above the 50th percentile of structures at high fire risk." That designation sits behind everything a mountain homeowner runs into at renewal time.

The department's data shows the strain. In that same January 2025 fact sheet, working from 2023 data, it found that the FAIR Plan, the state's fallback fire insurer, grew "from 1.6% of the residential market to 3.7% of the residential market" through 2023, noting the increase is "mostly occurring in counties that have more structures at high wildfire risk." More homeowners in places like ours were being pushed out of the regular market and onto the fallback.

The FAIR Plan has kept growing since. Its own reporting puts it at 696,562 policies in force and roughly $768 billion in exposure as of June 2026.

The cause and effect is messier than it looks, though, and that matters when you're trying to read your own situation. In the January 2025 fact sheet, again using 2023 data, the department reports that most non-renewals are routine: "75-80% of non-renewals are initiated by policyholders," for instance when they buy or sell a home or switch companies, while the remaining "20-25%" are initiated by insurers for reasons that include wildfire risk. The department also notes that non-renewals fluctuate year to year, dropping after 2019 "before climbing again in 2023 as some larger insurers began to reduce their presence in California."

Coverage is tighter in high-fire zones. But no one can tell you why a particular insurer made a particular decision. If you were non-renewed, the reason is specific to your insurer and your policy, and you're entitled to ask them for it in writing.

Those percentages are a snapshot of 2023, published in January 2025. They describe the shape of the problem, not the state of the market this month. Your own address is the only number that decides your renewal.

The Market Is Moving in Both Directions Now

The pullback is real, and it isn't the whole story anymore. Under the Department of Insurance's Sustainable Insurance Strategy, insurers may use catastrophe models and the net cost of reinsurance when they file for rates, which they could not do before, but only if they commit to writing at least 85% of their statewide market share in wildfire-distressed areas. The trade is explicit: better rate math in exchange for writing business in places like the San Lorenzo Valley.

Whether that is turning into an offer at any particular address is a month-to-month question, and the department tracks the market publicly. What that means for you is practical, and it's the single most useful thing on this page.

Re-shop the admitted market before you settle for the FAIR Plan, because a carrier that had nothing for your address a year ago may have something now. And if you're already on the FAIR Plan, re-shop every year anyway. Nobody will call to tell you the market reopened. None of this guarantees a carrier will write your house. It means the door is worth pushing on more than once.

If You Just Got a Non-Renewal Notice

First, don't let your coverage lapse while you sort it out. A lapse can make you look riskier to the next insurer and can violate your mortgage terms.

Second, check whether you're protected by California's wildfire non-renewal moratorium. The law behind it is California Insurance Code section 675.1, and it's worth knowing by name, because you can cite it to an insurer. After a governor declares a wildfire emergency, that statute can freeze non-renewals in the affected area. In a 2025 example, the Department of Insurance explained that homeowners in and around the ZIP codes covered by a declared wildfire emergency get at least one year of protection from the date of the Governor's emergency declaration, whether or not they suffered a loss, and that homeowners who suffered a total loss get up to 24 months. The protection is tied to specific ZIP codes and a specific declaration. Whether it covers you is a fact to confirm on the department's mandatory one-year moratorium page, which lists the active moratoriums and the ZIP codes each one covers, not an assumption to make.

Third, start shopping early with a licensed agent or broker who knows the mountains. Some brokers specialize in high-fire properties and can reach carriers you won't find on your own. If the regular market has nothing for you, that's where the FAIR Plan comes in.

The California FAIR Plan: The Insurer of Last Resort

The California FAIR Plan is not a state agency and it's not a charity. It's an insurance pool that exists as a backstop. In its own words, it "was established so that all California property owners have access to basic fire insurance when access to coverage in the traditional market is not available." It's blunt about its role: "The California FAIR Plan is an insurer of last resort. If you cannot obtain coverage in the traditional insurance market, the California FAIR Plan may be a temporary solution."

Two things to understand. It's meant to be temporary, a place to hold coverage while you keep looking for a regular policy, not a permanent home. And the FAIR Plan's basic policy covers fire and a short list of related perils. It is not a full homeowners policy. That gap is the reason the next section exists.

There's also a ceiling. The FAIR Plan's dwelling policy currently caps coverage at $3 million. If what it would actually cost to rebuild your house exceeds that number, the FAIR Plan on its own cannot cover the rebuild, and that's a conversation to have with a broker before you need it, not after. Mountain construction costs are not what they were, and a house that seemed comfortably under the cap a few years ago may not be.

One more thing on the horizon. News outlets have reported that the Department of Insurance approved an average dwelling rate increase of about 29.1% for the FAIR Plan, taking effect October 15, 2026, on new and renewal business, with wildfire-exposed properties potentially seeing more than the average and some properties seeing decreases. We have not found that figure in a department press release or on the FAIR Plan's own site, so treat it as reporting rather than an official announcement, and treat the "average" as an average. What it should change is your timing: ask your broker what the FAIR Plan would actually cost for your address today and what they expect after October, and get it in writing. Confirm current pricing with your broker before you budget around any number in a news story, including this one.

Why a FAIR Plan Policy Usually Isn't Enough on Its Own

A standard homeowners policy bundles a lot together: fire, yes, but also water damage, theft, and personal liability if someone is hurt on your property. The FAIR Plan's basic policy leaves those out. To rebuild something close to full coverage, homeowners pair a FAIR Plan policy with a second policy called a Difference in Conditions, or DIC, policy.

The FAIR Plan explains the split clearly: "DIC policies provide coverages that are not available through the California FAIR Plan, such as water damage, theft and liability coverage," and they're "designed to combine with a California FAIR Plan policy to provide coverage similar to that in a comprehensive homeowner's policy." One catch: "The California FAIR Plan does not offer DIC policies." You buy the wrap separately, through a licensed agent or broker, and it's a separate contract with its own carrier and its own deductible.

This is where a lot of mountain homeowners get exposed. In its January 2025 fact sheet, using 2023 data, the Department of Insurance counted the policies rather than the households: for every two FAIR Plan policies, the state counts roughly one DIC policy, meaning "many homeowners with FAIR Plan policies do not have an accompanying DIC policy." If you go the FAIR Plan route, treat the DIC wrap as part of the plan, not an optional extra, and ask your agent to quote both together so you can see the full picture.

You may hear that this two-policy structure is on its way out. Be careful with that. In December 2025 a California Court of Appeal held that the Insurance Commissioner does not have the authority to require the FAIR Plan to provide liability coverage, reading the FAIR Plan statute as limited to first-party property insurance. The FAIR Plan has been fighting the Commissioner in court over this expansion since 2019, by the department's own account, and it still does not write full homeowners policies. In February 2026, legislators announced AB 1680, the "Make It FAIR Act," which would require the FAIR Plan to offer comprehensive homeowners coverage and would remove the need for a separate DIC policy. It has not passed, and until it does the rules are the rules as they stand today. Plan around today's rules, and buy the wrap.

How Home Hardening and Defensible Space Fit In

You can't move your house out of the mountains, but you can make it measurably more resistant to fire, and California rules now tie that work to insurance. Under the Department of Insurance's Safer from Wildfires framework, "Every action under Safer from Wildfires will qualify you for an insurance discount. By doing more, you can save more."

The qualifying actions run from small to significant: a five-foot ember-resistant zone right around the house (the department describes "removing greenery and replacing wood chips with stone or decomposed granite 5 feet around your home"), a Class-A fire-rated roof, ember- and fire-resistant vents, and defensible space that follows state and local law by "trimming trees and removal of brush and debris from yard." Community-wide efforts count too, including recognized Firewise USA and Fire Risk Reduction Communities.

The tree and brush side of this is a big job in a redwood town, and it's worth doing right. Our guide to tree work in Boulder Creek walks through permits, licensing, and how defensible space works so you clear the right things without over-cutting, and our tree services directory lists local companies to start from.

One limit to be clear about: discounts vary by insurer and by the specifics of your property, and no one can promise a particular saving or that hardening alone will get you renewed. It improves your odds and can lower your bill. That's the accurate claim.

Questions to Ask a Licensed Agent

Specific questions get you further than "why is this so expensive." A few worth writing down:

  • Am I currently protected by any wildfire non-renewal moratorium, and when does it end?
  • Have you checked every admitted carrier and the surplus-lines market for my address, or just a couple?
  • Which carriers have started writing again in my area since the state's new rate rules took effect, and can we re-check next renewal?
  • What would it cost to rebuild my house today, and does that number sit above or below the FAIR Plan's $3 million dwelling cap?
  • If the FAIR Plan is my option, can you quote the FAIR Plan policy and a DIC wrap together, with both deductibles spelled out?
  • Which Safer from Wildfires actions would lower my premium, and by roughly how much for my property?
  • What exactly is and isn't covered, especially for water damage, theft, and liability?
  • Is my dwelling coverage limit enough to rebuild at today's mountain construction costs?

Where to Get Help

Two places to start. A licensed insurance agent or broker can shop the market and build the FAIR Plan and DIC combination if it comes to that, though a broker may have nothing to sell you on a given day, and that isn't the end of the search.
