And the California Department of Insurance helps consumers directly: its hotline is 800-927-4357, and its staff can explain your rights, tell you whether a moratorium covers your ZIP code, and take a complaint if an insurer isn't following the law.

Once more, because it matters: nothing here is insurance, legal, or financial advice, and nothing here promises you a price or a policy. It's a map of how the system works so you can walk into those conversations knowing the terms. The decisions belong to you and the licensed professionals you hire.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the California FAIR Plan?

It's the state's insurer of last resort for basic fire coverage. The FAIR Plan describes itself as a pool that gives property owners "access to basic fire insurance when access to coverage in the traditional market is not available," and calls itself "a temporary solution" for those who can't get a regular policy. It is not a full homeowners policy on its own.

Why do I need a second policy with the FAIR Plan?

Because the FAIR Plan covers fire and related perils but leaves out things a standard policy includes. A Difference in Conditions (DIC) "wrap" policy adds them back. The FAIR Plan says DIC policies cover "water damage, theft and liability coverage" and are "designed to combine with a California FAIR Plan policy." You buy the DIC separately through an agent, since the FAIR Plan doesn't sell it.

My insurer non-renewed me after a nearby fire. Is that allowed?

It depends. California Insurance Code section 675.1 creates a non-renewal moratorium that can protect homeowners "living within or adjacent to a declared wildfire emergency," for at least one year from the Governor's emergency declaration. The department's moratorium page lists the active declarations and the ZIP codes each covers. Whether it applies to your address and dates is specific. Confirm with the California Department of Insurance at 800-927-4357 before assuming either way.

Will clearing brush and hardening my home lower my premium?

It can, though results vary. Under the state's Safer from Wildfires framework, "Every action under Safer from Wildfires will qualify you for an insurance discount." The size of the discount depends on your insurer and your property, so no one can promise a specific number. Ask your agent which actions apply to you and keep records of the work.

Who do I call if I can't find any coverage?

Start with a licensed insurance agent or broker who works high-fire properties, and ask them to re-check the admitted market before defaulting to the FAIR Plan, since some carriers have been filing to write again in wildfire-distressed areas. If the regular market has nothing, ask them about a FAIR Plan policy plus a DIC wrap. For your rights and for help understanding your options, call the California Department of Insurance consumer hotline at 800-927-4357.

Are FAIR Plan rates going up?

News outlets have reported an approved average dwelling rate increase of about 29.1% effective October 15, 2026, on new and renewal business, with wildfire-exposed properties potentially seeing more than the average and some seeing decreases. That figure comes from reporting, not from a department press release or the FAIR Plan's own site, and an average is not a quote. Ask your broker what the FAIR Plan costs for your address now and what they expect after October.

This article draws on published guidance from the California Department of Insurance and the California FAIR Plan. Insurance rules, rates, court rulings, and moratoriums change; confirm the current specifics with a licensed agent or broker and the California Department of Insurance before you act.

free-green-waste-vegetation-clearing-bou.title: Free Green-Waste Disposal and Vegetation-Clearing in Boulder Creek
free-green-waste-vegetation-clearing-bou.html:
The short version

  • Free chipping (spring). The Resource Conservation District chips defensible-space cuttings for free, right at your property. Registration typically runs April 1 to 30, with chipping in early May.
  • Free disposal days (2026). The county runs them the last Saturday of the month at the Ben Lomond Transfer Station, 7:30am to 3:30pm, through September. Two-ton max per load, and bring ID showing you live here.
  • Everyday trimmings. Your GreenWaste Recovery green-waste cart takes yard waste on your normal pickup schedule.
  • Confirm before you cut. Dates and rules shift year to year, so check the current window before you start a big job.

Cut a season's worth of brush from around a Boulder Creek house and you end up with a pile that won't fit in anything you own. You don't have to pay to get rid of it. Between the Resource Conservation District's no-cost chipping program, periodic free green-waste disposal days for San Lorenzo Valley residents, and regular curbside pickup, there are several ways to move those cuttings without a dump fee. Most of these are tied to reducing wildfire fuel around homes, so the same work that clears your yard helps protect it. Here's how each one works, and how to plan for it.

Free chipping from the Resource Conservation District

The Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz County runs a community chipping program that will chip your defensible-space cuttings for free, right at your property. It's built specifically for wildfire fuel reduction, which means the material has to come from the defensible-space zone: within 100 feet of an occupied structure, or within 15 feet on either side of a private road.

The details that trip people up:

  • Timing. Registration typically runs April 1 to 30, with chipping in early May. It's a spring program, so plan your big cutting around it.
  • How much. Up to about three piles per household.
  • How to stack. Branches up to roughly 8 inches in diameter and 10 feet long, hand-stacked with the cut ends facing the same direction toward the road, and on the uphill side of sloped roads.

Dates and rules shift year to year. Confirm the current window and requirements on the RCD chipping page before you start cutting.

Free green-waste disposal days for the valley

Separately, the county has run free green-waste disposal days for residents of the unincorporated San Lorenzo Valley and Scotts Valley, a cooperative effort supporting vegetation management and defensible space in high fire-risk areas, coordinated with the District 5 County Supervisor's office.

For 2026 the county is running it on the last Saturday of the month at the Ben Lomond Transfer Station, 7:30am to 3:30pm, through September, with a two-ton maximum per load, no dump trucks or drop-boxes, and proof of residency for self-haulers. Dates and rules change year to year, so check the county's green waste disposal program page before you load up, and bring ID showing you live here.

Everyday trimmings: your curbside cart

For the everyday trimmings, GreenWaste Recovery is the county's hauler, and your green-waste cart takes yard waste on your normal pickup schedule. For bigger loads or specifics on what's accepted, check GreenWaste's Santa Cruz County page.

Why clearing brush matters here

This is more than tidiness. Clearing brush, limbing up trees, and hauling out dead material is the heart of defensible space, and these free programs exist largely to make that work easier and cheaper so more homes get it done. If you're clearing for fire season, pair this with our late-summer wildfire checklist. And before winter, moving cut vegetation also keeps it from washing into culverts and drainage during storms.

Frequently asked questions

How can I get rid of yard waste for free in Boulder Creek?

Three main ways: the Resource Conservation District's no-cost chipping program (spring, for defensible-space material), periodic free green-waste disposal days for San Lorenzo Valley residents, and your regular curbside green-waste cart through GreenWaste Recovery.

When is the chipping program?

Registration typically runs April 1 to 30 with chipping in early May, but confirm the current dates on the RCD chipping page, since they change year to year.

What material qualifies for free chipping?

Cuttings from the defensible-space zone: within 100 feet of an occupied structure or within 15 feet of a private road, branches up to about 8 inches in diameter and 10 feet long, hand-stacked toward the road.

Do I have to pay to use the green-waste disposal days?

The District 5 disposal days for valley residents are free within limits (a two-ton maximum per load and proof of residency). For 2026 they run the last Saturday of the month at the Ben Lomond Transfer Station through September; confirm on the county's program page.

Last reviewed July 20, 2026. Program details here link to the Resource Conservation District, Santa Cruz County Public Works, and the District 5 County Supervisor's office. Program dates and rules change; confirm with the RCD, the county, and District 5 before you haul. For the rest of what a mountain property needs before fire season, see our late-summer wildfire checklist and the Residents guide for county contacts in one place. Something out of date here? Tell us.

free-resources-boulder-creek.title: Free Resources in Boulder Creek
free-resources-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Free groceries every Friday, 3 p.m. until the food is gone, in the lot next to Jenna Sue's Cafe downtown. No sign-up, no questions. Junction Park if it's raining.
  • A free library card covers wifi, public computers, printing, museum and park passes, borrowable tools and equipment, and free garden seeds.
  • The BCRPD Community Tool Shed has wound down its weekly tool rentals, so don't plan a project around borrowing from it.
  • Valley Churches United Missions in Ben Lomond runs an every-other-week food pantry for San Lorenzo Valley residents.
  • Need help fast and don't know where to start? Dial 211 for food, housing, and benefits.

Printable version: where to get help in Boulder Creek gathers these on one printable page, which is easier to pass along than a URL. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

On Friday afternoons, folding tables go up in the open lot next to Jenna Sue's Cafe and the produce comes out at 3 p.m. Nobody asks who you are. That's the shape of a lot of the free help in Boulder Creek: small, run by neighbors, and easy to miss if nobody points you at it. Here's the running list, with a source for each one so you can check the current details yourself.

The Boulder Creek Branch Library

A library card is free, and it does more work than most people expect. The Boulder Creek Branch Library is at 13390 West Park Avenue (831-427-7703), open Monday through Thursday 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Friday 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Saturday 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

A card gets you a lot more than books:

  • Books, movies, audiobooks, and music, plus free wifi, public computers, and wireless printing.
  • Discover & Go: free and discounted passes to museums and parks around the region.
  • The Library of Things: borrowable objects and equipment, not just media.
  • The Felton Seed Library: free garden seeds you can take and grow, which is handy in a valley full of gardeners.
  • Story time, book groups, and craft and STEAM programs across all the branches.

Free Food Fridays

Every Friday, free food goes out to anyone who wants it, no questions asked. It runs from 3 p.m. until the food is gone, rain or shine, in front of the open lot next to Jenna Sue's Cafe downtown. If it's raining, the giveaway moves to Junction Park.

There's no proof of income and no sign-up. Come and take what you need, and donations are welcome but never required. The food is leftover produce and groceries from the Grey Bears Healthy Food program, distributed here through the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District, the local park district, thanks to a crew of volunteers who set it up every week.

Valley Churches United Missions food pantry (in Ben Lomond)

A few miles down Highway 9, Valley Churches United Missions (VCUM) runs a food pantry for San Lorenzo Valley residents at 9400 Highway 9 in Ben Lomond (831-336-8258). Enrolled households can pick up groceries every other week: staples like pasta, cereal, canned goods, and meat, plus fresh milk, eggs, and produce.

Pantry hours are Tuesday through Thursday 9 a.m. to noon, with a seniors-only window on the first and third Fridays from 9 to 11 a.m. VCUM also helps with clothing and seasonal programs, so it's worth a call if you need more than food.

The BCRPD Community Tool Shed

The BCRPD Community Tool Shed was born after the CZU fire and spent years lending tools out for free, everything from shovels and rakes to log splitters and cement mixers. The district announced that weekly rentals would close in August 2026, and the shed has since wound that program down, so it is no longer somewhere to borrow a tool for the weekend. Anything that continues will come through the district; bctoolshed@gmail.com is the contact on their page.

Heads up: the Rec District's own page says the shed's weekly rentals are closing in August 2026. Check the BCRPD site or email bctoolshed@gmail.com for the current status before you head over.

Little Free Libraries around town

The take-a-book, leave-a-book boxes are scattered all over Boulder Creek, and once you start noticing them you see them everywhere. Here's where to look:

  • Garrahan Park
  • The Boulder Creek Rec Center, near the swing set
  • Along Highway 9 northbound, just south of Bear Creek Road
  • A bookshelf inside the Treehouse Cafe
  • At Joe's Bar (note: Joe's is a 21-and-over bar)
  • Sunshine Lane, in the alley between Redwood and Hazel avenues
  • In front of Camp Joy

More of these are dotted through the rest of the valley in Ben Lomond and Felton, too.

A few more free things

  • Buy Nothing Boulder Creek: a local Facebook group where neighbors give away and ask for free stuff, from furniture to garden starts. Part of the Buy Nothing Project.
  • The BCRPD Foundation community potluck: a free, everyone-welcome community meal on the second Sunday of the month, 4 to 7 p.m. It's outdoors at Garrahan Park (15555 Highway 9) in the warm months and moves indoors from October through March, to a location the district announces each season. Bring a dish to share, and canned goods for the food drive if you can. Recurring free meals and community events also land on our community events calendar.
  • Junction Park and the town's other parks are open to everyone at no cost, and the park is also the rainy-day home for Free Food Fridays.
  • Free wifi is available at the library during open hours.

If you need a little more help

Most county services are down the highway in Santa Cruz. A few of them come up the valley or work over the phone, and those are the ones worth writing down:

  • 211 Santa Cruz County: dial 211 or search online for help with food, housing, benefits, and just about anything else. Start there if you don't know where else to start.
  • Second Harvest Food Bank: runs free grocery distributions across the county. Find the nearest one at thefoodbank.org or call 831-662-0991.
  • Meals on Wheels: hot weekday lunches for adults 60 and older at the Highlands Park Senior Center on Highway 9 in Ben Lomond, plus delivery for homebound seniors. Call 831-464-3180.
  • Grey Bears: county residents 55 and older can get a free weekly grocery bag. Call 831-479-1055.
  • CalFresh (SNAP): monthly grocery money if you qualify. Apply at BenefitsCal.com or call 888-421-8080.

Ways to give back

If you're on the other side of it and want to help, the Buy Nothing group is the easiest place to pass things on. Free Food Fridays and VCUM both take donations, and Grey Bears will pick up extra food or glean fruit from your trees (danielle@greybears.org).

Last reviewed July 19, 2026. Know a free resource we missed, or spot a detail that's changed? Tell us at hello@bouldercreeklocal.com and we'll add it. For utilities, county contacts, and more local services in one place, see the Residents guide. If work is the thing you need, our valley job board is free to browse with no account and no signup.

fun-things-boulder-creek.title: Fun Things to Do in and Around Boulder Creek
fun-things-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Warm day: the San Lorenzo River at Junction Park is the center of it, with a small beach and picnic tables. No lifeguards, so it's swim at your own risk.
  • In the redwoods: Big Basin, Castle Rock, and Fall Creek all sit within a short drive, but access keeps shifting since the 2020 CZU fire, so confirm each one on its official page before you go.
  • Downtown: a walkable loop of shops, galleries, and the Boulder Creek Farmers Market, every Thursday from 1:30 to 5:30 p.m. at Junction Park.
  • Evening: live music at Joe's Bar, dinner at Scopazzi's or the Sawmill, and weekend tastings at Big Basin Vineyards.
  • Before you head out: hours and conditions change with the weather and the season, so check the directory and the events calendar the day you go.

For a town you can walk end to end in ten minutes, Boulder Creek keeps a lot going, once you know where to look. Here's a roundup sorted by mood, from a slow afternoon by the river to a night of live music, pulled from our verified directory and the local pages we keep current. Access up here changes with the weather and the seasons, so confirm hours and conditions with each place the day you head out. None of this is a ranking, and inclusion isn't an endorsement.

On the water

When it's warm, the San Lorenzo River is the center of gravity. Junction Park, a block off the main street at Middleton Avenue and Railroad Avenue, has a small beach, river access, a lawn, and picnic tables, kept up by the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District. It's a popular summer swim spot, and it's swim at your own risk, so watch your footing on the rocks and keep an eye on kids near moving water.

Just downstream sits Barbara Day Park, a small park at the old dam, and up Highway 9 you'll find Garrahan Park, with a walking track, fields, shade, and barbecue areas.

For a pool instead of a river, the rec district runs Bear Creek Pool on Forest Hill Drive seasonally, and community swim nights turn up on the events calendar through the summer. Check the rec district for the current pool schedule, since it changes with the season.

In the trees

The redwoods are what draw a lot of people into these mountains, and three parks anchor the options. Access at all of them keeps shifting after the 2020 CZU fire, so confirm each one on its official page before you drive up.

Miller Property County Park, three miles north of town on Kings Creek Road, is the newest of them: 410 acres of redwood and creek that opened to the public in 2025, with nature trails and a bigger network under construction. Our Miller Property guide has the details, and the hiking guide covers the rest.

Big Basin Redwoods State Park, California's oldest state park, is open for limited day-use as it recovers, and much of it is still closed. Parking is limited and first come, first served, with reservations encouraged but not required. State Parks lists day-use fees of $6 plus a $2 reservation fee, or $10 without a reservation, and no fee to arrive on foot, by bike, or by bus. There's no drinking water on site except at the kiosk. Confirm the current status at State Parks before you count on it. We also have a full guide to a responsible Big Basin day trip.

Castle Rock State Park, up on Skyline about two and a half miles southeast of the Highway 9 junction, has sandstone formations and ridge-top views. Parking runs $10 a day at a self-serve kiosk, and the gate locks at sunset; weekdays are quieter.

Fall Creek, a day-use unit of Henry Cowell, offers about twenty miles of quiet trails through redwoods and old lime kilns, with a free trailhead on Felton Empire Road off Highway 9. There are no facilities there, and dogs, bikes, and fires are not allowed. Details for both Castle Rock and Fall Creek are at State Parks.

Around town

Downtown is walkable and easy to loop on foot, and the main stretch of Highway 9 rewards a slow lap:

  • Air & Fire: A Mystical Bazaar for crystals, jewelry, and gifts.
  • SWAG for vintage apparel, vinyl, and local art.
  • Viscosity Glass for locally made glass art.
  • Beck's Shoes for footwear, on its weekends-only schedule.
  • Scarborough Home & Garden for hardware, plants, and a little of everything.

Many keep limited days, so check posted hours or the directory before a special trip.

For art and history, the San Lorenzo Valley Museum presents valley history at its Grace Episcopal Gallery on Highway 9, with the office open Wednesday through Saturday afternoons; call or email for an appointment. Galleries and studios like Hennig Studios (ceramics) and lille aeske arthouse add to the scene, most by appointment or on limited days.

On any given week there's more happening than a list can hold. The Boulder Creek Farmers Market runs every Thursday from 1:30 to 5:30 p.m. at Junction Park with local vendors, farms, and music, and the events calendar tracks live music, library programs, First Fridays downtown, and seasonal festivals.

For the active

If you'd rather be doing than watching, Boulder Creek Golf & Country Club is a public course set into the redwoods off Big Basin Highway, open 6:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. daily, with a clubhouse, a restaurant and bar, and event facilities; call ahead for tee times. For a class instead, Mountain Sangha offers yoga, pilates, and breathwork on Highway 9, Treetop Pilates & Wellness runs reformer and mat classes on Forest Street, and Lone Wolf Kenpo Academy teaches martial arts in town. Our fitness guide covers all of them.

Looking for a full gym? Those are down valley in Felton and Scotts Valley, and we've compared the closest gyms to Boulder Creek so you can pick the drive that fits.

In the evening

Boulder Creek keeps a real nightlife for its size. Joe's Bar downtown hosts live bands most Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday nights, with karaoke on Tuesdays and a Thursday pool tournament; it's a 21-and-over room.

Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge pairs a historic Italian dining room with a lounge, and The Sawmill Restaurant & Alehouse up Highway 9 has craft beer, pub fare, outdoor seating, and a music stage. For wine, Big Basin Vineyards pours estate tastings at its Boulder Creek vineyard on weekends from noon to 5 p.m.

For the full rundown, including live-music venues down valley, see our guide to a night out in and around Boulder Creek.

Make a day of it

You don't have to pick just one. A classic Boulder Creek day stacks a few of these: coffee downtown, a morning on the trails or the golf course, lunch on the main drag, a slow lap through the shops, and dinner or live music to close it out. Our Visit page lays out a choose-your-own perfect day with several options at each stop, built for exactly this kind of mixing and matching.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Big Basin open right now?

Partly. Big Basin is open for limited day-use as it recovers from the 2020 CZU fire, and large portions remain closed. Parking is first come, first served and reservations are encouraged. Always confirm the current status at State Parks before you drive up, because access changes.

Can you swim in the river at Junction Park?

People do swim there in summer, and it's swim at your own risk. There are no lifeguards, currents and depths change with the season, and you should watch footing on the rocks and keep close watch on children near the water.

What's the one thing happening every week?

The Boulder Creek Farmers Market at Junction Park, every Thursday from 1:30 to 5:30 p.m., with local vendors, farms, music, and activities. Only service dogs are allowed at the park during the market. Everything else, from live music to library programs, is on our events calendar.

Where can I hear live music?

Joe's Bar downtown has bands most Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday nights (21 and over), the Sawmill has a music stage, and SWAG runs a summer concert series. The events calendar lists specific acts and dates, and our night out guide covers the venues.

None of this is a ranking, and inclusion isn't an endorsement, just verified places to plan around. Full details and hours for every spot are in the directory, what's happening this week is on the events calendar, and if we've missed a place or something has changed, tell us through the submit page.

gardeners-yard-help-boulder-creek.title: Finding a Gardener or Yard Help in Boulder Creek
gardeners-yard-help-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • For mowing, weeding, pruning, seasonal cleanups, and hauling, you want a maintenance gardener. Routine upkeep doesn't need a contractor's license as long as the work stays under California's threshold.
  • For a patio, a retaining wall, grading, drainage, or irrigation installed from scratch, you want a licensed C-27 landscape contractor.
  • Brush clearing and defensible space are maintenance-gardener work. Cutting down trees, removing large limbs, or working near power lines is a job for a tree service.
  • Verify any contractor's license for free at the Contractors State License Board before you sign anything.
  • Inclusion here isn't an endorsement. Get a clear scope and price in writing before any work begins.

The first mistake is calling the wrong kind of person. "Gardener" and "landscaper" are two different trades, and you hire them two different ways. Figure out which one your yard needs and the rest of the search gets a lot simpler.

Most of the outfits below are home-based or mobile, so we list the community and phone number, not a home address. Inclusion isn't an endorsement, just a starting point. A quick call is how you'd sort out fit and scheduling anyway.

Gardener or landscaper: which one you need

Here's the distinction that saves confusion. A maintenance gardener keeps an existing yard healthy and tidy: mowing, weeding, pruning shrubs and small trees, seasonal cleanups, and hauling away green waste. In California, routine gardening and maintenance can be done without a contractor's license, as long as the jobs stay under the state's threshold and don't involve the structural or installation work that requires one.

A landscape contractor, licensed by the state under the C-27 classification, does the bigger stuff: design and installation, hardscaping, retaining walls, drainage and grading, and irrigation systems. If your project involves building, installing, or moving earth at any real scale, that's licensed-contractor territory, and you can verify any license at the Contractors State License Board. The listings below are split along that line.

Maintenance gardeners and yard help

These are the crews and independent gardeners for ongoing care and cleanups.

  • Simple Wonders Landscape and Design (831-333-6709) is a Boulder Creek yard-maintenance and design service run by Ariana and Shawn, covering garden maintenance and design work from Boulder Creek down to Santa Cruz, with free consultations.
  • Greenman Gardening (831-566-6045) is a San Lorenzo Valley gardening service with more than 20 years of local experience, offering ornamental tree pruning and irrigation installation and maintenance. It comes owner-recommended, and details are best confirmed by phone.
  • Silverfern Gardens (831-239-8221), run by Aileen Addleman, is a local garden-care business that came recommended through community referrals. Call or text to talk through your garden.
  • Dragonfly Landscape Services (831-227-3848) is a permaculture-certified garden and landscape service, also owner-recommended from community referrals, with details to confirm by phone.
  • Hannah Soriano Gardens (303-882-8161) is a landscape gardener with an agroecology degree and an edible-landscaping background. She's reachable by text or on Instagram.

One note on the "owner-recommended" framing: where a listing says that, it means the business surfaced through neighbor referrals rather than a formal vetting of work quality. It's a starting point for your own conversation, not a guarantee. Get a clear scope and price before any work begins.

Landscape design and build (licensed contractors)

For projects rather than upkeep, these are licensed C-27 landscape contractors serving the valley.

  • Baxter Landscaping, Inc. (831-246-0537, CSLB #829811) lists a Scotts Valley office and handles residential and commercial landscape installation and grounds work across the valley.
  • Good Earth Landscape and Design (831-359-6211, CSLB #874175) is a Ben Lomond landscape design and installation contractor.
  • Angus Hill Landscapes (650-799-0477, CSLB #1127823) is a Boulder Creek landscaping contractor.

All three hold active C-27 licenses, which you can confirm any time at the state license board. For a bigger build, a written contract, a license check, and a couple of references are the basics worth doing before you commit.

Yard help and defensible space

A lot of yard work up here is really fire-safety work. Clearing brush, cutting back weeds and grass, and creating defensible space around your home is exactly the kind of ongoing job a maintenance gardener can take on.

Where it crosses into cutting down trees, removing large limbs, or working near power lines, that's a job for a tree service, not a gardener. We cover that separately in Tree Services in Boulder Creek, and the wider fire-readiness picture, including what defensible space means for a mountain parcel, lives on our Residents page. Matching the right trade to the job keeps you safer and usually cheaper.

The lay of the land

Boulder Creek is decently covered for both kinds of help. The maintenance-gardener bench is mostly small, independent, home-based operations, which means you'll do your scheduling by phone or text and should confirm availability rather than expect a storefront.

The licensed landscape-contractor options for design-and-build projects are spread out rather than clustered: one works from Boulder Creek, one from Ben Lomond, and one from Scotts Valley. If you can't reach anyone, or you have a specialized job, the directory has the full current list, and the county and state license lookups are always there to verify anyone you're considering.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a licensed contractor to mow and weed my yard?

No. Routine gardening and maintenance, like mowing, weeding, pruning, and cleanups, can generally be done by a maintenance gardener without a contractor's license, as long as the work stays under California's threshold and doesn't involve structural or installation work. Bigger installation, hardscaping, grading, or irrigation-system jobs call for a licensed C-27 landscape contractor.

What's the difference between a gardener and a landscaper here?

A maintenance gardener keeps an existing yard healthy: mowing, weeding, pruning, and hauling. A landscape contractor designs and builds: patios, walls, drainage, grading, and full irrigation installs, and holds a state C-27 license. Match the person to the job, and verify any license at the Contractors State License Board.

Can a gardener help with fire defensible space?

Yes, for the brush-and-weed side of it. Clearing grass, cutting back brush, and maintaining defensible space around a home is standard maintenance-gardener work. Cutting down trees or removing large limbs, especially near power lines, is a job for a licensed tree service instead. See our tree services and Residents guides for the fire-readiness details.

How do I check that a contractor is licensed?

Use the free license lookup at the Contractors State License Board (cslb.ca.gov). Each licensed contractor above lists its CSLB number, and you can confirm the license is active and in the right classification before you sign anything.

Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, just a starting point. See the full directory for contact details, and if a listing has changed, tell us at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact so the next neighbor gets it right. For the full rundown of trades, see Every Home Service You Need in the Mountains.

general-contractors-boulder-creek.title: General Contractors Based in the Valley
general-contractors-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • The San Lorenzo Valley has 14 general building contractors based in Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, or Felton, plus a dedicated roofer in Ben Lomond, most with an active California "B" license. They're listed by town below.
  • A "B" General Building license is the right one for whole-house work: builds, additions, and remodels. Specialty scopes like septic, wells, roofing, and tree work carry their own classifications.
  • Look up any contractor in the free CSLB license lookup before you sign or hand over a deposit. Status, bond, and complaint history can change.
  • Get at least three written bids on identical plans, and never put down more than $1,000 or 10 percent of the contract price, whichever is less.
  • A listing here is a verified place to start, not an endorsement. Run the checks no matter who you call.

Printable version: the hiring a contractor checklist is worth printing before you call anyone on this list, since the verification steps are the same whoever you hire. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

A builder who's already patched a washed-out driveway in February knows things a resume can't teach. If you're planning a build, remodel, or addition and you want a general contractor who lives with these slopes, driveways, and winters, you don't have to hire a stranger from over the hill. The valley has a deep local roster.

This page lists 14 general building contractors based in Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, or Felton, and most carry an active California "B" General Building license we've noted below. It's a selected roster, not a complete count, because the CSLB database carries valley builders we haven't written up yet. The listings are grouped by town, nothing more, and a spot here isn't an endorsement. For how to vet whichever one you call, read its companion, our guide on hiring a contractor in the Santa Cruz Mountains, which walks through licenses, bids, deposits, and permits in detail.

A quick word on the license numbers. Where our data has a contractor's CSLB number, we list it so you can confirm it yourself. A license number in a directory is a convenience, not a substitute for the free, real-time CSLB license lookup, which shows current status, classifications, bond, workers' compensation, and any complaint disclosure. Always look it up before you sign or hand over a deposit.

Boulder Creek

Geist Builders Group at 13119 Highway 9 (831-218-5730) is a licensed general contractor doing residential construction, remodeling, and project services, open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. It's one of the few on this list with a listed street address in town.

Robert Bimbi Construction at 13200 Highway 9, Suite 2 (CSLB #798373, active B) is a Boulder Creek general building contractor, sole owner, licensed here since the 1990s.

LK Construction and Management, Inc. (831-901-1030, CSLB #1010899, active B) handles ground-up builds, remodels, and tenant improvements, and adds construction-management services.

Meadows Custom Builders (408-489-8145, CSLB #1077781, active B) focuses on custom home construction, renovations, and additions.

Markey Construction (831-359-1634) is a licensed general contractor for home builds, remodels, decks, fences, retaining walls, and concrete work. On valley lots, retaining walls and concrete carry a lot of the load.

The rest of Boulder Creek's general builders work from the field rather than a storefront, so contact runs by phone. All handle residential construction and remodeling, and each is in our directory.

  • Kevin Foster Construction (831-588-2055, CSLB #936857, active B)
  • JRG Construction (831-345-2917, CSLB #967855, active B)
  • GNN Construction (831-247-9771, CSLB #997768, active B)
  • Aaron Chase Construction (831-566-1336, CSLB #1063144, active B)
  • Platinum Contracting Services (650-732-2168, CSLB #1037868, active B)
  • VSG Builder (831-818-5733, CSLB #1141184, active B), run by Victor Soto, adds framing and concrete work including pumping

Ben Lomond

Eric Martin Construction, Inc. (408-768-3905, CSLB #981846, active B) is a Ben Lomond general building contractor for residential construction and remodeling. Lotz Construction (831-252-3767, CSLB #865919, active B) is a second Ben Lomond general building contractor covering the same residential work.

Felton

Dixon Construction (831-335-3162, CSLB #635141, active B) is a Felton general building contractor handling remodels, additions, decks, and new construction across the valley. Oliveira & Sons (831-239-9655, CSLB #940607, active B) is a second Felton general building contractor for residential construction and remodeling.

What This Roster Covers, and What It Doesn't

Every contractor above holds a general building classification, the right license for whole-house work: builds, additions, remodels, and the structural pieces around them. That's a deep bench for a small mountain community, and it's an advantage. A builder who already knows valley soils, steep access, septic setbacks, and storm-season scheduling starts ahead of one who doesn't.

Two gaps to plan around:

  • Roofing: For a reroof, Christopher A New Roofing (CSLB #668255, C-39, Ben Lomond, 831-336-3553) has held a roofing license here since 1993 and is the closest dedicated roofer to town. Beyond that the local list is thin, so a general builder's subcontractor may be the other route.
  • Flooring: No flooring contractor is based in the valley, so plan to bring one in from the wider county for flooring-specific jobs.

Several of the general contractors above take on remodels that include roofing and flooring scopes, so ask directly whether the job you have fits under their license and their crew, or whether they'll subcontract it.

Also worth remembering: the general building license isn't the license for every job. Septic work is a C-42 classification, wells are C-57, and tree work is C-49, as we cover in the hiring-a-contractor guide and the tree-work questions guide. If a bid's scope doesn't match the license's classification, that's your cue to keep asking.

Before You Hire Any of Them

Being valley-based is a real plus, but it doesn't replace the checks.

  • Verify the license. Look up each contractor in the CSLB license lookup and confirm status, classification, and workers' compensation.
  • Get three written bids on identical plans.
  • Watch the deposit. Never put down more than $1,000 or 10 percent of the contract price, whichever is less.
  • Ask the mountain questions that reveal local experience, about your septic system, slope drainage, well or district water, and winter scheduling.

The full checklist, including how Santa Cruz County permits work on unincorporated parcels, is in our hiring-a-contractor guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many general contractors are based in the San Lorenzo Valley?

More than we've written up. This page covers 14 general building contractors based in Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, or Felton, most with an active California "B" license, and the CSLB database lists valley builders we haven't added yet. New businesses appear and licenses change, so confirm any contractor's current status in the CSLB lookup before hiring.

What license should a general contractor have for my remodel or addition?

For whole-house work like remodels, additions, and new builds, the right classification is a "B" General Building license, which every contractor on this page holds. Specialty scopes carry their own classifications, such as C-42 for septic, C-57 for wells, C-39 for roofing, and C-49 for tree work. Check that the license classification matches the job in the CSLB lookup.

Are there local roofers and flooring contractors in the valley?

Dedicated valley-based roofing contractors are thin, and there's no flooring specialist based in the valley, so those jobs may mean bringing someone in from the wider county or asking one of the general contractors here who they use. Several of these general builders take on remodels that include roofing and flooring scopes; ask directly whether your job fits their license and crew.

How do I check a contractor's license and deposit rules?

Use the free CSLB license lookup to confirm status, classifications, bond, and workers' compensation. On a California home improvement contract, the down payment is capped at $1,000 or 10 percent of the price, whichever is less, and later payments can't run ahead of the work done. A request for a large sum up front is a serious red flag. Our hiring-a-contractor guide covers the money and permit rules in full.

Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, just a verified place to start. Browse the full directory for local trades, read the hiring-a-contractor guide before you sign anything, and send corrections or additions through the submit page so the next neighbor gets accurate information.

gyms-near-boulder-creek.title: The Closest Gyms to Boulder Creek, Compared
gyms-near-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • In town: no weight room, but more than nothing. Mountain Sangha for yoga and movement, Treetop Pilates for mat and reformer work, Lone Wolf Kenpo for karate, plus a slate of rec district classes and a summer pool.
  • Closest real gym: SCM Community Fitness in Felton, about 15 minutes down Highway 9, for coached strength and conditioning.
  • Weight room and 24/7 access: Scotts Valley Gym, roughly 25 minutes.
  • Childcare while you train: Toadal Fitness in Scotts Valley.
  • A pool, courts, and the most under one roof: Enterprise Sports Club in Scotts Valley.
  • Drive times are ballpark. Highway 9 traffic, weather, and road work all move them, so give yourself margin.

You can walk to a yoga class, a Pilates reformer, and a karate mat in Boulder Creek. You can't walk to a squat rack.

There's no full gym in town, so a weight room or machines means a drive down Highway 9. The closest of those is about 15 minutes out in Felton, with a bigger cluster around 25 minutes on in Scotts Valley.

Here's what exists and roughly how far it is, grouped by drive time from downtown Boulder Creek. Those drive times bend with traffic, weather, and whatever mood Highway 9 is in, so treat them as ballpark, not a schedule.

In town

Boulder Creek has no weight room, but "nothing in town" is wrong. There are three fitness businesses here plus a full slate of classes at the rec district, and in summer there's a pool.

Mountain Sangha (Boulder Creek)

  • Address: 12788 Highway 9, Suite 1, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-217-3018
  • Hours: Monday through Friday 6 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., Saturday and Sunday 8 a.m. to 1 p.m.; the class schedule controls access

A community yoga and movement studio with regular classes, workshops, and wellness programs. It isn't a gym in the weights-and-machines sense, so set expectations accordingly. Access follows the posted class schedule, so check what's on before you go.

Treetop Pilates and Wellness (Boulder Creek)

  • Address: 125 Forest Street, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-419-0202, or 831-421-1224

A classical Pilates studio with mat, tower, and reformer work, running private lessons and small classes rather than open-floor time. Call to schedule. If you're looking for structured, low-impact strength work, this is the closest thing to it in town, and it's a walk from downtown.

Lone Wolf Kenpo Academy (Boulder Creek)

  • Address: 13089 Highway 9, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-703-4372
  • Website: karatebouldercreek.com

A kenpo karate school right downtown, teaching a range of ages, open Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 8:45 p.m. Alongside karate it runs cardio kickboxing and pilates, and it posts free women's self-defense classes. Call for the current class schedule rather than turning up cold. For families, a martial arts class in town beats driving to a gym with childcare twice a week.

Classes at the rec district

The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District runs the closest thing in town to a group-class schedule, and several are free. Most meet at the downtown rec center at 13333 Middleton Avenue:

  • Jazzercise, Monday to Friday 8:30 to 9:30 a.m., Saturday and Sunday 9 to 10 a.m., Monday 5:45 p.m., and Tuesday and Thursday 6 to 7 p.m. Conditioning, aerobics, and toning to choreography that's built to be easy to pick up.
  • Body sculpting, Monday, Wednesday, and Thursday 7 to 8 a.m., free, with Beatrice White and Arcelia Rudy. Bring your own weights and mat.
  • Morning yoga with Joan Donato, Mondays 11 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., $8 a class on a six-week commitment or $10 to drop in. Bring a mat and a bolster.
  • Adult recess, Sundays 11:45 a.m., women 18 and over. Bodyweight strength, balance work, rope climbing, and no pretence of seriousness. Beginners welcome.
  • Adult indoor soccer Thursdays 7 to 9 p.m. and ping pong Tuesdays 7:30 to 9 p.m., both free and community-run.

Two more meet up at Bear Creek, 15685 Forest Hill Drive: pickleball on Tuesdays and Thursdays 2 to 5 p.m. for $3, and water fitness in the pool on Mondays 5:30 to 6:30 p.m., which runs in registered sessions rather than drop-in. The lineup rotates and most classes are run by an individual instructor, so check the district's page for the current schedule, fees, and who to contact.

The pool, in summer

The district's pool at 15685 Forest Hill Drive runs roughly June through late September, closed Mondays, with adult swim in the mornings and evenings, rec swim through the afternoons, and a hot tub. Out of season, a pool does mean a drive.

About 15 minutes: Felton

SCM Community Fitness (Felton)

  • Address: 6500 Highway 9, Felton
  • Phone: 831-334-0264
  • Hours: Monday through Friday 6 a.m. to 6:30 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m. to 11 a.m., closed Sunday

SCM Community Fitness is the closest thing to a true gym to Boulder Creek, a functional-fitness gym running CrossFit-style group classes that combine strength training, conditioning, and mobility work, plus yoga sessions. It's coached group training rather than an open floor you wander into alone, which suits people who want structure and someone counting on them to show up. At roughly 15 minutes down Highway 9, it's the nearest strength-and-conditioning option.

San Lorenzo Valley Martial Arts (Felton)

  • Address: 6116 Highway 9, Suite 2B, Felton
  • Phone: 831-704-7924
  • Hours: not confirmed. At least one online listing shows it as closed, so call before you drive down.

If your idea of a workout involves a heavy bag, San Lorenzo Valley Martial Arts offers Tae Kwon Do for all ages, plus cardio kickboxing, Tabata bootcamp, and after-school programs. That mix works for families as well as adults who want a conditioning class that isn't a standard gym. The schedule leans afternoon and evening, so check the class times against your own.

Oakstrong Martial Arts (Felton)

  • Address: 6191 Highway 9, at the Felton Community Hall
  • Website: oakstrong.net
  • Hours: Tuesday 5:30 p.m. to 7 p.m. (Basic Karate and Self-Defense), Thursday 5:30 p.m. to 7 p.m. (open gym and office hours), Saturday 10 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. (Karate, Weapons and Self-Defense)

Oakstrong Martial Arts is a Tang Soo Do karate school teaching self-defense and weapons classes for teens and adults out of the Felton Community Hall. It runs a limited weekly class schedule rather than open hours, so think of it as a set of standing classes to join, not a drop-in facility. For adults who want a disciplined martial-arts track close to home, it's the nearest of its kind.

About 25 minutes: Scotts Valley

Scotts Valley Gym (Scotts Valley)

  • Address: 105 Whispering Pines Drive, Scotts Valley
  • Phone: 831-332-5555
  • Hours: 24/7 member access, with staffed hours posted on site

Scotts Valley Gym is a strength and powerlifting gym with Rogue equipment, personal training, and small-group coaching, open around the clock to members. If you want a serious weight room and the freedom to train at 5 a.m. or 10 p.m., this is the closest 24/7 access to Boulder Creek. The tradeoff is the drive, roughly 25 minutes each way.

Toadal Fitness Scotts Valley (Scotts Valley)

  • Address: 269 Mount Hermon Road, Scotts Valley
  • Phone: 831-430-9200
  • Hours: Monday through Friday 6 a.m. to 8 p.m., Saturday and Sunday 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Toadal Fitness is a family-oriented full-service health club with group classes and a supervised kids area for ages 3 months to 12 years. For parents, that childcare is the whole argument, since it's rare this close to the valley. Otherwise it's a broad general-membership club, covering most everyday fitness under one roof.

MADabolic Scotts Valley (Scotts Valley)

  • Address: 262 Mount Hermon Road, Suite 101, Scotts Valley
  • Phone: 831-202-5234
  • Website: madabolic.com

MADabolic is a strength-driven interval training studio built around structured work-to-rest ratios, and it's noted as the franchise's first California location. Like SCM Community Fitness, it's coached class training rather than an open gym floor, aimed at people who want the session programmed for them. We don't have its current class hours confirmed, so check the website or call before planning a visit.

Enterprise Sports Club (Scotts Valley)

  • Address: 100 Enterprise Way, Suite G100, Scotts Valley
  • Phone: 831-920-0912
  • Hours: Monday through Friday 5:30 a.m. to 9 p.m., Saturday and Sunday 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Enterprise Sports Club is the largest facility on this list, a 26,000-square-foot athletic club with exercise equipment, group fitness classes, personal training, a heated outdoor pool, a spa and sauna, and tennis, pickleball, and basketball courts. It was a private employee club before opening to the public in 2020. If you want the most under one roof and don't mind the drive, this is the full-service end of the spectrum.

How to think about the drive

A real gym means leaving Boulder Creek. There's no arranging around that.

For the shortest trip and a strength-and-conditioning focus, Felton's SCM Community Fitness is the closest bet at about 15 minutes. For a traditional weight room, 24/7 access, childcare, or a pool, the Scotts Valley cluster at roughly 25 minutes covers every style. And if you'd rather not drive at all, Mountain Sangha keeps a yoga practice available in town.

The right pick is whichever one you'll use often enough to justify the miles.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a gym in Boulder Creek?

Not a full gym. Mountain Sangha does yoga and movement, Treetop Pilates does mat, tower, and reformer work, and Lone Wolf Kenpo Academy teaches karate, all in town. The rec district runs adult classes including Jazzercise, body sculpting, yoga, and pickleball, and its pool is open in summer. For a weight room and machines, the nearest options are Felton, about 15 minutes away, and Scotts Valley, roughly 25 minutes.

What's the closest gym to Boulder Creek?

SCM Community Fitness in Felton, at about a 15-minute drive down Highway 9. It's a functional-fitness gym with coached CrossFit-style classes rather than an open-floor gym, so it suits people who want structured group training.

Which nearby gym has childcare or a pool?

For childcare, Toadal Fitness in Scotts Valley has a supervised kids area for ages 3 months to 12 years. For a pool, Enterprise Sports Club in Scotts Valley has a heated outdoor pool along with a spa, sauna, and courts. Both are about a 25-minute drive from downtown Boulder Creek.

Are the drive times exact?

No, they're approximate. 15 minutes to Felton and 25 to Scotts Valley are typical estimates from downtown Boulder Creek under normal conditions, but Highway 9 traffic, weather, and road work all change that. Give yourself margin, especially in winter.

Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, just a verified place to start. For what's in Boulder Creek itself, from pilates to hot yoga, see fitness and movement in town. See the full business directory for contact details, and send corrections or new listings through the submit page so this stays accurate for the next neighbor.

halloween-downtown-boulder-creek.title: Downtown Boulder Creek Trick-or-Treat
halloween-downtown-boulder-creek.html:
On Halloween evening the sidewalk along Highway 9 fills up with costumed kids, costumed parents, and a good number of costumed dogs. Instead of sending families down long, dark mountain driveways, downtown Boulder Creek turns its main street into one walkable trick-or-treat route.

Merchants hand out candy in the early evening, usually from about 5 to 7 p.m., and volunteers help families cross the highway. The Boulder Creek Business Association and the town's merchants run it. The reason it exists is a mountain one: homes up here sit too far apart for door-to-door, so the town brings the candy to one strip instead.

This year (2026)

Halloween 2026 falls on Saturday, October 31. In past years the downtown trick-or-treat has run from about 5 to 7 p.m. along Highway 9, hosted by the Boulder Creek Business Association and downtown merchants.

The exact hours, participating businesses, and any after-event activities are usually confirmed closer to the date. For this year's confirmed times and details, watch the Boulder Creek Business Association.

What to expect

The evening keeps a simple shape. Downtown businesses along Highway 9 prop their doors open and hand out candy, and families work the strip storefront by storefront. Over 20 downtown merchants have taken part in recent years, and the Press Banner has named stops like The Adventure Gift Store, Air and Fire, Boulder Creek Outfitters, Treasures from the Attic, Viscosity, lille aeske, and the Springy Girl among them. That roster shifts year to year, so treat those as examples rather than a guaranteed list.

The crowd is wider than the kids. Adults dress up, dogs get dressed up, and some years there are activities afterward at the Boulder Creek Recreation Hall behind the firehouse. The whole thing is compact and walkable, which suits short legs and early bedtimes.

I did this walk every Halloween of my childhood, and the two things I remember are the two things kids still get: the candy, obviously, and the shop owners you see all year suddenly out on the sidewalk in costume. Half the fun was working out who was under the makeup.

Crossing Highway 9

The trick-or-treat happens right along Highway 9, in the early evening as the light goes, and traffic keeps moving through downtown the whole time. A few habits keep it manageable:

  • Cross at the crossing points, not mid-block, and give yourself extra time as it gets dark.
  • Keep younger kids by the hand. For years the Valley Women's Club of San Lorenzo Valley has stationed volunteer crossing guards to help families across Highway 9, but they're a help, not a substitute for watching your own group.
  • Drivers, slow down. Expect kids on the street through the early evening.

If there's ever a real emergency, call 911.

History

The downtown trick-or-treat has a clear reason to exist. As one merchant told the Press Banner, "in the mountains, homes are spaced too far apart, and kids are not safe to go trick-or-treating," so the merchants gather the candy into one downtown strip instead. It's become an annual event run by the Business Association and the town's shops.

The safety side of it has a history of its own. The Valley Women's Club says it has been "conjuring safety and smiles in downtown Boulder Creek since 1985," standing at the Highway 9 crossings so generations of kids could get across. We haven't found a verified first year for the trick-or-treat itself, and we're not going to guess one, but the crossing-guard tradition alone goes back four decades.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Boulder Creek downtown trick-or-treat?

It's on Halloween, October 31, every year. In past years it has run from about 5 to 7 p.m. For the coming year's confirmed hours, check the Boulder Creek Business Association.

Where is it?

Along Highway 9 in downtown Boulder Creek. Downtown merchants hand out candy from their storefronts, and families walk the strip.

Is it safe to cross Highway 9 with kids?

The event runs on a working highway in the evening, so treat it with care: cross at the crossing points, hold little ones' hands, and go slow as it gets dark. The Valley Women's Club has provided volunteer crossing guards since 1985 to help families across Highway 9, and drivers should expect kids on the street. Watch your own group, and call 911 for any emergency.

Which businesses hand out candy?

Over 20 downtown businesses have taken part in recent years, and the list changes annually. Past coverage has named The Adventure Gift Store, Air and Fire, Boulder Creek Outfitters, Treasures from the Attic, Viscosity, lille aeske, and the Springy Girl, among others.

Why not trick-or-treat around the neighborhood?

Mountain homes are spread far apart, which makes door-to-door trick-or-treating hard and, as local merchants put it, less safe. The downtown event gathers the candy into one walkable place so families can do it together.

Planning your October? See what else is on the calendar on the Boulder Creek Local events page. Hosting something, or spot a detail here that needs fixing? Send it to us. For this event's official source, check the Boulder Creek Business Association.

healthcare-near-boulder-creek.title: Healthcare Near Boulder Creek: Pharmacy, Urgent Care, and the Nearest ER
healthcare-near-boulder-creek.html:
If you're new to the mountain, sort this out before you ever need it: there's no hospital, emergency room, or urgent care anywhere in the San Lorenzo Valley. Care is real, but most of it is down the highway, and the drive is longer than newcomers expect. The time to learn where it all is isn't the night you're bleeding or your kid swallows something.

Here's where the care is, how far, and who to call first.

The short version

  • Real emergency: call 911 and let them come to you. Don't drive yourself over Highway 9 and Highway 17.
  • Pharmacy in town: Boulder Creek Pharmacy, 13081 Central Avenue, 831-338-2144, with free delivery throughout the valley.
  • Primary care in the valley: Santa Cruz Mountain Health Center in Ben Lomond, by appointment, 831-427-3500.
  • Nearest walk-in urgent care: Santa Cruz, about a 30-minute drive. Kaiser members have one closer, in Scotts Valley.
  • Nearest 24-hour ER: Dominican Hospital in Santa Cruz, roughly 30 to 40 minutes away.
  • Poisoning or overdose: California Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222, free and staffed 24 hours.

This guide doesn't diagnose anything or promise that any provider can see you. It points you to where care is and how far. Hours and details change, so treat each link as the source of truth.

Call 911 first for a real emergency

Some things don't wait for a drive to Santa Cruz. Call 911 right away for chest pain or pressure, signs of a stroke (face drooping, arm weakness, or slurred and difficult speech), severe or uncontrolled bleeding, or trouble breathing.

Up here, where the nearest ER is a good half hour away on a clear day, that call matters more than it did wherever you lived before. Paramedics can start care at your door, get you to the right hospital faster than you can, and radio ahead. Don't talk yourself out of it, and don't get behind the wheel with a sick passenger if it's serious.

For a possible poisoning, an accidental overdose, or a "what did the toddler just swallow" moment, the California Poison Control System is free, staffed by pharmacists and physicians, and open 24 hours a day at 1-800-222-1222. It's worth putting in your phone right now.

The pharmacy in town

You don't have to leave Boulder Creek to fill a prescription. Boulder Creek Pharmacy is an independent pharmacy at 13081 Central Avenue, open weekdays 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Saturday 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed Sunday. The number is 831-338-2144.

The part that matters most when you live up a long driveway: they deliver free throughout the San Lorenzo Valley, and they've extended complimentary delivery to Felton and Scotts Valley for former Rite Aid customers. If you'd rather not drive down the valley sick, or you're caring for someone who can't, a local pharmacy that brings the medicine to you is a genuine asset.

Primary care in the valley

For the ordinary stuff, checkups, a nagging cough, managing an ongoing condition, there's a community clinic without leaving the valley. Santa Cruz Mountain Health Center, run by the nonprofit Santa Cruz Community Health, sits at 231 Main Street, Suite A, in Ben Lomond, a few minutes south on Highway 9. It's open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. (closed 11 to noon for lunch), with Saturday morning hours offered at the group's Live Oak location. The number is 831-427-3500.

They handle primary care for adults and kids, prenatal care, and behavioral health, and they accept Medi-Cal, Medicare, and most commercial plans, with a sliding scale for people without insurance. It runs by appointment, so call to book rather than dropping in.

One thing to be clear about: this is a primary-care clinic, not an urgent care and not an emergency room. It's the right call for a scheduled visit or an ongoing health need, not for a middle-of-the-night crisis.

The nearest urgent care

When it's more than a phone call to the doctor but less than a 911 emergency, a sprain, a deep cut that might need stitches, a fever that won't quit, you're driving down the highway for a walk-in urgent care. There isn't one in the valley, so plan on a longer drive than you might expect. Sutter Health closed its Scotts Valley walk-in urgent care in 2021, but two others in Santa Cruz are open to the general public.

Doctors on Duty is at 615 Ocean Street, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. and weekends 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., at 831-425-7991. Sutter's Westside Center urgent care is at 1301 Mission Street, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. and weekends 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., at 831-458-6310, which makes it the later option if something flares up in the evening. Either is roughly a thirty-minute drive down Highway 9 and Highway 17. Call before you go, especially late in the day, since hours shift.

If you're a Kaiser Permanente member, Kaiser runs urgent care closer, at its Scotts Valley Medical Offices, 5615 Scotts Valley Drive (2nd floor), about twenty minutes down Highway 9, at 831-430-2700, with a 24-hour advice line for members at 831-430-2740. Kaiser members can walk in without an appointment, and it's open weekdays 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. and weekends and holidays 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Hours can change, so confirm through Kaiser before heading over.

The nearest emergency room

For anything that needs a real emergency room, broken bones, deep wounds, severe pain, a bad reaction, chest or breathing trouble that a paramedic tells you to bring in, the closest ER is in Santa Cruz. Dignity Health's Dominican Hospital has an emergency room at 1555 Soquel Drive that's open 24 hours a day, every day, with specially trained teams for stroke and heart care. The hospital's number is 831-462-7700. From Boulder Creek, plan on thirty to forty minutes down Highway 9 and Highway 17, longer in traffic or bad weather.

There's a second 24-hour ER farther south at Watsonville Community Hospital, 75 Nielson Street, at 831-724-4741. It's a longer drive, closer to an hour, so for most Boulder Creek residents Dominican is the practical choice. Either way, if it's a genuine emergency, the fastest route to an ER is often the ambulance, not your own car. Call 911.

Telehealth and the nurse-line question

There's no telehealth service that belongs to the valley, but you may already have one and not know it. Most health plans include a nurse advice line and video visits, which are the fastest way to get a real answer at 10 p.m. without a drive.

Kaiser members have that 24-hour advice line at 831-430-2740. Sutter and PAMF patients can do video visits through My Health Online. Check your insurance card and your plan's app; the option is usually there, and it can save you a trip down the highway or tell you when it's time to make one.

The bottom line on distance

None of this is meant to scare anyone off mountain living. It's the trade you make for the redwoods: care is real, but it's down the highway.

A few habits close most of the gap. Keep the pharmacy's number and the poison line in your phone. Know that walk-in urgent care and the ER are both down in Santa Cruz, with Kaiser members closer in Scotts Valley. And keep a small first-aid kit and any critical medications stocked at home, along with a plan for when the power goes out, so a minor thing doesn't become a midnight drive. For the serious stuff, 911 is always the right first move.

Save these numbers before you need them, and see the Residents guide for the rest of the mountain's essential contacts, from utilities to county services. If you haven't built one yet, our power-outage plan is a good companion for anyone relying on refrigerated medications or medical equipment up here.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there an urgent care in Boulder Creek?

No. There's no urgent care, emergency room, or hospital anywhere in the San Lorenzo Valley. The nearest walk-in urgent cares open to everyone are Doctors on Duty (615 Ocean Street) and Sutter's Westside Center (1301 Mission Street), both in Santa Cruz, about thirty minutes down the highway; Kaiser members have one closer, in Scotts Valley. The nearest 24-hour ER is Dominican Hospital in Santa Cruz.

Where's the closest emergency room to Boulder Creek?

Dignity Health's Dominican Hospital at 1555 Soquel Drive in Santa Cruz has a 24-hour ER, roughly thirty to forty minutes away. Watsonville Community Hospital also has a 24-hour ER, but it's a longer drive. For a true emergency, call 911 rather than driving yourself.

Does the Boulder Creek pharmacy deliver?

Yes. Boulder Creek Pharmacy, at 13081 Central Avenue, delivers free throughout the San Lorenzo Valley, and it has extended free delivery to Felton and Scotts Valley for former Rite Aid customers. Call 831-338-2144.

Is there a doctor's office in the valley?

Yes. Santa Cruz Mountain Health Center in Ben Lomond offers primary care for adults and children, takes Medi-Cal and most insurance, and has a sliding scale for the uninsured. It's appointment-based at 831-427-3500. It's a primary-care clinic, not an urgent care or ER.

What should I do for a poisoning or if my kid swallows something?

Call the California Poison Control System at 1-800-222-1222. It's free, open 24 hours, and staffed by pharmacists and physicians. If the person is unconscious, not breathing, or having a seizure, call 911 first.

For the dentist, chiropractor, and other providers working right in town, see health services in Boulder Creek.

highway-9-construction-boulder-creek.title: What Is All the Construction on Highway 9?
highway-9-construction-boulder-creek.html:
You come around the bend north of town and there it is: a temporary signal glowing red over a single open lane, a line of cars idling, and somebody's truck up ahead already three-quarters of the way through a podcast. That's the bridge job.

Caltrans is rebuilding the aging San Lorenzo River and Kings Creek bridges one half at a time, which is why you're stopped at a signal on a one-way stretch. It's a different project from the planned work downtown to widen sidewalks and calm traffic through the middle of town, which is still in the design and funding stage. Conditions change week to week, so check Caltrans QuickMap before you drive, and see Mountain Status for live road links.

The bridge replacement (the work happening now)

The big one is the State Route 9 San Lorenzo River and Kings Creek Bridge Replacement, a Caltrans project a couple of miles north of downtown Boulder Creek. Both bridges have run out of road. Caltrans describes the San Lorenzo River bridge as roughly 80 years old and the Kings Creek bridge as roughly 90, both past the typical 75-year service life and found to be structurally deficient. Rather than patch them, Caltrans is replacing both.

Highway 9 is the only real route here, so crews can't close it and start over. They're rebuilding each bridge one half at a time, starting with the southbound side, and running traffic on the remaining lane. That's what the temporary signals at the bridges are for: they've been holding one-way reversing traffic under 24/7 signal control while work continues. Expect to wait your turn, and expect that wait to be longer at busy times.

Every so often the work needs a full overnight closure. On the night of July 1, 2026, Caltrans closed Highway 9 near the Kings Creek bridge from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. so crews could set the heavy precast girders for the new southbound span, with a detour routed via Highway 17. An overnight closure with a detour usually means the crew is doing something big and precise, like setting girders, that can't happen with traffic moving through.

The downtown project (coming, not yet built)

The second thing people lump in as "the Highway 9 construction" is the Boulder Creek Complete Streets project, and it's a different animal: it's about downtown, and it hasn't started building yet. It grew out of the 2019 Highway 9 San Lorenzo Valley Complete Streets Corridor Plan and focuses on the stretch through town between River Street and Bear Creek Road. The plan includes:

  • Wider sidewalks through downtown
  • Enhanced crosswalks with curb extensions to shorten the crossing distance
  • Gateway median islands to slow cars entering town
  • A look at whether a stop sign belongs at Highway 9 and Bear Creek Road

It has partial funding lined up, including $1.5 million secured by Representative Anna Eshoo, now paying for environmental review and initial design, and $850,000 in federal funding secured by Representative Jimmy Panetta and announced in Boulder Creek in March 2026 for the next phase of preconstruction, plus anticipated matching money from voter-approved Measure D. But it's still in environmental review and design, with staff pursuing additional grant funding to carry it through to construction. Real, funded in part, and coming. Not the thing tearing up the road right now.

What to expect when you drive it

Treat the bridge area as a chokepoint. Give yourself extra time, expect to stop at the signal, and don't count on squeezing through quickly at commute hours or on weekends when the valley fills up.

A practical note from one family's experience: the stop-and-go through the work zone can add a solid twenty minutes to a drive down the valley, and if you have a passenger prone to carsickness, plan for it. Our baby handles the mountain curves fine and the idling crawl not at all, and we've pulled over more than once just past the cones for a full cleanup and change. Pack accordingly, time your trips around the work windows if you can, and know that the finished project will be worth the season of patience.

Overnight closures come and go with the work, so if you're driving late, check for a closure and detour first. And because Highway 9 is the lifeline in and out of Boulder Creek, a single incident here can back things up fast, which is all the more reason to check conditions before you leave.

For anything time-sensitive, the live sources beat any article:

  • Caltrans QuickMap, live closures and cameras
  • Caltrans District 5 news, the weekly Highway 9 notices
  • Santa Cruz County road closures dashboard
  • Our Mountain Status page, which pulls these together

Frequently asked questions

Why is Highway 9 down to one lane near Boulder Creek?

Caltrans is replacing the aging San Lorenzo River and Kings Creek bridges just north of town, rebuilding each one half at a time. A temporary signal holds one-way traffic on the open lane while crews work. Check QuickMap for the current status.

How long will the Highway 9 bridge work take?

Caltrans lists the job as running from August 2025 to March 2028. Schedules on work like this move with weather and materials, so treat that as the plan, not a promise. Watch Caltrans District 5 news for schedule updates.

Is the downtown sidewalk project the same thing?

No. The Boulder Creek Complete Streets project (wider sidewalks, crosswalks, and traffic calming through downtown) is a separate effort that's still in environmental review and design. It hasn't begun construction.

Will Highway 9 be closed overnight again?

Possibly. Caltrans schedules occasional full overnight closures, with a detour, for work that can't happen with traffic moving, like setting bridge girders. Check for closures before driving late, and watch Caltrans notices.

For live conditions, always check Mountain Status and Caltrans QuickMap before you go. For the wider picture on getting around the valley, permits, and county contacts, see the Residents guide. Notice a change on the road we haven't caught? Tell us. In an emergency, call 911. Last reviewed August 12, 2026.

highway-9-winter-storms-boulder-creek.title: What to Know About Highway 9 During Winter Storms
highway-9-winter-storms-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Check before you drive. Use Caltrans QuickMap and our Mountain Status page for live closures. This page never tells you a road is open; only the official trackers do.
  • Never drive through water or around a barricade. Both hide hazards you can't see from the car. Turn around.
  • When a big storm is on, often the safest move is not to drive at all. Delaying a trip is usually the right call.
  • Keep the tank at least half full all winter, and carry water, a charger, and warm layers in case the road closes with you on it.
  • Factor in the bridge work north of town, with one-way signal control and occasional overnight closures.

When a real winter storm settles over the San Lorenzo Valley, Highway 9 is the road everyone watches, because it's Boulder Creek's lifeline and also the thing most likely to strand you. It runs the length of the valley through steep, forested, slide-prone terrain, and storms can close it, sometimes with no warning, from flooding, mudslides, downed trees and power lines, or rockfall. Add the ongoing bridge work north of town and there's less slack in the system than usual.

Why Highway 9 is the weak link

There aren't many ways in and out of Boulder Creek. Highway 9 north connects toward Saratoga and south toward Felton and Santa Cruz; Highway 236 loops toward Big Basin; and Highway 17 is the alternate over the hill, reached via other routes. In a bad storm, several of these can be compromised at once.

Because so much traffic funnels onto Highway 9, a single fallen redwood or a flooded low spot can cut the valley off or force long detours, and crews can't always clear it quickly in the middle of a storm.

Right now there's an added pinch point. Caltrans is replacing the San Lorenzo River and Kings Creek bridges north of town, with one-way signal control and occasional overnight closures. In a storm, factor that in.

How to read the risk before you go

  • Check the live trackers. Caltrans QuickMap shows state-highway closures and cameras; the county road dashboard covers county roads. Our Mountain Status page links both.
  • Watch the forecast. A strong atmospheric river or wind event is exactly when closures happen. The National Weather Service is the source.
  • Time it. If you must travel, go before or after the worst of a storm, not during the peak, and give yourself extra time for signals and slow going.

The hard rules

  • Never drive through a flooded road. It takes very little moving water to float or stall a vehicle, and you can't see if the road beneath is washed out. Turn around.
  • Never drive around a barricade or closure sign. They mark real hazards, often a washout or a downed line you can't see from your car.
  • Assume downed lines are live. If a tree or line is across the road, keep back and report it. Don't try to move it.
  • When in doubt, stay home. If a major storm is hitting, delaying a trip is almost always the right call.

If you get cut off

Storms sometimes close the road with people on the wrong side of it. Keep your car's tank at least half full through the winter, carry water, a charger, and warm layers, and have the power-outage and storm basics at home, so being stuck for a while is an inconvenience, not an emergency. After the storm, see what to do after a major storm.

Frequently asked questions

Does Highway 9 close in winter storms?

It can, from flooding, mudslides, downed trees and lines, or rockfall, sometimes with little warning. Always check Caltrans QuickMap before driving; it's the live source.

What are the detour options if Highway 9 closes?

Depending on where the closure is, alternates include Highway 236 and, over the hill, Highway 17, but several routes can be affected at once in a bad storm. Use the live trackers, since the best detour depends on the specific closure.

Is it safe to drive through water on the road?

No. Turn around. Even shallow moving water can sweep a car away or hide a washed-out road. Never drive around a closure barricade either.

This page never tells you a road is open or safe; only the live official trackers do. Check Caltrans QuickMap and Mountain Status before you go, and in an emergency call 911. Last reviewed July 20, 2026.

Storm-ready is a habit, not a single page. Keep the winter storm checklist handy, and find utilities, county contacts, and the rest of the season's prep in the Residents guide. For how the season is running against the long record, see our rain tracker.

hiring-contractor-santa-cruz-mountains.title: Hiring a Contractor in the Santa Cruz Mountains: What's Different Up Here
hiring-contractor-santa-cruz-mountains.html:
The short version

  • Check the license for free at the Contractors State License Board license lookup before anyone sets foot on your property.
  • Get at least three written bids on identical plans, and be wary of the low one; it often means the slope, the access, or the septic setbacks weren't priced.
  • Never put more than $1,000 or 10 percent of the contract price down, whichever is less. A request for half up front is a red flag, not a negotiation.
  • Confirm the license classification matches the job. C-42 for septic, C-12 for grading and driveways, and so on.
  • Ask the mountain questions: where the septic sits, where the water goes, whether they've worked on wells, and what their winter plan is.

Printable version: the hiring a contractor checklist has the licence and insurance questions in an order you can work through with someone standing in your driveway. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

A contractor who does beautiful work in a Willow Glen subdivision can still get in real trouble on a Boulder Creek parcel with a septic system, a steep driveway, and a creek at the bottom of the yard. The license, the deposit rules, and the classifications are the same statewide, but the ways a mountain job goes sideways are not. This isn't legal advice, just a neighbor's checklist for asking better questions before you sign anything.

One piece of advice outranks the rest of this article, and every longtime local will tell you the same thing. Plenty of contractors up here are great people who are not great project managers; the work is fine, but it starts late, drifts past deadlines, and stretches a two-month job across most of a year.
