Parking and getting there

Garrahan Park has limited on-site parking, and Highway 9 runs right through town, so give yourself extra time. If you live close, walking or biking saves the hunt for a spot. Follow any event parking directions on the day.

What to bring

A low chair or blanket, sun protection, and water. Bring cash for anything your ticket doesn't cover, and pack a layer for when the afternoon cools off under the redwoods.

Who it supports

The festival comes from KBCZ, Boulder Creek's volunteer-run community radio station, and it's the station's signature fundraiser. Your ticket helps keep local radio on the air, including the community and emergency information the station provides.

Make an afternoon of it

Garrahan Park sits close to downtown, so it's easy to fold the festival into a longer day. See where to eat in Boulder Creek before or after, and check what else is open in town.

Details change; confirm the date, lineup, and tickets with KBCZ and the Eventbrite listing before you go. Something off here? Tell us. Last reviewed: 2026-07-22.

kids-birthday-party-boulder-creek.title: Planning a Kids Birthday Party in Boulder Creek
kids-birthday-party-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • In town: parks, the community center, and the pool book through the Boulder Creek Recreation & Park District, by application and usually by quote, not online checkout. Downtown office: 831-338-4144.
  • In Felton: Roaring Camp runs package birthday parties. Book through group sales at 831-335-4484, extension 135.
  • Need a roof: rent Felton Community Hall or the Highlands Park center in Ben Lomond, or book a turnkey indoor party at Haven Play Lounge in Scotts Valley.
  • The party comes to you: entertainers, face painters, balloon stylists, and bounce-house companies deliver up the hill. Most are county-wide, so call to confirm they reach your address and ask about any distance fee.
  • Keep it local: custom cakes and kids gifts are both available from Boulder Creek shops.

Throwing a kids party up here used to mean a drive out of the valley. It doesn't anymore. In town you can reserve a park or the community center; in Felton, Roaring Camp runs package parties; and if you want a full-service play venue, there's one a short drive out in Scotts Valley or Santa Cruz. The rest of it travels to you now, from face painters and entertainers to balloon stylists and bounce houses.

One thing to sort out before you build a plan around a date: most in-town spots book by application or by phone, not by clicking a button, and several don't post flat prices, so you'll be asking for a quote. What follows is where to reserve, how each place books, and then cake, entertainment, balloons, and rentals. Being listed here isn't an endorsement, only a place to start.

Where to Reserve in Town

The Boulder Creek Recreation & Park District (BCRPD) handles reservations for in-town party spots. It rents Junction Park, Garrahan Park, the Bear Creek Community Center, and the Downtown Rec Center, plus the Bear Creek pool.

There's a sequence to it: read the posted rental policy first (the pool has its own separate rules), then submit the rental application. BCRPD doesn't publish flat fees online, so expect a quote. The downtown office answers at 831-338-4144 (Tuesday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.); the Bear Creek office is at 831-703-4135. Current forms are at bcrpd.org/rentals.

Junction Park is the default outdoor pick, a downtown riverside park with a small beach, river access, lawn, and picnic facilities. Garrahan Park on Highway 9 has a walking track, play structures, a gazebo, and a barbecue area. Both open sunrise to sunset, and both run through the same BCRPD application. Pool parties come with one gate: read the pool rental policy before you apply, so start there if water's the plan.

Roaring Camp Party Packages (Felton)

Roaring Camp Railroads at 5401 Graham Hill Road in Felton (831-335-4484) runs two birthday packages. The outdoor picnic package covers party favors (paper hats and train whistles) for up to 28 kids, an engineer's cap for the birthday child, and up to six checkered picnic tables. The train package adds a Roaring Camp engineer hat and scarf for the honoree plus 28 train tickets for a scheduled train.

Add-ons run to face painting, puppet shows, gold panning, candle making, and a bounce house. Book through group sales at 831-335-4484, extension 135; pricing is quote-on-request. It's a longtime valley fixture, and it books ahead in peak season.

Indoor and Rain-Proof Options

When you need a roof, the valley's community halls rent out for parties. Felton Community Hall at 6191 Highway 9 (831-335-5621) has been a Felton institution since 1926, and it rents its auditorium and meeting room. Email reservations@feltonhall.org or call, check the online calendar, then complete the rental agreement, policies, and required event insurance. The kitchen comes only with a room rental, and nonprofits get a discount.

A little farther down the road, the Highlands Park Senior & Community Center at 8500 Highway 9 in Ben Lomond (831-336-8900) rents reasonably priced rooms and welcomes all ages, not seniors only. Rates are by inquiry at seniorcenterslv8500@gmail.com.

For a full-service indoor party with almost nothing to set up, Haven Play Lounge and Cafe in Scotts Valley (108 Whispering Pines Drive, Suite 125; 831-331-7349) runs birthday and event packages of two, three, or four hours for ages 0 to 10, with decor, cleaning, and food handled by the venue. It's the closest turnkey indoor-play option, about 25 minutes down the valley, and hours vary by day, so confirm party availability directly.

And Camp Harmon on Highway 9 in Boulder Creek (831-338-3383), the Easterseals accessible camp, arranges group and facility use; for an accessible outdoor setting, ask them directly whether party rentals fit their calendar.

Full-Service Party Venues (a short drive)

If you'd rather book a package and let the venue do the work, a handful of spots are worth the drive down the valley. Closest is Vargas Academy in Scotts Valley (831-438-8242), a gymnastics and parkour gym whose parties include an in-gym bounce house, gym apparatus, decorated tables, and staff coaches.

In Santa Cruz, JuneBugs Gym (831-464-2847) and the Santa Cruz Gymnastics Center both run coach-led gymnastics parties with foam pits and obstacle courses, the Santa Cruz Roller Palladium does roller-skating parties, and Kianti's Pizza & Pasta Bar (831-469-4400) runs a pizza-making party with a kitchen tour and a dough-spinning lesson. For a bigger group, the Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk has party packages for bowling, Neptune's Kingdom mini-golf and arcade, and laser tag. Confirm ages, minimums, and dates when you book.

Cake and Treats

The cake itself has real options in town. Dessert First Bakery makes custom celebration cakes, cupcakes, and cookies to order; it has no shopfront, so contact it through its own page rather than turning up. Butter Late Than Never Baking Co. is a licensed Boulder Creek cottage bakery that takes custom orders (510-390-5548), and Wildstone Bakery turns out naturally fermented breads and pastries you can catch at regional farmers markets.

Entertainment

Entertainment used to be the hard part in the valley, and it isn't anymore. One company lists the San Lorenzo Valley right in its service area, which is the line you're hoping to find. Special Memories Children's Entertainment names Boulder Creek, Felton, Ben Lomond, and Scotts Valley, and it brings costumed characters, magicians, puppet shows, exotic-animal and reptile shows, pony rides, and balloon twisting, enough to cover most of a party in one booking.

Plenty of solid Santa Cruz companies serve the wider county without naming the valley specifically, so book them the way you'd book any of them: call first, and confirm they'll drive to your address. Those include Santa Cruz Party Company (clowns, princesses, magic, face paint, balloons), Happily Ever Laughter (characters, magic, puppets, sing-alongs), the Surfing Magician (a Santa Cruz magic show with a live rabbit), Fiesta Face Paint, SmileyOrca Facepaint & Henna, Brenda's Face Painting, and Primal Henna Arts.

For an animal theme, Pet Shop Santa Cruz (831-429-1242) brings reptiles and animals to parties and classrooms, and Tails of Redwood Trails in Felton runs horse and farm-animal experiences and travels through the valley. And Roaring Camp, again, bundles its own entertainers into its party packages if you want it all in one place.

Balloons and Decor

For balloons and styling, Luzovich Celebrations handles custom balloon work and party decor (831-818-5407, luzovichcelebrations@gmail.com). Bash Works (831-234-0530) does balloon garlands, arches, and marquee letters, and it also rents bounce houses, so it can pull double duty. And Aesthetic Events & Co. does balloon garlands plus party and sleepover rentals.

Party Rentals and Bounce Houses

Bounce houses, tents, tables, and chairs are the other piece to line up early. A few Santa Cruz County companies deliver: Astro Jump of Santa Cruz (831-475-5055), Santa Cruz Bounce House Rentals (831-515-6869), and Bash Works (831-234-0530) all rent inflatables and handle setup and takedown. For tables, chairs, and tents, A to Z Party Rental is a longtime Central Coast option.

One thing to keep in mind: these are county-wide operators, and delivery up a winding mountain road sometimes carries a distance fee or a minimum order, so confirm delivery to your exact address and ZIP before you count on it.

Gifts From Local Shops

The gift can stay local too. Boulder Creek's downtown shops carry toys, books, and kid-friendly finds, and our directory lists the current retailers in town. Buying the present a few doors from the party keeps the money in the valley and saves you the drive.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I reserve a Boulder Creek park for a birthday party?

Go through the Boulder Creek Recreation & Park District. Review the posted rental policy for the park or facility you want (the pool has its own rules), then submit the rental application. There's no online flat-fee list, so you'll get a quote. Call the downtown office at 831-338-4144 or the Bear Creek office at 831-703-4135, or start at bcrpd.org.

Is there a kids party entertainer who comes to Boulder Creek?

Yes. Special Memories Children's Entertainment lists the San Lorenzo Valley in its service area. Several other Santa Cruz companies, including SmileyOrca Facepaint & Henna and Brenda's Face Painting, serve the wider county and will usually travel up here, so call to confirm they'll come to your address. Roaring Camp also bundles its own entertainers into its party packages.

Where can I rent a bounce house in Boulder Creek?

There's no bounce-house company based in the valley, but Astro Jump of Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz Bounce House Rentals, and Bash Works all deliver in Santa Cruz County. Because Boulder Creek is a longer drive, confirm they deliver to your address and ask about any distance fee or minimum before you book.

What's the best rain-proof party option in the valley?

For an indoor room you set up yourself, rent Felton Community Hall or the Highlands Park Senior & Community Center in Ben Lomond, both of which have kitchens available with a room rental. For a fully handled indoor party, Haven Play Lounge in Scotts Valley runs packages with decor, cleaning, and food included. Confirm dates and policies directly with each.

Where can I order a custom birthday cake in town?

Dessert First Bakery does custom celebration cakes to order, with no shopfront to visit, and Butter Late Than Never Baking Co. is a licensed local cottage bakery taking custom orders. Order ahead, especially for a specific date or design.

Hours, prices, and party availability change, so confirm the details directly with each venue before you book. Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, only a verified place to start. Browse the full directory for local shops and services, keep an eye on the community events calendar for what else is happening around town, and send corrections or additions through the submit page so the next family gets accurate information.

late-summer-wildfire-checklist-boulder-c.title: Late-Summer Wildfire Checklist for Boulder Creek
late-summer-wildfire-checklist-boulder-c.html:
The short version

  • Clear defensible space, closest zones first. Move firewood, mulch, and anything flammable off the house and out from under decks, and clear needles from the roof and gutters. Keep it lean within 30 feet.
  • Harden against embers. Cover vents with fine metal mesh, screen under decks and eaves, and keep the roof and gutters clear. Do the roof, gutters, and vents first.
  • Pack a go-bag now and know two ways out. Highway 9 and Highway 236 carry most of the traffic out, and either can jam or close; Bear Creek Road is another way out.
  • Look up your evacuation zone and sign up for alerts before you need them. Check your address on Genasys Protect, and register for the county's emergency notifications and PG&E outage alerts.
  • When conditions turn dangerous, leave early. The plan in these mountains is to go, not to stay and fight.

Printable version: the defensible space and home hardening checklist covers the yard work here zone by zone, in a form you can carry around the property. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

The work that protects a mountain home from wildfire, clearing defensible space, hardening against embers, packing a go-bag, and knowing your evacuation zone, is the kind you want finished before a red-flag day, not scrambled together during one. Peak fire season in the Santa Cruz Mountains runs through late summer and fall, so the quiet weekends now are the ones to spend on it.

Here's a checklist you can work through over a few weekends. None of it guarantees your home survives a fire. What it does is stack the odds in your favor and buy you time to leave safely. When conditions turn dangerous, the plan is always to go early, not to stay and fight.

Clear your defensible space

CAL FIRE breaks the area around your home into zones, and the closest ones matter most:

  • Zone 0, the first 5 feet (ember-resistant): keep it as non-combustible as you can. Move firewood, wood mulch, dead plants, and anything flammable away from the house and out from under decks. Clear leaves and needles from the roof, gutters, and deck.
  • Zone 1, 5 to 30 feet (lean, clean, and green): remove dead plants and debris, keep grass low, prune tree limbs up off the ground, and don't let branches overhang the roof or touch the house.
  • Zone 2, 30 to 100 feet (reduce fuels): thin vegetation, break up continuous brush, and keep it from forming a fuel ladder from the ground into the trees.

In a redwood canyon that's easier said than done, but even partial work helps. Details and diagrams are at CAL FIRE's Ready for Wildfire.

Harden the house against embers

Most homes that burn in a wildfire are ignited by wind-blown embers, not a wall of flame. The fixes are unglamorous but effective over time: cover vents with fine metal mesh so embers can't get in, keep the roof and gutters free of needles, clear anything flammable off decks, and screen the space under decks and eaves.

You don't have to do it all at once. Do the roof, gutters, and vents first.

Pack a go-bag and plan your exit

Assume you may get very little notice. Keep a go-bag ready with medications, important documents, phone chargers, water, and essentials for everyone in the household, including pets.

Think through CAL FIRE's "6 P's" when you pack:

  • People and pets
  • Papers, phone numbers, and important documents
  • Prescriptions, vitamins, and eyeglasses
  • Pictures and irreplaceable memorabilia
  • Personal computer, hard drive, and disks
  • "Plastic," meaning credit and ATM cards and cash

Because Highway 9 and Highway 236 carry most of the traffic out and either can jam or close, know more than one route (Highway 9 runs both north and south, and Bear Creek Road leads out too), follow the directions officials give for that particular fire, and don't wait for a mandatory order to leave if you feel unsafe.

Know your zone and sign up for alerts, now

  • Know your evacuation zone. Look up your address on Genasys Protect (the system formerly called Zonehaven) so that when officials call an evacuation warning or order for a zone, you know instantly whether it's yours.
  • Sign up for alerts before you need them. Register for the county's emergency notifications and for PG&E outage alerts, which also warn of Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS) during high fire risk.
  • Watch for red-flag warnings. On hot, dry, windy days the National Weather Service issues red-flag warnings. Those are the days to be packed, alert, and ready to go.

Don't forget power

Fire-season power shutoffs are a fact of mountain life, and a de-energized grid during a heat wave brings its own problems. Get ahead of it with our power-outage preparation guide, and when it's time to leave, our wildfire evacuation guide covers zones, warnings, and orders.

Frequently asked questions

What's the most important wildfire prep for a Boulder Creek home?

Defensible space in the first 5 to 30 feet and hardening the house against embers (roof, gutters, vents) do the most to help a home survive. Just as important: a packed go-bag and a plan to leave early.

How do I find my evacuation zone?

Look up your address on Genasys Protect, formerly Zonehaven. Officials issue evacuation warnings and orders by zone, so knowing yours means you'll know right away when it applies to you.

Should I stay and defend my home?

No. The safe plan in the Santa Cruz Mountains is to leave early. Roads here are narrow and can close fast, and staying puts you and first responders at risk.

Where do I sign up for emergency alerts?

Register for the county's emergency notification system and PG&E alerts now, before fire season peaks. Also watch for National Weather Service red-flag warnings.

This is a checklist, not a guarantee of safety. For official guidance, see CAL FIRE's Ready for Wildfire; for live conditions, see Mountain Status. In a fire emergency, call 911. Last reviewed July 20, 2026.

Ready your home before the season peaks, then keep the rest of your fire-season plan in one place with our power-outage preparation guide and the Residents guide for county contacts, alerts, and local resources.

mary-pickford-boulder-creek.title: Mary Pickford in Boulder Creek: A Romance of the Redwoods
mary-pickford-boulder-creek.html:
In 1917, the most famous woman in the world came to Boulder Creek to make a movie. Mary Pickford was earning $10,000 a week plus half the profits, enough that her distributor built a whole new company around her releases. Cecil B. DeMille directed.

The film was A Romance of the Redwoods, and its exteriors were shot near Boulder Creek on the Poverty Flat set, a fake gold-rush town a film company had built here two years earlier. Unlike most silent films made in these mountains, this one survives.

What was filmed here

UCSC's Santa Cruz Silent Cinema project states it directly: "The exteriors were shot in northern California near Boulder Creek, in Santa Cruz County, on sets built by the California Motion Picture Corporation."

Those sets were Poverty Flat, the roughly 25-building mining town that George Middleton and Beatriz Michelena put up on family land outside Boulder Creek in early 1915. In A Romance of the Redwoods it plays a fictional camp called Strawberry Flats. When you see the town in this film, you're looking at a structure that stood in Boulder Creek.

What was not filmed here

This part matters, and most write-ups get it wrong.

The stagecoach holdup sequence, one of the film's set pieces, was shot in Ben Lomond, at a spot UCSC's researchers haven't been able to identify. That's a different town, seven miles down Highway 9, and we don't relabel Ben Lomond history as Boulder Creek history.

Beyond that, we can't currently give you a scene-by-scene breakdown. What we can say is this: the town exteriors are Poverty Flat near Boulder Creek, at least one major sequence is Ben Lomond, and interiors were studio work. Anyone claiming a precise shot list for a 1917 production should be asked what document they're reading.

Why DeMille came to the redwoods

The commercial logic was Pickford. In 1916 she'd negotiated a deal that made her the highest-paid performer in the industry: roughly $10,000 per week against 50 percent of the profits, with Artcraft Pictures Corporation formed specifically to release her films. At that price, the production needed to look like something.

The story is a Gold Rush romance: Pickford as a young woman who travels west to join an uncle and finds a road agent living under his name instead. It needed a mining camp and mountain forest. Southern California was already the industry's center by 1917, but a standing, purpose-built gold-rush town in genuine old-forest country was a real asset, and the California Motion Picture Corporation had one sitting in the Santa Cruz Mountains.

It was also early DeMille. The Biblical spectacles that define his reputation were years away. In 1917 he was a working director building a résumé, and this was one of many films made in Santa Cruz County during that period.

What Boulder Creek looked like to a film crew in 1917

The town they came to was a lumber town in decline and a resort town on the rise. The railroad still ran to Boulder Creek. Big Basin had been California's first state park for fifteen years. The big mills were running out of accessible old growth, and the valley was learning to sell scenery instead of board feet.

For a production, that combination was ideal: rail access for people and equipment, hotels and boarding houses that could absorb a crew, local labor experienced with timber and teams, and forest that photographed as wilderness within a short haul of a working town.

We haven't yet found local newspaper coverage of the 1917 shoot. Mountain Echo issues from that year are a live research target, and a crew of that profile arriving in a town this size would almost certainly have been reported.

Where to see it

A Romance of the Redwoods is one of the rare survivors. silentera.com records a 35mm positive at the George Eastman Museum and a 16mm reduction positive at the Mary Pickford Institute for Film Education. Lower-quality copies circulate online.

Two notes on that. First, quality matters a lot for location identification: a soft, cropped transfer isn't much use for matching a ridgeline. Second, Boulder Creek Local doesn't link to uploads whose rights status we can't verify. If you want to see it properly, watch for archival screenings and silent film festival programming, which is where preserved prints of this era surface.

Compare that to the rest of the Poverty Flat filmography: a 1931 nitrate fire in the California Motion Picture Corporation's San Rafael vault destroyed nearly everything else shot at that set. A Romance of the Redwoods survives largely because it was a Pickford picture on a major distributor's release schedule, and Pickford's films got looked after.

What we're still looking for

This is where the story is still open, and where a local reader might have what an archive doesn't:

  • Newspaper items: Mountain Echo pieces from 1917 reporting the production's arrival, lodging or hiring.
  • Family memories: relatives who worked as extras, teamsters or laborers on the production.
  • The Ben Lomond location: the stagecoach holdup site, which remains unidentified.
  • Production paperwork: any correspondence or call sheets held in DeMille or Artcraft collections.

If you have a clipping or a family story that touches any of this, send it through the contribution link below. Corrections and leads from residents are how these pages get more accurate over time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Mary Pickford film in Boulder Creek?

Yes. UCSC's silent cinema research states that the exteriors for A Romance of the Redwoods (1917) were shot near Boulder Creek on sets built by the California Motion Picture Corporation, the Poverty Flat set.

Which scenes were shot in Boulder Creek?

The town exteriors, standing in for the fictional Strawberry Flats. The stagecoach holdup sequence was filmed in Ben Lomond, and interiors were studio work. A complete scene-by-scene breakdown hasn't been established.

Can I watch A Romance of the Redwoods?

The film survives. A complete 35mm print is held by the George Eastman Museum, and the Mary Pickford Institute for Film Education holds a 16mm reduction print. It appears occasionally in archival and silent film festival programming. Copies of varying quality circulate online; we don't link to uploads whose rights we can't verify.

Can I visit the filming location?

No. The Poverty Flat set was dismantled, and the probable site is private residential property with no marker or public access. This site doesn't publish a location for it.

Did Mary Pickford live in Boulder Creek?

No. She came for a production. There's no evidence of any residence here, and we treat that claim as false unless documents establish otherwise.

What else was filmed at the Poverty Flat set?

At least eight productions between 1915 and the early 1920s, including The Lily of Poverty Flat (1915), The Half-Breed (1916), The Flame of Hellgate (1920) and Soul of the Beast (1923). Most of that footage was destroyed in a 1931 vault fire. For the full story of the town that hosted them, see our history of the Poverty Flat film set near Boulder Creek.

mountain-home-maintenance-calendar.title: The Mountain Home Maintenance Calendar
mountain-home-maintenance-calendar.html:
The short version

  • Before the rains (September and October): clear gutters, downspouts, ditches, drains, and culverts; deal with dead limbs over the house; book roof and tree work early. Early October is the single most important maintenance weekend of the year.
  • Before fire season (spring): clear defensible space out to 100 feet, the amount required by Public Resources Code 4291, while the growth is still green and easy to cut.
  • Before Public Safety Power Shutoff season (June): start the generator and run it under load, and test it outdoors only, never plugged into house wiring without a proper transfer switch.
  • Year-round: test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms monthly, and replace any alarm over 10 years old.
  • On septic, like most of Boulder Creek: inspect at least every three years and pump the tank every three to five.

Printable version: the mountain home maintenance calendar lays the whole year out month by month, which is easier to keep on the wall than in a browser tab. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

Owning a home in Boulder Creek runs on two seasons, not four: the wet one and the dry one. Get your drainage, roof, and trees ready before the rains, get your defensible space and generator ready before fire season, and most of the year takes care of itself.

What follows is that rhythm, month by month. One caveat before we start: every parcel here is different. A house on a sunny ridge and a cabin in a creek-bottom redwood grove have different problems, so treat this as the rhythm, not a rulebook, and lean on the pros and the official sources linked below for anything specific to your property.

Every rule in this calendar is a lesson I learned by missing it once. Septic pumping on a schedule, because the alternative announces itself. Propane refilled before the gauge hits 20 percent, not after. Gas on hand for the generator, canned and boxed food and water put by for outages, and dried firewood stacked before the season starts, not during the first cold week when everyone else wants it too. None of this is complicated. All of it is easier in September than in January.

January and February: Storm Season, Eyes Open

Deep winter is less about projects and more about watching your systems work. During and after each big storm, walk the property when it's safe to do so. Check that gutters are overflowing nowhere, that downspouts are moving water away from the foundation, and that the ditches and culverts draining your driveway are running clear. A culvert that plugs mid-January is how driveways disappear, and clearing leaves now is far cheaper than repairing washout later.

Keep an eye on the trees you flagged in fall. Saturated ground plus wind is when limbs and whole trees come down. If anything falls into power lines, stay away and call 911; our emergency contacts list has the numbers for everything less urgent, including county road dispatch at (831) 477-3999.

Indoors, make this the season you're strict about alarms. The U.S. Fire Administration says to test smoke alarms monthly, whatever type you have, and if anything in your house burns fuel or you run a generator, a carbon monoxide detector near every sleeping area is non-negotiable. The CDC counts more than 400 American deaths a year from CO, a gas you can't see or smell.

March and April: Assess the Damage, Start the Fire Work

When the storm train slows down, take stock. Look at the roof from the ground with binoculars for lifted shingles, debris dams, and moss that holds moisture against the roofing. Check decks, railings, and stairs for winter rot. Note where water pooled or cut channels this winter and fix the grading or drainage while the memory is fresh; the county's storm preparedness page links a good home drainage guide if you want a starting point.

This is also when defensible space season begins in earnest, while the vegetation is still green and soft. CAL FIRE's defensible space guidance organizes the work in zones:

  • The first 5 feet from the house should be ember-resistant, with hardscape instead of combustible mulch and nothing dead or dry against the structure.
  • Within 30 feet, keep things lean, clean, and green.
  • Out to 100 feet or your property line, reduce fuel, with grass mowed to four inches or less.

State law, Public Resources Code 4291, requires 100 feet of defensible space, and it's a year-round obligation, not a one-day deadline. Spring is when the work is most pleasant and the growth is easiest to cut.

May and June: Finish Defensible Space Before the Heat

By late spring, the goal is to have the heavy defensible space work done: dead vegetation removed, tree branches limbed up at least 6 feet from the ground per CAL FIRE, wood piles relocated out of the first 30 feet, and the roof and gutters cleared of needles again, because they're ember beds in summer and dams in winter. CAL FIRE and its partners conduct defensible space inspections in the State Responsibility Area that covers much of our valley, so if an inspector visits, this is the work they're looking at. Don't count on a warning before an inspection, and don't need one.

June is also generator month, because Public Safety Power Shutoff season arrives with the dry winds. Start the generator, run it under load, check your fuel supply, and reread the two safety rules that matter most: outdoors only, more than 20 feet from windows, doors, and vents per the CDC, and never plugged into house wiring without a proper transfer switch. Your owner's manual sets the maintenance schedule; the habit of testing before you need it is the part we'll insist on. The whole setup is covered in our power outage plan.

July and August: Vigilance, Water, and the Small Stuff

High summer is maintenance-light and awareness-heavy. Keep the first five feet around the house bare of dry debris, since redwood duff keeps falling all summer. Confirm your CruzAware alert registration is current, especially if you've changed phones or carriers, and make sure your PG&E outage alerts are set.

Use the slow months for the unglamorous items. Refresh the emergency kit against ready.gov's list, rotating stored water, one gallon per person per day for several days, and swapping out expired food and medications. If you're on a private well, summer is a sensible time for any pump or tank service, when a day without water is an annoyance instead of a crisis. If you're on district water, the San Lorenzo Valley Water District at (831) 338-2153 can answer system questions; our utilities guide sorts out who serves what.

September and October: The Big Push Before the Rains

This is the most important stretch of the calendar, and the one where procrastination costs real money. Before the first atmospheric river arrives, clean gutters and downspouts, clear every ditch, drain, and culvert you own, and get roof repairs done while roofers can still get to you. Walk the property and deal with dead limbs over the house, cars, and power drops; tree crews book out quickly once storms are in the forecast, so call early. If your place heats with a wood stove, have the stove and chimney serviced before burning season starts.

Two more fall jobs. First, if you heat with propane, get the tank filled before winter, when delivery schedules tighten for everyone. Second, restock the storm side of your kit: flashlights, batteries, a radio, and sandbags if your parcel needs them, which the county distributes at posted locations each storm season via the storm preparedness page. Our winter storm checklist turns this whole section into a single afternoon's work.

November and December: Switch to Storm Mode

By Thanksgiving, you want to be done preparing and into operating. Keep vehicles fueled ahead of big systems, check drainage after each of the first storms, and keep the generator's fuel fresh and its extension cords where you can find them in the dark. Test the smoke and CO alarms with the monthly routine, and if you have a 9-volt-battery alarm, the USFA says replace that battery at least once a year, so pick a date you'll remember and make it annual.

December is also a good month for the paperwork nobody enjoys: photograph the house and outbuildings for insurance, back up the photos somewhere off the mountain, and confirm your policy reflects what's actually on the parcel.

The Recurring Beat, All Year

A few items ignore the seasons. Test smoke alarms monthly and replace any alarm that's 10 years old, per the USFA. If you're on septic, like most of Boulder Creek, the EPA says to have the system inspected at least every three years and expect to pump the tank every three to five, with yearly checks for systems that have pumps or floats. Put both on a calendar you'll see, because neither one reminds you until it fails, and a failed drainfield is one of the most expensive failures a mountain house can serve up.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the deadline for defensible space work?

There isn't a single statewide date. CAL FIRE frames the 100 feet of defensible space required by Public Resources Code 4291 as an ongoing obligation, maintained year-round, and its crews inspect properties in the State Responsibility Area on their own schedule. Practically, do the heavy cutting in spring and keep it maintained through fire season.

How often should a septic system be pumped in Boulder Creek?

The EPA's guidance is an inspection at least every three years and pumping typically every three to five years, more often for systems with mechanical parts. Your actual interval depends on tank size and household size, so ask your septic professional to put a recommendation in writing after the next inspection.

What's the most important maintenance month of the year?

October, and it's not close. Gutters, culverts, roof, trees, and storm supplies all need to be squared away before the first big rain, and every trade you might need is busiest right then. If you only ever plan one maintenance weekend a year, make it early October and work from our winter storm checklist.

Do I really need to test smoke alarms every month?

That's the U.S. Fire Administration's standing guidance for every alarm type: test monthly, replace 9-volt and backup batteries at least yearly, and replace the whole unit every 10 years. In a wooden house surrounded by forest, with winter fires burning and generators running, it's cheap discipline.

My property doesn't match this calendar. What then?

That's normal up here. Slope, sun, trees, water source, and road access change the priorities parcel by parcel, and this calendar can't see your land. Use it as the skeleton, then let a good local arborist, septic professional, and the official sources linked above fill in the specifics for your place.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This calendar links to official sources from CAL FIRE, the U.S. Fire Administration, the CDC, the EPA, ready.gov, and Santa Cruz County. Local requirements and property-specific advice come from the responsible agency and qualified professionals.

One weekend of the year carries most of this list. If you do nothing else, block out early October and work through our winter storm checklist. For utilities, permits, and county contacts gathered in one place, see the Residents guide. For where the water year currently stands, see our rain tracker.

movies-filmed-in-boulder-creek.title: Every Movie, Short Film and Music Video Filmed in Boulder Creek
movies-filmed-in-boulder-creek.html:
Boulder Creek has been a filming location for more than a century. A studio built a permanent gold-rush town outside of town in 1915. Mary Pickford shot here in 1917. Hitchcock filmed the redwood scene in Vertigo nine miles up Highway 236. Downtown played a fictional town called Buzzsaw in a 1992 Matthew Broderick comedy. This page is the working database: every production we can document, what part of the area it actually used, and how solid the evidence is.

It's not finished, and it says so where it isn't. If you know something we don't, there's a contribution link at the bottom.

How to read this page

Two things trip up every other list of movies filmed in Boulder Creek.

Geography. Big Basin Redwoods State Park has a Boulder Creek mailing address, but it's nine miles up Highway 236 and it's not downtown. A scene shot among the park's old-growth redwoods is a Big Basin scene. We label the actual place. The same goes for Ben Lomond, Brookdale, Felton and Bonny Doon, all part of this valley's film history, none of them Boulder Creek.

Evidence. A production shows up in one blog, which gets copied into five more, and suddenly it's a fact. Each entry below carries a status:

  • Confirmed: official or primary source, or multiple strong independent sources
  • Well documented: reputable researcher or strong secondary source
  • Local firsthand: confirmed by a named or internally documented local source, not yet in formal records
  • Research lead: plausible, evidence incomplete, do not repeat as fact

Silent era: 1914–1923

Nearly all of this activity traces to one thing: the Poverty Flat set, a roughly 25-building gold-rush town that George Middleton and Beatriz Michelena built on family land outside Boulder Creek in early 1915 for the California Motion Picture Corporation. UCSC's Santa Cruz Silent Cinema project is the core research on it, and also records the main drag of Highway 9 doubling as a western mining town.

Film titles link to IMDb. Where a film has entered the public domain and a legitimate copy exists, we link that too.

Film Year Location used Evidence Survives? Where to watch
Salomy Jane 1914 Boulder Creek area filming reported; scene-level detail unresolved Research lead Yes. Print found in Australia 1996, preserved by the Library of Congress. Watch free via the National Film Preservation Foundation
The Lily of Poverty Flat 1915 Poverty Flat set, Boulder Creek Well documented Presumed lost
The Rose of the Misty Pool 1915 Poverty Flat set Well documented Presumed lost
A Phyllis of the Sierras 1915 Poverty Flat set Well documented Presumed lost
The Half-Breed 1916 Poverty Flat set Well documented Survives; restored by the San Francisco Silent Film Festival. No authorized free stream
A Romance of the Redwoods 1917 Poverty Flat set (town exteriors); stagecoach holdup in Ben Lomond Well documented Yes. 35mm print at the George Eastman Museum; public domain copy at the Internet Archive
Sudden Jim 1917 Boulder Creek reported as a fictional lumber town Research lead Lost
The Sunset Trail 1917 Boulder Creek Confirmed: IMDb carries a Boulder Creek filming-location credit Unresolved
Just Squaw 1919 Poverty Flat set Well documented Survives; print held by the Library of Congress. Reported as the only surviving Beatriz Michelena Features production
Heart of Juanita 1919 Poverty Flat set Well documented Presumed lost
The Flame of Hellgate 1920 Poverty Flat set Well documented Presumed lost. Michelena's final film
Soul of the Beast 1923 Boulder Creek, incl. Poverty Flat area; elephant performer Anna May Well documented Yes. Public domain copy at the Internet Archive
Salomy Jane (remake) 1923 Expanded settlement in the Boulder Creek area Research lead Lost
Evangeline 1929 Big Basin forest and waterfall sequences are claimed locally; the documented location photography was at Point Lobos, near Carmel Research lead Survives; entered US public domain in 2025. Copy at the Internet Archive

Two notes on that table. The Sunset Trail is the one silent title where IMDb itself records Boulder Creek as a filming location, which makes it better evidenced than the surrounding entries even though it's less discussed locally. And the two Salomy Jane films are different pictures a decade apart (the 1914 original survives, the 1923 remake is lost), so check the year before citing either.

Two titles above use language that is offensive today. We keep them as released because that's how the films are cataloged in archives, and because how these productions handled race is part of the record.

Most of this footage no longer exists. A 1931 fire in the California Motion Picture Corporation's San Rafael storage vault destroyed the nitrate negatives.

Big Basin on film

The park is its own filming location with its own history, and the biggest name in it is Hitchcock.

Production Year Location Evidence Where to watch
Vertigo 1958 Big Basin: the redwood forest sequence, which in the story represents Muir Woods Confirmed In copyright; rental or streaming
The Gnome-Mobile 1967 Big Basin redwood scenes Research lead Disney+ or paid rental
Cirque du Soleil: Journey of Man 2000 Big Basin: bungee sequence among the redwoods Research lead Subscription streaming
The Truth About Beef Jerky 2002 Big Basin area Research lead Not located
The Tripper 2006 Big Basin (21600 Big Basin Way) and Santa Cruz; filmed February 2006 Well documented Rental

The Vertigo correction is worth stating plainly, because it's one of the most persistent errors in Bay Area film geography: Scottie and Madeleine's scene at the cross-section of the felled redwood is not Muir Woods. Location research places it at Big Basin Redwoods State Park, with location filming running from late September into October 1957. Hitchcock's own ranch was near Scotts Valley, a short drive from the park.

The Tripper, David Arquette's 2006 horror comedy, used the park's forest for its hippie-festival encampment and chase sequences. Whether any of it was shot in Boulder Creek proper rather than the park is an open question we'd like to close. If you were around for that shoot, we want to hear from you.

Downtown Boulder Creek on screen

Production Year Location Evidence Where to watch
Out on a Limb 1992 Downtown Boulder Creek as the fictional town of Buzzsaw; the Boulder Creek Fire Protection District building at 13230 Highway 9 played the bank; chase sequences on Moon Drive off Highway 236 and beyond Well documented Paid rental
Graves End 2005 Downtown Boulder Creek and nearby mountain locations reported Research lead Not readily available
Motos 2025 Filmed in Boulder Creek on the director's own property; post-wildfire subject Well documented Free via Omeleto, a licensed short-film distributor

Out on a Limb is the best-documented modern production. Directed by Francis Veber and released by Universal in September 1992, it starred Matthew Broderick, Jeffrey Jones, Heidi Kling and John C. Reilly, and shot across Northern California with Boulder Creek supplying the town of Buzzsaw. Location listings also place work in Bonny Doon, Davenport and Big Basin.

If you were an extra, worked on the crew, or ran a business that got dressed as a Buzzsaw storefront, that's the material this page is missing.

Music videos

Artist Title Boulder Creek connection Evidence
Wolf Jett ft. The T Sisters Garden of Pain (2020) Shot on 16mm in Boulder Creek, on the foundation of the drummer's home destroyed by the CZU fire Confirmed: stated twice in the artist's official description
Avery Chapman In California (2021) Filmed in Half Moon Bay and Boulder Creek Confirmed: stated in the artist's official description
Rachel Platten Fight Song (2015) The bar sequence is identified locally as Joe's Bar, downtown Boulder Creek Local firsthand only: see below

All three links go to the artist's own channel or official VEVO upload. We don't link fan re-uploads; Garden of Pain in particular has a second copy on an unrelated channel, and it isn't the one to cite.

The Wolf Jett video is the strongest documented music-video connection this town has, and it's the one nobody talks about. The official description says it was shot on Kodak 16mm in Boulder Creek and dedicates the video to residents affected by the CZU Lightning Complex fire. It was filmed on the foundation of drummer Jon Payne's house, which the fire destroyed. That's a Boulder Creek story in its own right, and we'd like to talk to the band.

On Fight Song. A worldwide hit from 2015 contains a bar scene, and local firsthand knowledge supplied to Boulder Creek Local identifies that bar as Joe's. Corroboration is missing: the official video description is boilerplate credits, and no production or press source names a Boulder Creek location. So the label stays local firsthand: credible, locally sourced, not externally documented. If you worked on that shoot or remember it, you can settle this.

Removed from this list

TonyG, "Will You Be Mine Tonight?" (2013) previously appeared here on the basis that the official upload identified Boulder Creek. It does not. The entire official description is a one-line copyright credit, and we could find nothing connecting the artist or the video to Boulder Creek. We've taken it off rather than leave an unsupported entry sitting in a table, and we're recording the removal here so it doesn't get re-added.

Leads we have not resolved

These come up in conversation or in scattered sources. None is confirmed. Several may turn out to be somewhere else entirely.

  • The Primal Lure, The Narrow Trail, Melissa of the Hills: silent-era titles with reported Santa Cruz Mountains connections
  • Thunder Mountain: a persistent local claim with no located evidence
  • Beaver Run Café: reported production, details unknown
  • A CBS Eye on the Bay segment shot at the White Cockade
  • Commercials, student films and locally produced video not indexed anywhere online

Things that are not Boulder Creek

We keep this list so the same errors stop getting recycled:

  • Productions shot in Santa Cruz, Felton, Ben Lomond, Brookdale, Bonny Doon or Aptos with no Boulder Creek scene
  • References to a different Boulder Creek: there are towns by that name in Idaho and Colorado
  • Films set in redwoods but shot elsewhere
  • Big Basin scenes described as downtown Boulder Creek

Help us finish this

This is where you come in. We're looking for anything that turns a research lead into a documented fact:

  • Memories from extras and crew
  • Business owners who were paid for location use
  • Permits and local newspaper coverage

Use the contribution link below. Tell us whether your information is firsthand, family knowledge or something you heard, all three are useful, and we'll label them accordingly.

This page is reviewed quarterly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What movies were filmed in Boulder Creek?

The best-documented are A Romance of the Redwoods (1917, Mary Pickford and Cecil B. DeMille), Soul of the Beast (1923), and Out on a Limb (1992), in which downtown played the fictional town of Buzzsaw. At least eight silent films used the Poverty Flat set built outside town in 1915. Vertigo (1958) and The Tripper (2006) filmed at Big Basin, which has a Boulder Creek address but is nine miles up Highway 236.

Was Vertigo filmed at Muir Woods?

No. The redwood forest sequence was shot at Big Basin Redwoods State Park, though the story places it at Muir Woods. This is one of the most common mistakes in Bay Area film geography.

Where is the bar in Rachel Platten's Fight Song video?

Local firsthand knowledge identifies it as Joe's Bar in downtown Boulder Creek. We label this a local confirmation rather than a documented fact: we searched for external corroboration and found none, and the video's official description is only credits. If you were involved in that shoot, you can settle it.

Which Boulder Creek music video is best documented?

Wolf Jett's "Garden of Pain" (2020). The band's official description states it was shot on Kodak 16mm in Boulder Creek and dedicates it to residents affected by the CZU fire; it was filmed on the foundation of the drummer's home, which the fire destroyed.

Can I watch the old films for free?

Several are public domain. Salomy Jane (1914) streams free via the National Film Preservation Foundation, and A Romance of the Redwoods (1917), Soul of the Beast (1923) and Evangeline (1929) have copies at the Internet Archive. Links are in the tables above. We only link authorized or public-domain sources.

Can I visit any of the filming locations?

Big Basin Redwoods State Park is open for day use. Check parks.ca.gov for current access, since recovery from the 2020 CZU fire is ongoing. Downtown Boulder Creek is walkable. The Poverty Flat set is gone and its probable site is private property with no public access.

Why do so many old films from here no longer exist?

A 1931 fire in the California Motion Picture Corporation's San Rafael storage vault destroyed the nitrate negatives for nearly the entire studio output, which includes most of what was shot at Poverty Flat. Nitrate stock is also chemically unstable, and much American silent film was scrapped after sound arrived.

Is anything filmed in Boulder Creek today?

Independent and short-film production continues; the 2025 short Motos was filmed on private land in Boulder Creek. Productions of any size are far less common than during the silent era, and most local filming now happens without public announcement.

Two threads on this page reward a closer look on their own: the gold-rush set at Poverty Flat that made Boulder Creek a silent-film town for a decade, and the career of Beatriz Michelena, the star who helped build it. And if you have a memory or an old permit from any shoot listed here, the contribution link above is how a research lead becomes documented local history.

new-resident-quick-start-boulder-creek.title: New to Boulder Creek? The Quick-Start Guide
new-resident-quick-start-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Alerts first. Sign up for CruzAware, the county's emergency alert system, before you unpack a box. Add PG&E outage alerts while you're at it.
  • Utilities in your name. PG&E for electricity and gas; the San Lorenzo Valley Water District for water at most in-town homes.
  • Trash. Set up service with GreenWaste and confirm your street's collection day, since days vary route by route.
  • Kids? Enrollment starts with a phone call to your school's registrar, not an online portal.
  • Two things to keep handy: a Boulder Creek library card, and the county's 24-hour road dispatch line, 831-477-3999, saved in your phone.

Printable version: the new resident quick start collects the first-week essentials on one page, which is a kinder thing to hand a neighbour than a link. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

Nobody hands you a manual when you move to Boulder Creek, which is a shame, because a mountain town runs on a different set of rules than wherever you came from. There's no city hall. Your water may come from a district office on the main drag, your trash day probably won't match your neighbor's across the valley, and the smartest thing you can do in your first week is sign up for an emergency alert before you've unpacked a single box.

I've lived here my whole life, so take this guide as a neighbor's orientation rather than a brochure. The one mindset shift that matters most: up here you plan for the what-ifs, the outage, the closed road, the Monday the shop is dark, and once you do, each of them shrinks from crisis to inconvenience. Newcomers who learn that stay. The ones who don't tend to leave after their first hard winter.

Boulder Creek is unincorporated Santa Cruz County, so your services come from a patchwork of county departments and special districts rather than one city office. Hours and details change, so treat each link below as the last word.

Sign up for emergency alerts before you unpack

This is mountain country, and fire season, winter storms, and power outages come with the address. The county's wildfire preparedness page tells residents to register for CruzAware, the official Santa Cruz County alert system, and that's the first account to make at your new place. It takes a few minutes online, so get on CruzAware before the boxes are even open.

While you're at it, set up outage alerts from PG&E. Account holders get notified about outages at their service address automatically once their contact info is current, and you can follow any address on the outage map without an account. If PG&E calls a Public Safety Power Shutoff during high fire risk, alerts go to account holders without a separate signup.

One more number for your phone: the county's 24-hour road dispatch line, 831-477-3999, listed on the Public Works contact page. That's who you call when a tree or slide blocks a county road. If a line is down or anyone's in danger, call 911 first.

Put the utilities in your name

Electricity and gas come from PG&E. Start there if the previous owner or tenant hasn't already closed the account.

Water for most homes in town comes from the San Lorenzo Valley Water District, whose office sits right on the main drag at 13060 Highway 9. To start service, fill out the form on the district's Start/Stop Service page at least 24 business hours before you need water in your name, and expect a $20 establishment fee on your first monthly bill.

One quirk for renters: the district keeps accounts in the property owner's name, so if you're leasing, your landlord handles the water account. The office is open weekdays 8:30 a.m. to noon and 1 to 5 p.m., and the main number, 831-338-2153, routes to an answering service for water emergencies after hours.

Not every property is on district water, and plenty of homes up here run on septic rather than sewer. If you're buying, ask directly whether the house is on district water or a well, and where the septic tank and leach field sit. Get that in writing before escrow closes, not after.

Trash, recycling, and organics

Garbage service in unincorporated Santa Cruz County, Boulder Creek included, comes from GreenWaste. Call 831-426-2711 or email SantaCruzCS@GreenWaste.com to set up carts, confirm your collection day, and ask about backyard service if your driveway is the kind of driveway this town is famous for. Collection days vary street by street, so don't assume yours matches a neighbor's across the valley.

For big cleanouts, the county runs its own disposal facilities; the Public Works page lists 831-454-2430 for landfill and recycling questions.

Enrolling kids in school

Boulder Creek sits in the San Lorenzo Valley Unified School District, which covers TK through 12th grade for the whole valley. Enrollment starts with a person, not a portal: the district's enrollment page says to contact your school's registrar first to set up pre-enrollment, after which you'll get online registration instructions to finish within a week.

Have these ready: proof of your child's age, immunization records, an oral health assessment for TK, kindergarten, and first grade, and proof of address, which can be a utility bill, lease, property tax receipt, or similar. For the 2026-27 year, kindergartners need to be five on or before September 1, and TK students need to turn four by that date.

The neighborhood elementary school is Boulder Creek Elementary at 400 Lomond Street, a short walk from downtown, and its site carries current 2026-27 registration information. If you have enrollment questions the registrar can't answer, the district's Student Services office is at 831-336-9678.

Get a library card

The Boulder Creek branch of Santa Cruz Public Libraries sits at 13390 West Park Avenue, a block off the highway, and it punches well above its weight after a full remodel. Current hours are Monday through Thursday 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Friday 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Saturday 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Sunday. Free WiFi, computers, kids' programs, and a local history collection make it one of the best rainy-day rooms in the valley.

Getting to Santa Cruz without a car

Santa Cruz METRO runs Route 35, the Highway 9/Scotts Valley line, which connects Boulder Creek to Felton, Scotts Valley, and downtown Santa Cruz. Its Boulder Creek timepoints include Highway 9 at Middleton Avenue in the middle of town and stops out to the Country Club end of Big Basin Way. On weekdays there's also Route 35X, the Santa Cruz/Boulder Creek Express, which runs every 30 minutes from 6:30am to 5:30pm and carries most of the daytime service to town. Schedules shift with service changes, so check the live pages before you build a commute around them.

Fire, sheriff, and who to call

Fire protection comes from the Boulder Creek Fire Protection District, with its station at 13230 Central Avenue downtown. The office line, 831-338-7222, is for non-emergency business on weekdays 8 to 5; emergencies always go through 911.

There's no Boulder Creek police department. Law enforcement is the Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office, which staffs a Boulder Creek Service Center at 13210 Central Avenue with a community deputy; the center's number is 831-454-7440. For things that need a deputy but not lights and sirens, the non-emergency dispatch line is 831-471-1121, per Santa Cruz Regional 9-1-1.

Where to get the everyday basics

You can cover most errands without leaving town.

  • Johnnie's Super Market, 13225 Highway 9: a full grocery with produce, meat, a deli, and a serious wine and spirits section. It has anchored Boulder Creek since 1938 and opens daily at 8 a.m.
  • Wild Roots Market, 13159 Central Avenue: the natural-foods counterpart, open daily 9 to 9 with a deli kitchen and local produce.
  • Boulder Creek Pharmacy, 13081 Central Avenue: an independent pharmacy with free delivery throughout the San Lorenzo Valley, open weekdays 9 to 6 and Saturday 10 to 4.
  • Scarborough Home & Garden, 13110 Highway 9: Ace Hardware lines seven days a week, for the endless small fixes an older mountain house demands.

For more of what's open locally, browse the Boulder Creek business directory.

Your first weekend

Walk the town. The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District runs Junction Park at Middleton and Railroad Avenues, with a small beach and river access a block from downtown, and Garrahan Park at 15555 Highway 9, with a walking track, soccer field, and play structures, open sunrise to sunset. Dogs are welcome on leash at both.

The district's downtown office at 831-338-4144 can fill you in on classes, camps, and community events, which are the fastest way to stop feeling new here. The BCL community events calendar is another good place to see what's coming up.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who provides trash service in Boulder Creek?

GreenWaste handles garbage, recycling, and organics for unincorporated Santa Cruz County, including Boulder Creek. Call 831-426-2711 to set up service and confirm your street's collection day, since days vary by route.

What school district serves Boulder Creek?

San Lorenzo Valley Unified School District, headquartered in Ben Lomond. Start enrollment by contacting the registrar at your child's school; Boulder Creek Elementary is the in-town elementary campus.

Is there a bus from Boulder Creek to Santa Cruz?

Yes. METRO Route 35 runs along Highway 9 through Boulder Creek to Santa Cruz, and on weekdays the Route 35X express makes the trip faster, running every 30 minutes from 6:30am to 5:30pm. Check the live schedules on METRO's route pages before relying on a specific trip.

Who do I call when a tree comes down across the road?

For county-maintained roads, the 24-hour road dispatch line is 831-477-3999. If the tree took wires down with it, stay well away and call 911 first. Anything threatening life or property is a 911 call, full stop.

How do I sign up for emergency alerts?

Register at CruzAware, the county's official alert system, and add PG&E outage alerts through your account. Both take a few minutes, and they matter more here than almost anywhere else you've lived.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. Boulder Creek is unincorporated Santa Cruz County, so services come from a mix of county departments and special districts; hours, fees, and phone numbers change, so treat each linked official page as the last word.

Once the essentials are handled, the Residents guide keeps utilities, permits, and county contacts in one place for when you need them again. If you are still sorting out work or a longer-term place to live, the valley job board and our rental listings are both pulled from local sources and free to browse. Welcome to the valley.

night-out-boulder-creek.title: A Night Out in and Around Boulder Creek
night-out-boulder-creek.html:
Downtown Boulder Creek doesn't put out much of a marquee glow after dark, but a few doors stay lit and worth walking toward. Some nights you just want a drink, a stage, and somewhere to land, and you'd rather not guess who's open. Here's where to go in town, and where to head down the valley when Boulder Creek winds down before you're ready to.

My own version of a Boulder Creek night out, for the record: a nice dinner at Scopazzi's and a drink at the bar after, or live music at lille aeske or Joe's. These days, with a baby whose bedtime outranks everything, it's more of a fond memory than a weekly habit. The town will still be doing all of this when you're ready to come back out.

The short version

  • In town after dark: Joe's Bar for drinks and live music (21 and over), the lounge at Scopazzi's for a quieter sit-down evening, and The Sawmill Restaurant & Alehouse for craft beer and a patio stage.
  • Wine, mostly weekend afternoons: Big Basin Vineyards' tasting room pours Saturday and Sunday, noon to 5:00 p.m., April through October, and adds Fireside Fridays, 5:30 to 9:30 p.m., May through October.
  • Want a bigger stage or a later night: drive a few minutes down Highway 9 to Henflings Tavern in Ben Lomond (open daily until 1:30 a.m.) or Felton Music Hall in Felton.
  • Before you go: Joe's is 21 and over, so bring ID, and plan a designated driver or a ride for the Highway 9 stretch.
  • Joe's runs latest: open daily from 10 a.m. until 2 a.m., which makes it the only room in town still going after midnight.

Joe's Bar

13118 Highway 9, Boulder Creek. (831) 338-9417. Open daily, 10 a.m. to 2 a.m. This is a 21-and-over venue.

Joe's Bar is the downtown bar and live-music room, and it's the anchor of a Boulder Creek night out. Its own calendar posts karaoke every Tuesday at 8:30 p.m. and a pool tournament every Thursday at 8 p.m., with live music most weekends, so there's usually a reason to stop in.

It's a 21-and-over place, so bring ID. Our listing doesn't carry confirmed opening hours, so call (831) 338-9417 if you want to line up a specific night, and check Joe's current calendar for the week's lineup.

Scopazzi's lounge

13300 Big Basin Way, Boulder Creek. (831) 338-4444. Dinner and lounge Wednesday through Sunday from 4:00 p.m. Closed Monday and Tuesday.

Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge is the historic Italian restaurant in town, and the lounge is the quieter, sit-down side of an evening out: a drink and a table rather than a stage. It runs Wednesday through Sunday from 4 p.m. and closes Monday and Tuesday.

Think of it as the spot for a calmer evening or a nightcap after dinner, not a late night.

The Sawmill Restaurant & Alehouse

15520 Highway 9, Boulder Creek. (831) 610-8196.

The Sawmill Restaurant & Alehouse sits just north of downtown, an American restaurant and alehouse that pairs craft beer with outdoor seating and a music stage under the redwoods. On a warm evening it's the closest thing in town to dinner, drinks, and live music in one place.

One planning note: the Sawmill is expected to close temporarily for renovations after service on Friday, August 14, 2026, with reopening details not yet confirmed, so call 831-610-8196 before building a night around it.

We don't have verified current hours for it, so check by phone at (831) 610-8196 before you plan around a specific night or a show.

Lille Aeske Arthouse

13160 Highway 9, Boulder Creek.

Lille Aeske Arthouse is the town's other kind of evening out: a small arthouse hanging a rotating monthly show, with concerts, film nights, and events on its own calendar rather than a nightly schedule. It's the room to check when you'd rather see something than sit at a bar. Its gallery hours run weekend afternoons, and evening events are posted per show, so look at what's booked before you plan around it.

Big Basin Vineyards tasting room

830 Memory Lane, Boulder Creek. Phone: (831) 621-8028. Saturday and Sunday, 12:00 to 5:00 p.m., April through October; Saturdays only in November and December; closed to the public January through March. Fireside Fridays run 5:30 to 9:30 p.m., May through October.

Big Basin Vineyards Estate Vineyard & Tasting Room pours its mountain-grown wines at the estate vineyard. Most of the year it's a daytime stop that fits an early Saturday or Sunday plan, but Fireside Fridays through the warm months are a genuine evening option, wine by the fire under the redwoods. Worth checking the season before you drive out: the room closes to the public from January through March.

For bookings and current pours, use the winery's visit page to check current details and any reservation requirements.

Up the valley: Henflings Tavern, Ben Lomond

9450 Highway 9, Ben Lomond. (831) 289-3019. Open daily, 12:00 p.m. to 1:30 a.m.

Henflings Tavern has been a Santa Cruz Mountains tavern in downtown Ben Lomond since 1946, about ten minutes down Highway 9. You get live music every weekend, a recurring Sunday Pro Jam, a full bar, a food menu, and a covered patio, and it stays open daily until 1:30 a.m., which makes it the late-night option the valley doesn't have north of here.

If Boulder Creek is winding down and you're not ready to, this is where the night keeps going.

Up the valley: Felton Music Hall, Felton

6275 Highway 9, Felton. (831) 704-7113.

Felton Music Hall is the dedicated live-music venue in Felton, presenting local and touring acts across genres, with craft food and cocktails from a full bar served in-house. It's the room to check when you want a booked lineup and a proper stage.

Shows and hours vary by the calendar, so use the venue's site to see who's playing and when doors open before you drive down. Our events calendar is another place to catch what's coming up around the valley.

What a Boulder Creek night out doesn't include

A few things worth naming before you head out:

  • No nightclub. Boulder Creek doesn't have one, and the only place in town proper built for a late night is Joe's Bar.
  • Daytime and dinner hours wind down early. Big Basin Vineyards is weekend afternoons outside its Fireside Friday season, and Scopazzi's lounge keeps restaurant hours. Once those close, the late options are down the valley at Henflings.
  • The drive matters. Plan a designated driver or a ride for the Highway 9 stretch, and check ages, since Joe's Bar is 21 and over.

For where to eat before you go out, see our dinner guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where can I hear live music near Boulder Creek?

In town, Joe's Bar regularly hosts live music, and The Sawmill has a stage on its patio. Down the valley, Henflings Tavern in Ben Lomond has live music every weekend plus a Sunday Pro Jam, and Felton Music Hall in Felton books local and touring acts. Check each venue's site for the current lineup.

What's open latest for a night out?

Henflings Tavern in Ben Lomond is open daily until 1:30 a.m., the latest confirmed closing time in this guide. In Boulder Creek proper, Joe's Bar runs later still, open daily from 10 a.m. to 2 a.m.

Is there anywhere to go out on a weeknight?

Yes. Joe's Bar posts karaoke every Tuesday and a pool tournament every Thursday, and it regularly hosts live music, so check its current calendar for the week's lineup. Scopazzi's lounge is open Wednesday and Thursday evenings, and Henflings is open daily if you're up for the short drive.

Can I go wine tasting near Boulder Creek?

Yes. Big Basin Vineyards runs its estate tasting room at 830 Memory Lane, Saturday and Sunday noon to 5:00 p.m. from April through October, Saturdays only in November and December, and closed to the public January through March. Fireside Fridays, 5:30 to 9:30 p.m. May through October, are the one evening option.

A venue I know is missing. Why?

We list places we can point to through their own page or a current official listing. If a bar, tasting room, or music venue is missing or a detail has changed, tell us at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact. You can also browse the local business directory for more spots around town.

parks-playgrounds-boulder-creek.title: Every Park a Kid Can Play At in the Valley
parks-playgrounds-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • In-town playground: Garrahan Park, 15555 Highway 9, has play structures, a soccer field, a walking track, and barbecues, open sunrise to sunset.
  • River and downtown: Junction Park, at Middleton Avenue and Railroad Avenue, has a small beach and San Lorenzo River access. Swim at your own risk, no lifeguard.
  • Biggest playground nearby: Highlands County Park, 8500 Highway 9 in Ben Lomond, adds a skate park, ball fields, tennis courts, and a nature trail.
  • A pool: the Bear Creek pool at 15685 Forest Hill Drive opens seasonally in summer. Check BCRPD for hours and passes.
  • State parks are for hiking, not playgrounds, with day-use hours, parking fees, and dogs kept off most trails.
  • No indoor play space in Boulder Creek. Rainy days mean the library or a drive down the valley.

Ask around town for a park with a real playground and you'll get a few different answers, because it depends on what your kid wants that afternoon: a swing, a river to splash in, a field to run out, or a ramp to skate. So here's what each spot near Boulder Creek has, versus what people assume it has. The rec district runs three parks close to town, the county runs a bigger playground-and-skate-park stop a few minutes down the valley, and the state parks are for nature days with their own rules. We only list amenities we could confirm. If a park isn't described as having something, assume it doesn't until you check.

Junction Park (Boulder Creek)

Junction Park sits a block off the main street at Middleton Avenue and Railroad Avenue, and it's the heart of family life in town. There's a small beach, San Lorenzo River access, a lawn, and picnic facilities.

Junction is also the park I can vouch for across a few decades: the beach I grew up playing on is the same one the newest member of our house is currently learning to walk on.

The river draws a crowd on summer afternoons, and it's swim at your own risk, with no lifeguard and conditions that change through the season, so young kids need close supervision near the water.

Junction Park also hosts the Thursday Boulder Creek Farmers Market and, in summer, the free Water Park Wednesdays playgroup from the rec district. One thing worth knowing: during the Thursday market, only service dogs are allowed at Junction Park, per the county Health Department.

Barbara Day Park (Boulder Creek)

Barbara Day Park, also called Dam Park, is a small public park at the Boulder Creek dam, a short way downstream from Junction Park. It's a quieter riverside spot rather than a playground destination. Good to know when Junction is busy, but not the place to go looking for play structures.

Garrahan Park (Boulder Creek)

Garrahan Park at 15555 Highway 9 is where you go when you want playgrounds and space. It has a walking track, a soccer field, play structures, a gazebo, benches, and a barbecue area, and it's open sunrise to sunset.

That mix makes it the spot for a picnic-and-playground afternoon, a kids' soccer kickabout, or a birthday gathering with a grill. It's up Highway 9 from downtown, so it's a quick drive rather than a walk from the town center.

Bear Creek Community Center grounds (Boulder Creek)

The Bear Creek Community Center at 15685 Forest Hill Drive is the rec district's larger facility, and its grounds include the Bear Creek pool, open seasonally in summer with recreational swim most afternoons.

It's also where the rec district runs children's classes and community events such as summer pool-and-movie nights. Center and pool hours vary by season, so check the BCRPD site for the current schedule and pool passes before you go.

Highlands County Park (Ben Lomond)

A few minutes down Highway 9 in Ben Lomond, Highlands County Park at 8500 Highway 9 brings together a playground, a skate park, ball fields, tennis courts, a nature trail, and picnic areas, open sunrise to sunset.

The same property holds a couple of the valley's community buildings, the Highlands Park Senior and Community Center and the Highlands House event venue. (Wilder Hall, where the county runs its Kreative Kids preschool program, is at Ben Lomond Park, a separate county park up the road.) For a lot of valley families it's the default birthday-party and skate-session park, worth the short drive even if you rarely leave Boulder Creek.

State parks: nature days, not playgrounds

The redwood state parks around Boulder Creek are for hiking and nature, and they play by different rules than a neighborhood park. Here's what to plan for at each:

  • Henry Cowell Redwoods (Felton): the main entrance has a flat, family-friendly redwood loop. The Fall Creek unit has no facilities and allows no dogs, bikes, or fires.
  • Big Basin Redwoods: open for limited day use only as it recovers from the 2020 fire, with first-come parking, day-use fees, and no water except at the kiosk.
  • Castle Rock (Highway 35): $10 for parking, and the gate locks at sunset.

The pattern holds across all of them: state parks generally keep dogs off trails, run on day-use hours, and charge parking fees, so they're a plan-ahead nature outing rather than a swing-by playground. Confirm access and rules on each park's official page the day you go.

The gaps worth naming

A couple of things are worth being upfront about. Boulder Creek doesn't have an indoor play space, so rainy-day play means the library or a drive down the valley.

And while the valley has other county open spaces, the parks above are the ones we can describe from verified amenity data. If you're eyeing a spot we haven't detailed here, check the county parks site for what it offers before you count on a playground being there.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which park near Boulder Creek has the best playground?

For play structures and space in town, Garrahan Park has a walking track, soccer field, play structures, a gazebo, and barbecues. For the larger option, Highlands County Park in Ben Lomond adds a skate park, ball fields, tennis courts, and a nature trail. Both are open sunrise to sunset. It comes down to whether you want in-town convenience or the larger county stop.

Where can kids swim near Boulder Creek?

The river beach at Junction Park is the classic summer swim spot, and it's swim at your own risk with no lifeguard. The rec district's Bear Creek pool at 15685 Forest Hill Drive is open seasonally with afternoon recreational swim. Check BCRPD for current hours and passes.

Are dogs allowed at the parks?

Rules vary by park, so check each one. During the Thursday farmers market, only service dogs are allowed at Junction Park, per the county Health Department. State parks generally do not allow dogs on trails, and the Fall Creek unit at Henry Cowell prohibits dogs, bikes, and fires.

Is there an indoor place to play on a rainy day?

Not in Boulder Creek itself. The library is the best local indoor option, especially on program days. The nearest dedicated indoor play lounge is in Scotts Valley, about a 25 to 35 minute drive.

We list only amenities we could confirm, and park hours and rules can change with the season. Check each agency's official page the day you go.

Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, only a starting point. Browse the full directory for park and business details, keep an eye on the local events calendar for playgroups and summer programs, and if a park's amenities or hours have changed, tell us at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact so the next family gets it right.

poison-oak-and-plants-to-avoid.title: Poison Oak and the Plants to Avoid on Santa Cruz Mountains Trails
poison-oak-and-plants-to-avoid.html:
The short version

  • Leaves of three, let it be. Poison oak grows all over these mountains, changes with the seasons, and can still give you a rash in winter when it's just bare sticks.
  • Wash fast. If you touch it, wash the skin within minutes. After about 30 minutes the oil is mostly absorbed and it's too late.
  • Decontaminate the gear. The oil, urushiol, lingers for months or years on clothes, tools, and pets, so wash those too.
  • Never eat wild mushrooms here. Death caps grow in these hills, and deadly lookalikes fool experienced foragers.
  • Save the numbers. California Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222, free and staffed 24 hours a day. Trouble breathing or swallowing is a 911 call.

You spot it a mile up the trail: three leaves off a single stem at knee height, the middle one riding a little farther out than the two beside it. That plant is worth knowing cold before your next trail day. Poison oak is everywhere in these mountains, and it changes costume with the seasons, including a winter disguise as bare sticks that can still give you a rash.

If you touch it, washing within the first minutes matters enormously; after half an hour, the oil is mostly absorbed. And the phone number for any plant question or exposure is California Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours a day. Anything severe, especially trouble breathing, is a 911 call.

None of this is a reason to stay inside. Longtime residents hike here their whole lives with nothing worse than an occasional itchy forearm. They know the plant, and that's the whole trick.

Learning to See Poison Oak

"Leaves of three, let it be" is the right starting point. UC's statewide integrated pest management program describes Pacific poison oak's signature: leaflets in threes (occasionally more), with the middle leaflet on a longer stalk than the two side ones. The leaves are lobed a bit like a true oak's, and they can be glossy or dull, which is why shine alone isn't a reliable tell.
