How often should I pump my septic tank?

EPA's general range is every three to five years for a typical household tank, with an inspection at least every three years. Your real interval depends on tank size, household size, and water use, and a disposal shortens it. Let inspections set the schedule rather than guessing, and treat these as general ranges, not a rule for your specific parcel.

Are septic additives worth buying?

Per EPA, additives aren't necessary for a system to work properly when it's treating normal household wastewater. Regular pumping does what the additives promise. Put the money toward the next inspection instead.

I'm buying a house in Boulder Creek. What should I ask about the septic system?

Ask where the tank and drainfield are, when the tank was last pumped and inspected, and for any records, then confirm the property is on septic rather than the CSA 7 sewer by checking the tax bill for a sewer charge. Questions about permits, past repairs, and what's on file for the parcel go to County Environmental Health at (831) 454-2022.

What are the signs my septic system is failing?

Slow drains, gurgling pipes, sewage smells outside, backups, soggy ground or standing water near the drainfield, and unusually lush green grass over the system even in dry weather. Any of these means call a septic professional now, while it's still a small problem.

Can I plant a garden over the drainfield?

Keep it shallow-rooted; lawn or unirrigated groundcover is the safe zone, and EPA's core drainfield rules are no vehicles, no trees nearby, and no added drainage on top of it. Skip vegetable beds you'd water regularly, and give redwoods and other thirsty trees a wide berth, because their roots will find the pipes.

shop-local-holiday-gift-guide-boulder-cr.title: Shop Local: A Boulder Creek Holiday Gift Guide
shop-local-holiday-gift-guide-boulder-cr.html:
In December, downtown Boulder Creek gets dark early, and the shop windows do most of the lighting. That's the case for doing your holiday shopping here, in a few walkable blocks of the small business district, instead of Highway 9 and a mall parking lot over the hill.

The gifts are good, the money you spend stays in town, and you skip the drive. For the current list of what's open, start with the Boulder Creek business directory.

Why shop local here

It's not sentiment. A dollar spent at a locally owned Boulder Creek shop circulates back through the town in a way a big-box purchase never does. The people behind the counters on Central Avenue tend to be the same ones sponsoring the parade, turning out for fundraisers, and keeping the lights on downtown.

A strong shopping season is part of what keeps a small mountain town's storefronts full. You also get gifts with a story attached, and you skip the drive.

What you can find downtown

Downtown Boulder Creek fits a wide range into a short walk. Rosters change from season to season, so the directory is the place to confirm who's open, but the categories to browse are these:

  • Gifts and home goods from local boutiques and gift stores
  • Outdoor and adventure gear for the hikers and campers on your list
  • Art, crafts, and handmade goods from local makers, plus galleries and studios
  • Books, music, and curiosities at the town's independent shops
  • Food and drink as gifts: local coffee, baked goods, and treats from downtown's cafes and bakery
  • A meal out to cap the day. See our guide to where to eat in Boulder Creek.

For a fuller sense of the district, our guide to the essential shops in Boulder Creek and the downtown Boulder Creek guide are good starting points.

Make a day of it

Time it with one of the season's downtown happenings and the errand turns into an outing. The Winter Festival and the December First Friday both bring the tree lighting, music, and shops open late. Small Business Saturday, the weekend after Thanksgiving, is the other natural date to aim for.

A few tips

  • Bring cash and a little patience with parking. Downtown lots are small and Highway 9 runs through the middle, so give yourself time.
  • Check hours before you go. Small shops keep their own schedules, especially around the holidays. The directory and each shop's own page are your best bet.
  • Ask the owners. Shopkeepers here know their stock and their neighbors' stock, and they'll point you to the right gift.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I do holiday shopping in Boulder Creek?

Downtown along Highway 9, which is Central Avenue through town, where local gift shops, outdoor gear, art and craft sellers, bookstores, and cafes cluster in a few walkable blocks. See the directory for what's currently open.

Why shop local instead of driving over the hill?

Money spent at locally owned Boulder Creek businesses stays in the community and helps keep downtown's storefronts and character alive, and you skip the Highway 9 drive and a crowded mall.

When are the best times to shop local for the holidays?

Small Business Saturday (the weekend after Thanksgiving), the December First Friday, and the Winter Festival, when shops stay open late and downtown is at its most festive.

Shop rosters and hours change, so check the directory and each shop before you go. Own a downtown business we should feature? Tell us. Last reviewed: July 20, 2026.

six-years-after-czu-fire-boulder-creek.title: Six Years After the CZU Fire
six-years-after-czu-fire-boulder-creek.html:
Every morning I look out over the town from our deck, and the fire is still there. Six years of regrowth has softened the ridgelines across the valley, but the old burned trees still stand against the green, gray snags marking where the CZU Lightning Complex came through in August 2020. The lightning came first, a rare dry storm that set fires which merged and burned about 86,500 acres across the Santa Cruz and San Mateo mountains, destroyed roughly 1,490 structures, and killed one civilian. Boulder Creek, Bonny Doon, and the rest of the San Lorenzo Valley were hit hardest, and it all happened in the middle of the pandemic. Our home was spared, and so were our immediate neighbors. Recovery, from this deck, looks like a mountain healing in patches.

That patchiness describes the whole valley. Six years on, some households are fully rebuilt and others are still living the fire every day. What follows is where things stand, not a tidy ending, because for many families the recovery isn't over.

What happened, briefly

In mid-August 2020, a dry lightning storm sparked fires that merged into the CZU Lightning Complex. It forced mass evacuations across the valley, moved fast through steep, forested terrain, and burned for weeks before crews contained it that September.

When people were allowed home, whole neighborhoods were gone. For the fuller account, see our history of Boulder Creek's notable disasters.

What's come back

Drive the valley now and the recovery shows up in pieces. Rebuilt homes stand on lots that were bare foundations a few years ago. The forest, which many feared was lost, has come back further than expected: coast redwoods that looked dead have pushed new growth from scorched trunks, and green has returned to hillsides that were black. Redwoods are built for this. Most of the ancient giants at Big Basin survived even where the fire burned hottest. Ninety-seven percent of the park's 18,000 acres burned in the fire's first three days, yet a small ranger team evacuated the campgrounds ahead of it and no one in the park was lost. The story of that evacuation deserves its own telling, and Traci Bliss sets the account down in her history of the park, Big Basin Redwood Forest: California's Oldest State Park (The History Press, 2021).

The institutions are moving too. Big Basin, which lost nearly all of its buildings, reopened for limited day use and has an approved plan to rebuild. The town's businesses, fire department, and community groups are all still here.

What hasn't

Recovery has been uneven. Some families rebuilt within a couple of years; others are still not home. The obstacles have been the ones you'd expect, and some you wouldn't:

  • Underinsurance that left people short of what rebuilding actually costs.
  • A slow permitting and geologic-review process that has been, at times, contentious.
  • The sheer exhaustion of navigating agencies and paperwork for years.

County officials have themselves acknowledged flaws in the rebuilding system. One fire, people here learned, can contain several different recoveries at once, and not everyone got the same one.

The hardest part is the neighbors who never got the chance. Around the valley there are still families who haven't been able to rebuild, and others selling their properties as-is because they can't afford to, with the county's permitting and septic requirements adding costs that insurance never anticipated.

The volunteers who stayed

While the rest of us evacuated, Boulder Creek's volunteer firefighters stayed behind in a town with no power, no cell service, and at first, not much food, protecting homes as the fire front moved through and state resources stretched across hundreds of fires burning at once. Help found them as the days went on: donated food and water rolled in, and volunteers from other departments came up the hill to stand with them. Long after the town reopened and residents were let back in, they were still mopping up and containing spot fires. It was a long run. They saved the town and many of our homes, and along the way they fed the animals they found left behind.

What endures

The lasting story of the CZU fire in Boulder Creek isn't only loss, and it isn't only recovery. It's both, side by side.

It's the mutual aid that showed up when official help was slow. It's neighbors who grew close because they went through the same thing. It's a hard-won, practical respect for fire preparedness that shapes how people clear defensible space and pack a go-bag now. Six years on, the valley is still rebuilding, and still here. If you have a story from those years, or one about coming back, we'd like to hear it.

I evacuated that August with a car full of animals and came home a month later to a town that held. My partner was one of the volunteers who stayed. Six years later, the department's summer BBQ still fills the fire station, the ridge across from my deck gets a little greener every year, and some of my neighbors are still waiting. All three of those things are true at once. That's what recovery looks like here.

Frequently asked questions

When was the CZU fire?

The CZU Lightning Complex fire started in mid-August 2020 during a dry lightning storm and burned for weeks before containment that September.

How much did the CZU fire burn?

It burned about 86,500 acres across the Santa Cruz and San Mateo mountains and destroyed roughly 1,490 structures, with one civilian death. Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley were among the hardest-hit areas.

Has Boulder Creek recovered from the CZU fire?

Partly. Many homes have been rebuilt and the forest has regrown strongly, but recovery has been uneven, and some families are still working to rebuild six years later, slowed by insurance gaps and a difficult permitting process.

What about Big Basin?

Big Basin lost nearly all its buildings but most of its old-growth redwoods survived. It's open for limited day use, and State Parks approved a rebuilding plan in July 2026.

Have a CZU story, a rebuild update, or a correction? Share it with us. If you're preparing for fire season now, see our wildfire evacuation guide. In an emergency, call 911. Last reviewed August 12, 2026.

slv-family-resources.title: Family Resources in the San Lorenzo Valley
slv-family-resources.html:
The short version

  • Schools: Boulder Creek is part of SLVUSD (TK through 12th). Enrollment starts by phoning your school's registrar, not a portal. Boulder Creek Elementary is the in-town campus.
  • Childcare: Call the county's Child Development Resource Center at 831-466-5820 for referrals to licensed care anywhere in the county.
  • Free kids' programs: The Boulder Creek library branch runs storytime Wednesdays and a playgroup Fridays, both free.
  • Parks, pool, camps, scouts: Most of the town's kid activity runs through the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District, at 831-338-4144.
  • When you're stuck: Dial 211 for anything from childcare subsidies to food help to counseling referrals, 24 hours a day.

Printable version: where to get help in Boulder Creek is the one-page version, useful to keep a copy of for someone who is not going to go looking online. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

Raising kids here means assembling your own list out of a school district, a library branch, a recreation district, and a handful of nonprofits, mostly by word of mouth. Here's that list, checked. SLVUSD handles school, the Boulder Creek library branch runs free weekly kids' programs, the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District covers camps, a seasonal pool, and youth programs, and the county's Child Development Resource Center will connect you with licensed childcare. Programs change with the seasons, so treat the links as your source of truth.

Schools: SLVUSD and Boulder Creek Elementary

Boulder Creek sits in the San Lorenzo Valley Unified School District, which covers TK through 12th grade for the whole valley from its offices in Ben Lomond. Enrollment starts with a phone call, not a portal. The district's enrollment page is explicit: contact your school's registrar first, and once pre-enrollment is set up, the registrar emails you instructions to finish registration online.

For the 2026-27 year, kindergartners need to turn five on or before September 1, and TK students need their fourth birthday before that date. Have a few things ready before you call:

  • Proof of your child's age
  • Immunization records
  • An oral health assessment for TK, kindergarten, and first grade
  • Proof of address

The in-town campus is Boulder Creek Elementary at 400 Lomond Street, a short walk from downtown, with current registration information posted on its site. Middle and high schoolers head down the road to the SLV campus in Felton, and METRO Route 35 stops there. That's worth knowing because K-12 students ride METRO free. Our transit guide has the details.

Preschool and childcare

Start with the Child Development Resource Center, run by the Santa Cruz County Office of Education. Its referral specialists connect families with licensed childcare centers and licensed family child care homes anywhere in the county, and they can also walk you through subsidized programs and preschool options. Call 831-466-5820 or the toll-free line at 833-774-4596, weekdays 8 to 5.

In town, Seeds of Knowledge Preschool at 16900 Highway 9 runs a licensed weekday program, Monday through Friday from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., and welcomes visits from prospective families. Little People's School at 13155 Oak Street (831-566-4236) has looked after young children here for years and now focuses on infants and toddlers, roughly babies to age three, so call to confirm the current range. Adina's and Busy Bees round out the in-town options, both home-based. For the preschool-age crowd that isn't in a full program, the rec district's outdoor classes, covered below, fill part of that gap.

The library branch on West Park Avenue

The Boulder Creek branch of Santa Cruz Public Libraries, at 13390 West Park Avenue, runs a full slate of free kids' programming, all posted on the branch events calendar. The recurring lineup:

  • Toddler and Preschool Storytime: every Wednesday at 11 a.m., with stories and songs for little ones and their caregivers.
  • Discovery Zone Playgroup: a free-play hour for kids up to age five with a participating adult, Friday mornings at 11.
  • Make & Explore: a STEAM program for school-age kids on Wednesday afternoons.
  • R.E.A.D.: free one-on-one reading comprehension instruction for grades 1 through 12, by appointment at 831-427-7713.

Summer brings extra performances and reading-program events, and a Mobile Health Clinic visits the branch monthly. Schedules shift with the seasons, so check the calendar before you load up the car. Branch hours are Monday through Thursday 10 to 6, Friday 11 to 5, and Saturday 10 to 5.

BCRPD: parks, pool, camps, and scouts

The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District is where most of the town's kid activity lives. Its downtown office at 13333 Middleton Avenue is open Tuesday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., at 831-338-4144.

For outdoor time, Junction Park sits a block off downtown at Middleton and Railroad Avenues with a small beach and river access, and Garrahan Park at 15555 Highway 9 has play structures, a soccer field, and a walking track, open sunrise to sunset. Both allow leashed dogs.

The district's childcare and youth programs page is the current catalog, and offerings rotate by season. Right now it lists:

  • Summer camp registration and seasonal movement classes for elementary and middle schoolers.
  • Enchanted Little Forest Friends: an outdoor play-based program for ages 3 to 7 that runs Monday and Wednesday mornings.
  • Santa Cruz Mountain Learning Collective: a two-day-a-week enrichment program for homeschooling families with kids in K-5.
  • Scouting: Cub Scout Pack 623 for K-5 and Scout Troop 623, which meets Monday evenings at the rec center.

The district also runs the Bear Creek pool at 15685 Forest Hill Drive, open for the 2026 season from June 6 through September 27, with recreational swim most afternoons and the pool closed Mondays. Current pool hours and passes are posted here.

Camps in our backyard

Two established camps operate right on Highway 9 north of town. YMCA Camp Campbell at 16275 Highway 9 runs overnight summer camps for kids and family camp weekends, with 2026 registration open and financial assistance available for all programs. Camp Harmon, the Easterseals camp at 16403 Highway 9, calls itself a fully accessible campground for all ages and abilities, and its programs include summer camp, weekend camps, family camp, and social recreation events.

Both are registered-program camps rather than drop-in facilities, so plan ahead through their sites.

Down the valley: Highlands Park

Five minutes down Highway 9 in Ben Lomond, Highlands County Park at 8500 Highway 9 packs a playground, a skate park, ball fields, tennis courts, a nature trail, and picnic areas into one stop, open sunrise to sunset. It's where valley birthday parties and after-school skate sessions tend to end up, and it's worth knowing even if you rarely leave Boulder Creek.

When you don't know who to call

For everything else, from childcare subsidies to food assistance to family counseling referrals, dial 211 or text your ZIP code to 211211. 211 Santa Cruz County, a program of United Way of Santa Cruz, covers more than 500 local resources. Phone and text service runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and 211 offers phone interpretation in 150 languages. It's the fastest way to find out which agency handles the thing you need.

New to the valley entirely? Our new resident quick-start guide covers alerts, utilities, and the rest of week one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a storytime at the Boulder Creek library?

Yes. Toddler and Preschool Storytime runs every Wednesday at 11 a.m. at the branch on West Park Avenue, and a Friday-morning playgroup serves kids up to age five. Both are free; check the branch events calendar for the current schedule.

How do I enroll my child in school in Boulder Creek?

Contact the registrar at your assigned school first; for elementary-age kids in town that's Boulder Creek Elementary. The registrar sets up pre-enrollment and sends you online registration instructions. You'll need proof of age, immunization records, proof of address, and an oral health assessment for the youngest grades.

Where can I find childcare in the San Lorenzo Valley?

Call the Child Development Resource Center at 831-466-5820 for referrals to licensed centers and family child care homes. In Boulder Creek itself, Seeds of Knowledge Preschool runs a licensed weekday program, and BCRPD's Enchanted Little Forest Friends covers preschool-age kids two mornings a week.

Is there a public pool in Boulder Creek?

Yes, seasonally. BCRPD's Bear Creek pool at 15685 Forest Hill Drive is open June 6 through September 27 in 2026, with afternoon recreational swim most days and Mondays closed.

What summer camps operate near Boulder Creek?

BCRPD runs day camps in town, YMCA Camp Campbell offers overnight camp and family camps on Highway 9, and Easterseals' Camp Harmon runs fully accessible sessions for campers of all ages and abilities. All three post registration on their own sites.

Last reviewed July 16, 2026. Details here come from the school district, library, recreation district, and county resources linked throughout. Programs, hours, and fees change with the seasons, so confirm current specifics through each link before you go.

Once you've got the kids sorted, the rest of settling in lives in one place: see the Residents guide for utilities, alerts, and county contacts, and the local directory for businesses and services around town. If you are looking for work that fits around school hours, the valley job board carries the district and local business openings.

splashfest-boulder-creek.title: Splashfest 2026 in Boulder Creek: A Family Guide
splashfest-boulder-creek.html:
There's a stretch in early September when Boulder Creek is still holding onto summer, and for one afternoon Garrahan Park fills up with soaked, delighted kids. That's Splashfest, the end-of-summer water-play party, back on Saturday, September 5, 2026, from noon to 3 p.m., with a quieter low-sensory hour from 11 a.m. to noon. It's built for young children: hands-on, messy, and cheerfully wet, a way to send the warm season off before school pulls everyone back inside.

The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District runs it alongside Messy Play Kits. Plan on your kids getting wet, and confirm the details with BCRPD before you go.

The quick version

  • When: Saturday, September 5, 2026, noon to 3 p.m. The low-sensory hour runs 11 a.m. to noon.
  • Where: Garrahan Park, 15555 Highway 9, Boulder Creek.
  • Cost and registration: confirm current details with BCRPD. Community park events like this can fill up, so check ahead.
  • Bring: a towel, dry clothes, water shoes, sun protection, and water to drink.

What to expect

An afternoon of water play and messy, sensory fun aimed squarely at younger kids. The activities are hands-on and, as the name promises, wet, so plan around soggy children from the start.

The low-sensory hour from 11 a.m. to noon gives kids who do better with less crowd and noise a calmer window to enjoy it. Worth knowing if that fits your family.

Parking and getting there

Garrahan Park sits right on Highway 9, where the highway runs through the middle of town. Parking is limited, so give yourself extra time and follow any event parking directions on the day.

Who is organizing it

Splashfest is presented by the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District with Messy Play Kits. BCRPD runs Garrahan and Junction parks and much of the town's recreation programming.

More to do with the kids

If Splashfest sends you looking for the rest of the weekend, see our guide to a day with kids in Boulder Creek and our roundup of local parks and playgrounds.

Details change. Confirm the date and any cost with BCRPD before you go, and tell us if something's off. Last reviewed July 20, 2026.

summer-camps-san-lorenzo-valley.title: Summer Camps and Kids Classes in the San Lorenzo Valley: The 2026 Guide
summer-camps-san-lorenzo-valley.html:
The short version

  • Register in the off-season. Many camps open sign-ups between December and spring, and popular sessions are often full or waitlisted by mid-July. If a specific camp matters, get on its page over the winter.
  • Free options exist. The Boulder Creek library's summer reading program and Henry Cowell's drop-in Junior and Little Rangers cost nothing (Henry Cowell has a $10 parking fee).
  • Cheapest paid camps this summer: Community Mountain Gym's Friday drop-in at $50 a day, and Santa Cruz Learning Center's full week on a $200 to $300 sliding scale.
  • Ask about scholarships. Camp Harmon, Farm Discovery, Tails of Redwood Trails, the Santa Cruz Mountains Art Center, the YMCA, and Santa Cruz Learning Center all offer some form of financial help.
  • Treat the links as your source of truth. Camps change dates and prices year to year, so confirm on each program's page before you plan around it.

If a camp matters to your family, the thing that decides it usually isn't price or age range. It's timing. By the middle of the summer the rafting trip had a waitlist and half the overnight weeks in the county were gone, which is how camp season tends to go up here.

Between Boulder Creek and the towns down the valley, families had more than thirty summer camp and class options in 2026: recreation-district day camps in town, gymnastics and horse camps in Felton, art and nature programs, and a handful of overnight camps within a short drive. Below is that full list, grouped by type, with one-line facts and a link to each program's page. Most open registration between December and April and fill through the spring, so bookmark the ones that interest you over the winter.

In town: BCRPD, the pool, and the library

The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District is the closest thing the valley has to a home-base camp program, at 13333 Middleton Avenue (831-338-4144). This summer's BCRPD flyers listed four camps.

  • Adventure Camps served ages 2 to 5 in half-day themed weeks (Kids in the Kitchen, Ocean Explorers, Mini Makers), 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., at $240 a week.
  • Bear Creek Camp ran seven themed weeks for ages 6 to 11, full days 9 to 4 with daily pool time and snacks, at $310 a week.
  • Gymnastics and Dance Camp covered ages 3 to 6 over one late-June week, 10 to 2, at $250.
  • Whitewater Rafting Campout took older kids (the flyer listed ages 11 to 15) down the South Fork of the American River on a three-day, two-night trip in mid-July for $650.

Registration runs through Wufoo forms linked from the district site, and by mid-summer the rafting trip was already waitlisted.

The Bear Creek pool at 15685 Forest Hill Drive runs its own season, June 6 through September 27 in 2026, with recreational swim most afternoons and the pool closed Mondays. Current hours and season passes are posted here. One expectation to set: BCRPD doesn't publish swim lessons or a junior-lifeguard program anywhere on its site, so don't count on those.

The library is the free option worth building around. The Boulder Creek branch of Santa Cruz Public Libraries runs a summer reading program every year (2026's was "Plant a Seed, Read"), where kids log reading from June 1 through July 31 and earn prizes, with magicians, puppeteers, and craft events through the summer. Sign up at the branch or through Beanstack.

The branch also holds a Toddler and Preschool Storytime on Wednesday mornings. Check the branch calendar for the current week before you go.

Gymnastics and active camps

Community Mountain Gym runs day camps out of Felton (6171 Highway 9) and Scotts Valley. This summer's flyer listed an Active Kids Gymnastics Summer Camp across eight weeks, June 8 through July 31, at $325 a week, blending gymnastics with science, library trips, and games, plus a drop-in Kids Summer Camp on Fridays, 9 to 3 at the Felton Community Hall, for $50 a day. The gym's site confirms the format but doesn't publish dates or prices, so treat the flyer numbers as this-year figures and confirm on the weekly registration form.

La Madrona Athletic Club in the Scotts Valley area (1897 La Madrona Drive) ran three camps over ten weeks, June 1 through August 7, open to members and non-members. Sports Camp covered ages 6 to 10, 8:45 to 3, at $389 member and $466 non-member per week; a Summer Pool Guards Camp for roughly ages 6 to 12 ran mornings at $230 and $276; and a Tennis and Pickleball Camp for ages 6 to 12 ran 10 to 1 at $270 and $324. Registration packets are on the club's site.

Valley Sports Camp is a private operator running a multi-sports camp out of local school facilities. In 2026 it held three June weeks in Ben Lomond (June 8-12, 15-19, and 22-26) and three July weeks in Scotts Valley. It serves ages 4 through 13, with full days 9 to 3 at $390 a week and half days at $320, plus early-bird pricing for those who signed up by mid-March.

Horse camps

Tails of Redwood Trails runs horse programs out of the Covered Bridge Equestrian Center at 220 Covered Bridge Road in Felton. Its site lists school-break day programs, Pioneer Ponies for ages 5 to 7 and Horse Hollow for ages 8 to 13, covering riding, grooming, farm chores, and creek play. This summer's flyer described a fuller June-through-August horse camp with certified lifeguards, crafts, and Felton library visits, and noted full and partial scholarships. There's no online registration. Text Kristina Nielsen at 831-706-7482 about the current season.

Trinity Rivers Equestrian at White Rock Ranch ran horsemanship camps on a published 2026 schedule of six weeks between June 8 and July 24 (no camp the week of June 29). Days run 9 to 3:30, with extended care to 5 for an extra $100 a week, at $650 a week including instruction, lunch, pool time, and a Friday show. Register through the RegFox link on the ranch's page.

Art and making

The Santa Cruz Mountains Art Center in Ben Lomond (9341 Mill Street) ran youth art classes over two weeks in June 2026, for ages 7 to 14, with some specialized classes for ages 9 and up. The format is a-la-carte: kids stack individual classes (painting, drawing, ceramics, printmaking, jewelry, tie-dye, and more) back to back, with a supervised lunch option to make a full day. The center doesn't publish a price online and offers sliding-scale help through the Gloria Seneres Memorial Fund, so email info@mountainartcenter.org or call 831-336-3513 for pricing and scholarships.

Nature and farm camps

WOLF School runs a Summer Nature Day Camp for kindergarten through sixth grade, split into ages 5 to 7 and 8 to 11. It's a drop-off day camp, 8:30 to 3:30, across eight weekly sessions from June 8 through July 31, at $525 a week early-bird (through the end of April) or $575 after. One thing to know before you plan around it: the camp is held at Camp Monte Toyon in Aptos, not in the valley, so figure on a 20-to-30-minute drive from Ben Lomond.

Farm Discovery at Live Earth Farm runs a Farm Camp for ages 5 to 13 across ten weeks, June 1 through August 7, at $425 a week, with early- and late-care add-ons at $100 each and a Leaders-in-Training track for ages 13 and up. Scholarships are available. It's a day camp in Watsonville.

Quail Hollow Ranch County Park in Ben Lomond runs Santa Cruz County youth day camps for first through sixth graders, with hikes, science, games, and crafts. The county registers these through its ActiveNet portal rather than a static page, so the summer dates and prices live there. Check the county page or call 831-454-7941 for the session list.

Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park in Felton isn't a camp, but it's a free option worth knowing. From Memorial Day through Labor Day, interpreters lead drop-in programs in the campground, including Junior Rangers for ages 7 to 12 and Little Rangers for younger kids, where they explore and earn prizes. There's no pre-registration, only the $10 day-use parking fee. Times vary, so check the park's calendar or the visitor center (831-335-7077).

Water and ocean

Wave Warrior Camp, now run by OXA Training near Santa Cruz and Capitola, teaches ocean skills to kids ages 7 and up: surfing, bodysurfing, ocean safety, and basic first aid, 10 to 3 Monday through Friday, at $750 a week. There's also a lower-cost Wave Warrior Little's class at $165. The camp page can lag behind, so confirm the current summer's dates before you plan (831-291-0968). For an option closer to home, see the BCRPD rafting campout above.

Overnight and traditional camps

YMCA Camp Campbell on Highway 9 north of Boulder Creek runs both a day camp (8 to 5, campers grouped by age and folded into overnight-camp activities) and overnight camps in traditional, teen-adventure, and leadership tracks. Session dates and prices move around and sell through the YMCA registration portal; by mid-2026 the remaining bookable overnight weeks were six-day mini-camps for ages 7 to 16 around $1,024 for members, and those were waitlisted. Financial assistance is available, and a Labor Day family camp weekend closes the season.

Mount Hermon in Felton runs faith-based overnight camps. Redwood Camp serves grades 2 through 6 in weekly sessions at $799 a week (meals, lodging, and program included, with sibling and bring-a-friend discounts), and Ponderosa Lodge covers grades 7 through 12 at $990 a week. Registration opens in the off-season (a recent year opened in early December) through register.mounthermon.org.

Kennolyn Camps in Soquel is a regional staple with a day camp for kindergarten through 11th grade (from $745 a week), a residential overnight camp for grades 1 through 12 (from $3,325 a week), and a Huntington Lake overnight for older kids. It registers on a rolling basis, and by mid-summer 2026 many sessions were full with only a couple of open weeks left, so book early.

Camp Harmon in Boulder Creek, run by Easterseals Central California, is a fully accessible overnight camp built for children and adults with disabilities, with a 60-year history and a 1-to-3 staff-to-camper ratio (1-to-1 available). Its summer runs as nine five-day sessions, the youngest group starting at age 10, across an animal farm, garden, arts, and pool. Sessions in 2026 ran $1,450 each at the standard ratio, with Regional Center funding and scholarships available through the camp's scholarships page. Applications close once the season fills, so for next summer, watch campharmon.org and apply in the off-season.

Regional day camps down the valley

Santa Cruz Learning Center runs a day camp for ages 5 to 11, weekly from June 1 through July 31 plus a short August mini-session (no camp the week of June 29), 10 to 4 with extended care available. The center dropped its 2026 pricing to a sliding scale of $200 to $300 a week, one of the more affordable full-week camps around. It also runs short tween and teen camps like Forensics and Physiology and Coastal Crafts and Design.

Seven Directions in Santa Cruz ran a deep art-and-nature schedule in 2026: nineteen one-week day camps from June through mid-August for ages 5 to 18, most full days 10 to 3:30 at $425 to $440 a week, with some half-day camps from $220. Themes ranged from prehistoric animal art and anime to a nature adventure camp at Henry Cowell and end-of-summer eco art, and the studio offers multi-camp discounts. Each camp registers separately through the schedule page.

When registration opens

There's a rhythm worth knowing for next year. Many camps open registration in the off-season, roughly December through spring. Mount Hermon has opened as early as December, and Camp Harmon's applications open in the off-season too.

Early-bird pricing tends to cluster from late January (Farm Discovery's ended January 31) through spring (Valley Sports' ran through mid-March, WOLF's through the end of April). By mid-July, popular sessions are often full or waitlisted: this summer the BCRPD rafting campout, the YMCA mini-camps, and much of Kennolyn's schedule were already spoken for. If a specific camp matters to your family, get on its page over the winter and register by early spring.

Frequently asked questions

When should I register for summer camp in the San Lorenzo Valley?

Plan to register in the off-season, roughly December through early spring. Several camps open registration as early as December, early-bird deadlines cluster from late January through March, and by mid-summer the popular sessions are frequently full or waitlisted.

What are the cheapest summer options for kids?

The library's summer reading program and Henry Cowell's drop-in Junior and Little Rangers programs are free, apart from Henry Cowell's $10 parking. Among paid camps, Community Mountain Gym's Friday drop-in ran $50 a day this summer, and Santa Cruz Learning Center's full-week day camp ran a sliding $200 to $300. Several camps also offer scholarships.

What's available for toddlers and preschoolers?

The youngest camps in town were BCRPD's Adventure Camps for ages 2 to 5 and its Gymnastics and Dance Camp for ages 3 to 6. Community Mountain Gym runs ongoing tiny-tot and preschool classes outside of camp, and the Boulder Creek library's Wednesday-morning storytime is a free weekly option.

Which camps offer scholarships or financial help?

Several. Camp Harmon offers scholarships and Regional Center funding, Farm Discovery lists scholarships for its farm camp, and this summer's Tails of Redwood Trails flyer noted full and partial scholarships. The Santa Cruz Mountains Art Center runs a sliding scale through the Gloria Seneres Memorial Fund, the YMCA offers financial assistance, and Santa Cruz Learning Center moved to sliding-scale pricing. Ask each program directly, since terms change year to year.

For the broader picture on schools, childcare, and year-round kids' programs in the valley, see our family resources guide.

Planning the rest of your season? Check what's coming up on the Boulder Creek Local events page, find local businesses in the directory, see who is hiring for the season on the valley job board, and if a camp here has changed its dates or you know one we missed, send it to us.

swimming-boulder-creek-san-lorenzo-river.title: Where to Swim Near Boulder Creek
swimming-boulder-creek-san-lorenzo-river.html:
The short version

  • The closest place to swim is the San Lorenzo River at Junction Park, one block off Highway 9 downtown, where the Rec and Park District keeps a small river beach.
  • There are no lifeguards on the river anywhere, so it's swim at your own risk.
  • Never swim alone, keep young or weak swimmers within arm's reach, and pick one sober water watcher who puts the phone down.
  • After rain the river runs higher, faster, colder, and often dirtier for a few days. Give it time to settle, and don't jump where you can't see the bottom.
  • Want a pool instead? The district runs a seasonal community pool at its Bear Creek site, roughly early June into late September.

When the valley heat climbs and you need to cool off, the closest swimming water in town is the San Lorenzo River at Junction Park, a summer swimming hole a block off downtown. There are no lifeguards there, or anywhere on the river, so it's swim at your own risk. If you'd rather have a chlorinated pool with set hours, the district runs a seasonal community pool a couple of minutes away. Whichever you pick, the water safety basics below aren't fine print. They're the difference between a good afternoon and a bad one.

The river at Junction Park

Junction Park is the easy answer. The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District maintains it at Middleton and Railroad Avenues, one block off the main street, with a beach, San Lorenzo River access, a grassy area, and picnic tables. As the district puts it, in summer the river here is "a favorite swimming hole for many of our community members." It's walkable from downtown, shaded, and the natural place to spend a hot afternoon.

Just downstream, Barbara Day Park, which longtime residents still call the Dam Park, also touches the river. The district says it's currently undergoing some beautification and new features, so expect it to be a work in progress for now. Both parks are leashed-dogs-only.

One more district park people ask about: Garrahan Park, up Highway 9 north of town, is a fields-and-track park with a walking loop, play structures, a gazebo, and barbecues, not a developed river beach. It's a fine place for a picnic or to let kids run, but Junction Park is the swimming spot in town.

It's been the swimming spot for generations, including mine. I grew up on that beach, hunting salamanders along the bank with my sister while the big kids swam across to jump off the rocks, and the water is exactly as cold now as it was then. Bring a towel for the kid who swears they won't need one.

The safety part that matters

Nobody lifeguards the San Lorenzo River. That single fact shapes everything else, because drowning is not what most people picture.

The CDC says drowning is fast and often silent, and can happen in as little as 20 to 60 seconds, without the splashing and shouting movies train us to expect. It's the leading cause of death for children ages 1 to 4 and the second-leading cause of unintentional injury death for kids 5 to 14, and more than 40 percent of drownings among children 5 to 14 happen in natural water like rivers.

Natural water is riskier than a pool for reasons you can't always see. The CDC lists hidden hazards in rivers and lakes: currents, cold water, rocks and vegetation, and limited visibility that hides how deep or shallow the next step is. A few habits carry almost all the safety here, and every one of them comes straight from the CDC and the American Red Cross:

  • Never swim alone, and swim where you can. Choose spots with other people around, and when it's an option, swim where there are lifeguards.
  • Watch kids within arm's reach. For young or weak swimmers, an adult should stay within an arm's length in or near the water. Pick one adult to be the water watcher, and have them put the phone down and skip the drinks. Drowning happens too fast and too quietly to catch while you're distracted.
  • Respect cold water and current. Even in summer, mountain river water is colder than it looks, and a cold plunge can steal your breath and strength in seconds. After rain, the river runs higher, faster, and colder, sometimes for days, so give it time to settle.
  • Don't count on jumping. People do jump from rocks along the river, but depth changes with the season and with what the last storm moved, and a pool that was deep last August may not be this year. If you can't see the bottom, don't jump.
  • If someone's in trouble, reach or throw, don't go. The Red Cross rule is to extend a branch or throw something that floats rather than jump in after them, because panicked swimmers pull rescuers under. If it's an emergency, call 911.

None of this makes the river safe. It stays swim at your own risk. It stacks the odds in your favor.

What about the water quality

Santa Cruz County Environmental Health routinely tests rivers, creeks, and ocean swimming areas across the county for bacteria that signal pollution, and the San Lorenzo River watershed gets intensive monitoring under a long-running partnership that includes the county, the City of Santa Cruz, the Coastal Watershed Council, Surfrider, and the regional water board. When bacteria run high, the county posts advisory signs: a Warning sign, black lettering on white, when levels exceed the standard, and a Danger sign, red on white, for a confirmed sewage problem.

Two practical things follow from that. Water quality changes, especially after rain, when runoff can carry bacteria into the river for up to three days. So the answer to "is it clean today" is that it depends on the day, and we won't publish a number here that would be stale by the time you read it. Check the county's recreational water quality information or call the county for the current posting, look for any signs at the park, and when in doubt after a storm, wait a few dry days.

The other rule is simpler: don't swim with an open wound, and try not to swallow river water. That's good practice on any natural waterway.

If you'd rather have a pool

For a swim with more structure and no current, the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District runs a seasonal community pool at its Bear Creek site on Forest Hill Drive. It opens for a summer season, roughly early June into late September, with expanded summer hours and scheduled Adult Swim and Rec Swim sessions, plus a summer membership option. Hours shift year to year, so check the current schedule with BCRPD or call the office before you load the car.

Beyond the valley, La Madrona Athletic Club in Santa Cruz is a private membership club with heated outdoor pools and swim lessons, if a club setup and structured lessons are what you're after. And if you want lifeguarded open water, the nearest is the Santa Cruz coast, where city and state beaches staff lifeguards during the summer season. Guarded hours and locations vary, so confirm with the City of Santa Cruz or State Parks for the day you go.

A few more San Lorenzo River spots

The river runs the length of the valley, and there are well-known swim spots downstream of Boulder Creek, from Highlands County Park in Ben Lomond to the Garden of Eden area inside Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park near Felton. They're scenic and popular, and every one of them is unguarded, with the same cold-water, current, and changing-depth realities as the river in town. If you explore them, bring the same habits, check each park's official page for access and rules, and remember that state parks have their own regulations.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. The safety guidance here follows the CDC, the American Red Cross, and Santa Cruz County Environmental Health, all linked above. River conditions and posted advisories change day to day, so confirm the current status before you go.

Frequently asked questions

Can you swim in the San Lorenzo River at Boulder Creek?

Yes, at Junction Park the Rec and Park District keeps a small river beach that the community uses as a summer swimming hole. There are no lifeguards, so it's swim at your own risk. Watch the water safety basics above, especially with kids, and give the river time to settle after rain.

Are there lifeguards anywhere in Boulder Creek?

Not on the river. Junction Park and the other river beaches are unguarded. The district's seasonal pool has scheduled swim sessions, and the nearest lifeguarded open-water swimming is at the Santa Cruz coast in season. Confirm hours with each place before you go.

Is the water clean enough to swim in?

It depends on the day. The county monitors the San Lorenzo River for bacteria and posts advisory signs when levels are high, and runoff after rain can raise bacteria for a few days. Check the county's recreational water quality info, look for signs at the park, don't swallow the water, and skip it with an open wound.

When is the river best for swimming?

Deeper, colder, faster flow comes early in the season and after storms; by late summer the water is warmer but the pools get shallower. Early to mid-summer on a stretch of dry weather tends to be the sweet spot, but conditions vary year to year, so look before you wade in.

Is there a public pool near Boulder Creek?

Yes. The Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District runs a seasonal community pool at its Bear Creek site, open roughly June through late September with scheduled swim sessions. Check current hours with BCRPD.

Before you head down to the water, check conditions after any storm on Mountain Status, see how wet the winter was on our rain tracker since river levels follow it closely, and find parks, pools, and local services in the Boulder Creek Local directory and the Residents guide. In an emergency, call 911. Notice a detail here that needs fixing? Send it to us.

tree-services-boulder-creek.title: Tree Services in Boulder Creek
tree-services-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Four tree services are based right here in Boulder Creek: Christianson Tree Experts, Stellar Tree Care, Sunderland Tree Service, and Travis Tree Professionals.
  • Some removals need county sign-off. Check the rules before you assume a tree can come down at all.
  • In California, tree work over $1,000 is licensed contracting under the C-49 Tree and Palm classification, and tree contractors must carry workers' comp insurance even as one-person crews.
  • Verify license and insurance before you sign, and ask the insurer to send liability and workers' comp certificates directly.
  • For a 24-hour emergency, Travis Tree Professionals advertises round-the-clock response. Even then, slow down on the paperwork before you commit.

A redwood that starts leaning the wrong way after a winter storm isn't a problem you want to solve by grabbing the first name off a search page. Tree work is the most consequential home service up here, and the wrong crew, or the wrong call on a redwood, is an expensive mistake. The good news is that four tree services are based right here in town, which is a real advantage. Here's who works locally and what they say they do, grouped so you can start calling for bids.

Before you sign anything, read our companion guide on the questions to ask before anyone touches a redwood. It covers permits, licensing, and insurance in detail, and all of it applies to every company on this page.

One thing drives most tree work in these mountains, and that's fire. Clearing trees isn't the same as creating defensible space, and some removals need a permit. Our Residents page points to the Santa Cruz County tree protection and removal rules, which can require county sign-off depending on your parcel's overlays, creeks, and habitat. Start there before you assume a tree can come down at all.

Christianson Tree Experts (Boulder Creek)

Address: 13041 Pine Street, Boulder Creek. Phone: 831-338-6984. Website: christiansontreeexperts.com.

Christianson is a Boulder Creek tree-care company, and one of the few on this list with a listed street address in town rather than a service-only operation. Its own description covers pruning, removal, hazard assessment, cabling, and emergency services, a full range for storm-country work. The hazard assessment and cabling are worth a second look, because they point to keeping trees standing safely, not only felling them.

Stellar Tree Care (Boulder Creek)

Phone: 831-227-5414. Website: stellartreecare.com. Service area: Boulder Creek and the Santa Cruz Mountains. No public storefront address.

Stellar Tree Care is a Boulder Creek-based service that offers trimming, removal, firebreaks, and property-safety work. The firebreak focus speaks directly to defensible-space planning around a mountain home. Like several local tree outfits, it works from the field rather than a storefront, so contact runs through its site or by phone.

Sunderland Tree Service (Boulder Creek)

Phone: 831-338-2197. Website: sunderlandtree.com. Service area: Boulder Creek and the Santa Cruz Mountains. No public storefront address.

Sunderland Tree Service handles removal, pruning, firebreak, and defensible-space work for Boulder Creek and the surrounding mountains. Its description names defensible space directly, so it's a reasonable call when your goal is meeting fire-safety spacing rather than clearing a lot. Ask for a zone-by-zone plan rather than a blanket "take them all down" bid.

Travis Tree Professionals (Boulder Creek)

Phone: 831-338-6361. Website: travistreeprofessionals.com. Hours: daily, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with 24-hour emergency response advertised. Service area: Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley.

Travis Tree Professionals offers pruning, removal, fire mitigation, land clearing, and emergency response, and it's the one company here that advertises a daily schedule plus round-the-clock emergency service. That kind of availability matters at 2 a.m., when a winter storm has dropped a limb across your driveway. Storm season or not, slow down on the paperwork even when the situation feels urgent, and verify before you commit.

Before You Hire Any of Them

Every company here is Boulder Creek based, which is a real plus for local knowledge of our slopes, soils, and creeks. It doesn't replace the checks, though.

In California, tree work over $1,000 is licensed contracting under the C-49 Tree and Palm classification, and tree contractors are required to carry workers' compensation insurance whether or not they have employees. Verify any company's license and workers' comp status in the state licensing lookup, and ask their insurer to send liability and workers' comp certificates directly.

Our tree-work questions guide walks through exactly how, and the Residents page links the county permit rules you may need to clear first. Being listed in our directory is a starting point, not an endorsement, so run the checks regardless of who you call.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a permit to remove a tree in Boulder Creek?

Sometimes, and it's parcel-specific. Santa Cruz County can require a permit depending on the Coastal Zone, riparian corridors along creeks, sensitive habitat, and tree size. Check your parcel and the county rules before cutting. Our Residents page links the county's tree protection and removal information, and our tree-work questions guide explains the thresholds. Don't rely on a contractor's verbal "no permit needed."

Will these companies handle defensible-space and fire clearing?

Several name firebreak or defensible-space work directly, including Stellar Tree Care and Sunderland Tree Service, with Travis Tree Professionals listing fire mitigation. Keep in mind that defensible space is about spacing, limbing, and fuel reduction across zones, not blanket removal, so ask any bidder for a zone-by-zone plan rather than a clear-cut quote.

How do I check that a tree company is licensed and insured?

Look up the C-49 license and workers' comp status in the state contractor license system, and ask for insurance certificates sent directly from the company's insurer. Tree contractors must carry workers' comp even as one-person operations, so verify it rather than taking a business card's word. The full step-by-step is in our tree-work questions guide.

Who do I call for an emergency, like a tree on a structure or across the road?

For a true emergency, safety comes first. If the tree is on power lines, stay clear and call PG&E; if it's blocking a public road, that's a county road matter. Among local companies, Travis Tree Professionals advertises 24-hour emergency response. Document the situation with photos before any work, and note that genuine emergencies are treated differently under the county code.

Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, only a verified place to start. See the full directory for local tree services and other trades, and send corrections or additions through the submit page so the next neighbor gets accurate information.

twenty-years-of-rain-san-lorenzo-valley.title: What Twenty Years of Rain Looks Like in the San Lorenzo Valley
twenty-years-of-rain-san-lorenzo-valley.html:
What Twenty Years of Rain Looks Like in the San Lorenzo Valley

Two years apart, this valley recorded its second-driest year in living memory and its third-wettest. Water year 2021 brought 21.51 inches to the Ben Lomond gauge. Water year 2023 brought 85.13. Nothing about the way we talk about rain up here prepares you for a four-fold swing inside two winters, and yet that is the actual record.

The National Weather Service and the water district both keep this data, but almost nobody sees it laid out. So here it is: nearly ninety years of rainfall from the valley's longest continuous gauge, what the typical year really looks like, and why the word "average" is close to useless for planning a mountain property.

I've lived every one of these winters. The chart below is the same story my culverts, my generator, and my firewood stack would tell you, just with better data.

Where these numbers come from

The valley's long record belongs to a National Weather Service cooperative station called Ben Lomond No. 4, at 435 feet, which has been logging daily rainfall since 1937. It is about five miles down-canyon from downtown Boulder Creek, and it is the only gauge nearby with a record long enough to say anything about normal.

Rain here is measured by water year, October 1 through September 30, named for the calendar year it ends in. That matters: a water year holds one winter, which is how storms actually arrive. Splitting rainfall by calendar year cuts every wet season in half.

Of the 86 water years in the record, 67 are complete enough to report, meaning five or fewer missing days. The gaps are honest gaps, mostly 2011, 2012 and 2024, and they are excluded rather than patched.

The typical year is drier than the average year

  • Mean water-year total: 49.1 inches
  • Median water-year total: 42.7 inches

A handful of enormous years drag the mean upward, so the "average" year is wetter than most years actually are. If you are sizing a culvert or deciding whether your drainage can cope, the median is the better number, and the extremes are what break things.

The extremes

Wettest water years Inches
1983 95.65
2017 94.62
2023 85.13
1998 82.80
1958 80.61
Driest water years Inches
1977 19.97
2021 21.51
1976 21.60
2014 22.83
1990 24.30

Three things jump out. Two of the five wettest years on an eighty-six-year record have happened since 2017. So has one of the five driest. And 1976 and 1977 sit back to back, the two-year drought older residents still measure other dry spells against.

The last twenty years, in order

Water year Inches Against the 42.7-inch median
2006 74.62 well above
2007 29.03 well below
2008 38.79 below
2009 38.55 below
2010 56.20 above
2013 36.85 below
2014 22.83 4th driest on record
2015 34.44 below
2016 46.62 near median
2017 94.62 2nd wettest on record
2018 33.77 below
2019 65.26 well above
2020 31.38 well below
2021 21.51 2nd driest on record
2022 44.58 near median
2023 85.13 3rd wettest on record

Water years 2011, 2012 and 2024 are missing too many days at this station to report. Water year 2025 came in around 37 inches with fifteen days missing, so treat it as approximate and probably a slight undercount. The current water year, 2026, stood at about 45 inches through July, and since August and September are reliably dry here, that is close to its final figure.

Is Boulder Creek different from Ben Lomond?

Less than you would guess. A volunteer gauge three miles northwest of Boulder Creek, up at 875 feet, has overlapped the Ben Lomond record for seven reportable years. Boulder Creek came in an average of six percent lower, and within a few percent in five of those seven years.

Two cautions before anyone reads that as "Boulder Creek is drier." Volunteer gauges miss days, and a missed day during an atmospheric river costs inches, which is the likeliest explanation for the one big outlier, 2017. The fair conclusion is narrower and more useful: the valley moves together. A wet year in Ben Lomond is a wet year in Boulder Creek, so the long Ben Lomond record is a reasonable stand-in for the whole valley, and the exact inches at your own house will differ with elevation, canyon and aspect.

What this means for a house up here

The record does not say the climate is getting steadily wetter or drier. It says the swings are what you plan for. A 21-inch year and an 85-inch year are both normal here, and they can arrive two winters apart.

Practically, that argues for the unglamorous work: clear culverts and ditches before the first atmospheric river, because a 40-inch year and an 85-inch year both come through the same pipe. Know where water goes on your parcel. And treat any single dry winter as a pause rather than a trend, because 1977 was followed by decades that included four of the five wettest years on record.

Our maintenance calendar puts the drainage work in the right months, and the before the first major rain checklist covers the September and October push.

Frequently asked questions

How much rain does Boulder Creek get in a year?

The valley's long gauge at Ben Lomond averages 49.1 inches per water year across 67 complete years since 1940, but the median is 42.7 inches, and individual years have ranged from about 20 to about 96 inches. There is no single normal.

What was the wettest year on record?

Water year 1983, at 95.65 inches. Water year 2017 came within an inch of it at 94.62, and 2023 was third at 85.13.

What was the driest?

Water year 1977, at 19.97 inches, part of the back-to-back 1976 and 1977 drought. Water year 2021, at 21.51 inches, is the second driest in the record.

Why measure by water year instead of calendar year?

Because a water year, October through September, contains exactly one winter. Calendar years split each wet season across two totals and make comparison meaningless.

Data pulled 2026-07-25 from NOAA cooperative station Ben Lomond No. 4 (GHCN identifier USC00040673) through the NOAA Regional Climate Centers ACIS service, with a Boulder Creek volunteer station (US1CASZ0021) used for comparison. Water-year totals were computed from daily records, and any year missing more than five days is excluded rather than estimated. Rainfall at your own property will differ. For current conditions and forecasts, use the National Weather Service, and for road and storm conditions see Mountain Status.

vets-pet-services-boulder-creek.title: Vets and Pet Services In and Around Boulder Creek
vets-pet-services-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Vet in town: Boulder Creek Veterinary Clinic, 12870 Highway 9, 831-338-7205. Full-service, six days a week, with two late nights.
  • Backup vet: Felton Veterinary Hospital, about fifteen minutes south, 831-335-3466.
  • Overnight emergency: no 24-hour ER in the valley. The nearest is Pacific and Santa Cruz Veterinary Specialists in Santa Cruz, 831-475-5400, open 24/7. Save that number now.
  • Injured wildlife: Native Animal Rescue hotline, 831-462-0726. Call before you touch anything.
  • Stray or lost pet: Santa Cruz County Animal Shelter, 831-454-7224.
  • Grooming: Bowzer Baths right in town, plus options in Felton and Ben Lomond. Boarding and sitting: valley-wide services and both vet clinics. Call ahead; most are appointment-based.

Most mountain towns send you down the mountain for a vet. Boulder Creek doesn't. There's a full-service veterinary clinic right on Highway 9 in town, and another a few minutes south in Felton, so routine care, shots, dental work, and daytime sick visits are all handled close to home. The one gap is overnight: neither valley clinic is a 24-hour hospital, so for a middle-of-the-night crisis you're driving to Santa Cruz. Here's who does what, grouped by need. Hours change, so call ahead.

The vet in town

Boulder Creek Veterinary Clinic is the full-service clinic right in town at 12870 Highway 9, reachable at 831-338-7205. It's open Monday and Wednesday 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., and Saturday 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Sunday. Those two late nights a week are handy in a valley where most things close early.

They cover the whole range of companion-animal care: puppy and kitten wellness, spay and neuter, dental cleanings with digital x-rays, laser therapy, in-house lab work, ultrasound, and even exotic pets, plus therapeutic bathing and boarding. Their site says they're staffed and equipped to handle emergencies during open hours, so if something happens on a weekday, call them first. Just know that "emergencies during open hours" isn't the same as an overnight ER, which is covered further down.

The vet in Felton

A short drive south, Felton Veterinary Hospital at 5996 Highway 9 is the valley's other clinic, at 831-335-3466. It's open weekdays 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Saturday 8 a.m. to 2 p.m.

Along with preventive care, diagnostics, dentistry, surgery, and exotics, they also offer boarding and grooming, so your dog can get a checkup and a bath in the same trip. It's about fifteen minutes down Highway 9 from Boulder Creek, a reasonable backup if the in-town clinic is booked or closed on the day you need them.

After-hours and overnight emergencies

There's no 24-hour animal hospital in the San Lorenzo Valley. If your pet has an emergency at night, on a Sunday, or after the local clinics close, the nearest round-the-clock animal ER is Pacific and Santa Cruz Veterinary Specialists at 2585 Soquel Drive in Santa Cruz. They're open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, all year, at 831-475-5400.

They take walk-ins, and while they recommend calling ahead so their team can prepare, they know emergencies don't wait. From Boulder Creek, plan on thirty to forty minutes down Highway 9 and Highway 17. Put that number and address in your phone now, before you need it at 2 a.m. with a scared animal in the back seat.

Grooming

For grooming, the first option is right in town, with more within a short drive.

  • Bowzer Baths (Boulder Creek): the in-town dog groomer at 13156 Highway 9, doing mountain grooming since 1998, open Tuesday through Friday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. at 831-338-0717. Small dogs can book a full bath and haircut; medium dogs are bath only for now. More in our Bowzer Baths profile.
  • Dapper Dogs and Divas (Felton): an appointment-based dog grooming shop at 6144 Highway 9, Unit B, run by groomer Jackson Hamilton, open Tuesday through Saturday 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., at 831-216-6462. Find them on Facebook.
  • Mountain Paw Spa (Ben Lomond): a home-based grooming business run by Kristin Miller, offering full grooms, bath and brush, nail trims, and ear cleaning by appointment at 831-266-7998. Since it works out of a home, there's no walk-in storefront, so book ahead. Details are on their booking site.
  • Felton Veterinary Hospital: offers grooming alongside its boarding, handy if you'd rather keep everything under one roof.

Boarding, daycare, and pet sitting

If you're heading out of town, you have both dedicated services and the vet clinics to choose from.

  • Camp Happy Tails: covers the San Lorenzo Valley with doggy daycare, boarding, grooming, and in-home pet sitting. It's a licensed, bonded, and insured operation reachable at 831-247-8245. Because it serves the valley rather than running a public storefront, call to arrange details. See Camp Happy Tails for what they cover.
  • The two valley vet clinics: Boulder Creek Veterinary Clinic boards in town, and Felton Veterinary Hospital offers supervised dog and cat boarding. That can be reassuring if your pet has a medical condition and you'd rather it stay somewhere with a vet on site. The full rundown, including in-home sitting, lives in our boarding and sitting guide.

Pet food and supplies in town

You can cover the basics without leaving Boulder Creek. Boulder Creek Veterinary Clinic keeps a small pet shop inside the clinic with food, treats, and toys, so you can restock while you're in for an appointment. And Scarborough Home and Garden at 13110 Highway 9 stocks dog food, cat food, chicken feed, and horse feed alongside the hardware and garden aisles. For specialty diets or a bulk run, it's still a drive to Scotts Valley or Santa Cruz.

Wildlife: injured, sick, or orphaned wild animals

This is redwood country, so sooner or later you'll find a wild animal that seems to be in trouble: a fledgling bird, a fawn, an injured raccoon. Wildlife doesn't go to the vet or the pound. It goes to Native Animal Rescue, the licensed nonprofit that cares for Santa Cruz County's sick, injured, and orphaned wildlife, at their hotline, 831-462-0726.

Their guidance is worth following: not every wild animal needs rescue, and picking one up can do more harm than good. Take a photo, call the hotline first, and let their wildlife dispatcher tell you what to do before you touch anything. Their intake is at 1855 17th Avenue in Santa Cruz, but the call comes first.

Strays, lost pets, and animal control

For a stray dog, a lost cat, or a domestic animal in trouble, that's the Santa Cruz County Animal Shelter at 831-454-7224. The main shelter is at 1001 Rodriguez Street in Santa Cruz, and because Boulder Creek is unincorporated county, the shelter and its animal control officers serve our area. They're who you call to report a stray, look for a lost pet, or ask about a dangerous or aggressive animal.

The shelter also points wildlife calls to Native Animal Rescue and to Wildlife Emergency Services at 831-498-9453. A rule of thumb: if it's someone's pet, or should be, call the county shelter; if it's wild, call Native Animal Rescue first.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a vet in Boulder Creek?

Yes. Boulder Creek Veterinary Clinic is a full-service companion-animal clinic in town at 12870 Highway 9, open six days a week with two late nights, at 831-338-7205. Felton Veterinary Hospital is a second option about fifteen minutes south on Highway 9.

Where do I take my pet for an emergency at night?

Neither valley clinic is open 24 hours. The nearest round-the-clock animal ER is Pacific and Santa Cruz Veterinary Specialists at 2585 Soquel Drive in Santa Cruz, open 24/7 at 831-475-5400, about thirty to forty minutes away. They take walk-ins but appreciate a call ahead.

Who do I call about an injured wild animal?

Native Animal Rescue, at 831-462-0726. They handle the county's sick, injured, and orphaned wildlife. Take a photo and call before you try to help, since not every animal needs rescue and handling can hurt. Wildlife doesn't go to a vet clinic or the animal shelter.

What about a stray or lost dog?

Call the Santa Cruz County Animal Shelter at 831-454-7224. Boulder Creek is unincorporated county, so the shelter and its animal control officers cover our area for strays, lost and found pets, and dangerous-animal reports.

Where can I get my dog groomed near Boulder Creek?

Bowzer Baths grooms right in Boulder Creek at 13156 Highway 9. Dapper Dogs and Divas in Felton and Mountain Paw Spa in Ben Lomond both groom by appointment, and Felton Veterinary Hospital offers grooming with its boarding. Camp Happy Tails also grooms as part of its valley pet-care services. Call ahead at any of them, since these are small, appointment-driven shops.

Details here come from each provider's own listings and the official contacts for the Santa Cruz County Animal Shelter and Native Animal Rescue. Hours and availability change often at small local businesses, so call ahead to confirm before you drive.

Keep this page handy for the next time something goes sideways with a pet. For more local contacts and services, browse the Boulder Creek Local directory and the Residents guide for the rest of the valley's everyday essentials.

wedding-venues-san-lorenzo-valley.title: Getting Married in the San Lorenzo Valley: Venues and Local Vendors
wedding-venues-san-lorenzo-valley.html:
A steam train carries your guests into a grove in Felton, and the ceremony starts when it stops. That's one of nine verified venues within a short drive of Boulder Creek if you want to get married under redwoods, a run that goes from a historic Brookdale hotel to county park halls you rent yourself.

The venues were never the hard part. It's the rest of a wedding, the florals, cake, photos, music, hair and makeup, officiant, and rentals, that used to feel thin up here. That's changed: we've since verified vendors in every one of those categories who serve the valley.

What follows are the venues operating in the area, then local vendors grouped by what you're booking. Everything comes from each business's own information, so treat it as a place to start making calls rather than a verdict on anybody. Every listing is in our directory, and where a vendor's status is uncertain we say so instead of guessing.

The Venues

Brookdale Lodge (Brookdale)

Address: 11570 Highway 9, Brookdale. Phone: 831-609-6010. Website: brookdalelodge.com.

The historic Brookdale Lodge hosts weddings and parties in its River Run lounge and event space, and its remodeled rooms mean guests can stay on site. The on-site Brookdale Diner can handle catering. It's the closest full-service wedding-and-lodging venue to Boulder Creek.

Roaring Camp Railroads (Felton)

Address: 5401 Graham Hill Road, Felton. Phone: 831-335-4484. Website: roaringcamp.com.

Roaring Camp runs ceremonies at Cathedral Grove, reached by steam train, or at the Redwood Grove, with receptions in Bret Harte Hall. Its published wedding packages run from about 75 guests up to 275 depending on the ceremony site, so ask which combination fits your count. Its wedding coordinator is Stacey Mabuhay (staceym@roaringcamp.com). This is the marquee redwood-railroad option, and it books well ahead.

The Sequoia Retreat Center (Ben Lomond)

Address: 11445 Alba Road, Ben Lomond. Phone: 831-218-5872. Website: sequoiaretreatcenter.com.

The Sequoia Retreat Center holds ceremonies at Peace Park among old-growth sequoias, with receptions in Las Alas Lodge or the string-lit Pixie's Garden patio. On-site cabins give the wedding party a place to get ready and guests a place to sleep, and the venue supplies tables and chairs.

Waterfall Lodge and Retreat (Ben Lomond)

Address: 325 Hidden Falls Trail, Ben Lomond. Phone: 831-212-3895. Website: waterfallsantacruz.com.

Waterfall Lodge is a private 80-acre redwood property with a sunny ceremony meadow and 32 cabins and cottages that sleep up to 86 overnight. It's a bring-your-own-vendor venue and hosts weddings of up to 150 daytime guests, plus retreats.

The Barn at River House (Ben Lomond)

Locality: Ben Lomond. Phone: 831-688-0355. Booking is by phone (ask for Casey). Web presence: Facebook page.

The Barn at River House centers on a 3,500-square-foot barn on a private stretch of the San Lorenzo River, with a wisteria arbor, a gazebo over the water, a redwood ceremony grove, and about 10,000 square feet of lawn seating up to 250 for dinner. It's available April through December and includes a bridal cottage and catering station. The exact street address isn't published, so confirm details by phone.

Highlands House at Highlands County Park (Ben Lomond)

Address: 8500 Highway 9, Ben Lomond. Booking phone: 831-454-7901 (Santa Cruz County Parks). Website: Highlands County Park.

Highlands House is a 1940s house you rent for weddings and parties at a county park, with a grand room for dancing, a prep kitchen, stored tables and chairs, and two upstairs rooms for the wedding party. One thing to know before you fall for it: you book through Santa Cruz County Parks at 831-454-7901, not a private event company, so the process runs on the county's reservation system. County Parks currently lists a maximum capacity of 75 people for the Highlands Park house, well under what the room looks like it could hold, so confirm the number for your date before you plan around it.

Sydalyn Hill (Felton)

Locality: Felton (exact address not published; tours by appointment). Phone: 408-892-1994. Website: sydalynhill.com.

Sydalyn Hill is a family-run farm venue on a sunny hilltop off Highway 9, surrounded by Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park, with valley views, orchards, gardens, and an open meadow. It hosts a limited number of weddings each year, up to 150 guests for full packages, plus micro-weddings and intimate day events for up to 30. Its site currently shows full-size weddings booking for 2027, so ask about dates early.

Felton Guild (Felton)

Address: 5449 Highway 9, Felton. Phone: 831-336-8093. Website: feltonguildweddings.com.

Felton Guild has hosted outdoor weddings since 1994, built around a redwood cathedral ceremony space seating about 130 and a reception lawn that holds more than 200. The on-site Cowboy Bar & Grill provides catering and full bar service, with couples building a menu directly with the restaurant.

Kennolyn Events (Soquel)

Address: 8400 Glen Haven Road, Soquel. Phone: 831-479-6700. Website: kennolyn.com.

Kennolyn is a 450-acre estate and camp venue with two settings: the hilltop Hacienda Estate overlooking Monterey Bay, and Stone Creek Village, a redwood setting suited to weekend-long destination weddings of roughly 75 to 150. It sits over the ridge in Soquel rather than in the valley itself, included here as the nearby regional option for couples who want scale.

A few more venues are worth a call if you'll travel a little: the Amphitheater of the Redwoods at Pema Osel Ling in Watsonville (a 104-acre redwood retreat with on-site lodging and catering), Quail Hollow Ranch County Park in Felton (a county-permit ranch house and lawn), and the Hilton Santa Cruz / Scotts Valley for a full-service hotel wedding.

Florists

Boulder Creek has in-town floral makers plus reliable valley delivery.

  • In Boulder Creek: Boulder Creek Flowers & Lokahi Designs (also known as Everly Designs) does wedding and event flowers by appointment. Woodland Floral & Creations (801-564-9944) makes hand-painted sola wood flower bouquets and arch pieces, a keepsake alternative to fresh flowers. Camp Joy Gardens (831-338-3651), the organic farm nonprofit since 1971, arranges flowers for weddings and events.
  • Down the valley: Wild Iris Floral and Botanical in Felton (831-278-0151) serves Ben Lomond and the valley.
  • County-wide studios: Ferrari Florist & Gardens (since 1946), Redwood & Ranunculus, Quaintrelle Farms, Dahlias & Details, and Seascape Flowers in Aptos.

Cakes and Desserts

  • In Boulder Creek: Dessert First Bakery makes custom wedding and celebration cakes to order and shares a kitchen with Jenna Sue's Cafe rather than keeping a shopfront, and Butter Late Than Never Baking Co. is a licensed cottage bakery taking custom orders.
  • Across the county: verified wedding-cake makers include Edith Meyer Wedding Cakes (a Santa Cruz wedding-cake specialist by appointment), The Buttery, Companion Bakeshop, Sugar Bakery Co. in Soquel, Gayle's Bakery in Capitola, and Freedom Bakery & Confections in Watsonville.

Catering and Bar

Couples here tend to mix dedicated caterers with restaurant catering lines.

  • Closest: Wylder Space, farm-to-table wedding catering from Chef Molly Bravo in the Felton and Scotts Valley area.
  • Around the county: Humble Bumble Catering, Feel Good Foods Catering, Santa Cruz Catering Company, Sunny's Catering, Aptos St. BBQ for barbecue, and D'La Colmena for Mexican catering. The Wild Bite is a women-owned small-bites caterer who also does day-of coordination, and Busy Bee's Cafe & Catering caters county-wide.
  • Restaurant catering: the Brookdale Diner caters at 831-609-6126, and Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge in Boulder Creek (831-338-4444) has private-event rooms.
  • Bar: Tip Top Taps is a mobile tap bar covering the county.

Photographers and Video

Several wedding photographers work the valley, and a few are Boulder Creek locals. Kassandra Thomsen Photography names San Lorenzo Valley redwood weddings in her own service list, and Kyer Wiltshire specializes in redwood-forest weddings and shoots both photo and video. De Joy Photography (Amber Amelingmeier) brings 18-plus years and 300-plus events, Sand and Stone Media covers photo and video, and Kelly Griffiths Photography travels throughout the county.

Music and DJs

ICON DJ serves Felton, Scotts Valley, and redwood estates with no local travel fee, and DJ Warwick keeps a dedicated Ben Lomond wedding page, which makes both natural first calls for a valley wedding. Santa Cruz DJ Company in Scotts Valley (founded 2008) runs 200-plus events a year, and SIM Events is a full-service DJ and entertainment company covering Santa Cruz and Monterey.

Hair and Makeup

Wedding hair and makeup here is mobile, coming to your venue or getting-ready suite. Kelly Jo Beauty works studio and mobile, Cristal Stephani is a mobile makeup artist, Meghan Elisabeth (the Nomadic Stylist) does mobile bridal hair, and Kala Ketchum and Malina Terra both do on-location wedding hair and makeup.
