Spa Bella Mobile Spa serves the Santa Cruz area; confirm it covers your valley venue when you book.

Planners and Coordinators

Weddings By Aimee names the San Lorenzo Valley on its site and works with a low-waste focus, the closest local fit of the planners we found. Mia Jasmine Weddings specializes in redwood and mountain weddings, and Wedding Connection and Event by Dawn both plan across the county. For day-of coordination specifically, A Paper Flower Wedding (Sarah G.) and The Wild Bite both offer it.

Officiants

You do have valley-serving officiants. Santa Cruz Officiant lists Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, and Felton directly in its service area. Marry Me In Santa Cruz (Jane Bendick) performs ceremonies and elopements across the county, and Elope Santa Cruz and Monterey Bay is a separate officiant-and-photographer team focused on elopements.

Balloons, Decor, and Rentals

  • Balloons and styling: Luzovich Celebrations is a San Lorenzo Valley stylist who also makes party favors, and Bash Works and Aesthetic Events & Co. do balloon garlands and event styling (Bash Works also rents bounce houses and marquee letters).
  • Tables, chairs, tents, and lighting: verified rental companies serving the county include M&M Party Rentals in Watsonville, Alexis Party Rental, A to Z Party Rental, Special Events Rentals, and Chic Event Rentals.

Delivery up a mountain road can carry a distance fee, so confirm your exact venue address when you book.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which valley venues let you bring your own caterer and vendors?

Waterfall Lodge is explicitly a bring-your-own-vendor property, and Highlands House through the county is self-catered by design. Others, like Felton Guild with its Cowboy Bar & Grill and Brookdale Lodge with the Brookdale Diner, pair you with in-house food and bar. Always confirm the vendor policy with the venue before booking outside help.

How do I book Highlands House for a wedding?

Highlands House sits in Highlands County Park and is reserved through Santa Cruz County Parks, not a private operator. Call the county parks reservation line at 831-454-7901 to check availability and the rental process. County Parks currently lists a maximum capacity of 75 people for the house, so confirm the number for your date.

Are there any wedding venues in Boulder Creek?

Brookdale Lodge in neighboring Brookdale is the closest full-service hotel-and-event venue, and Boulder Creek itself has florists, bakeries, and photographers who live in town. The dedicated ceremony-and-reception estates cluster south in Ben Lomond, Felton, and Soquel, a short drive down Highway 9.

Is there a wedding officiant who serves the San Lorenzo Valley?

Yes. Santa Cruz Officiant lists Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, and Felton in its service area, and Marry Me In Santa Cruz and Elope Santa Cruz both perform ceremonies and elopements across the county. Contact each to confirm your date and location.

Who bakes wedding cakes near Boulder Creek?

Dessert First Bakery in Boulder Creek specializes in custom wedding and celebration cakes, ordered direct rather than from a shopfront, and Butter Late Than Never Baking Co. is a licensed Boulder Creek cottage bakery. For more options, Edith Meyer Wedding Cakes, The Buttery, Companion Bakeshop, Sugar Bakery Co., Gayle's, and Freedom Bakery all make wedding cakes across the county.

Everything above is a verified place to start, not a recommendation. Browse the full Boulder Creek Local directory for local vendors, and send corrections or additions through the submit page so the next couple gets accurate information.

what-are-the-sirens-for-boulder-creek.title: What Are the Sirens For? How to Look Up Boulder Creek Emergency Calls
what-are-the-sirens-for-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • A siren just went by? Open PulsePoint's web feed for Boulder Creek Fire in any browser. No app, no account. It shows the fire district's calls, usually within a minute or two of dispatch.
  • Wildfire or smoke: use Watch Duty, which tells you whether a fire is growing, staffed, and mapped.
  • Crash on Highway 9 or Highway 236: check the CHP Traffic Incident page and pick the Monterey center.
  • Sheriff calls: there's no live public feed, only an address-history search going back three years.
  • The fixed siren at the fire station is different. It's a community warning, tested Tuesdays at 7 p.m. Hear it any other time and go get information.
  • An actual emergency? Don't open an app. Call 911. Evacuation decisions come from CruzAware alerts and official orders, never from counting sirens.

A siren climbs Highway 9, a couple of engines pull out of the station on Central Avenue, and half the town lands on the same question at once: what's going on? The fastest answer we know of is PulsePoint's web feed for Boulder Creek Fire. It shows the fire district's active and recent calls, usually within a minute or two of dispatch: the incident type, the time, the street, and which units are responding. Most days you'll find a medical call, because that's most of what our fire district does.

That single link answers the question maybe eight times out of ten. The other two times, the sirens belong to an agency whose calls show up somewhere else, or nowhere at all. Below is who responds in Boulder Creek, where each agency's calls can be looked up, and what stays off the public record on purpose.

This is how I use these tools. Long, extended sirens up the highway, and PulsePoint is already open in my hand. Heading out on a drive with a tight timeline, I check it first to see if a crash is about to cost me twenty minutes. And any time there's a fire nearby, Watch Duty goes on with notifications enabled until it's out. Both have earned permanent spots on my home screen.

Two Different Sirens, and Only One Is a Warning

Before anything else, know that "siren" in Boulder Creek means two different things.

The fixed siren at the fire station is a community warning. Boulder Creek Fire Protection District sounds it in a disaster or large-scale emergency to tell residents to go get information. It was used during the CZU fire. If you hear it outside the weekly test, treat it as real.

What to do when the station siren sounds:

  1. Stay calm and get information. The tone is the same no matter the emergency, so the siren itself doesn't tell you what happened or which way to go.
  2. Tune in: KBCZ 89.3 FM, KSCO 1080 AM, or KSCO 104.1 FM, plus local TV.
  3. Check your phone for a CruzAware alert and look up your evacuation zone at Genasys Protect.
  4. Don't call 911 to ask what the siren was. 911 is for a life-threatening emergency, and asking ties up a line someone else needs.

The weekly test is Tuesdays at 7 p.m. A siren at that time is a test. A siren at any other time is not, so go get information. The district also sounds it occasionally for ceremonial reasons, such as opening the Fourth of July pancake breakfast or honoring a member who has died.

Moving sirens are something else entirely. An engine, medic unit, or patrol car on its way to a call isn't a warning to anyone. That's what the rest of this page is about, and what PulsePoint will usually explain in under a minute.

Who Responds Here

Boulder Creek doesn't have one emergency service. It has several, and knowing which is which tells you where to look.

  • Boulder Creek Fire Protection District is the first responder for most of it. The district's volunteers cover 21 square miles of mountain terrain, including Brookdale, and answered more than 1,300 calls last year. Per the district's own site, that workload runs from medical aids and vehicle accidents to hazmat, vehicle fires, wildland fires, and structure fires. The station is at 13230 Central Ave, business line (831) 338-7222.
  • American Medical Response runs the ambulances. Santa Cruz Regional 9-1-1, the dispatch center for the county, describes AMR as "the local paramedic and ambulance transport provider," and dispatches it alongside every fire district in the county. On a medical call you'll typically see both: a BCFD engine plus an AMR medic unit.
  • CAL FIRE CZU, headquartered in Felton at (831) 335-5353, covers wildland fire and backs up local districts. On a recent Boulder Creek structure fire, the PulsePoint feed showed CZU units in the response alongside district engines. During fire season, a column of smoke can draw a response that looks enormous from the road. That's by design up here.
  • The Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office handles law enforcement, since Boulder Creek is unincorporated. Non-emergency dispatch is (831) 471-1121.
  • The CHP covers the state highways, which in our case means Highway 9 and Highway 236. A crash on 9 is usually a CHP incident with fire and AMR responding too.

Nearly all of it funnels through one room: Santa Cruz Regional 9-1-1, also called NetCom, answers the 911 calls and dispatches the sheriff, the county's fire districts, and AMR.

Fire and Medical Calls: PulsePoint

PulsePoint is a service that participating fire agencies use to publish their dispatch activity in close to real time, and Boulder Creek FPD is a participating agency. You can see the feed two ways.

In a browser, use web.pulsepoint.org and select Boulder Creek FPD, or jump straight to the saved Boulder Creek feed. On your phone, download PulsePoint Respond for iOS or Android, then follow Boulder Creek FPD as your agency. The app can notify you of significant incidents; the web view is better for a quick "what was that" check.

Each entry lists the call type (medical emergency, traffic collision, fire alarm, structure fire, vegetation fire, and so on), when it came in, where, and the responding units. Two details worth knowing. First, medical calls are shown at the street level only, no house numbers, which is a reasonable privacy line for what are usually someone's worst days. Fires show the full address. Second, closed calls stay visible in the recent list with their duration, so you can still check an hour after the sirens passed.

If you want a wider view, the same picker offers neighboring agencies: Felton FD, a Santa Cruz County agency covering unincorporated areas like Bonny Doon and Davenport, Central Fire, and Santa Cruz FD. Adding Felton and Santa Cruz County catches most of what BCFD gets called to assist on.

Wildfire: Watch Duty

For anything that smells like wildfire, Watch Duty is the tool this valley reaches for, and the Fire Safe Council of Santa Cruz County recommends it for that use. Watch Duty is a nonprofit. Its updates are posted by humans, largely retired dispatchers, firefighters, and reporters listening to radio traffic and verifying before they publish. It covers all 50 states, Santa Cruz County included, and it'll alert you to a new fire start near you faster than most official channels will.

PulsePoint tells you an engine went somewhere. Watch Duty tells you whether a vegetation fire is growing, staffed, and mapped. They're complementary, and both belong on a Boulder Creek phone.

Highway 9 and 236: The CHP Incident Page

Crashes and hazards on the state highways live on the CHP Traffic Incident Information Page. It's a plain, old-school page, and it works. From the Communications Centers menu, choose Monterey, which is the CHP center that covers Santa Cruz County, and click OK. You'll get a live table of incidents; the Area column shows "Santa Cruz" for our county's calls, and the page refreshes every 60 seconds. When traffic stops dead on 9 south of town, this page usually says why before anything else does.

Sheriff Calls: Mostly Not Public, and That's Deliberate

Here's the gap people run into. There's no live public feed of sheriff calls in Santa Cruz County. If deputies fly past with lights on, no app will tell you where they're going. Law enforcement calls stay off public feeds for practical reasons: officer safety on in-progress calls, victim and reporting-party privacy, and open investigations.

What does exist is a lookback tool. The Sheriff's Office runs a Civilian Calls for Service search where you can enter a street address and see calls from the last three years. It's useful for questions like "what's the history on that property," not "what's happening right now." The office's own disclaimer says it doesn't include all calls and excludes certain incident types entirely, so treat an empty result as not shown, not as nothing happened.

For anything you need to report or ask about, the non-emergency dispatch line is (831) 471-1121. The full local list, including the Boulder Creek service center, is in our emergency contacts one-pager.

If you're the scanner type, a live Santa Cruz County Fire audio feed runs on Broadcastify, carrying the county fire channels. Radio traffic is raw and easy to misread, so treat it as background, not fact.

The Hard Rule

All of these tools are for curiosity and awareness. None of them is how you should decide to evacuate. Feeds lag, calls get typed under generic categories, and no service guarantees completeness or timeliness.

When something big is happening, evacuation decisions come from CruzAware alerts and official orders from the Sheriff's Office and CAL FIRE, period. Know your evacuation zone before you need it: look up your address at Genasys Protect, the tool the fire district points residents to. If you haven't registered for alerts yet, our CruzAware setup guide walks through it in about ten minutes.

And if you're looking at an actual emergency, don't check an app first. Call 911.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do fire engines respond to medical calls?

Because in Boulder Creek, the fire district is the medical first responder. BCFD lists medical aids among its core call types, and its engines carry trained personnel who are usually closer than the ambulance, which may be coming from elsewhere in the valley. Watch the PulsePoint feed for a week and you'll see the pattern: a district engine and an AMR medic unit on the same call, with the engine often arriving first. The engine isn't there because of a fire. It's there because it's the fastest help.

Why can't I see sheriff or CHP calls in PulsePoint?

PulsePoint publishes fire and EMS dispatches from participating fire agencies only. CHP incidents have their own page at cad.chp.ca.gov. Sheriff calls have no live public feed at all, only the address-history search above.

Sirens went by and nothing shows in any app. What happened?

It happens. The call may be law enforcement (not published), a CHP incident filed under the Monterey center page, units passing through to another district, or a feed running behind. A blank screen means not shown, nothing more. If you're worried something nearby is serious, check CruzAware and Watch Duty rather than refreshing a quiet feed.

Do I need the app, or is there a website?

Both exist. The web feed at web.pulsepoint.org needs nothing installed and is the fastest one-time check. The app adds notifications, which are worth having if you want to know about structure fires and vegetation fires the moment they're dispatched.

Are sirens ever a warning to residents, like an evacuation signal?

The fixed siren at the fire station is. Boulder Creek Fire sounds it in a disaster or large-scale emergency, as it did during CZU, to tell residents to go get information. It's tested Tuesdays at 7 p.m.; outside that, treat it as real. It doesn't tell you what happened or which way to go, so tune to KBCZ 89.3 FM or KSCO 1080 AM / 104.1 FM, check for a CruzAware alert, and look up your zone. Don't call 911 to ask about the siren.

Moving sirens are not a warning. Those are response vehicles on their way to a call: engines, medics, patrol cars. Evacuation orders arrive through CruzAware, wireless emergency alerts, and official announcements from the Sheriff's Office and CAL FIRE, never by counting sirens on Highway 9.

Save the two tools you'll reach for most, the PulsePoint feed and Watch Duty, to your phone now, while nothing is happening. For the full list of local numbers, see our Boulder Creek emergency contacts one-pager, and the CruzAware setup guide gets you registered for the alerts that order an evacuation.

what-is-boulder-creek-known-for.title: What Is Boulder Creek Known For?
what-is-boulder-creek-known-for.html:
Boulder Creek is known for five things: it's the gateway town to Big Basin Redwoods State Park, California's oldest state park; it was one of the biggest lumber-shipping points in the United States during a thirty-year boom; it briefly was an incorporated city and voted to stop; it hosted a purpose-built silent-film town that put Mary Pickford in these redwoods; and it survived the CZU Lightning Complex fire of 2020. Downtown still looks like the railroad-era lumber town it was, because that's what it is.

Below is the short version of each, and every one links out to the full story.

The gateway to California's oldest state park

The single thing Boulder Creek is best known for isn't in Boulder Creek. Big Basin Redwoods State Park sits nine miles up Highway 236, which leaves Highway 9 right in the middle of downtown. The park has a Boulder Creek mailing address, and this town has been its front door for well over a century.

Big Basin became a park in 1902, when the state bought the heart of the basin and created California Redwood Park, the first park in what became the California state park system. The campaign behind it started in May 1900, when a group led by San Jose photographer Andrew P. Hill camped in the basin, formed the Sempervirens Club and passed a hat that raised 32 dollars.

The gateway role is older than the park's pavement. By 1886, a Boulder Creek livery stable was hauling visitors from the railroad terminus up toward the basin. Trains never reached Big Basin. Surveys came and went, and the 1906 earthquake killed the last serious plan, so the transfer from rail to stage happened here. When the trains stopped, the cars kept coming through town anyway.

Some of the park's redwoods are estimated at 1,000 to 1,800 years old.

→ How Big Basin became California's first state park · Is Big Basin open? · A responsible Big Basin day trip

A lumber boomtown at the end of the line

The redwoods explain everything about how this town got here.

A sawmill went up across from Bear Creek in the early 1860s. A post office opened in December 1872 and fixed the name. In 1875 a gravity-powered flume, a V-shaped wooden trough, began floating rough lumber roughly twelve miles down the valley to Felton. It leaked, jammed and ran dry every summer, so in April 1885 the railroad arrived instead, and Boulder Creek became the northern terminus, the end of the line.

What followed was the boom. From 1885 to 1915, Boulder Creek ranked among the largest exporters of lumber in the United States, with a freight yard at the center of town and a year-round population over 800, plus the floating population of a mill and woods economy.

Then it ended, the way extraction economies do. The accessible old growth near the rail line gave out. Passenger trains were replaced by buses in March 1931. The last freight train left in January 1934, closing 49 years of rail service. The town, in rail historian Derek Whaley's phrase, "transitioned begrudgingly from a lumber town to a tourist town."

→ The logging boom · Railroads of the San Lorenzo Valley · How Boulder Creek got its name

The town that voted to stop being a city

Boulder Creek used to be an incorporated city, and in 1915 the residents voted to disincorporate.

It's been unincorporated ever since: no mayor, no city council, no city hall. Santa Cruz County governs, the Sheriff's Office is the police department, and independent special districts handle fire, water, schools and parks. Felton did the same thing two years later, in 1917.

The incorporation year is 1902, and we have the vote. The Santa Cruz Morning Sentinel of February 16, 1902 reported that incorporation "won the day in Boulder Creek Saturday," 107 votes in favor to 45 against, and named the town's first trustees. The 1910 Census footnotes the same year.

→ Why isn't Boulder Creek a city?

A silent-film town, literally

In early 1915 the California Motion Picture Corporation built an entire gold-rush settlement outside Boulder Creek, roughly 25 log and frame buildings, complete with stores, offices and saloons. They called it Poverty Flat, and it worked as an outdoor studio, with roofless cabins covered by sheets to diffuse daylight for interior shots.

At least eight films were made there. In 1917, Cecil B. DeMille brought Mary Pickford, then the most famous woman in the world, to shoot exteriors for A Romance of the Redwoods. The town's own main street doubled as a western mining town on camera.

Nearly all of that footage burned in a 1931 vault fire at the studio in San Rafael. The set is gone too, and its exact location is not established.

Boulder Creek's screen career didn't stop in the silent era. Hitchcock shot Vertigo's redwood scene at Big Basin in 1957, not Muir Woods, whatever the film tells you. Downtown played a fictional town called Buzzsaw in the 1992 Universal comedy Out on a Limb.

→ Poverty Flat · Every movie and music video filmed here · Beatriz Michelena · Mary Pickford in Boulder Creek

A downtown that still looks like 1900

Visitors regularly describe downtown Boulder Creek as looking like a western movie set. The reason is unglamorous: it's a surviving railroad-and-lumber-era commercial strip that never got redeveloped. False fronts, covered walks, narrow lots, the shape the railroad laid out, still doing business.

The town's commercial core sits where the freight yard put it, with the road to Big Basin splitting off at the center. The old station grounds were behind today's fire department.

One building carries the name of the town that used to be here: the Grace Episcopal Church, built in 1906 on ground that had been Lorenzo, a rival town founded in 1875 that was gradually absorbed into Boulder Creek in the early 1900s. The church now houses a San Lorenzo Valley Museum gallery on Highway 9.

→ Downtown Boulder Creek in an afternoon · The San Lorenzo Valley Museum

Fire, water, and what it takes to live here

Boulder Creek is also known, locally and increasingly beyond, for disaster and recovery.

On August 16, 2020, the CZU Lightning Complex fire ignited. It burned more than 86,000 acres across the Santa Cruz Mountains, destroyed homes throughout the valley, and swept through 97 percent of Big Basin, taking every historic structure in the park.

Most of the old-growth redwoods survived; the buildings didn't. Recovery is still underway six years later, and a 2024 county Grand Jury report on the aftermath was titled Four Years Later The Flame Still Burns.

Fire isn't the only one. The Christmas flood of December 1955 and the January 1982 storm that triggered the Love Creek landslide are both permanent fixtures of local memory, and atmospheric rivers hitting the burn scar in January 2023 brought debris flows and road damage.

This is the part of Boulder Creek's reputation that residents feel most and tourists see least: it's a beautiful place that asks something of you.

→ Fires, floods and storms · Six years after the CZU fire · Wildfire evacuation

And what it's like now

Boulder Creek is a small mountain community of roughly 5,400 people in the redwoods of the San Lorenzo Valley, about halfway between Silicon Valley and the beach and not especially convenient to either. It has a downtown you can walk in ten minutes, one main road in and out plus a few narrow back routes, a volunteer fire tradition, a community radio station, and a Fourth of July parade people plan their summer around.

It also has a counterculture streak that never fully left: an experimental college operated here in the 1970s and 80s, a working physicist wrote books about quantum reality from a desk in town, and a computer-history museum ran for two decades out of a redwood barn.

→ Is Boulder Creek a good place to live? · New to Boulder Creek? Quick-start guide · Famous people from Boulder Creek · Full history timeline

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Boulder Creek, California known for?

Being the gateway to Big Basin Redwoods State Park, California's oldest state park; a redwood logging boom between 1885 and 1915 that made it one of the country's largest lumber shipping points; a silent-film set called Poverty Flat that hosted Mary Pickford; voting to stop being a city in 1915; and surviving the 2020 CZU fire.

Is Boulder Creek worth visiting?

If you like redwoods, a walkable historic main street and a non-touristy mountain town, yes. Most visitors come through on the way to Big Basin. Check park access before you plan around it, since recovery from the 2020 fire is ongoing.

How far is Boulder Creek from Big Basin?

Nine miles up Highway 236, which leaves Highway 9 in downtown Boulder Creek. The road is narrow and winding, so allow more time than the mileage suggests.

Why does downtown Boulder Creek look like an old western town?

Because it largely is one. The commercial strip is surviving railroad-and-lumber-era fabric (false fronts, covered walks, narrow lots) that never got redeveloped. It also played a fictional western-ish town on film more than once, which reinforces the impression.

Is Boulder Creek a city?

No. It's an unincorporated community and a census-designated place in Santa Cruz County. It was an incorporated city in the early 1900s until residents voted to disincorporate in 1915.

What movies were filmed in Boulder Creek?

At least eight silent films used the Poverty Flat set built here in 1915, including A Romance of the Redwoods (1917) with Mary Pickford. Downtown played the town of Buzzsaw in Out on a Limb (1992). Vertigo (1958) and The Tripper (2006) filmed at Big Basin.

How big is Boulder Creek?

About 5,400 residents as of the 2020 Census, in a census-designated place in the upper San Lorenzo Valley.

Want to go deeper than the highlights? The full Boulder Creek history timeline lays out the dates end to end, and the Residents guide covers what it's like to live in the San Lorenzo Valley now.

where-to-eat-boulder-creek.title: Where to Eat in Boulder Creek Right Now
where-to-eat-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • A local's defaults: Los Gallos is my weekly stop, the Sawmill is where we meet friends on weekends, and when I'm sick, nothing but Jenny's hot and sour soup at the Red Pearl will do.
  • Sit-down restaurants (four): Scopazzi's (Italian), the Red Pearl (Chinese), Tae's Edo Sushi, and the Sawmill (pub fare and craft beer).
  • Quick and casual: El Rey Leon, a food truck parked downtown with outdoor seating, plus River Dogs for Chicago-style hot dogs by a fire pit. Taqueria Los Gallos is a sit-down taqueria if you'd rather eat inside.
  • Coffee and baked goods: two coffee shops (Jenna Sue's and the Tree House), Bella's for a sit-down breakfast, and three bakers who work by order or market stall rather than a shop counter (Dessert First, Butter Late Than Never, Wildstone).
  • Markets, deli, and a drink: two full markets and a deli (Johnnie's, Wild Roots, the Redwood Keg), plus Joe's Bar and Big Basin Vineyards' estate tasting room up the mountain.
  • Before you go: hours shift with the season and staffing. Where we couldn't confirm hours to a current source, we've left them out and listed the phone number instead, so call ahead.

For a town this size, Boulder Creek keeps a real kitchen running. I've eaten my way through everything on this list, some of it weekly, so this is a local's guide, not a compiled one. If you're hungry today, downtown and the stretch of Highway 9 just north of it can cover breakfast, lunch, dinner, and a drink without a drive down the valley. The sections below group every spot by type, with a link to each business's own page where one exists. Just remember that mountain-town hours move with the seasons, the weather, and the occasional staffing crunch, so check before you drive.

Sit-down restaurants

Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge at 13300 Big Basin Way is the historic special-occasion room, an Italian restaurant and lounge that's fed Boulder Creek for generations, mine included. Every December since 2006, the partners of the fire department's volunteers take over a table there for our annual ladies night, and for years I ordered the same plate of gnocchi. It's off the menu now and I still crave it, but the menu runs deep enough that losing a favorite mostly means finding a new one. Breakfast runs Wednesday through Sunday from 10:30 to 2, lunch Wednesday through Saturday, and dinner Wednesday through Sunday starting at 4. It's closed Monday and Tuesday. There are private rooms if you're planning something bigger than dinner.

The Red Pearl at 13151 Highway 9 handles Chinese food for the whole valley, dine-in or takeout, Wednesday through Sunday 11 to 9. When a cold gets me, nothing else in town will do but Jenny's hot and sour soup. It's closed Monday and Tuesday, and the site is clear that it doesn't deliver, so plan on picking up.

Tae's Edo Sushi at 13271 Highway 9 is the sushi bar in town. Dinner runs 4 to 8 Tuesday through Thursday and Sunday. Friday and Saturday add a lunch window from noon to 3 ahead of the usual dinner hours. It's closed Monday.

The Sawmill Restaurant & Alehouse at 15520 Highway 9, a few minutes north of downtown, does burgers, pub fare, and craft beer, with a big outdoor area and a music stage under the redwoods. It's our standing weekend spot with friends from down the street; the outdoor setup makes it easy to arrive as two households and leave as one long table. One planning note: the Sawmill is expected to close temporarily for renovations after service on Friday, August 14, 2026. A reopening is planned, and community posts indicate it may return with a counter-service model, but the reopening date, incoming ownership, and final format haven't been publicly confirmed. Check its website or call 831-610-8196 before you head over, and we'll update this page as details firm up.

Counter service, tacos, and hot dogs

El Rey Leon at 12890 Central Avenue is a Mexican food truck at its downtown spot on set days each week, with outdoor seating and counter service. Hours are Monday through Saturday, 11 to 3 and again 4 to 7, closed Sunday. Order at the truck or call; online ordering is currently unavailable.

Taqueria Los Gallos at 13070 Central Avenue downtown is a sit-down taqueria and, in my house, the weekly quick stop. I could eat Mexican food every day of the week, if I'm being honest, and this is where it usually lands. It doesn't keep a website, but it's on the Boulder Creek Business Association's current food listings. Call 831-217-5000 for hours before you go.

River Dogs of Boulder Creek at 123 Forest Street, tucked behind Joe's Bar and Scarborough's, is an outdoor stand doing Chicago-style Vienna Beef hot dogs and sausages, with a fire pit and a small stage for acoustic music. Its posted winter schedule is Tuesday through Thursday 11:30 to 3 and Friday through Sunday 11:30 to 5. It closes for bad weather and special events, which is what you'd expect from a place that's genuinely outdoors.

Coffee, breakfast, and lunch

Three cafes cover the morning shift. All three are small enough that calling ahead beats trusting the internet.

Jenna Sue's Cafe at 13090 Highway 9 is the downtown coffeehouse, pouring Java Bob's coffee alongside breakfast, lunch, and baked goods. The oatmeal, loaded with fresh fruit, is the breakfast I keep trying to replicate at home and keep failing to match. My partner doesn't even open the menu; the astronaut breakfast wins every time. Its own page posts 831-338-7008 and hours of 6:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. on weekdays, 7:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. on weekends.

Bella's Cafe at 13132 Central Avenue is the sit-down breakfast and lunch spot downtown, a diner rather than a coffee bar. It serves 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday, and closes Mondays.

The Tree House Cafe at 13266 Highway 9 sits creekside at the north end of the business district, with coffee, breakfast, and sandwiches. It runs on Facebook rather than a website. The business association listing has it current at 831-610-8912.

Bakeries

Dessert First Bakery makes custom cakes and desserts with all-natural, locally sourced ingredients. There is no shop to walk into: it works out of the kitchen it shares with Jenna Sue's Cafe, so you order through the bakery directly, and some of its goods turn up in the case at Jenna Sue's.

Butter Late Than Never Baking Co. is a licensed cottage bakery working out of a Boulder Creek home kitchen, which means online orders rather than a storefront, and no published address. Expect cookies, brownies, mini donuts, and cookie cakes, with seasonal flavors rotating through the shop page, local delivery, and California-only shipping under cottage food rules.

Wildstone Bakery is Boulder Creek's naturally fermented bread and pastry maker, also without a storefront. You'll find its loaves, bagels, and seasonal tarts at the Downtown Santa Cruz Farmers Market on Wednesdays from 12:30 to 5, and at the Ben Lomond Village Market on first Saturdays, June through October 2026, from 10 to 2.

Markets and delis

Johnnie's Super Market at 13225 Highway 9 has been the town grocery since 1938: produce, meat and seafood, a deli making sandwiches from family recipes, a bakery case, cheese, and a deep beer, wine, and spirits selection. Hours are Monday through Thursday and Sunday 8 to 9, Friday and Saturday 8 to 10, which makes it the latest food in town most nights.

Wild Roots Market at 13159 Central Avenue is the natural grocery, open daily 9 to 9, organic and heavily locally sourced, with a bulk section of beans, grains, and dried fruit worth bringing your own jars for. For a few short weeks each summer its dry farmed tomatoes arrive, sweet enough to eat like fruit, and locals plan around them. The deli's prepared case is our first stop when a last minute gathering needs feeding: a fresh kale salad, some veggie empanadas, done.

The Redwood Keg at 12980 Highway 9 is the local liquor store with a deli counter, listed on the SLV Chamber's food and takeout page. There's no website, so call 831-338-2727 to check deli hours before you make the trip for a sandwich.

A bar and a winery

Joe's Bar at 13118 Highway 9 is the downtown bar and live music room, the sort of place locals will tell you defines the town. It appears on Visit Santa Cruz County's current dining pages, and its listing shows daily hours from 10 a.m., though that listing hasn't been refreshed recently, so confirm by phone at 831-338-9417 if timing matters.

Big Basin Vineyards' estate tasting room at 830 Memory Lane pours its mountain-grown wines at the vineyard itself on Saturdays and Sundays from noon to 5. Reservations go through the booking system on its site. This is the Boulder Creek estate, separate from the winery's Santa Cruz tasting room.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's open on Monday in Boulder Creek?

Monday is the quiet day. Scopazzi's, the Red Pearl, and Tae's Edo are all closed, and River Dogs' winter schedule starts Tuesday. Your reliable Monday options are the markets, with Johnnie's and Wild Roots both open daily, plus El Rey Leon's posted Monday hours.

Which restaurants deliver?

Plan on pickup. The Red Pearl doesn't deliver, the Sawmill runs online ordering for pickup only, and El Rey Leon takes orders at the truck or by phone. The exception is baked goods: Butter Late Than Never delivers its cottage bakery orders locally.

Where can I eat early in the morning?

Jenna Sue's posts the earliest open in town at 6 a.m. on weekdays. Bella's listing shows 8 a.m., and Johnnie's opens at 8 daily if a deli sandwich counts as breakfast. Call the cafes to confirm their current opening times.

Why aren't hours printed for every place on this list?

Because a wrong hour is worse than no hour, and some of these places don't post a current schedule anywhere. Where a business's posted schedule conflicted across sources or hadn't been updated recently, we left it out and gave you the phone number instead.

A place I know is missing. Why?

We list businesses we can point to through their own site or a current official listing. A few local food makers without any public web presence didn't make the cut yet, and we'll add them as soon as they have a page we can point to. If you run one of them, get in touch.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. Hours and details here follow each business's own page or a current official listing where one exists. Call ahead for anything time-sensitive.

Hungry for more of Boulder Creek? Browse the full business directory for hours and contacts, check our bakery guide for the town's bread and dessert makers, the events calendar for live music and pop-ups around town, and see the rest of our Around Town guides. Spot an hour that's changed or a spot we missed? Tell us and we'll fix it.

where-to-eat-breakfast-boulder-creek.title: Where to Eat Breakfast in Boulder Creek
where-to-eat-breakfast-boulder-creek.html:
For a sit-down breakfast in Boulder Creek, you've got three downtown cafes: Bella's Cafe, Jenna Sue's Cafe, and The Tree House Cafe. Want coffee and something to eat on your way through instead? Johnnie's runs a deli counter that makes sandwiches fresh daily. Mountain-town cafe hours move with the season, so we list what we can verify and give you a phone number for the rest.

Our house has assignments for all three: Bella's when breakfast is the event (the French toast and the scrambles are the move), Jenna Sue's when it's fuel for an errand run (the oatmeal for me, the astronaut breakfast for my partner, every single time), and the Tree House when the point is to sit under the trees a while.

Jenna Sue's Cafe

Address: 13090 Highway 9, Boulder Creek, CA 95006. Phone: (831) 338-7008. Posted hours are 6:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Monday through Friday and 7:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. on weekends.

Jenna Sue's Cafe is the downtown coffee shop and breakfast cafe, pouring espresso drinks alongside breakfast, sandwiches, and house-baked goods. It's a good place to land if you're up before the mountain is. It opens at 6 a.m. on weekdays and 7 a.m. on weekends, closing at 2:30 p.m.

Bella's Cafe

Address: 13132 Central Ave, Boulder Creek, CA 95006. Phone: (831) 217-5070. Hours: Tuesday through Sunday, 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Closed Monday.

Bella's Cafe is a locally owned American breakfast and lunch cafe in the heart of downtown. It's the classic sit-down morning plate, eggs and the rest of it, in a small room a block off Highway 9. Our listing doesn't carry confirmed current hours, so call ahead at (831) 217-5070 before you make the drive, especially early or late in the day.

The Tree House Cafe

Address: 13266 CA-9, Boulder Creek, CA 95006. Phone: (831) 610-8912.

The Tree House Cafe is the cafe and espresso bar at the north edge of the business district, and it's a genuine Boulder Creek landmark: giant redwoods grow up through the interior of the building. Coffee and a light breakfast here come with a setting no chain can copy. We don't have verified current hours, so check by phone at (831) 610-8912 before heading over.

Johnnie's deli counter, for grab-and-go

Address: 13225 Highway 9, Boulder Creek. Hours: Monday to Thursday 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m.; Friday and Saturday 8:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.; Sunday 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m.

Not every morning needs a table. Johnnie's Super Market & Liquor is the town grocery, and its deli counter makes fresh sandwiches daily. It's the reliable option when you'd rather eat in the truck or at the trailhead than in a dining room. The store opens at 8 a.m. every day, so it covers the mornings you're moving early and don't want to sit down. It's a full grocery too, so you can grab coffee, fruit, and a pastry from the bakery case in the same stop.

A later start: Scopazzi's brunch

If you're closer to a late-morning brunch than a sunrise breakfast, Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge at 13300 Big Basin Way serves breakfast Wednesday through Sunday from 10:30 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. It's the historic Italian room in town, and it's closed Monday and Tuesday. On a weekend morning when you want to linger rather than rush, it's the sit-down brunch table. Its dinner service is covered in our dinner guide.

What Boulder Creek doesn't have for breakfast

Worth setting expectations: our directory doesn't list a national coffee chain or a drive-through anywhere in town. Breakfast in Boulder Creek means an independent cafe, a grocery deli counter, or a weekend brunch table, not a franchise window. That's part of the character of the place, and it's why calling ahead beats assuming. Cafe hours here move with the season, the weather, and staffing, so a quick phone check saves a wasted drive.

For every meal beyond the morning, our full where to eat in Boulder Creek guide covers the sit-down restaurants, taquerias, markets, and the rest. You can also browse hours and contacts for local spots in the Boulder Creek business directory.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the earliest breakfast in Boulder Creek?

Jenna Sue's Cafe posts the earliest opening in town, 6:00 a.m. on weekdays and 7:00 a.m. on weekends. Johnnie's Super Market opens its doors at 8:00 a.m. daily if a deli sandwich or a bakery-case pastry counts as breakfast for you.

Is there anywhere open for breakfast on Monday?

Jenna Sue's Cafe is open Monday, from 6:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Johnnie's is open daily from 8:00 a.m. The Tree House opens at 6 a.m. Scopazzi's brunch runs Wednesday through Sunday, and Bella's Cafe is closed Mondays, so those two are out at the start of the week.

Where can I get coffee to go?

Jenna Sue's and The Tree House Cafe are both espresso bars, and Johnnie's carries coffee in the store. There's no national coffee chain or drive-through in Boulder Creek, so a to-go cup comes from one of the local cafes or the market.

Why aren't hours listed for every cafe here?

Because we only publish hours we can verify to a current source, and a wrong hour is worse than none. Where our listing doesn't carry confirmed current hours, as with Bella's Cafe and The Tree House Cafe, we've given you the phone number instead so you can check directly.

A breakfast spot I know is missing. Why?

We list places we can point to through their own page or a current official listing. If a local morning spot doesn't have a page we can point to yet, it isn't here, and we'll add it as soon as it does. If coffee is the whole point of the morning, our coffee guide covers who pours what and who opens earliest. If you run one, or spot a detail that's changed, tell us at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact.

where-to-eat-dinner-boulder-creek.title: Dinner in Boulder Creek: Every Sit-Down Option in Town
where-to-eat-dinner-boulder-creek.html:
Once the light goes off the redwoods, dinner in Boulder Creek comes down to five kitchens plus a truck: Red Pearl Chinese Cuisine, Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge, Tae's Edo Sushi Bar, Taqueria Los Gallos, and The Sawmill Restaurant & Alehouse, with El Rey Leon's Mexican food truck downtown for takeout rather than a table. That's the whole evening roster in town, running Italian, Chinese, Japanese, Mexican, and American pub fare. The thing to know before you head out: most kitchens close early, and several take Monday and Tuesday off.

Our own rotation, for calibration: Los Gallos is the weeknight default, the Red Pearl is non-negotiable when anyone is sick, Tae's Edo is the birthday table, and Scopazzi's is for the occasions. One planning note: the Sawmill is expected to close temporarily for renovations after service on Friday, August 14, 2026, with reopening details not yet confirmed, so call before you count on it.

The short version

  • Five kitchens serve dinner at a table, from Scopazzi's special-occasion dining room to an unfussy taqueria, plus a food truck for takeout.
  • Nobody runs late. The kitchens that post hours close by 8 or 9 p.m., and El Rey Leon wraps up at 7.
  • Monday is the quietest night: Red Pearl, Scopazzi's, and Tae's Edo are all closed.
  • Taqueria Los Gallos runs latest on weeknights, to 8:45 p.m. The Sawmill closes at 8 p.m. and opens late on Wednesdays.

Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge

Address: 13300 Big Basin Way, Boulder Creek. Phone: (831) 338-4444. Dinner hours: Wednesday through Sunday, 4:00 p.m. to closing. Closed Monday and Tuesday.

Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge is the historic Italian restaurant and lounge in town, the special-occasion room that's fed Boulder Creek for generations. Dinner runs Wednesday through Sunday starting at 4 p.m. There's a lounge on site, plus private-event rooms if you're planning something bigger than a table for two. It's closed Monday and Tuesday, so a weekend reservation is the safe bet.

Red Pearl Chinese Cuisine

Address: 13151 Highway 9, Boulder Creek. Phone: (831) 338-9800. Hours: Wednesday through Sunday, 11:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. Closed Monday and Tuesday.

Red Pearl Chinese Cuisine handles Chinese food for the valley, dine-in or takeout, from downtown Boulder Creek. The kitchen runs to 9 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday, which makes it one of the latest dinners in town on the nights it's open. Like several places here, it takes Monday and Tuesday off.

Tae's Edo Sushi Bar

Address: 13271 Highway 9, Boulder Creek. Phone: (831) 338-2099. Hours: Tuesday through Thursday and Sunday 4:00 to 8:00 p.m.; Friday and Saturday 12:00 to 3:00 p.m. and 4:00 to 8:00 p.m. Closed Monday.

Tae's Edo Sushi Bar is the Japanese and sushi spot in town, serving sushi and other Japanese dishes for dinner, with an added lunch window on Friday and Saturday. Dinner service ends at 8 p.m., earlier than the pub and the Chinese kitchen, so think of it as an earlier-evening plan rather than a late one. It's closed Monday.

El Rey Leon

Address: 12890 Central Avenue, Boulder Creek. Phone: (831) 282-7792. Hours: Monday through Saturday, 11:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. and 4:00 to 7:00 p.m.

El Rey Leon is a Mexican food truck at its downtown spot on set days each week, with outdoor seating and counter service. Its posted evening window runs to 7 p.m., Monday through Saturday, which makes it more of an early-dinner or takeout-home option than a linger-late one. It's also one of the few kitchens in town posting Monday hours, so keep it in mind at the start of the week.

Taqueria Los Gallos

Address: 13070 Central Ave, Boulder Creek, CA 95006. Phone: (831) 217-5000. Hours: open daily at 8:30 a.m., serving until 8:45 p.m. Monday through Friday and 7:45 p.m. Saturday and Sunday.

Taqueria Los Gallos is the downtown sit-down taqueria, serving tacos, burritos, and other Mexican dishes. It's an unfussy dining room, and a solid pick when you want dinner without any ceremony. Those weeknight hours make it the latest kitchen in town, and one of the few places serving before 9 a.m. as well. Hours shift, so call (831) 217-5000 before a special trip.

The Sawmill Restaurant & Alehouse

Address: 15520 Highway 9, Boulder Creek. Phone: (831) 610-8196. Hours: 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, except Wednesday when it opens at 4 p.m.

The Sawmill Restaurant & Alehouse sits a few minutes north of downtown and does burgers, pub fare, and craft beer, with outdoor seating and a music stage under the trees. On a warm evening on the patio, it's the closest thing to a dinner-and-a-night-out combination in town. We don't have verified current hours online, so call (831) 610-8196 if you're cutting it close, and see our Boulder Creek night out guide for the after-dinner side of the Sawmill.

What dinner in Boulder Creek doesn't include

A few things worth knowing before you head out:

  • No late-night dining. The kitchens that post hours close by 8 or 9 p.m., and El Rey Leon wraps up at 7.
  • Monday is the quietest night. Red Pearl, Scopazzi's, and Tae's are all closed, which leaves the taqueria until 8:45, the Sawmill until 8, and El Rey Leon's truck until 7.

For grab-and-go, deli counters, markets, and the rest of the food picture, our full where to eat in Boulder Creek guide has it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's open for dinner on Monday in Boulder Creek?

Monday is the slow night. Red Pearl, Scopazzi's, and Tae's Edo are all closed. Taqueria Los Gallos serves until 8:45 p.m., El Rey Leon's truck posts Monday hours until 7:00 p.m., and The Sawmill serves until 8:00 p.m.

Which Boulder Creek restaurants are open latest?

Red Pearl runs to 9:00 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday, the latest dinner service in town, with Taqueria Los Gallos close behind at 8:45 p.m. on weeknights. Tae's Edo closes at 8:00 p.m. and El Rey Leon at 7:00 p.m. There's no late-night dining in Boulder Creek, so plan on an earlier evening.

Is there a sit-down restaurant open every night?

No. Several kitchens close Monday and Tuesday, so there's no single restaurant open seven nights a week. Check the day-by-day hours above, and remember that El Rey Leon is one of the few posting Monday service.

Why aren't hours listed for every restaurant?

Hours come from each kitchen's own posting or from the restaurant directly. They shift with the season and the staffing, so the phone numbers are here too.

A restaurant I know is missing. Why?

We list sit-down places we can point to through their own page or a current official listing. Grab-and-go spots, markets, and food stands are covered in our main eating guide. If a dinner spot is missing or a detail has changed, let us know at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact.

Want the whole evening mapped out, not just the meal? Our Boulder Creek night out guide covers what happens after dinner, and the local business directory lists hours and contacts for everything else open in town.

where-to-find-sourdough-boulder-creek.title: Where to Find Real Sourdough Around Boulder Creek
where-to-find-sourdough-boulder-creek.html:
Go looking for a bakery counter and a fresh sourdough loaf on a random Tuesday in Boulder Creek, and you'll come up empty. The town doesn't have one. What it has instead is a small network of cottage bakers and farm stands, and once you know the schedule, you eat well. Here's where the naturally leavened bread comes from around here, and how to get it.

The short version

  • No walk-in counter in town. Sourdough here comes from cottage bakers, farmers-market stalls, and farm stands, so it rewards a little planning.
  • Wildstone Bakery is the closest thing to a dedicated sourdough bakery. It sells at regional farmers markets; call (831) 252-0706 to ask about ordering.
  • Doughlicious Farmstand runs on weekends with sourdough, cookies, cakes, and sweet breads, by preorder or pickup. It's a home-based stand, so check its social pages for days and details rather than turning up.
  • Butter Late Than Never does local delivery and custom orders. Ask about a sourdough loaf directly at (510) 390-5548.
  • Dough and Dahlias, a short drive down in Ben Lomond, arranges sourdough pickup through Instagram, @doughandahlias.

Wildstone Bakery

Base: Boulder Creek. Phone: (831) 252-0706. Where to find it: Downtown Santa Cruz Farmers Market, Wednesdays 12:30 to 5:00 p.m.; Ben Lomond Village Market, first Saturdays June through October 2026, 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.

Wildstone Bakery is the Boulder Creek maker most squarely built around naturally fermented bread. The loaves, bagels, pastries, and seasonal tarts go out to regional farmers markets rather than a storefront, so you catch it at a market stall, not a shop counter.

Plan around the market schedule above, or call ahead at (831) 252-0706 about ordering. This is the closest thing the town has to a dedicated sourdough bakery.

Butter Late Than Never Baking Co.

Base: Boulder Creek. Phone: (510) 390-5548. Reach: local delivery and California distribution.

Butter Late Than Never Baking Co. is a licensed Boulder Creek cottage bakery selling small-batch baked goods, custom orders, and wholesale. Our listing describes it as a small-batch and custom bakery rather than naming a specific sourdough line, so if a sourdough loaf is what you're after, ask about it as a custom order when you get in touch.

As a cottage operation it works from a home kitchen, which means orders and delivery rather than a storefront, and no published address. Reach it at (510) 390-5548 or through its site to ask what's available.

Dough and Dahlias, Ben Lomond

Base: Ben Lomond, local pickup. Order and updates: Instagram, @doughandahlias.

Dough and Dahlias is a home-based Ben Lomond cottage operation offering homemade sourdough breads and baked goods for local pickup, along with cut-flower bouquets grown in the owner's garden. Being home-based, it has no storefront and no public address; ordering and pickup are arranged through its Instagram page.

It's a short drive down Highway 9 from Boulder Creek, and the sourdough-and-flowers pairing is the kind of small mountain operation this valley runs on.

Doughlicious Farmstand

Where: a home-based stand on the north side of Boulder Creek. Details and stand days come from its social pages.

Doughlicious Farmstand is a neighborhood farm stand known for sourdough and seasonal goods, on the north side of Boulder Creek. It typically runs weekends, with sourdough, cookies, cakes, and sweet breads available to preorder or pick up. Because it works out of a home, we don't publish the address: it's active on Facebook and Instagram, and that's where stand days and what's-available news appear.

Our listing doesn't carry set hours or a phone number for it, so those social pages are the place to check before you head over. Farm stands run on their own rhythm.

What Boulder Creek doesn't have

There's no daily walk-in bakery counter for sourdough in Boulder Creek. The bread here comes from cottage bakers, farmers-market stalls, and farm stands, which means it rewards a little planning: following an Instagram page, catching a market day, or placing an order ahead.

That's not a knock on the town. It's how small-batch, naturally leavened baking tends to work in a mountain community, and it's the difference between driving down the valley for a supermarket loaf and getting bread made by someone a few streets away.

For everything else food-related in town, see our where to eat in Boulder Creek guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a sourdough bakery in Boulder Creek?

Not a storefront one. Wildstone Bakery is the Boulder Creek maker built around naturally fermented bread, but it sells at regional farmers markets rather than from a shop counter. The closest thing to buying local sourdough in town is the Doughlicious Farmstand, which runs weekend stand days, lately Saturday and Sunday with the occasional Friday, by preorder or honor-system walk-up (cash or Venmo), and posts each week's details on its own social pages.

Where can I buy sourdough near Boulder Creek right now?

Catch Wildstone Bakery at the Downtown Santa Cruz Farmers Market on Wednesdays or the Ben Lomond Village Market on first Saturdays in season, check the Doughlicious Farmstand's social pages for stand days, or arrange pickup from Dough and Dahlias in Ben Lomond through its Instagram.

Does anyone deliver sourdough locally?

Butter Late Than Never offers local delivery and California distribution for its cottage-bakery orders, and it takes custom orders, so a sourdough loaf is worth asking about directly. Dough and Dahlias and Doughlicious work on local pickup rather than delivery.

Why don't these bakers have storefronts?

Most are cottage or home-based operations, which under California cottage food rules work from home kitchens with pickup, delivery, or market stalls rather than a public shop. That's also why we don't publish addresses for the home-based ones. It keeps small local baking possible in a town this size.

A baker I know is missing. Why?

We list makers we can point to through their own page or a current official listing. If a local sourdough baker has a page we can point to, or a detail here has changed, tell us at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact.

Chasing down a good loaf is half the fun of a valley this size. Once you've got your bread, our where to eat in Boulder Creek guide covers the rest of a day's meals in town.

where-to-get-haircut-boulder-creek.title: Where to Get a Haircut in and Around Boulder Creek
where-to-get-haircut-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • In Boulder Creek: three full-service salons downtown, all within an easy walk of Highway 9. Hair Hut keeps the most regular posted hours; Central Avenue Salon and Oh Suzannah round out the block.
  • A few minutes south in Ben Lomond: VIP Hair Studio and the home-based K-Salon, both good backups when the Boulder Creek shops are booked.
  • Want a real barbershop with fades, tapers, and beard work? There isn't one in Boulder Creek or Ben Lomond. The nearest is Society Barbershop in Felton, about 15 minutes south, by appointment only with online booking.
  • Call first. Nearly everything on this list is appointment-driven, and a single stylist can be booked solid on the day you need them.

You can walk to a haircut in Boulder Creek. Three salons work downtown, close enough that you could pass all three on one errand, and not a barber pole among them. Two more sit a few minutes south in Ben Lomond, and the valley's one dedicated barbershop is in Felton. Below is who cuts hair and where, grouped by community, with the details we could confirm. Most of these are small, appointment-driven shops, so booking beats walking in almost everywhere on this list.

One thing worth saying up front: if you want a barbershop, with fades, tapers, beard work, and a straight-razor shave, there isn't a dedicated one in Boulder Creek or Ben Lomond. The in-valley shops are full-service hair salons that cut men's, women's, and kids' hair. The nearest true barbershop is in Felton, covered at the end.

Hair Hut (Boulder Creek)

Address: 13266 Highway 9, Suite A. Phone: 831-239-0317. Hours: Tuesday through Thursday 9am to 7pm, Friday 9am to 5:30pm, Saturday 10am to 5pm, closed Sunday and Monday.

Hair Hut is the long-running full-service salon at the north end of downtown. It handles cuts, color, highlights, perms, and extensions for men, women, and children, which makes it the closest thing in town to a one-stop shop for a whole family. It also keeps the most regular posted hours of any salon in Boulder Creek, so it's a reasonable first call.

Central Avenue Salon (Boulder Creek)

Address: 13162 Central Avenue. Phone: 415-725-0850. Hours: by appointment.

Central Avenue Salon is stylist Dana Bernhardt's shop, a block off the main drag on Central. It does cuts, color, and extensions by appointment rather than drop-in, so plan to book ahead. It's a single-stylist operation, which some people prefer for the consistency of seeing the same person every time.

Oh Suzannah Hair Designers (Boulder Creek)

Address: 13090 Highway 9. Phone: 831-338-3883. Hours: Tuesday through Friday 10am to 5pm, Saturday 10am to 4pm, closed Sunday and Monday.

Oh Suzannah is the third downtown salon, offering color, cuts, perms, and relaxers, plus facial waxing if you want to add it to a visit. Relaxers are worth underlining, since plenty of salons down the valley have quietly dropped them, and finding one in the valley saves a real drive. Its posted hours run a bit later in the week than some, with Saturday appointments available. As with the others, a quick call to confirm the day's schedule is the safe bet before you drive in.

VIP Hair Studio (Ben Lomond)

Address: 10090 Highway 9, Suite 2, Ben Lomond. Phone: 831-609-6563. Hours: by appointment only.

A few minutes south in Ben Lomond, VIP Hair Studio is run by longtime San Lorenzo Valley stylist Melissa Bumbaca. It's an appointment-only cut-and-color salon, worth knowing about when the downtown Boulder Creek shops are booked or closed on the day you need them. Being in Ben Lomond, it's a short drive down Highway 9 rather than an in-town option.

K-Salon (Ben Lomond)

Location: Ben Lomond (home-based, no public storefront address). Website: ksalon.us.

K-Salon is a home-based salon run by stylist Krishna, offering cut and color services in a private redwood setting. Because it works out of a home rather than a storefront, there's no walk-in address to list. Book through the site or by texting or calling (831) 325-9664, and directions come with your confirmation. It's a good fit if you like a quieter, one-on-one setting over a busy shop floor.

Society Barbershop (Felton)

Address: 6287 Highway 9, Felton. Online booking available at societybarbershop.com. Phone: (408) 800-2219.

If a barbershop is what you're after, Society Barbershop in Felton is the closest one, about a fifteen-minute drive down Highway 9. It's a full-service shop offering fades and tapers, with online booking through its site. We don't have its current daily hours confirmed, so book online or call before heading down.

Where the valley comes up short

For everyday cuts, color, and kids' trims, Boulder Creek is covered without leaving town. The gap is barbering as its own craft. None of the Boulder Creek or Ben Lomond shops is a dedicated barbershop, so a classic barber experience means driving to Felton.

That's no knock on the local salons, which cut men's hair too. It's the arithmetic of a small town, and worth knowing before you go looking for a barber pole downtown.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a barbershop in Boulder Creek?

Not a dedicated one. The three hair salons in town cut men's, women's, and children's hair, but the nearest shop that specializes in barbering, with fades and tapers, is Society Barbershop in Felton, roughly fifteen minutes south on Highway 9.

Can I walk in for a haircut, or do I need an appointment?

Most of these shops lean toward appointments. Central Avenue Salon, VIP Hair Studio, and K-Salon are appointment-based, and Society Barbershop takes online bookings. Hair Hut and Oh Suzannah keep posted hours, but calling ahead is still the safe move at any small salon, since a single stylist can be fully booked on a given day.

Which salons are in Boulder Creek versus nearby?

Hair Hut, Central Avenue Salon, and Oh Suzannah Hair Designers are all in Boulder Creek proper. VIP Hair Studio and K-Salon are in Ben Lomond, and Society Barbershop is in Felton, all a short drive down Highway 9.

A shop I know is missing. Why?

This list only includes hair businesses we could verify as current listings in our directory. If a stylist or shop near Boulder Creek isn't here, it may not have a public listing we can confirm yet. If you run one, or want a correction, tell us at bouldercreeklocal.com/contact.

Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, it's a starting point. Browse the full Boulder Creek business directory for contact details on these shops and more, and if anything above has changed, let us know through the submit page so the next neighbor gets it right.

where-to-stay-boulder-creek.title: Where to Stay in and Around Boulder Creek
where-to-stay-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • In town: Masood's Lodge is the small lodge you can walk to downtown from. Brookdale Lodge, in neighboring Brookdale, is the historic option.
  • Standard hotel amenities: the Quality Inn & Suites in Ben Lomond is the closest chain hotel, a few miles south on Highway 9.
  • Camping: Redwood Resort is right in town; Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park Campground has 107 sites and fills up, so reserve ahead.
  • Most stays are vacation rentals. We point you to the Airbnb and VRBO searches rather than naming individual listings.
  • Book for the mountains, not the flatlands: plan for spotty cell service, aim to arrive in daylight, and favor a flexible cancellation policy for fire season and winter storms.

There's no strip of hotels on the way into Boulder Creek. The town keeps its lodging small and scattered under the redwoods: a handful of creekside lodges and cabin resorts, the closest chain hotel a few miles south in Ben Lomond, and a good number of visitors filling in the rest with a vacation rental. Match the stay to your trip and the mountains are easy to enjoy. Book blind and a steep, unlit driveway at 10 p.m. can teach the lesson the hard way. Listing a place here isn't an endorsement, only a factual starting point so you can pick well.

Lodges and Cabins

Masood's Lodge at 13420 Big Basin Way in Boulder Creek (831-246-4517) is a small lodge offering cabin and studio rooms in a wooded creekside setting, with check-in from 3 to 9 p.m. and check-out at 11 a.m. It's the in-town pick if you want to walk to downtown Boulder Creek.

Brookdale Lodge at 11570 Highway 9 in Brookdale (831-609-6010) is the historic landmark hotel just south of town, with remodeled, pet-friendly rooms and the on-site 1950s-style Brookdale Diner. One detail worth knowing before you book: the rooms, the diner, and the River Run lounge and event space are operating, but the storied Brook Room dining hall, the one with a creek running through it, isn't currently running as a standalone restaurant. Book it for the rooms and the history, and check ahead on which spaces are open during your dates.

Fern River Resort at 5250 Highway 9 in Felton (831-335-4412) is a third-generation, family-owned resort with rustic cabins in the redwoods along the San Lorenzo River. Cabin features and river activities vary by unit and season, and the resort doesn't post general office hours, so call before you count on reaching someone.

Quality Inn & Suites Santa Cruz Mountains at 9733 Highway 9 in Ben Lomond (831-336-2292) is the closest chain hotel to Boulder Creek, with rooms and suites, free hot breakfast, an outdoor pool, and a 24-hour front desk. It's the predictable pick when you want standard hotel amenities.

Camping and RV

Redwood Resort RV Park and Campground at 150 Grove Street in Boulder Creek (831-338-3413) offers seasonal tent and RV sites plus year-round monthly RV spaces, right in town.

For state-park camping, the Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park Campground has 107 sites in a pine and oak forest. It has its own entrance at 2591 Graham Hill Road in Scotts Valley, separate from the Felton day-use area, and the campground kiosk is 831-438-2396. State Parks says reservations are highly recommended between Memorial Day and Labor Day, and books them through ReserveCalifornia at 800-444-7275. Check the park page for the current season, site amenities, and nightly rate before you plan around a site.

Group and Retreat Centers (and What They Are Not)

A few large properties in the valley look like lodging on a map but are really group and retreat centers, so it helps to know what they are before you call.

  • The Sequoia Retreat Center in Ben Lomond (831-218-5872) is a redwood wedding and retreat venue with on-site cabins, geared to booked events and groups rather than nightly walk-up rooms.
  • Mount Hermon Christian Camps & Conference Center (831-335-4466) offers cabin and lodge stays with meals, but primarily for retreats, conferences, and organized groups.
  • Redwood Christian Park in Boulder Creek (831-338-2134) is a Christian retreat and family-camp center that rents to church, youth, and family groups, not as an open hotel.

These are a good fit for a reunion, a retreat, or a group getaway, and not the place to book a single room for a weekend.

Vacation Rentals: Airbnb and VRBO

Beyond the fixed lodges, most Boulder Creek stays happen in vacation rentals, cabins and homes tucked into the redwoods. We don't name individual listings, because a rental that exists only on a booking platform, with no independent website or identity of its own, isn't something we can verify and stand behind the way we do a named business. What we can do is point you to the search and tell you how to book a mountain rental well.

Start with an area search on Airbnb or VRBO for Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, Brookdale, or Felton, and read recent reviews closely. Then keep a few mountain realities in mind that flatland trips don't have:

  • Cell coverage is spotty. Download your directions and the host's check-in instructions before you leave a reliable signal, and get a phone number you can call from a landline or Wi-Fi if you get turned around.
  • Arriving after dark on Highway 9 is harder than it looks. The road is winding, narrow in spots, and unlit, and many rental driveways are steep and unmarked. Aim to arrive in daylight for a first-time stay, and ask the host for a landmark, not just an address.
  • Fire season is real from roughly late summer into fall. Ask the host about their evacuation plan and access road, note that red-flag conditions can prompt precautionary power shutoffs, and check current conditions before and during your stay. Our Mountain Status page links the official sources for weather, roads, power, and air quality.
  • Build in flexibility. Winter storms can close or delay Highway 9, and summer wildfire activity can change plans fast, so favor a rental with a reasonable cancellation policy and confirm it before you book.

For live road and condition updates near your dates, check the Mountain Status page, and see our roads and parking notes for the durable patterns on Highway 9.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the closest hotel to Boulder Creek?

For an in-town small lodge, Masood's Lodge is right in Boulder Creek. For a full-service chain hotel with predictable amenities, the Quality Inn & Suites in Ben Lomond is the closest, a few miles south on Highway 9, with free breakfast, a pool, and a 24-hour front desk. Brookdale Lodge in neighboring Brookdale is the historic hotel option.

Can I camp near Boulder Creek?

Yes. Redwood Resort RV Park and Campground is in town with tent, RV, and monthly sites. Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park Campground has 107 sites, reached by its own entrance off Graham Hill Road in Scotts Valley, and books through ReserveCalifornia at 800-444-7275. Check the park page for the current season and nightly rate before you plan around a site.

Is Brookdale Lodge open?

Yes, with a caveat. The remodeled, pet-friendly rooms, the Brookdale Diner, and the River Run lounge and event space are operating. The historic Brook Room dining hall, the one with the creek running through it, isn't currently running as a standalone restaurant. Confirm which spaces are open for your dates when you book.

Should I book an Airbnb or a lodge?

It depends on your trip. A named lodge or resort gives you a front desk, set check-in, and a known operator, which is simpler for a short or first-time visit. A vacation rental can offer more space, a kitchen, and privacy, which suits families and longer stays, as long as you plan for spotty cell service, a daylight arrival, and a flexible cancellation policy. We don't rank individual rentals; search the platforms and read recent reviews.

Inclusion here isn't an endorsement, only a verified place to start. Browse the full directory for local lodging and services, plan the rest of your trip with our events calendar, and send corrections or additions through the submit page so the next visitor gets accurate information.

why-isnt-boulder-creek-a-city.title: Why Isn't Boulder Creek a City?
why-isnt-boulder-creek-a-city.html:
Boulder Creek isn't a city because the people who lived here voted to stop being one.

That's the short answer, and even some of the people who write about Boulder Creek don't know it. This town was an incorporated California city in the early twentieth century. In 1915, residents voted to disincorporate: to abolish the city and hand the area back to county government. It's been unincorporated ever since, and it has never gone back.

First, a correction

We need to own something. An earlier Boulder Creek Local article stated that Boulder Creek never incorporated as a city. That was wrong, and we're fixing it.

It's an easy error to make, because it's the natural assumption. Boulder Creek looks like every other unincorporated mountain community, it's been unincorporated for over a century, and most casual sources just describe it as "an unincorporated community in Santa Cruz County" without mentioning that it used to be something else. We repeated the assumption instead of checking it. Consider this the check.

What the record shows

Here's where we have to be careful, because the sources don't fully agree.

Well documented: the 1915 disincorporation. The Wikipedia entry states that "in 1915, residents of Boulder Creek voted to disincorporate the city (the process of abolishing the city and returning the area back to county rule)." More usefully, Boulder Creek appears with a 1915 date in the standard reference list of California municipal disincorporations compiled in Michael Coleman's survey of the subject, a public-finance document that exists for reasons entirely unrelated to Santa Cruz Mountains local history. That's exactly what makes it good corroboration.

Settled: the incorporation year. The 1910 Census marks Boulder Creek town with a footnote reading "Incorporated in 1902," which matches the 1902 date in Santa Cruz County's own Boulder Creek Town Plan. Other pages online give 1905, and at least one gives a 1920s incorporation with a 1941 disincorporation. Those trace back to low-quality aggregators, and the 1941 claim contradicts the 1915 date in the disincorporation literature.

So the record reads: Boulder Creek incorporated in 1902 and disincorporated in 1915.

The vote itself: 107 to 45

An earlier version of this article said the 1902 election returns were an archive job still on our list. They aren't any more.

The Santa Cruz Morning Sentinel of February 16, 1902 ran the result the morning after the polls closed:

BOULDER CREEK VOTES IN FAVOR OF INCORPORATION. Incorporation won the day in Boulder Creek Saturday. The vote in favor of it was 107, while those who opposed could only muster up 45 votes.

That fixes the date as Saturday, February 15, 1902, which the Santa Cruz Surf had flagged in advance: on the Friday it reported two special elections set for the next day, Boulder Creek's held under the general election law with the county clerk getting things ready. On Monday the seventeenth the Board of Supervisors canvassed the returns and certified the legality of the proceedings to the Secretary of State. Boulder Creek was the third town in Santa Cruz County to incorporate, after Santa Cruz and Watsonville.

The same report names the town's first officers. Five trustees were elected from a field of six, I. T. Bloom, J. H. Fuller, W. H. Dool, S. Hubbs and W. O. McAbee, with J. Iliff the only candidate to lose. A. M. Anthony became clerk, J. H. Armistead treasurer, and A. L. Seidlinger marshal. They held their first meeting the following Monday night. (The Sentinel printed a vote count beside each name, but those digits sit at the edge of the page and the scan is not clean enough to publish, so we're giving names and outcomes only.)

The paper's own read on the campaign is worth keeping. The election, it said, "was free from all bossism or gerrymandering. Boulder Creek has yet to learn these metropolitan methods." The new town's first order of business was better streets and sidewalks.

The 1915 disincorporation is separately corroborated by the California League of Cities list of municipal disincorporations, which names Boulder Creek at 1915.

Why a town would quit being a city

Incorporation makes sense for a boomtown. Between 1885 and 1915 Boulder Creek was one of the largest lumber-exporting points in the country, with a railroad terminus, a freight yard, hotels, saloons and a year-round population over 800, plus a floating population of mill and woods workers.

A place like that has real municipal problems: fire in a town built of wood and full of mills, plus water, streets, sidewalks, drainage, and the policing of a rowdy industrial town. A city government can tax, borrow and build to handle those.

Disincorporation makes sense when the boom ends. And it was ending exactly then. The accessible old growth near the rail line was giving out, the mills were closing, and the same decade brought the end of the town's rail-driven economy. A shrinking town still owes whatever a city government committed it to, and the tax base to pay for it walks out with the industry.

That's the general shape of early-1900s California disincorporations, and Boulder Creek wasn't alone in the valley: Felton disincorporated two years later, in 1917. Two neighboring San Lorenzo Valley towns gave up cityhood within 24 months of each other, as the timber economy that justified it collapsed.

The part the economics leaves out: whiskey

There is a second thread running through those thirteen years, and it involves the saloons.

Local historian Ross Eric Gibson, writing in the Santa Cruz Sentinel, records that the town had sixteen saloons when it incorporated. The new council added a quarterly saloon licence fee, which closed three of them and brought in cash from the rest, then raised that fee to $75. The saloons answered by backing an initiative to disincorporate the town in 1906. It failed. The council then doubled the fee again to $150, and the number of saloons fell to eight, with their customers "harassed" by enforcement of the public drunkenness laws.

Sixteen to eight, by licence fee, in a few years. That is a town government being used as a temperance instrument, and it explains why the liquor trade wanted rid of it.

The saloons tried twice. A second attempt to disincorporate, in 1912, failed to reach the two-thirds majority the law required. Three years later they got their result, and by then the argument had changed hands entirely.

Read that alongside 1915 and a different story appears. The 1902 vote was not only about streets and sidewalks, and the 1915 vote was not only about a collapsing tax base. A town government with the power to tax and licence had spent more than a decade using it against the liquor trade, and the trade had tried to abolish that government twice and lost both times. When cityhood was finally given up, the industry that had most wanted it gone got what it had been asking for since 1906.

The 1915 vote, and what it was sold on

By 1915 the town's revenues were down and its debts were up. Gibson records the argument that carried the day: that if Boulder Creek gave up cityhood, the county would maintain its roads, sewers and street lights, and would build the town a library.

The vote, the first here in which women took part, was 173 to 72 to disincorporate. Set against the 107 to 45 of 1902, more than twice as many people turned out to end the town's government as had turned out to create it.

The library took rather longer than promised. Boulder Creek's reading room closed after disincorporation and came back in 1917 by public demand, and the branch library the town eventually got is a 1980s building, campaigned for across years of public meetings and opened in March 1985. Seventy years is a long time to wait on a ballot argument.

Two caveats worth stating plainly. These figures come from Gibson's column of October 22, 2023 rather than from the 1906, 1912 and 1915 papers themselves, and we have not yet found the contemporary reporting of any of the three votes. And the tallies above are Gibson's; the certified returns are still an archive job.

What we still need to prove the local story: the contemporary election returns for 1906, 1912 and 1915, the Mountain Echo's reporting on those campaigns, city council minutes, and any record of municipal debt.

So what governs Boulder Creek now?
