Boulder Creek is an unincorporated community and a census-designated place (CDP), a boundary the Census Bureau draws for statistical purposes, first applied to Boulder Creek in the 1980 Census. A CDP is not a government. It has no mayor, no city council, no city hall, and no city limits in any legal sense.

Practically, that means:

  • Santa Cruz County governs. Land use, planning, building permits and county roads run through county departments, and Boulder Creek is represented by a member of the county Board of Supervisors rather than by a local council.
  • The Sheriff's Office is the police department. There is no Boulder Creek PD.
  • Special districts do much of the local work. Fire protection, water, schools and parks and recreation are delivered by independent districts with their own boards and their own boundaries, which is why the fire district, the water district, the school district and the rec district don't all cover the same map.
  • Your ballot reflects all of that. Local elections here are district elections and county elections, not city elections.

If you're new and trying to work out who to call about a given problem, that district-by-district split is the thing to understand. Our new resident quick-start guide and utilities guide map it out.

Could Boulder Creek incorporate again?

In theory, yes. California has a process for it, run through each county's Local Agency Formation Commission, and it requires a fiscal analysis showing the proposed city could pay for itself, plus a vote of the affected residents.

In practice, nobody is proposing it, and the arithmetic is the reason. A new city has to fund police, roads, planning and administration out of its own revenue. Boulder Creek's population is small, its commercial tax base is modest, its road mileage per resident is high, and its terrain is expensive to maintain. The services residents care about most, fire, water, schools, parks, are already run by districts that would continue regardless.

The 1915 voters made a call about what this community could afford to run. More than a century later, nobody has made a serious case that the answer changed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Was Boulder Creek ever a city?

Yes. It was an incorporated California city in the early twentieth century, and residents voted to disincorporate in 1915. It has been unincorporated ever since.

When did Boulder Creek disincorporate?

In 1915. Local historian Ross Eric Gibson gives the vote as 173 to 72, in the first Boulder Creek election in which women took part. Incorporation had come on Saturday, February 15, 1902, when the town voted for it 107 to 45.

Did Boulder Creek try to disincorporate before 1915?

Twice. The town's saloons backed an initiative in 1906, after the council raised their quarterly licence fee, and it failed. A second attempt in 1912 failed to reach the required two-thirds majority. The 1915 vote succeeded.

What does "unincorporated" mean for Boulder Creek?

It means there is no city government. Santa Cruz County handles land use, planning and county roads, the Sheriff's Office provides law enforcement, and independent special districts provide fire protection, water, schools, and parks and recreation.

What is a census-designated place?

A boundary the U.S. Census Bureau draws around a recognizable unincorporated community so it can be counted and reported statistically. Boulder Creek was first designated in the 1980 Census. A CDP has no government or legal authority of its own.

Does Boulder Creek have a mayor?

No. There is no mayor, city council or city hall. Boulder Creek is represented on the Santa Cruz County Board of Supervisors, and the special districts serving the area each have their own elected or appointed boards.

Did other towns near here disincorporate too?

Yes. Felton disincorporated in 1917, two years after Boulder Creek, as the valley's timber economy declined. Disincorporation is rare in California overall, which makes two in one valley notable.

Why do other sources give a different incorporation date?

Because aggregator pages repeat 1905, and one even gives a 1920s date. Two independent records settle it: the 1910 Census footnotes Boulder Creek town as "Incorporated in 1902," and the Santa Cruz Morning Sentinel of February 16, 1902 reports the vote that did it. We publish the primary record rather than the most-copied number.

Who were Boulder Creek's first town officials?

Elected February 15, 1902: trustees I. T. Bloom, J. H. Fuller, W. H. Dool, S. Hubbs and W. O. McAbee; A. M. Anthony as clerk; J. H. Armistead as treasurer; A. L. Seidlinger as marshal. J. Iliff ran for trustee and was the only candidate defeated. The board held its first meeting the following Monday night.

Last reviewed July 27, 2026. The incorporation date and vote are drawn from the Santa Cruz Morning Sentinel of February 16, 1902 and the Santa Cruz Surf of February 14 and 17, 1902, held by the California Digital Newspaper Collection, and corroborated by the 1910 U.S. Census and Santa Cruz County's Boulder Creek Town Plan. The disincorporation date comes from the standard reference list of California municipal disincorporations. We'll update this article if archival records add detail.

Still sorting out who runs what up here? Start with our new resident quick-start guide, and see the Residents guide for county contacts, special districts, and utilities in one place.

why-so-many-orange-butterflies-boulder-c.title: Why Were There So Many Orange Butterflies in Boulder Creek?
why-so-many-orange-butterflies-boulder-c.html:
You notice the movement before you understand it. Some warm afternoon this month, the air over Boulder Creek fills with small orange butterflies, dozens and then hundreds of them, all headed the same direction.

They didn't hatch here. They're painted ladies, and this spring they're moving through California by the thousands. What you're watching isn't a local hatch so much as a migration passing overhead, and it only turns up big in certain years. This is one of them.

In our house the migration had a soundtrack. Our daughter greeted them at every daycare pickup with a squeal, a point, and her own word for them, buhbuhbuh, and for a few weeks they were the highlight of her day in town.

What you're seeing

The butterfly is the painted lady, Vanessa cardui, one of the most widespread butterflies in the world. Up close it's orange and brown with white spots and black-tipped forewings, a bit ragged and mottled rather than boldly patterned.

It flies fast, low, and erratically, rarely stopping for long. That restless flight in a steady direction is the tell. You're watching a migration, not butterflies drifting around a garden.

They're easy to mistake for monarchs, so here's the quick way to sort them:

  • Painted ladies are smaller, roughly a two-inch wingspan, mottled orange-brown with white flecks.
  • Monarchs are larger, closer to four inches, with bold black veins across deep orange and a border of white dots.

Monarchs are the ones that overwinter on the coast, at spots like Natural Bridges. The fast orange river pouring through the valley in March is painted ladies.

Why so many this year

Painted lady numbers swing wildly from year to year, and the switch is rain, hundreds of miles away. These butterflies spend the winter in the deserts of the Southwest and northern Mexico. When those deserts get a wet winter, the spring wildflower bloom explodes, and all that fresh growth feeds an enormous crop of painted lady caterpillars. A few weeks later, that boom takes to the air and heads north.

UC's naturalists tie the huge years directly to big wildflower blooms, and the butterfly biologist Art Shapiro has long noted their numbers are enormous in years with large blooms.

So this isn't an every-year show. Big migrations are irregular, with standout years like 2005 and 2019, and long stretches in between when you'd barely notice them. This spring is a strong year, though the old-timers among butterfly watchers say it's not quite the wall-to-wall spectacle of 2019.

Where they're all going

They're passing through, not moving in. The main California migration runs north from the desert through the Central Valley toward Oregon and the Pacific Northwest, with a branch that swings through the Bay Area and over the Santa Cruz Mountains.

The round trip takes several generations. The butterflies you're seeing now will breed to the north, and their descendants make the return trip south in the fall. The ones crossing Boulder Creek today are one leg of a relay that spans the West and the seasons.

If you want to give them a hand, the same thing that helps them helps everything else: native, nectar-rich plants and no pesticides. Thistles and mallows are classic painted lady host plants, and a patch of blooming natives gives migrants a place to refuel.

Will it happen again?

Maybe, and it comes down to the deserts, not to us. Another big migration needs another wet desert winter to trigger the wildflower bloom that feeds the caterpillars, and that varies year to year in ways no one can promise in advance.

One thing is worth watching for next year. Forecasters are calling for a strong El Niño this coming winter, and wet winters can prime the Southwest deserts for exactly the kind of bloom that produces a painted lady boom. That's a genuine possibility, not a prediction, since it depends on where and when the rain falls.

Their numbers are a kind of weather report from a place you can't see. Watch the deserts this winter. If they green up, next spring could be another good one.

Frequently asked questions

What are the orange butterflies all over Boulder Creek?

They're painted ladies (Vanessa cardui) on their spring migration, small orange-and-brown butterflies with white spots and black forewing tips. In big years, thousands stream north through the Santa Cruz Mountains.

Are they monarchs?

No. Painted ladies are smaller and mottled orange-brown; monarchs are larger with bold black veins and a white-dotted border. Monarchs overwinter on the coast, while the fast-moving spring swarms are painted ladies.

Why are there so many this year?

A wet winter in the Southwest deserts produced a big wildflower bloom, which fed a huge crop of caterpillars. That population boom becomes the spring migration. Numbers vary a lot year to year.

Will there be another big migration next year?

Possibly. It depends on whether the deserts get another wet winter and a strong bloom. A strong El Niño is forecast, which could set that up, but it's not guaranteed.

How can I help the butterflies?

Plant native, nectar-rich flowers, including painted lady favorites like thistles and mallows, and skip the pesticides. Migrants need places to refuel along the way.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. The painted lady biology here follows longstanding observations from University of California naturalists and butterfly biologist Art Shapiro.

Seen something worth noting in the valley's wildlife? Tell us, and browse more Boulder Creek nature and seasonal notes while the migration is still passing through.

wildfire-evacuation-boulder-creek.title: How Boulder Creek Prepares for a Wildfire Evacuation
wildfire-evacuation-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Know your zone now. Look up your address on Genasys Protect. Boulder Creek zone IDs start with BOU. Write down the zones for home, work, and family.
  • Sign up for the alerts. Register for CruzAware and leave Wireless Emergency Alerts on. Orders come from the Sheriff and CAL FIRE, not from this site. For a fire you can see or smell right now, call 911.
  • Learn the three levels. Watch ("Ready"), Warning ("Set"), Order ("GO"). Leave early. Don't wait for a mandatory order to decide.
  • Know more than one way out. Highway 9 isn't the only route, and any road can close.
  • Prep before fire season. Pack a go-bag, keep at least half a tank of gas, and work through defensible space and home hardening on the calm days.

Printable version: the wildfire go-bag and evacuation checklist puts this on paper, which is what you want when the power is out and you are packing in a hurry. It is one of nine local guides on the downloads page.

I evacuated in August 2020 without a go bag. When the order came, I grabbed the animals and left, and everything I know about evacuation prep comes from doing it wrong in real time. It took two trips, one with the first load of animals and a second back up the hill for the chickens and ducks. That first night I had a cranky cat, no cat food, and no open stores until morning. Nobody needs that extra stressor on the worst day of the year.

So this guide is what I'd tell my 2020 self. One thing it will never be is an evacuation order: those come from the Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office and CAL FIRE, and they reach you through CruzAware, the county's alert system.

This site can't tell you a road is clear, a zone is safe, or that it's fine to stay. What it can do is help you get ready now, so that when an alert comes, you already know your zone, you have a bag packed, and you're not making big decisions for the first time in the dark.

For anything happening right now, a fire you can see or smell, call 911. Everything below is for the calm days before a fire, which are the only days to do this.

Know Your Zone Before There's Ever a Fire

Santa Cruz County divides the whole county into small evacuation zones, and every address sits in one. During an emergency, the Sheriff and fire agencies issue warnings and orders zone by zone, so the most useful thing you can do ahead of time is learn yours.

Look it up on Genasys Protect, the county's evacuation map (formerly called Zonehaven), or through the county's "Know Your Zone" page. Type in your address, and the map shows your Zone ID along with the fire and law enforcement agencies that cover you. Boulder Creek zone IDs look like BOU-E028, sometimes with a letter on the end, like BOU-E021A.

The zones are small, so look up your own address rather than assuming a neighbor's zone is yours, and write it down. Learn the zones your kids' school, your work, and your parents' place fall in too, because an order for one zone tells you nothing about the next one over.

Knowing your zone helps, but learn your surroundings too. The county notes it has more than 200 zones and sub-zones, and says public messaging should lean on recognizable streets and landmarks rather than zone numbers. So an alert may name your zone ID or it may describe the area in plain geography. Know both: your Zone ID, and the roads that bound your neighborhood.

Watch, Warning, Order: Three Levels, Not Two

Santa Cruz County uses three evacuation levels, and they don't mean the same thing. Learn all three now. Ready, Set, GO is the shorthand the county attaches to them.

Evacuation Watch ("Ready"). Notification of a possible threat to life or property. Get ready. If you need extra time to leave, consider evacuating early, at this stage. That includes people with disabilities, people with access and functional needs, and anyone with pets or livestock.

Evacuation Warning ("Set"). Notification of a potential threat to life or property. If you need extra time to leave, begin evacuating immediately. Everyone else: be packed, be fueled, be ready to move the moment an order comes. A warning is your cue to load the car, not to keep an eye on it.

Evacuation Order ("GO"). Mandatory. Leave immediately. There is an immediate threat to life, and the area is legally closed to public access. Don't stop to pack more, don't wait to see how it develops, and don't drive around road barricades. In a fast-moving mountain fire there may be no time for anyone to knock on your door, so the order is the knock.

Two more statuses come at the other end, and the difference matters:

Evacuation Orders Lifted means you may return, but some hazards or restrictions may remain. Downed lines, damaged roads, unstable trees, and closed areas are all still possible. Lifted is not safe.

All Clear means all hazards have been fully mitigated. Only this status means the incident hazards are resolved. Never read an all clear into a lifted order, and never read either one off a neighbor's post. Wait for the county to say it.

Shelter in place means stay where you are because leaving is riskier than going. If officials tell you to shelter in place: go indoors, close all doors and windows, stay put, keep your phone on and charged, and follow the instructions that come with the alert. In a wildfire, CAL FIRE says to keep doors and windows closed but unlocked so firefighters can get in. That instruction, like the others, comes from officials, not from this site.

If an evacuation is ordered, officials may designate a Temporary Evacuation Point, a location announced at the time of the incident where evacuees can gather and get information. Its location is decided during the emergency, so there is no standing site to plan around. Watch CruzAware and the Sheriff's Office for where it is. This site will never name one in advance.

If You Can't Get Out

Plan to leave early so this never applies. If it does apply, if your route is blocked or you are cut off, do this:

  1. Call 911.
  2. Follow CAL FIRE's guidance for being trapped at home: gather everyone inside, fill sinks and tubs with cold water, keep doors and windows closed but unlocked so firefighters can get in, and stay inside, away from outside walls and windows.

Do not drive into smoke to force a route. Low visibility, downed lines, and stopped traffic ahead of you are how people get trapped in a car. CAL FIRE publishes separate survival steps for being trapped in a vehicle, on foot, and at home, so read all three in its Go Evacuation Guide before you ever need them.

The county's own evacuation planning notes that residents of this area may have to shelter in place until roads are cleared. That is a real possibility here, and it's another argument for leaving at the watch or the warning rather than the order.

Where the Real Orders and Information Come From

In an emergency, rumors move faster than fire. A neighbor's group text, a screenshot of a screenshot, a well-meaning post with no source behind it: none of that is an evacuation order. Get your information from the places that issue it.

  • CruzAware is the county's alert system and the main way evacuation warnings and orders reach your phone by text, call, and email. If you do nothing else after reading this, sign up at cruzaware.org. Register more than one contact method and more than one address. We have a full walkthrough in our CruzAware setup guide.
  • Wireless Emergency Alerts are the loud, buzzing alerts that arrive on your phone with no signup at all. Officials can push them to every capable phone in an area, which means they reach visitors, guests, and phones that were never registered for anything. Leave them turned on. They are a different channel from CruzAware, and they cover the people CruzAware can't. CruzAware is the one you have to register for.
  • The Genasys Protect map shows the current status of every zone during an incident, color-coded, so you can see whether your zone is under a warning or an order.
  • The Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office and CAL FIRE are the agencies that make and announce evacuation decisions. CAL FIRE's Active Incidents page tracks fires across the state.
  • 911 is for reporting a fire or an emergency and for a life-threatening situation right now. It is not a general information line, so keep it clear for people who need it.
  • Non-emergency questions go elsewhere: the Sheriff's Office main line is (831) 454-7600, and the Boulder Creek Fire Protection District is (831) 338-7222. Neither line issues evacuation orders, and neither can tell you a road is clear.

No alert system is perfect. Phones lose signal, texts fail, and power goes out, which is common in a mountain fire. That's exactly why you sign up for more than one channel and why knowing your zone and your plan ahead of time matters so much. Treat every alert as one layer, not the whole safety net.

The Highway 9 Reality: Know More Than One Way Out

Boulder Creek is a canyon town with limited roads, and most traffic funnels onto Highway 9. It isn't the only way out. Highway 9 runs both north and south, and Highway 236 and Bear Creek Road lead out too. All of them are narrow, and any of them can close. In a large evacuation, that road carries a lot of cars at once, and it can also be the road firefighters need. This is not a reason to panic. It's a reason to leave early and to know your options before you need them.

Learn more than one route away from your home, and drive them on an ordinary day so they're familiar. Keep at least half a tank of gas in the car through fire season, because a full evacuation is no time to be hunting for an open station. Back your car into the driveway or park it facing out, so you're ready to pull away without a three-point turn.

One thing this site will never do is map a "safe route" out of town, because no one can promise a given road is passable or clear when a fire is moving. Conditions change by the minute, and only the officials running the incident have the full picture. When an order comes, follow the routes and directions they give you, obey road closures and barricades, and if you're told a road is closed, believe it. The whole point of leaving early is to be gone before the roads are the problem.

Leave Early. Don't Wait to Be Sure

The hardest part of evacuating is deciding to do it. It always feels too soon, right up until it's too late. Every fire agency says the same thing: if you feel at risk, don't wait for a mandatory order, and if an order comes, don't wait at all.

Leaving early is safer for you and for everyone else. It keeps the roads clearer for the people still coming out behind you and for the trucks coming in. It gives you time to move calmly instead of racing. And it means a stressful evening at a friend's house instead of being caught on the road. If you ever find yourself weighing whether it's "bad enough" to go, that hesitation is your answer. Go.

If you have animals, medical needs, young kids, or anyone in the house who moves slowly, build your plan around leaving at the watch or the warning, not the order. The extra hour is the whole game.

Get Your Home and Your Go-Bag Ready Now

Two kinds of preparation make the biggest difference, and both are done long before any smoke: hardening your home and the space around it, and having a bag ready to grab.

Defensible space and home hardening. CAL FIRE's Ready for Wildfire program lays out the buffer zones around a house, from the ember-resistant five feet closest to the walls out to 100 feet, plus the home-hardening details like vents, gutters, roofs, and decks that decide whether flying embers find a way in. We've pulled all of it into a printable home-prep and defensible-space checklist so you can walk your property with it in hand. Some of this work, especially limbing up and removing trees near the house, is a job for a professional. Our guide to hiring local tree services can help you find someone reputable up here, and our local directory is a place to start.

Your go-bag. A go-bag is the kit you can grab and be out the door with in two minutes. It holds a few days of essentials, your medications, copies of key documents, phone chargers, cash, and supplies for your pets. Our printable go-bag checklist, built from CAL FIRE and American Red Cross guidance, lays it out item by item. Pack it once, keep it by the door, and check it a couple of times a year.

The list I'd pack first now: important papers, medications, animal food, and electronics. Everything else is replaceable. If you keep animals, know your trip math. I needed two trips in 2020; we've since sized up the car so that, if there's ever a next time, everyone hopefully goes in one load. Count your carriers, count your seats, and do the dry run before fire season, not during it.

Do these two things and you've handled most of what's in your control. Keep sturdy shoes and a flashlight by your bed, too, in case an alert comes at 2 a.m.

Pets and Livestock

Animals are part of the plan, and the plan has to account for them before an emergency, not during one.

For pets, keep a carrier for each one, and store their food, water, medications, and vaccination records with your go-bag. Make sure collars and ID tags are current. When a warning comes, bring pets inside and keep them close so you're not chasing a scared cat under the porch when it's time to leave.

Livestock and horses take more lead time, which is the main reason to leave at the warning, not the order. Arrange transport ahead of season if you don't have your own trailer, and know where you'd take animals, whether that's a fairground, a friend's property, or a boarding facility out of the area. CAL FIRE's Go Evacuation Guide has detailed livestock and pet checklists worth reading before you need them. Firefighters focus on the fire and may not be able to move your animals, so their safety comes down to your own advance planning.

Why This Matters So Much Here

Boulder Creek doesn't need to be told that wildfire is real. In August 2020, the CZU Lightning Complex burned through the Santa Cruz Mountains, and our community was among the hardest hit. According to CAL FIRE, the fire covered about 86,000 acres before it was contained that September, and it destroyed 1,490 structures and took one life. Many neighbors are still rebuilding, and many more carry the memory of that evacuation.

We raise this plainly and without drama because the lesson from CZU is a practical one, not a fearful one. The people who had already looked up their zone, packed a bag, and decided in advance that they'd leave early were the ones who moved fastest and with the least panic when it counted. Preparation didn't stop the fire, but it gave people room to make good decisions. That's the whole aim of this page: not to frighten anyone, and never to tell you it's safe, but to help you be ready and to know exactly where to look when the county speaks.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I find my evacuation zone in Boulder Creek?

Go to Genasys Protect and type in your address. The map shows your Zone ID, which for Boulder Creek starts with BOU, along with the agencies that cover you. Look up your home, work, and family members' addresses now, while it's calm, and write the zones down.

Who issues evacuation orders here?

The Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office and CAL FIRE make and announce evacuation decisions. They reach you mainly through CruzAware alerts and the Genasys Protect map. This site does not issue orders and can't tell you it's safe to stay or go. For a fire or an emergency right now, call 911.

What's the difference between an evacuation watch, warning, and order?

There are three levels. A watch ("Ready") means a possible threat: get ready, and consider leaving early if you need extra time, have animals, or have access and functional needs. A warning ("Set") means a potential threat: if you need extra time, begin evacuating immediately. An order ("GO") is mandatory: leave immediately, the threat to life is immediate and the area is legally closed to public access. Afterward, "Evacuation Orders Lifted" means you may return but hazards or restrictions may remain, while "All Clear" means all hazards have been fully mitigated. A lifted order is not an all clear.

Should I wait for an official order before I leave?

No. Every fire agency advises leaving before a mandatory order if you feel at risk, and leaving immediately once an order is issued. Leaving early keeps you safer and keeps the roads clear for others and for firefighters. If you're unsure whether it's time, that uncertainty is your cue to go.

Is Highway 9 the only way out of Boulder Creek?

No. Highway 9 runs both north and south from town, and Highway 236 and Bear Creek Road are also routes out. All of them are narrow mountain roads, and any of them can close, so treat none of them as guaranteed. Know more than one way out and drive your routes on ordinary days so they're familiar. Keep at least half a tank of gas through fire season and park facing out. In an actual evacuation, follow the routes officials give you and obey every road closure. This site won't map a "safe route," because no one can promise a road is clear when a fire is moving.

How do I get ready before fire season?

Sign up for CruzAware, look up your zone, pack a go-bag, and work through defensible space and home hardening around your house. Our printable go-bag checklist and home-prep checklist walk through both, and our CruzAware setup guide covers the alert signup step by step.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This page links to official sources from CAL FIRE, the Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office, and the county's evacuation-zone resources. Evacuation warnings, orders, and all-clear decisions come only from those agencies, not from this site.

Do the calm-day steps once and you've done the hard part: sign up for CruzAware, look up your BOU zone on Genasys Protect, and pack a bag. For the rest of the county contacts, utilities, and emergency resources in one place, see the Residents guide.

wildlife-around-boulder-creek.title: Wildlife Around Boulder Creek: Who You'll Meet and How to Be a Good Neighbor
wildlife-around-boulder-creek.html:
The short version

  • Secure the food supply. Keep trash and recycling in latched or secured bins and set them out the morning of pickup, feed pets indoors, and pick up fallen fruit.
  • Bring cats and small dogs in at night, when coyotes, bobcats, and mountain lions do their moving around.
  • Never feed wild animals. It's illegal in the state parks, and everywhere else it's how a normal animal becomes a problem animal.
  • Injured wild animal: call Native Animal Rescue at (831) 462-0726. Take a photo and call before you drive anywhere.
  • Any emergency involving people, including a mountain lion that's an immediate threat: call 911.

A flock of turkeys can hold a driveway for an entire afternoon, and there's no negotiating with them. That's most of what sharing a neighborhood with wildlife up here amounts to, and it works out fine almost all the time. Deer will eat your roses, raccoons will test your trash cans, and once in a long while a mountain lion will pass through without you ever knowing. Get a few habits right and the arrangement mostly runs itself. Here's who you'll meet and what's normal.

The Everyday Neighbors

Black-tailed deer are the animal you'll see most, browsing yards and road edges at all hours. They're generally calm around people, and that's normal, but don't help it along. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) warns that fed deer "can also lose their fear of humans or attract predators," and around here the predator that follows deer is the mountain lion. Admire them, fence the garden, and let them stay wild. They're also the main reason to drive Highway 9 gently at dawn and dusk, which our guide to driving the mountain roads covers.

Wild turkeys move through in loud, confident flocks. Mostly they're comedy, but a habituated flock can turn pushy. UC's integrated pest management program explains that turkeys used to people "may see human beings as part of the flock and, therefore, part of their pecking order," which is how you get a tom charging a mail carrier in spring. The fix is the same as everything else on this page. Don't feed them, and know that it's legal to shoo them off your property as long as they aren't physically harmed. Clapping, a hose, or letting the dog escort them out all work.

Raccoons are the valley's night shift, smart and persistent. CDFW notes they "easily become food conditioned" when they find accessible food, so the answer is prevention: latched cans, no pet food outside overnight, closed pet doors after dark. One habit worth knowing about: CDFW says raccoons leave droppings in a shared spot called a latrine, which can expose people and pets to raccoon roundworm. If one appears in your yard, clean it up carefully with gloves rather than ignoring it.

Banana slugs are the mascot of the whole forest, the bright yellow ones you'll find on any damp trail. Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park lists them alongside deer, coyotes, and bobcats as the wildlife visitors most often spot. They need nothing from you except to not get stepped on.

The Shy Ones

Bobcats live here and want nothing to do with you. CDFW describes them as solitary animals that typically avoid humans. The realistic concern isn't people, it's that "unsecured poultry or small pets can be preyed upon," so the chicken run needs a roof and the cat sleeps inside.

Coyotes are around more than they're seen, and the CDFW coyote guidance reads like a neighbor's advice: put trash, recycling, and pet food in secure bins, don't leave small pets unsupervised outside, and bring pets in at night. If a coyote lingers near people, haze it. Yell, clap, wave your arms to look bigger, and it should move off. A coyote that's lost its wariness is almost always a coyote someone has been feeding, which is why not feeding is the most neighborly wildlife policy there is.

Mountain lions are the resident everyone asks about, so here are the facts without the horror-movie lighting. Lions live in these mountains because deer do, and they're built to avoid us. Encounters are rare, and attacks are rarer still: CDFW puts it memorably, "a person is one thousand times more likely to be struck by lightning than attacked by a mountain lion," and counts fewer than 50 verified attacks in California since 1890.

For a record of how these encounters usually go: lions pass through our place regularly, whole families some years, and one has bounced off the chicken run. The closest call belonged to our old pitbull rescue, who jumped a lion barely ten feet from me, before I'd seen it at all, chased it up the hillside, and trotted back twenty-five minutes later looking extremely pleased with herself. Then she took a long nap. I don't recommend her method; the guidance below works better. And if you're new here, the sound that will one day stop your heart from the deck at night, a scream like a woman's, is a mountain lion saying nothing is wrong. It's unsettling, and it's normal.

If you do meet one, CDFW's instructions are specific and worth memorizing:

  • Don't run. Running can trigger a chase. Stay calm and stand your ground.
  • Face the animal. Don't turn your back, make noise, and try to look bigger.
  • Pick up small children. Put them on your shoulders.
  • Give it an exit. Leave the lion a clear escape route; most encounters end with the cat taking it.
  • Don't crouch or bend over.

CDFW's prevention advice doubles as a mountain-life checklist: avoid hiking, biking, or jogging alone at dawn, dusk, or night, deer-proof your property so you're not stocking the lion's pantry, trim dense vegetation near the house, add outdoor lighting, and give livestock and outdoor animals a sturdy covered shelter at night. If a lion is an immediate threat to people, that's a 911 call.

The Habits That Make Coexistence Work

Almost every wildlife problem in a mountain town traces back to food, so the whole playbook is short.

  • Trash and recycling: keep it in latched or secured bins, and put it out the morning of pickup rather than the night before.
  • Pet food: feed pets indoors, and never leave bowls out overnight.
  • Pets at night: bring cats and small dogs in after dark, when coyotes, bobcats, and lions do their commuting.
  • Fallen fruit: pick it up if you have trees.
  • Openings: close up crawl spaces and pet doors after dark.
  • Feeding: never intentionally feed wild animals, anywhere. In the state parks it's explicitly illegal, State Parks regulations prohibit feeding or disturbing any animal, and everywhere else it's how a normal animal becomes a problem animal that ends up relocated or killed.

Feeding wildlife is the opposite of kindness in these mountains. None of this requires fear. It requires the same tidiness you'd apply to keeping mice out of the pantry, applied at yard scale.

When You Find an Injured or Orphaned Animal

This is the section to bookmark, because it always happens on a Sunday.

For most hurt or orphaned wildlife, songbirds, squirrels, opossums, young raccoons, reptiles, the county's rehabilitator is Native Animal Rescue of Santa Cruz County at 1855 17th Avenue, Santa Cruz, (831) 462-0726, urgent line extension 0. Their own guidance on what to do when you find an animal comes down to three steps: take a photo, call, and their wildlife dispatcher will give you a number to text the photo to so they can tell you the right next move. Call before you drive; the county animal shelter lists their receiving hours as 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Don't try to feed or water a rescued animal, and don't handle anything you're not confident about. The phone call comes first.

Some animals route elsewhere, and Native Animal Rescue publishes the referrals:

  • Adult large mammals such as deer, mountain lions, bobcats, and adult raccoons: Santa Cruz County Animal Services at (831) 454-7200.
  • Injured deer specifically: the county shelter directs residents to CDFW dispatch at (916) 358-1312.
  • Marine mammals: the Marine Mammal Center at (415) 289-7325.
  • Oiled birds: the Oiled Wildlife Care Network at (877) 823-6926.
  • Ongoing wildlife conflicts, or to reach the state directly: our area is CDFW's Bay Delta Region, (707) 428-2002, and sightings or incidents can be reported through CDFW's Wildlife Incident Reporting system.

And the standing rule: if an animal situation is endangering people right now, on the road or otherwise, call 911 first.

We can't promise any animal can be saved, and neither can the rehabilitators. But this county is lucky to have a licensed wildlife hospital twenty minutes down the highway, and knowing the number is half the rescue.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I be worried about mountain lions in Boulder Creek?

Aware, not worried. Lions live here and mostly avoid people entirely; CDFW notes attacks are extraordinarily rare statewide. Follow the basics, supervise kids outside at dusk, keep pets in at night, don't feed deer, and know the encounter drill: don't run, look big, make noise, give it an exit. Report a lion that's threatening people or pets to 911 or CDFW.

Who do I call about an injured wild animal?

Native Animal Rescue at (831) 462-0726 (ext 0 for urgent), 1855 17th Avenue in Santa Cruz. Take a photo and call first; their dispatcher will tell you whether and how to bring the animal in. Injured deer and other large animals route to county Animal Services at (831) 454-7200 or CDFW dispatch at (916) 358-1312.

Is it really that bad to feed the deer or turkeys?

Yes, and it's the one habit that causes most of the rest. CDFW warns fed deer lose their fear of people and attract predators, and UC's wildlife guidance notes feeding wildlife is illegal and turns turkeys aggressive. Feeding also draws the coyotes and lions that follow prey. A wild animal's respect for your space is the thing you're protecting.

What keeps raccoons out of my trash?

Latched or locking bins, stored in a shed or against a wall if possible, and set out the morning of pickup. No pet food outside overnight, pet doors closed after dark. Raccoons give up on properties that never pay out; CDFW notes they become persistent exactly where food access teaches them to be.

A coyote walked through my yard in daylight. Is that abnormal?

Not by itself; coyotes move around the clock. What matters is behavior. A coyote that ignores you and keeps moving is being a coyote. One that approaches people or lingers after you haze it has likely been fed somewhere, and that's worth reporting through CDFW's Wildlife Incident Reporting system. Keep small pets supervised regardless.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This article links to official sources from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the UC integrated pest management program, California State Parks, and Native Animal Rescue of Santa Cruz County. Phone numbers, agency roles, and local requirements can change; the responsible agency is the authority for your situation.

Wildlife is one piece of settling into mountain living. For utilities, permits, road conditions, and county contacts in one place, see the Residents guide, and keep the mountain roads driving guide handy for the deer at dawn.

winter-landslide-warning-signs-boulder-c.title: Winter Landslide Warning Signs Around Your Property
winter-landslide-warning-signs-boulder-c.html:
The short version

  • Learn your property's baseline before winter so you can spot what's new. One odd crack can be nothing; a cluster, or anything getting worse during a storm, is a warning.
  • Watch for movement: new ground cracks or bulges, soil pulling away from foundations, tilting trees and fences, sticking doors, new seeps or saturated ground, a creek that suddenly runs muddy, and rumbling or cracking sounds.
  • Active movement or an imminent slide: leave immediately and call 911. Don't stop to investigate or grab things.
  • Below or near a CZU burn scar: treat a Flash Flood Warning as an evacuate-now alert, and know your evacuation zone before the season starts.
  • This is a homeowner's guide to noticing trouble early, not a substitute for a professional geologic assessment.

When heavy winter rain settles over a forested slope in the Santa Cruz Mountains, the ground you live on can start to move, and that risk rises sharply during and after the storm, especially below hillsides burned in the CZU fire. The reassuring part is that many slides give warning signs before they let go, and knowing what to look for can buy you time to act. This isn't a substitute for a professional geologic assessment; it's a homeowner's guide to noticing trouble early. If the ground is actively moving or a slide looks imminent, don't investigate. Leave and call 911.

What to watch for

The U.S. Geological Survey and slope experts point to a consistent set of warning signs. Around your home and yard, watch for:

  • New cracks or bulges in the ground, pavement, driveway, or the base of slopes.
  • Soil or fill pulling away from foundations, decks, or stairs, or new gaps opening up.
  • Tilting or leaning trees, fences, retaining walls, utility poles, or decks that were straight before.
  • Doors or windows that suddenly stick or jam, or new cracks in walls, foundations, or tile, a sign the structure is shifting.
  • Water showing up where it didn't before: new springs or seeps, unusually saturated ground, or water breaking out of a hillside.
  • Changes in a creek or drainage: water that suddenly turns muddy, or flow that rises or drops sharply, can signal movement upstream.
  • Sounds: faint rumbling, cracking, or trees popping, which can grow louder as movement increases, is a reason to get out now.
  • Cracking or bulging retaining walls, or a wall that's begun to lean.

Any one of these can have an innocent explanation. A cluster of them, or any that are getting worse during a storm, deserves serious attention.

What to do if you see the signs

  • If movement is active or a slide seems imminent (ground shifting, growing cracks, rumbling), get everyone out of the path immediately, if it is safe to do so, and call 911. Don't stop to gather things. If debris is already hitting the building you're in, the U.S. Geological Survey says not to go outside: get to the highest floor, or up onto something solid, and stay there.
  • If you notice worrying but not active signs, keep people away from the area, document them with photos, and consult a geotechnical or geologic professional. On a county road or right-of-way, report it to the county.
  • Reduce your exposure ahead of storms. Know which rooms and which side of the house are most exposed to an uphill slope. During a storm that could cause a slide, the National Weather Service's advice is to stay alert and awake rather than to sleep through it, because many landslide deaths happen while people are asleep. If you have real concerns about your slope, leave before the storm rather than waiting it out.

The burn-scar factor

Hillsides burned in 2020 shed water fast and are more prone to debris flows, fast and destructive slurries of mud, rock, and trees, during intense rain. The alert to watch for is a Flash Flood Warning: that is the product the National Weather Service issues for this hazard, there is no separate "debris-flow warning," and it can arrive with very little lead time. If you live below or near a burn scar, treat one as an evacuate-now alert, and know your evacuation zone before the season.

Before and after storms

Before winter, walk your property and note the baseline so you can spot changes. Clear culverts and drainage so water doesn't saturate a slope unnecessarily. After a big storm, walk it again, and remember that ground can keep moving for days after the rain stops, part of what to do after a major storm.

Frequently asked questions

What are the warning signs of a landslide?

New ground cracks or bulges, soil pulling away from foundations, tilting trees or fences, sticking doors and new wall cracks, new seeps or saturated ground, sudden muddy or changed creek flow, and rumbling or cracking sounds. A cluster of these, or any worsening during a storm, is a warning.

What should I do if I think a slide is starting?

If the ground is actively moving or a slide looks imminent, leave immediately, as long as leaving is safe, and call 911. If debris is already striking the building, don't go outside; get to the highest floor. For worrying but non-active signs, keep people away, document them, and consult a geologic professional.

Why is Boulder Creek at higher landslide risk?

Steep, forested slopes plus heavy winter rain, and hillsides burned in the 2020 CZU fire that shed water and can produce debris flows. Risk peaks during and just after big storms.

Last reviewed July 20, 2026. This guide draws on official guidance from the U.S. Geological Survey and the National Weather Service. It is not a geologic assessment.

For active danger, call 911. For forecasts, watch the National Weather Service, and for local road and slope conditions before you travel, check Mountain Status. For context on how much rain the ground has already taken this season, see our rain tracker.

pizza-in-boulder-creek.title: Is There Pizza in Boulder Creek?
pizza-in-boulder-creek.html:
Boulder Creek doesn't have a pizzeria right now. Boulder Creek Pizza & Pub, the place most people mean when they ask, closed permanently in May 2026. Nothing has replaced it downtown. If you want pizza tonight, you'll need to head down Highway 9.

You don't have to go far. One Friday-night option is closer than many people realize.

What happened to Boulder Creek Pizza & Pub

Boulder Creek Pizza & Pub had been downtown since 2012. When it closed in May 2026, nineteen people lost their jobs.

Owner Justin Acton is a Ben Lomond resident who led the Boulder Creek Business Association, served with Rotary, and sat on the Mountain Parks Foundation board. He was seriously injured in December 2025 when a drunk driver struck him outside his home, and the business couldn't carry on through such a long recovery. The shop gave the community more than pizza. Its kitchen supported school fundraisers, fed the fire department, and helped make Grad Night happen year after year. Boulder Creek got a lot of dinners from that oven, along with years of service. Justin and everyone who kept the shop going deserve the town’s gratitude and respect.

For our household the closure was personal in the ordinary way: Boulder Creek Pizza and Pub was our regular, the standing answer to pizza night for years, and we haven't had a true pizza night since. The baby and I did make the trip to Pizza Series in Scotts Valley recently to try their more unusual pies, which softened the blow without filling the hole. A town this size deserves its pizzeria back.

The closest thing to pizza night: Fridays in Ben Lomond

Coffee Nine at 9505 Highway 9 in Ben Lomond holds C9 Pizza Nights every Friday from 5 to 8 p.m. Its page lists “fresh, handcrafted pizzas, crisp salads, and a full lineup of beer, wine, and ice-cold drinks.” You can eat dinner there or take it home.

For a Boulder Creek family, this is the shortest pizza drive on the list. It also feels more like a valley pizza night than an errand.

C9 Pizza Night is a weekly event, not a permanent menu. Check the page before planning your Friday around it.

A note on La Placa

La Placa Bakery in Ben Lomond has sold take-and-bake pizzas for years, and plenty of local customers still make the drive for them. The bakery is closing its Ben Lomond location in early August 2026 and moving to Scotts Valley.

Check its location before you go so you don't make a wasted trip. The Ben Lomond closure is a real loss for the valley. La Placa will still be worth visiting at its new address once it opens.

The nearest pizzerias

Redwood Pizzeria at 6205 Highway 9 in Felton is the closest full pizzeria to Boulder Creek. It takes online orders for dine-in and pickup, but it doesn't deliver to Boulder Creek. Call 831-335-1500.

Round Table Pizza at 6267 Graham Hill Road in Felton is the chain option. You can order through the store’s own page or call 831-335-4771.

The Pizza Series at 226 Mt. Hermon Road in Scotts Valley is the furthest of the three. It's useful when you're already headed that way. Its site lists dine in and take out. Call 831-600-8318.

Does anyone deliver to Boulder Creek?

Yes. Round Table’s Felton store delivers to Boulder Creek through the store’s own ordering page. The Pizza Series delivers from Scotts Valley through DoorDash. Mountain Mike's Pizza in Scotts Valley delivers through Grubhub.

Redwood Pizzeria doesn't deliver to Boulder Creek. Plan to eat there or pick up your order in Felton.

Delivery areas change. They can shrink on rainy winter nights along Highway 9. If an ordering page rejects your address, call the store and ask. For options beyond pizza, our guide to what food delivery works in Boulder Creek covers restaurants and groceries.

What is open in town instead

Boulder Creek has no pizza, but it does have dinner. Four sit-down restaurants, a taqueria, a food truck, a hot dog stand, and two markets with deli counters operate within town limits.

Start with where to eat in Boulder Creek for the full picture. You can also browse the food and drink listings if you already know what you want.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Boulder Creek Pizza & Pub reopening?

No. It closed permanently in May 2026. No replacement pizzeria has opened downtown since.

Where is the closest pizza to Boulder Creek?

Coffee Nine’s Friday pizza night in Ben Lomond is the shortest drive. It runs only on Fridays from 5 to 8 p.m. Redwood Pizzeria in Felton is the nearest pizzeria operating on a regular schedule.

Can I get pizza delivered to Boulder Creek?

Yes. Round Table in Felton delivers to Boulder Creek. The Pizza Series in Scotts Valley delivers through DoorDash, and Mountain Mike’s in Scotts Valley delivers through Grubhub.

Redwood Pizzeria doesn't deliver up here, so it requires a dine-in or pickup trip. If an ordering page rejects your address, call the store. Delivery areas change with weather and staffing.

Does anywhere in Boulder Creek sell pizza by the slice?

No current source confirms a place selling pizza by the slice in Boulder Creek. If that changes, or if a market or cafe in town begins offering slices, tell us and we'll add it here.

Why does this page not list hours for every pizzeria?

Hours change, and a wrong hour is worse than no hour. Each business above links to its own page. That's the schedule to check before leaving home.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. Details follow each business’s own page where one exists. Where something couldn't be verified, it has been left unstated rather than guessed.

scopazzis-boulder-creek.title: Scopazzi's Restaurant & Lounge: Boulder Creek's Hundred-Year Dining Room
scopazzis-boulder-creek.html:
Scopazzi's is the special-occasion restaurant in Boulder Creek, an Italian dining room and lounge at 13300 Big Basin Way that has been feeding this town out of the same wooden building since 1915. People go there for anniversaries, visits from out-of-town parents, and dinners meant to mark something important.

The building came first

In June of 1915, Joe Locatelli laid the foundation for a hotel on Big Basin Highway. It opened as a boarding house called The Italia Hotel, built to house the loggers working the surrounding hillsides at the height of the timber years. One address holds much of the town's origin story.

The Locatellis saw the town changing. With the northern route to Big Basin State Park opening up, they shifted the emphasis from a bunkhouse to a travelers' hotel. In 1924 they added the redwood-windowed dining room and the patio on the east side, then renamed the place The Locatelli Inn. That dining room is still the room diners eat in.

The building also connects to two distinct parts of local history. Boulder Creek had a movie studio during the silent film years of 1914 to 1925. The restaurant's own history names Wallace Beery, Henry Fonda, Slim Summerville, Mary Pickford, and Tom Mix among the Hollywood people who visited the hotel while pictures were being shot here.

During Prohibition, in the restaurant's own careful phrasing, the site was known as THE place to go for the forbidden distribution from the local stills.

How it became Scopazzi's

The Locatellis ran the hotel and dining room until 1955, when they sold it to the Scopazzi family. The Scopazzis were experienced restaurateurs who turned it into the restaurant that stands today. John "Nono" Scopazzi added the lounge and the bar and closed out the hotel rooms for good.

In 1986, the current owners bought the restaurant and the name: Paul Violante, a long-time chef, and front-of-house manager Talal Janbay, who started there as a busboy. The building is square and vernacular, built entirely of wood. Its full second floor remains above the dining room.

The room, and what it is for

The dining room is dim, wood-lined, and unhurried. Scopazzi's isn't a quick weeknight stop. It's a restaurant for a two-hour sit-down meal, with a full lounge attached and pacing built around that kind of evening.

The menu is organized into House Specialties, entrees, salads and appetizers, luncheon specials, and desserts. There's also a young people's menu for kids and a Sunday champagne brunch that locals treat as its own occasion. For a first visit, the House Specialties list gives the clearest sense of the restaurant.

The bar is The Barrel Room. Wine by the glass splits between imported bottles and Santa Cruz Mountains labels. The local list deserves a look. This appellation grows serious wine, and the restaurant has been pouring it for decades.

When to plan around it

Scopazzi's isn't open every day of the week. It runs separate breakfast, lunch, and dinner services rather than one continuous kitchen, so check the schedule on the restaurant's own site before making plans.

It's also the town's banquet room. Private dining is available in the Banquet Room, the Creekside Room, and the patio, with capacity up to 200. In a town this size, that makes Scopazzi's the default venue for many memorials, receptions, and fiftieth birthdays. Custom menus are available, so arrangements start with a phone call.

Hours, menus, and prices change. Go to Scopazzi's own site or call 831-338-4444 for anything time-sensitive.

The menu

The full menu is on Scopazzi's own site; here is the shape of it, with August 2026 prices that will move.

  • House specialties are the headliners: pasta (ravioli a la Genovese or in gorgonzola cream, fettuccine Alfredo), chicken piccata and marsala, fish from calamari fritti to calamari steak in lemon beurre blanc and prawns scampi, and the veal that anchors the old-school side of the menu, scallopini or piccata ($43). Saturday adds roast prime rib au jus ($49).
  • Salads and appetizers run from soups and dinner salads through a seafood appetizer list.
  • Sunday brunch is its own 12-item card, eggs Benedict included.
  • Lunch, Wednesday through Saturday, has its own specials board, sandwiches (a calamari steak sandwich among them), and lighter entrees.
  • A young people's menu covers the kids at a flat price, and the dessert card runs long, with dessert wines and ports alongside.

The kitchen notes it never adds service charges to the bill.

Frequently Asked Questions

How old is Scopazzi's?

The building dates to 1915, when it opened as The Italia Hotel. The restaurant has operated under the Scopazzi name since 1955, when the Scopazzi family bought it from the Locatellis.

Does Scopazzi's take reservations or do private events?

It hosts private events regularly in the Banquet Room, the Creekside Room, and the patio, with capacity up to 200. Custom menus are available. Contact the restaurant directly to make arrangements.

Is Scopazzi's open every day?

No. It closes early in the week, and breakfast, lunch, and dinner run as separate services on different days. Check the restaurant's site or call before you go.

Where is Scopazzi's, and is there a bar?

13300 Big Basin Way, at the north end of Boulder Creek, phone 831-338-4444. The lounge is The Barrel Room, with wine by the glass covering both imported and Santa Cruz Mountains bottles.

Last reviewed August 5, 2026. History here is drawn from the restaurant's own published account and corroborated where possible. Hours, menus, and prices live on the business's own page.

More of the town's kitchens are in where to eat in Boulder Creek and the food and drink listings. See the rest of our Around Town guides, or tell us if something needs fixing.

red-pearl-boulder-creek.title: The Red Pearl: Boulder Creek's Chinese Restaurant
red-pearl-boulder-creek.html:
If you want Chinese food anywhere in the San Lorenzo Valley, the Red Pearl is where you go. It's at 13151 Highway 9 in downtown Boulder Creek, with dine-in and takeout service. It doesn't deliver, which is the most useful thing to know before you order.

It's dine-in and takeout only. Plan on driving.

The dragon on the wall

The Red Pearl's website gives the hours and tells the restaurant's story:

"In the Northern reaches of the San Lorenzo Valley, Located in the mystical mountains of Santa Cruz, is the Long ago town of Boulder Creek. It's there, at The Red Pearl, that the most delicious Chinese Food is Prepared fresh daily. Also there, is Zhujiang the Pearl Dragon, He has now come to these mystical mountains to dwell as protector of The Red Pearl, the owners, Jenny & Ren, and all who partake of its wondrous food."

Jenny and Ren are the owners. Zhujiang the Pearl Dragon is the guardian. The site calls these mountains mystical, a description that fits easily around here.

What kind of Chinese restaurant it is

The Red Pearl serves American-Chinese cooking with a broad menu. The categories include appetizers and soups, beef, chicken, lamb, pork and spareribs, seafood, mu shu, egg foo young, chop suey, noodles and chow fun, rice and fried rice, and vegetable and tofu.

Two parts of the menu are especially useful for locals. There's a vegan section including mock chicken, which isn't a given in a mountain town where the vegetarian option is often a side salad. There are also family dinner specials, built for a familiar situation: a household on a weeknight when nobody wants to cook.

The kitchen advertises food prepared fresh daily rather than a steam table. The room is small and plain. People come for the food, and because the valley has one Chinese restaurant and it holds up.

Ordering, and the drive

The restaurant's site has an online ordering link, and you can order by phone at 831-338-9800. Either way, the order is for pickup. The Red Pearl sits on Highway 9 in the middle of downtown. It's a short walk from most of the shops if you're already in town, and it's directly on the main road if you're coming up the valley.

The restaurant closes early in the week rather than running seven days, so a Monday craving needs a different plan. Its site carries the current schedule.

Hours and menu items change. Check the Red Pearl's own page or call 831-338-9800 before relying on anything time-sensitive.

The menu

The full menu runs past four hundred items across seventeen categories, and the current version with prices lives on the ordering site. The shape of it:

  • Lunch specials, daily 11 to 3: dozens of plates with steamed rice and soup or a fried wonton included, Kung Pao and Mongolian classics and General chicken among them, most under $10.
  • The classics, deep: appetizers, soups, beef, poultry, lamb, seafood, pork and spareribs, chop suey, mu shu, egg foo young, noodles and chow fun, and rice plates.
  • The vegetarian side is unusually serious: a full vegetables-and-tofu section plus an entire soy mock chicken category running to more than two dozen dishes, which is why the vegan section got its own mention above.
  • Family dinner specials bundle multi-course meals for the table.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the Red Pearl deliver?

No. Red Pearl doesn't deliver. Order for pickup, or eat in.

Can I order online?

Yes. There's an online ordering link on the restaurant's site. You can also order by phone at 831-338-9800.

Is the Red Pearl open every day?

No. It closes early in the week, so check the current schedule before driving up.

Are there vegetarian or vegan options?

Yes. The menu has a vegetable and tofu section and vegan dishes including mock chicken, which is unusual for the valley.

Where exactly is it?

13151 Highway 9, in downtown Boulder Creek, on the main block. Phone 831-338-9800.

Last reviewed August 5, 2026. Details follow the restaurant's own page. Hours and menus live there, not here.
