jenna-sues-cafe-boulder-creek.title: Jenna Sue's Cafe: Where the Morning Crowd Goes in Boulder Creek
jenna-sues-cafe-boulder-creek.html:
Jenna Sue's opens at 6 a.m. on weekdays, tied with the Tree House for the earliest door in Boulder Creek. The cafe sits at 13090 Highway 9 in the middle of the downtown shops, and its own site calls it the place "where friends meet in Boulder Creek," describing its job in town as hosting the morning crowd.

The menu

This is a full coffee house, not a counter with a pot on it, and the food is breakfast and lunch built for people who are on their way somewhere. The cafe doesn't post prices online, so ask at the counter.

  • Breakfast: biscuits and gravy, breakfast burritos, breakfast bagels, and something called the Astronauts Breakfast.
  • Sandwiches: BLT, turkey club, hot ham and swiss, Reuben on rye, avocado and cheese, hummus, and whole wheat wraps, with bagels and soup and salad alongside.
  • From the in-house bakery: the baking happens on site. Lori's coffee cake is named on the menu in its own right, and Dessert First Bakery shares the kitchen here, which is why some of its cookies and pastries turn up in the case even though the bakery itself has no shopfront.
  • Coffee and drinks: espresso drinks run the usual range, americano through mocha, plus drip and cold drinks. The beans are Java Bob's, the Santa Cruz small-batch roaster, and you can buy them by the bag as well as the cup.

Where it fits in town

Boulder Creek has three morning rooms and they're not interchangeable. Bella's is the sit-down diner, a plate and a table. The Tree House is the larger cafe at the north end, redwoods growing through the floor and room to sit, work, and socialize. Jenna Sue's is the downtown one and the early one, a small shop with only a handful of seats, an in-house bakery, and food that outruns the square footage.

It's also a landmark for something other than coffee. The free grocery giveaway runs every Friday at 3 p.m. in the open lot next to the cafe, no sign-up and no questions, moving to Junction Park if it rains. If someone gives you directions to it, Jenna Sue's is how they will describe the spot.

Hours and menu items change. Check Jenna Sue's own page or call 831-338-7008 for anything time-sensitive.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time does Jenna Sue's open?

Doors open at 6:00 a.m. Monday through Friday and 7:00 a.m. on weekends, and close at 2:30 p.m. daily. The Tree House keeps the same schedule, so the two cafes share the earliest opening in town.

Whose coffee do they pour?

Java Bob's, a small-batch roaster based in Santa Cruz. Bulk coffee is sold by the bag as well as brewed by the cup.

Is it open on Monday?

Yes. Jenna Sue's posts Monday hours, which isn't true of most of the town's dining rooms.

Is this where the Friday free groceries are?

Next door. The giveaway runs from 3 p.m. until the food is gone, in the open lot beside the cafe, and moves to Junction Park in the rain. See our free resources guide.

Where is it exactly?

13090 Highway 9, downtown Boulder Creek, in the middle of the shops. Phone 831-338-7008.

Last reviewed August 5, 2026. Hours and details follow the cafe's own page. Where other listings disagreed, the cafe's own page was used.

bellas-cafe-boulder-creek.title: Bella's Cafe: Boulder Creek's Sit-Down Breakfast
bellas-cafe-boulder-creek.html:
Bella's is the one place in Boulder Creek where breakfast means sitting down to a plate. Not a paper cup and a bagel on the way out, but eggs, a table, and someone bringing them to you. It's at 13132 Central Avenue, downtown, and it describes itself as "a local Santa Cruz County owned American breakfast and lunch joint."

What it is, and what it is not

Boulder Creek has three morning rooms and they do different jobs. Jenna Sue's is the coffee house in the middle of the shops, open at 6 and built for people on their way somewhere. The Tree House is the espresso bar at the north end with redwoods coming up through the floor. Bella's is the diner.

That's the useful distinction. If you want a full breakfast and an hour, this is the room. If you want a latte and a laptop, one of the other two is a better fit.

The French toast and the scrambles are the move. I can also report that Bella's eggs have the enthusiastic approval of the youngest and most brutally honest critic in our family.

American breakfast and lunch is the whole of it. Here is the shape of the breakfast board; prices move, and the counter is current.

  • From the griddle: pancakes by the short stack ($7.25) or full stack ($8.25) and French toast ($8.25), with a combo add-on of two eggs and a breakfast meat.
  • Omelets: large three-egg omelets served with home fries or hash browns and toast or an English muffin: plain ($8.25), Denver with ham, bell peppers, onions, and cheese ($10.95), Californian with avocado, tomato, bacon, and garlic ($11.25), Greek with black olives, tomatoes, and feta ($9.95), Spanish with mushrooms and cheese ($9.75), meat lovers ($11.50), and the mixer with avocado and mushroom ($10.25).
  • Breakfast plates: two eggs, or eggs with sausage, bacon, or ham ($7.50 to $9.75), all with home fries and toast.
  • Breakfast favorites: huevos rancheros ($10.95), eggs Benedict with smoked Canadian bacon ($11.25), cafe Florentine with poached eggs and grilled tomatoes ($11.25), and huevos mexicanos with jalapenos and avocado ($10.95).
  • Scrambles ($8.50 to $10.75): eight builds from jack-and-cheddar through pesto-and-tomato, and any of them can be made with fresh tofu instead of eggs for 75 cents.
  • Fruit and granola: granola with cold milk, fresh fruit bowls, and cups of fruit ($3.95 to $7.25).

Lunch runs alongside it; ask at the counter for the day's board.

Hours, and how to check them

Bella's keeps no website, and its social pages have gone quiet, so the phone is the channel: 831-217-5070.

Both the Visit Santa Cruz County listing and the business association's food page put it at 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. daily. Neither listing has been refreshed this year, so treat that as a starting point and call before you drive in for it, especially at the ends of the day.

If those hours are right, Bella's would be open seven days in a town where most of the dining rooms close Monday and Tuesday. Confirm by phone before you plan a Monday around it.

Hours and menu items change. Call 831-217-5070 for anything time-sensitive.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Bella's Cafe have a website?

No, and its Facebook page is out of date, so calling 831-217-5070 is the reliable route.

What are the hours?

The listings we can point to show 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. daily, but they predate this year. Call 831-217-5070 to confirm before you go.

Is Bella's a coffee shop?

No, it's a sit-down breakfast and lunch diner. For espresso and a counter, Jenna Sue's and the Tree House Cafe are the coffee shops in town.

Is it open on Monday?

The published listings say daily, which would include Monday. Because those listings aren't current, call first.

Where is it exactly?

13132 Central Avenue, downtown Boulder Creek. Phone 831-217-5070.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. This cafe keeps no website. The hours above come from official listings that predate this year and aren't confirmed current, so the phone number is the reliable source.

air-and-fire-boulder-creek.title: Air & Fire: The Mystical Bazaar on Highway 9
air-and-fire-boulder-creek.html:
Air & Fire has been on the downtown block long enough that the smell gives it away before the sign does. It's at 13150 Highway 9, and it calls itself a mystical bazaar, which turns out to be an accurate description of a room holding soap, crystals, tarot decks, and the work of local artists all at once.

What is inside

The shop makes a good deal of its own stock. Natural soaps, oil blends, candles, incense, and mists and potions are handcrafted on site with pure essential oils. Alongside that are crystals and stones both loose and set into jewelry, sterling silver pieces with specialty stones, and what the shop counts as more than 200 tarot and oracle decks, plus books, runes, and ritual supplies.

The other half of the floor is local. Air & Fire says it carries work from over 50 area artists, running from incense and jewelry to ceramics, wood carvings, cards, prints, and original paintings. Ginia's Gems, the handmade jewelry maker down the street at 13133 Highway 9, says her designs are among them.

There's a public altar in the shop for customers to use, and tarot readings, energy healing, body therapy, and hypnotherapy are offered by appointment. The shop also posts classes now and then.

Air & Fire posts its door policy on its homepage: "We welcome all humans regardless of race, gender, color, religion and sexual choices, all are safe here."

Hours

Air & Fire runs two seasons, and it dates them by the wheel of the year rather than the calendar.

  • Spring Equinox through Samhain, roughly March 20 to October 31: Tuesday through Sunday 11:00 to 6:30, Mondays 11:00 to 4:00.
  • Samhain through Spring Equinox, roughly November through March 19: Tuesday through Sunday 11:00 to 5:30, Mondays 11:00 to 4:00.

Those are the hours posted on the shop's own site as of August 5, 2026. Call 831-338-7567 before a special trip.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Air & Fire?

13150 Highway 9, in downtown Boulder Creek. Phone 831-338-7567.

What does it sell?

Handmade soaps, oils, candles, and incense; crystals and stones; sterling silver jewelry; tarot and oracle decks, books, runes, and ritual supplies; and artwork from local makers.

Does it do readings?

Yes, by appointment. Tarot readings, energy healing, body therapy, and hypnotherapy are all listed on its site.

Are the hours the same all year?

No. The shop closes an hour earlier in the winter season. Both schedules are posted on its own site.

Last reviewed August 5, 2026. Hours and stock follow the shop's own site. Seasonal hours change twice a year, so check before a special trip.

becks-shoes-boulder-creek.title: Beck's Shoes: The Weekends Only Store at the South End of Town
becks-shoes-boulder-creek.html:
Beck's Shoes is the reason you don't have to drive to Scotts Valley for work boots. It sits at 12550 Highway 9, at the south end of Boulder Creek, and it's one of two stores Beck's runs under its Weekends Only format. The other is in Capitola.

What Weekends Only means

It's an outlet format rather than a full-line store. The layout is a showroom of sale shoes up front, then back rooms where deeper discounts are sorted by dot color. Everything is in-store only, so there's no ordering the deal you saw and picking it up here.

The chain's stock leans practical, which suits the valley. Work and safety footwear, comfort and orthopedic brands, and outdoor and casual shoes, from names Beck's lists including HOKA, Birkenstock, New Balance, Brooks, UGG, Aetrex, Brunt, and Dansko. What's on the racks in Boulder Creek on any given weekend is a different question, and it turns over.

Hours

Thursday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., closed Monday through Wednesday. The "Weekends Only" in the name is the outlet format, not the schedule; the store runs four days a week. If you're making a special trip, 831-703-4307 reaches the store.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Beck's Shoes in Boulder Creek?

12550 Highway 9, at the south end of town. Phone 831-703-4307.

What are the hours?

Thursday through Sunday, 10 to 6. It's closed Monday through Wednesday, despite the Weekends Only name.

Can I order online and pick up here?

No. Weekends Only stores are in-store only.

What kind of shoes does it carry?

Work and safety footwear, comfort and orthopedic brands, and outdoor and casual shoes, sold at outlet pricing.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026.

boulder-creek-pharmacy.title: Boulder Creek Pharmacy: The Independent That Delivers
boulder-creek-pharmacy.html:
Boulder Creek Pharmacy is the independent at 13081 Central Avenue, and the single most useful thing about it is that it delivers prescriptions for free. That matters here more than it would down the valley. When a car is in the shop or Highway 9 is a mess, the medication still arrives.

What it does

It's locally owned and family operated, and it describes itself as serving the town for over 40 years.

Beyond filling and transferring prescriptions, the pharmacy handles medication synchronization, which lines your refills up so they all come due on one visit, and multi-dose blister packaging, which is the service it says it specializes in. It also does medication therapy management, medication adherence support, Medicare open enrollment help, and consultations by appointment. There's a free app for refills and reminders.

The front of the store is a real store. Over-the-counter basics, first aid, vitamins, infant care, sunscreen, and school and office supplies, plus a gift boutique with greeting cards, home decor, candles, kids' toys, and seasonal merchandise. It's a reasonable place to solve a birthday card and a prescription in one stop.

Delivery, hours, and the Rite Aid question

Free delivery runs throughout the San Lorenzo Valley. The pharmacy's own site also posts a banner welcoming former Rite Aid patients and naming free delivery to Felton and Scotts Valley, so if the closure moved your prescriptions, this is the local answer.

Monday through Friday 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., Saturday 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed Sunday. Sourced August 5, 2026. Phone 831-338-2144, fax 831-338-0901.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Boulder Creek Pharmacy deliver?

Yes, free, throughout the San Lorenzo Valley. Its own site also names free delivery to Felton and Scotts Valley. Call 831-338-2144 to set it up.

What are the hours?

Monday through Friday 9 to 6, Saturday 10 to 4, closed Sunday, as posted on the pharmacy's own site on August 5, 2026.

Can I transfer a prescription from another pharmacy?

Yes. Refills and transfers are both listed services. Call 831-338-2144.

What is multi-dose packaging?

The pharmacy sorts a person's medications into dated blister or bubble packs rather than separate bottles. It lists this as a specialty.

Is there anything to buy besides prescriptions?

Yes. A full over-the-counter section and a gift boutique inside the store, including cards, candles, home decor, toys, and seasonal items.

Last reviewed August 5, 2026. Hours and services follow the pharmacy's own site. Nothing here is medical advice; call the pharmacy or your prescriber with health questions.

creekside-wellness-boulder-creek.title: Creekside Wellness: Boulder Creek's Licensed Dispensary
creekside-wellness-boulder-creek.html:
Creekside Wellness is the licensed cannabis dispensary at 12603 Highway 9, toward the south end of Boulder Creek. It has operated since 2018 and it serves adults 21 and older only.

The details

The store publishes its state license number on every page of its site: C10-0000008-LIC. That number is worth knowing, because it's the difference between a licensed retailer and an unlicensed one, and it's checkable against the state's own license search.

Hours as posted on the shop's own site: Monday through Saturday 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., Sunday noon to 6 p.m. Sourced August 5, 2026. Phone (831) 338-3840.

The site carries a product menu and an online ordering link. It also puts a 21-and-over age gate in front of everything, so expect one before you can browse.

Where is Creekside Wellness?

12603 Highway 9, Boulder Creek. Phone (831) 338-3840.

What are the hours?

Monday through Saturday 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. and Sunday noon to 6 p.m., as posted on its own site on August 5, 2026.

Do I need to be 21?

Yes. It's an adult-use dispensary for customers 21 and older.

Is it licensed?

It publishes California license C10-0000008-LIC on its site.

Creekside is the one in Boulder Creek. For everything else in town, the business directory is the full list.

swag-boulder-creek.title: SWAG: The Eclectic Collective on Highway 9
swag-boulder-creek.html:
SWAG is the store you can't summarize in one word, which is why its owner settled on "the eclectic collective." It's at 13026 Highway 9, in the middle of the downtown block, and in 2026 it's in its tenth year.

What is on the floor

The shop's own list runs: restored mid-century stereos, vinyl, vintage apparel, local apparel, jewelry, art, and consignment. In practice it's a room you browse rather than shop, and the stock moves.

One part of that list is changing. Jeff Brough, who runs the shop, posted at the start of 2026 that console stereo sales had declined and that he was redirecting his attention toward on-site music events and away from restoration work, with the remaining consoles due to sell off through the year. If you're coming specifically for a restored console, call first; there may be a handful left, and there may not.

SWAG also carries select pieces from Stumptown Supply, the local apparel brand, which is the only place in town you can see those shirts in person.

The music

The other half of the business is a room with a stage in it. SWAG has been running live music, including a monthly Saturday series through the warm months of its tenth year and a set at Boulder Creek's First Friday. The shop states plainly that 100 percent of the door goes to the musicians.

Where the current lineup is posted changes, so its Facebook page is the channel to watch.

Hours, and the building

SWAG doesn't post hours. Call 831-295-9191 before a special trip.

what-the-directory-says-about-boulder-cr.title: What 315 Listings Say About the Boulder Creek Economy
what-the-directory-says-about-boulder-cr.html:
What 315 Listings Say About the Boulder Creek Economy

Sixty businesses in this directory have a street address in Boulder Creek. Thirty-eight of those sixty are on Highway 9/Central Avenue. That's the town you can walk: two connected stretches of road, and everything else scattered up the canyons or run out of a truck.

We keep a directory of 315 businesses and services across Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley, each one checked against a first-party source before it goes in. Counting them turns out to say something about the place. Here is what the list looks like when you add it up.

What is being counted

The directory holds 315 listings across 36 categories and 211 distinct subcategories, as it stood on July 29, 2026. A listing is a business, agency, park or service that we have verified and published. It's not a business license, a tax record or an employment figure, and it counts a one-person mobile welder exactly the same as a school district.

208 of the 315 listings, 66 percent, sit in the San Lorenzo Valley: Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, Felton, Brookdale and Mount Hermon. 117 of the 315, 37 percent, give Boulder Creek as their location. The rest are in Santa Cruz, Scotts Valley and a scattering further out.

Restaurants, cafes, bars and markets aren't in these counts. They live in a separate food guide with its own hours and its own checking schedule, which is why you won't find a restaurant category below.

The valley builds things and throws parties

Grouping the 36 categories into broader kinds of work, one block dwarfs the others.

80 of 315 listings, 25 percent, exist to build or maintain a building: general contractors, plumbers, electricians and solar installers, landscapers, excavators, tree crews, house cleaners, handymen and well-and-pump companies. General contractors alone are the largest single category at 25 listings, 8 percent of the directory. Fifty listings carry a license number, 21 of them contractors.

That's what a housing stock of steep parcels, private roads, septic systems, well water and post-fire rebuilds produces. It's also a decent proxy for what people up here spend money on.

The second block is stranger and easy to miss until you count it. 54 of 315 listings, 17 percent, serve weddings, parties and events: 11 venues, 8 wedding services, 8 kids-party businesses, 7 caterers and bar services, 7 cake and dessert makers, 7 party rental companies, 6 florists. One in six businesses in this directory exists because people get married under redwoods.

Not one of the 11 event venues has a Boulder Creek address. Four are in Ben Lomond, four in Felton, and one each in Soquel, Scotts Valley and Watsonville. The wedding economy is a valley economy, and its center of gravity is downstream of us.

Group Listings Share of 315
Building and maintaining property 80 25%
Weddings, parties and events 54 17%
Beauty, health and fitness 36 11%
Civic, emergency and community 30 10%
Money, professional and real estate 20 6%
Shopping and errands 19 6%
Education and childcare 18 6%
Wineries and lodging 18 6%
Cars and getting around 12 4%
Arts and culture 10 3%
Parks and recreation 10 3%
Pets and animals 8 3%

The grouping is ours. The underlying category counts are published in full alongside the directory so you can regroup them if you disagree.

Two in five have no front door

Every listing falls into one of three states.

  • 157 of 315, 50 percent, have a street address. A door, a lot, a gate.
  • 124 of 315, 39 percent, are marked as having no storefront. They come to you, or you meet them at your site, or the work happens in their garage.
  • 34 of 315, 11 percent, have neither. Mostly hotlines, utilities and county services, plus a handful whose address we haven't confirmed.

In Boulder Creek itself the split is sharper: of the 117 listings located in Boulder Creek, 50 have no storefront, 43 percent. And 23 of the 25 general contractors in the whole directory have no storefront at all.

That's the part worth carrying around. If you judge a mountain town by what you can see from the road, you'll conclude there's almost nothing here. Most of the economy is a phone number and a truck.

What the town has, and what it does not

Three categories are entirely Boulder Creek: tree care and defensible space (all 5 listings), handyman and property maintenance (all 4), and real estate (all 3). Retail concentrates here too. 13 of the 15 shopping listings are in Boulder Creek: building supply and hardware, a pharmacy, a shoe store, an antique store, and a run of gift and clothing shops. The other two are in Felton.

Nine categories have no business based in Boulder Creek: event venues, home services and repair, wedding services, kids parties, catering and bar, party rentals and decor, government and public services, transportation, and well and pump work.

Read that carefully. It means no business in that category is based in Boulder Creek. It doesn't mean you can't get the service. Most of those listings are mobile, and a good share name Boulder Creek or the San Lorenzo Valley in the area they cover. If you want a well drilled, someone will drive up. There's nobody in town to call first.

What this count cannot tell you

Plenty.

The directory is a curated list, not a registry. A business is in it because we found it and verified it, so the count measures our coverage as much as it measures the local economy. The trades are probably undercounted worst, since a solo operator with no website is the hardest kind of business to confirm.

A listing is one unit regardless of size. Boulder Creek Fire Protection District and a one-person nail studio each count once. Nothing here measures revenue, employees or how busy anyone is.

And it's a snapshot. 266 of the 315 listings, 84 percent, have a website, and 260, 83 percent, have a phone number we've confirmed. Every listing carries the date it was last checked, and most of these were checked in mid-July 2026. Businesses close. If you find one that has, tell us and we'll fix it.

Frequently asked questions

How many businesses are in Boulder Creek?

Our directory holds 117 listings located in Boulder Creek: 60 with a street address, 50 mobile or by appointment, and 7 with neither recorded. Restaurants and markets are counted separately in the food guide. The true number of businesses is higher than any directory can capture, since one-person operations without a website are hard to verify.

What kind of businesses does Boulder Creek have?

By count, the biggest block is building and property work: 80 of the 315 valley-wide listings, 25 percent. Weddings and events are second at 54, 17 percent. Retail is small but concentrated in town, with 13 of the 15 shopping listings located in Boulder Creek.

Is there anything Boulder Creek does not have?

Nine of the 36 categories have no business based in town, including event venues, transportation, and well and pump companies. Most of those services are available anyway from businesses based elsewhere in the valley that will drive up.

How current is this?

The counts come from the directory snapshot dated July 29, 2026, and the listings in it were verified between July 15 and August 5, 2026. Each listing on the site shows its own verification date.

Counted from the Boulder Creek Local business directory, snapshot dated July 29, 2026. Every figure and chart value in this article comes from that count. what-jobs-near-boulder-creek-pay.title: What Jobs Near Boulder Creek Pay, According to 327 Listings
what-jobs-near-boulder-creek-pay.html:
What Jobs Near Boulder Creek Pay, According to 327 Listings

On the morning of August 5, 2026, our jobs board carried 327 openings within reach of Boulder Creek. Not one of them was in Boulder Creek. The closest were nine listings at San Lorenzo Valley Unified, a nine-minute drive down to Ben Lomond.

That's the first thing the data says about working up here, and it sets up the second. Of those 327 listings, 199 post a pay figure, 61 percent. That sounds like a healthy disclosure rate until you see who is doing the disclosing. Almost every employer posting a number is a public agency.

Here is the whole board, counted.

Who posts pay, and who does not

Split the 327 listings by where the work happens and the pattern is stark.

Where Listings Post a pay figure Share
Core, within about 45 minutes 137 109 80%
Extended, further out in the county or over the hill 87 79 91%
Remote 103 11 11%

224 of the 327 listings are on-site, and 188 of those post pay, 84 percent. Every single one of those 188 comes from a public employer: 182 from the county schools feed, 4 from the City of Scotts Valley, 1 from the County of Santa Cruz, and 1 from Second Harvest.

The 36 on-site listings that post no pay come from six employers, and five of the six are private. Safeway has 10 openings and no rate on any of them. Community Bridges has 10, Seascape Beach Resort has 8, and there's one each from Central Fire District and Dream Inn. The exception is Cabrillo College, which leaves the pay off 6 of its 19 postings.

The remote side is worse. 103 of the 327 listings are remote, 31 percent, and only 11 of them post pay. In the Technology category, 6 of 57 listings post a figure, 11 percent. In Education, 160 of 166 do, 96 percent.

So this isn't a picture of what work pays around Boulder Creek. It's a sharp picture of what public-sector work pays, and a near-total blank everywhere else.

What hourly work pays

80 listings post an hourly rate. 76 of them are on-site, and all 76 are school district positions. The other four are remote contract rates, which run from $14 to $170 an hour and belong to a different world.

Across those 76 local hourly listings, the median posted rate is $22.66 an hour, using the midpoint where a range is given. Half the postings fall between $19.75 and $26.64. The lowest posted rate is $16.84 and the highest is $50.61, for an adult-education Spanish GED instructor.

Hourly band Listings Share of 76
Under $20 20 26%
$20 to under $25 31 41%
$25 to under $30 18 24%
$30 and up 7 9%

58 of the 76 are classroom roles, and 24 of the 76 are instructional assistants, paraeducators or paraprofessionals. The other 18 are the jobs that keep a school running: bus drivers, custodians, cafeteria staff, office and payroll technicians, a health care assistant. Those pay $17.06 to $30.49.

The nine listings at San Lorenzo Valley Unified, the closest employer on the board, follow the same shape. Six post an hourly rate, from $19.94 for an instructional assistant to $29.47 for a bus operator. One posts $160 a day for math intervention support, and two are flat coaching stipends of $1,176 for a season.

What salaried work pays, and why there are fewer figures than listings

70 listings post an annual figure, and 63 of those are on-site. Before quoting a median, one thing has to be said out loud: those 63 figures aren't 63 independent data points. There are only 29 distinct salary ranges among them, because a district publishes one salary schedule and then attaches it to every opening. 27 of the 63 carry the exact same range, $58,520 to $97,574, the Pajaro Valley Unified teacher schedule.

So the median annual figure on this board is that schedule, more or less by definition. The useful version is the list of the actual schedules.

Employer and role Posted annual range Listings
Pajaro Valley Unified, teacher schedule $58,520 to $97,574 27
Live Oak Elementary, teacher schedule $57,461 to $103,800 3
County Office of Education, specialist schedule $55,104 to $115,074 3
Pajaro Valley Unified, special education $29,260 to $48,787 3
Scotts Valley Police Department, police officer $101,280 to $135,732 2

The top of the on-site range is a Chief Business Officer at Pajaro Valley Unified, $211,100 to $248,418. The bottom is a 0.20 FTE elementary music position at $10,897 to $19,728, which is a real annual figure for a one-day-a-week job and a good reminder that an annual number without an FTE next to it means very little.

A note on the ranges themselves. 62 of the 63 on-site annual listings post a band rather than a single number, and the median band is $39,054 wide. That's a salary schedule, not a negotiation: the bottom is what a new hire gets, the top is what someone gets after twenty years and a master's degree. Read the bottom number as the offer.

The pay figure is not always a wage

Of the 199 listings that post a figure, the figure means six different things.

What's posted Listings
An hourly rate 80
An annual salary or schedule 70
A flat stipend for a season or assignment 38
A monthly salary 6
A daily rate 4
A rate per teaching unit per semester 1

The stipends are worth pulling out. 38 listings pay a flat stipend, and 29 of those are coaching or athletics roles. They run from $1,176 to $5,641 for an entire season. A high school head coach isn't being paid a wage in any normal sense, and anyone reading a job board that averages everything together would never know these rows were in there.

How far you would be driving

Nobody on this board is hiring in Boulder Creek. The 224 on-site listings sit in eight cities.

Where the work is Listings Drive from Boulder Creek
Watsonville 87 about 50 minutes
Santa Cruz 75 about 30 minutes
Aptos 33 about 40 minutes
Scotts Valley 10 about 20 minutes
Ben Lomond 9 about 9 minutes
Capitola 7 about 35 minutes
Los Gatos 2 about 25 minutes
Soquel 1 about 35 minutes

The median on-site listing is a 40-minute drive. 203 of the 224, 91 percent, are 30 minutes or more. Only 19 are within 20 minutes. Put the $22.66 median hourly rate next to a daily round trip over Highway 9 and the arithmetic of working down the valley gets real fast.

What this count cannot tell you

This is a board, not a labor market. It carries what 11 sources publish in a structured feed, and 188 of the 327 listings come from one of them, the county schools feed on EDJOIN. Schools dominate this board partly because schools are big employers and partly because schools publish complete, structured, pay-included feeds while a hardware store tapes a card to the window.

So: 166 of 327 listings are in Education, 51 percent. That's a fact about the board. It's not a claim that half the jobs near Boulder Creek are in schools.

Two more limits. The feed's own pay parser disagrees with a careful reading of the posted text on 36 rows, usually where a signing bonus or a master's stipend sits at the end of the line, so every figure here was re-derived from the posted text rather than taken from the parsed field. And two posted figures were set aside as unusable: a $200 monthly reserve officer position and a "$3k to $10k" sales listing.

None of this is an average salary for Boulder Creek, and we're not going to compute one. It's 327 specific openings on one specific morning.

Frequently asked questions

Are there any jobs in Boulder Creek itself?

Not on this board, as of August 5, 2026. The closest listings were nine at San Lorenzo Valley Unified in Ben Lomond, about a nine-minute drive. An opening in town that never reaches a published feed won't appear here, and plenty of them never do.

What is the typical hourly rate?

Among the 76 local listings that post an hourly rate, all of them school district jobs, the median is $22.66 an hour and half fall between $19.75 and $26.64. That's the median of what is posted, not of what's paid.

Why do so few remote jobs post pay?

We don't know why, only that they do not: 11 of 103 remote listings post a figure, 11 percent, against 188 of 224 on-site listings. The on-site employers posting rates are almost entirely public agencies whose salary schedules are published documents.

How often does this change?

The board refreshes automatically and the counts move daily. Everything here describes the August 5, 2026 snapshot. For live openings, use the jobs board.

Counted from the Boulder Creek Local jobs board, snapshot dated August 5, 2026. Every figure and chart value in this article comes from that count. The board aggregates 11 published sources and isn't a census of local employment. Pay figures were re-derived from each listing's posted salary text. Openings change daily; see /jobs for what's live now.

joes-bar-boulder-creek.title: Joe's Bar: Live Music, Karaoke, and a Thursday Pool Tournament
joes-bar-boulder-creek.html:
Joe's runs on a weekly rhythm, and once you know it you don't need to check anything. Karaoke Tuesday. Pool Thursday. A band Wednesday, Friday, and most Saturdays. It's at 13118 Highway 9, in the middle of the downtown block, and it's 21 and over.

The week

Tuesday: karaoke, 8:30pm.

Wednesday: Neighborhood Night, 8pm. A solo player or a duo rather than a full band, and it runs most weeks straight through the fall.

Thursday: pool, sign-ups close at 8pm. A weekly double-elimination 8-ball tournament with a $5 entry that goes back out as prize money to the top three. The full eight-ball rule set is posted where you can read it in advance, which tells you how seriously it's taken.

Friday and Saturday: bands, usually 8:30pm. This is the busiest end of the week and the lineup turns over constantly: Americana, blues, reggae fusion, classic rock covers, tribute sets.

There's no cover charge on music nights. The bar asks you to tip the bands and the bartenders instead.

Boulder Creek Local carries the Joe's calendar on the events page, and the bar's own site at drinkatjoes.com lists every booked act with a short write-up and a link to the artist.

The building and the bar

Joe's has been Joe's since before 1977, when Lucille and Joe Kamisha owned it and gave it the name. Karin Ann Park joined her uncle David in the business in 1977 and went on to run it as sole owner for 38 years. Diane and Gina took over on June 1, 2015.

The building goes back further, and the bar tells the story itself: a late-1800s structure that served as a community center and the garage for the volunteer fire department's pump wagon, rebuilt in the early 1900s to the size it is now, holding the bar plus two smaller storefronts. Joe's own account lists a blacksmith, a bakery, a commission store, and at least two earlier bars in the same walls. That's the bar's history as the bar tells it, and we haven't matched it against our own records yet.

Joe's also hosts fundraisers for Valley Churches United, which runs the food pantry serving the San Lorenzo Valley, Scotts Valley, and Bonny Doon.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Joe's Bar?

13118 Highway 9, Boulder Creek, CA 95006. Phone 831-338-9417. The bar's directions page puts it at milepost 13 on Highway 9, on the right if you're coming up from Santa Cruz.

What are the hours?

10am to 2am, daily. That comes from the business rather than from anything published on its site, so call 831-338-9417 if you're planning around an early or a late arrival.

Is Joe's 21 and over?

Yes. Bring ID.

Does Joe's serve food?

No. Joe's is a bar, not a kitchen. The food answer sits directly behind the building: River Dogs, the hot dog stand, shares the lot out back, and its winter hours run to 5 on weekends. Time it right and the two work as a pair.

Is there a cover charge for live music?

No. The bar asks that you tip the musicians and the bar staff.

When is karaoke?

Every Tuesday at 8:30pm.

How does the Thursday pool tournament work?

Double-elimination 8-ball. Sign-ups close at 8pm, entry is $5, and the entry money becomes prize money for the top three finishers.

I'm a musician. How do I get booked?

The booking page on the bar's own site names the person to contact and how to reach them.

Which website is the real one?

drinkatjoes.com. The older joesbc.com address just forwards to it.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. Hours and the age policy come from the business, not from its website. Lineups change weekly, so check the bar's own site or our events page before you go.

kitten-kornher-rescue-boulder-creek.title: Kitten Kornher Rescue: The Kittens in the Corner Window
kitten-kornher-rescue-boulder-creek.html:
There's a corner in downtown Boulder Creek where the window has kittens in it. That's the whole landmark, and it works: people who can't remember the address remember the window.

The corner is Highway 9 and Forest Street, and the rescue is Kitten Kornher Rescue. The name is the family's, not a play on "corner." Jeanette Kornher runs it.

What it is

Kitten Kornher Rescue is a nonprofit, not a shop. Its stated purpose is to rescue, rehabilitate, and rehome abandoned, stray, and at-risk kittens, and it's a partner in the Best Friends Animal Society network. It became a 501(c)(3) in December 2024, which is the change that lets it issue tax-deductible receipts for donations.

The work is more than housing kittens until someone takes one. Reporting on the rescue describes a partnership with Project Purr's spay/neuter program for feral cats, a microchip program aimed at reuniting lost cats with their owners, and taking in pregnant mothers so they have somewhere safe to give birth. Boulder Creek Veterinary Clinic is the veterinary partner.

The storefront it shares

The same address is Boulder Creek Glass. The San Lorenzo Valley Post reported in 2022 that the glass business has been at it since 1982, that it passed to John Kornher from his parents, and that he holds a C-17 glazing license. Skylights, doors, showers, windows, and stained-glass work on the one side; kittens on the other.

That's also how the rescue started. The Post's account has Jeanette moving back to Boulder Creek from Pennsylvania with John to take over the glass shop, meeting a feral litter she couldn't walk away from, and going from there.

Full disclosure: my household is not a neutral party here. Our cat Biscuit came home from Kitten Kornher, and the rescue remains one of the two most requested stops in the family. Our baby ranks the kittens in the corner window somewhere above most of the town's other attractions, with only the pharmacy's toy shelf as real competition. If you have a small child and twenty minutes, you know where to go. And if you leave with a cat, you'll be in good company.

How to help

Three ways, and a call settles all of them.

Adopt. Ask what's available now. A list published in January tells you nothing useful in August.

Donate. Money, since December 2024, is tax-deductible. Cat food and litter have long been left at the store by neighbors, and a January 2026 vet bill over $1,000 is the kind of thing that prompts a fundraising push, so ask what's short this month rather than guessing.

Foster or volunteer. Not published anywhere. Worth asking.

Phone 831-428-4726. Email kittenkornher@gmail.com. The Facebook page is the only channel the rescue keeps, and it's where anything current gets posted.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Kitten Kornher Rescue?

13101 Highway 9, Boulder Creek, on the corner of Highway 9 and Forest Street. It shares the storefront with Boulder Creek Glass.

What are the hours?

Not published. Call 831-428-4726 before making a trip, especially if you're coming with a carrier or a car full of donations.

Is it a registered charity?

Yes. It obtained 501(c)(3) status in December 2024, so donations can be receipted as tax-deductible. Ask for a receipt at the time you give.

How do I adopt?

Call 831-428-4726 or message the Facebook page. The rescue publishes no adoption form or fee schedule, so the process starts with a conversation.

Can I just come and see the kittens?

The window is on the sidewalk and free to anyone walking past. Going inside depends on whether the storefront is open, which is why the phone number is the first thing on this page.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. Hours, adoption process, and current needs are not published anywhere first-party, so call before you go.

viscosity-art-glass-boulder-creek.title: Viscosity Art Glass: Blown Glass, and an Hour to Make Your Own
viscosity-art-glass-boulder-creek.html:
Most of the shops downtown sell things somebody else made. Viscosity sells things made in the building, and for an hour it'll let you make one.

Scott Graham and Cristy Aloysi blow contemporary glass in Boulder Creek and sell it out of a gallery on the downtown block: bubble bowls, vases, drinking glasses, garden glass, wall pieces, and jewelry.

The gallery

Open Fridays 1 to 3 and Saturdays 1 to 5, plus Sundays in December, and by appointment otherwise. The studio's own advice, which is worth repeating: call before you drive a distance, because a retail show can pull them out on a shop day.

Viscosity also opens to the public during two annual events, the San Lorenzo Valley Art Tour in May and Santa Cruz County Open Studios in October.

The classes

An hour, one on one with a glassblower, two students to a slot, and you leave with the thing you made. You book an hour somewhere between 10 and 2 and pick a project going in.

Project Price
Bowl or vase $120
Garden accent $140
Pumpkin $110
Tumbler or drinking glass $95
Float, paperweight, ornament, sun catcher, or gift $80

Ages 6 and up, and the studio notes that children under 10 may need help from an adult. Groups of six or more can book a private party, which runs with two instructors and lets everyone choose their own project. Gift certificates are available, which is the obvious answer to a hard-to-buy-for person in a town this size.

Booking goes through the studio's online scheduler, or call 206-669-1955 or email viscositystudio@yahoo.com.

Finding it

Viscosity is at 13158 Central Avenue, in historic downtown Boulder Creek, and the phone is 206-669-1955.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Viscosity Art Glass?

13158 Central Avenue, downtown Boulder Creek. The phone is 206-669-1955.

When is the gallery open?

Fridays 1 to 3, Saturdays 1 to 5, Sundays as well in December, and other times by appointment.

Can I take a glassblowing class?

Yes. Sessions are one hour with one-on-one help from a glassblower, two students per slot, scheduled between 10am and 2pm, from $80 depending on what you make.

How old do you have to be?

Ages 6 and up. The studio says children under 10 may need help from an adult.

Can I book it for a group?

Groups of six or more can book a private party with two instructors, and everyone picks their own project.

Can I buy the work online?

Yes, through the studio's Etsy shop, linked from viscositystudio.com.

Who are the artists?

Scott Graham and Cristy Aloysi.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. Prices, hours, and class dates come from the studio's own site. The street address is in dispute between sources, so call before making a special trip.

lille-aeske-arthouse-boulder-creek.title: Lille Aeske Arthouse: The Gallery and Listening Room on Highway 9
lille-aeske-arthouse-boulder-creek.html:
Boulder Creek has two rooms where you go to hear something. Joe's is the bar, where the band plays over the noise of a good night. Lille Aeske is a 350 square foot gallery with a stage in it, where the room exists for the music: the lights go down, the show is the whole evening, and the art on the walls listens with you.

The name is Danish for "little box," which is the joke and also the accurate description. The arthouse writes it lowercase with a ligature, lille æske, and sits at 13160 Highway 9.

The gallery

The gallery is open Saturday and Sunday, 11 to 3. It's a white-cube room with adjustable theater lighting, and it has shown paintings and prints alongside ceramics, sculpture, and installation work.

The rotating show hangs for the whole month rather than for one evening, so the weekend hours are a real chance to see it properly. Work is for sale during gallery hours and during events.

The music

Concerts are ticketed and they're the reason to plan ahead. The pattern is consistent: doors at 7, show at 8, $30 in advance or $35 at the door, with food and drinks at the show.

Two are booked for this autumn. Maya DeVitry and Mark Erelli play Thursday, October 8. Liz Longley plays Friday, October 23. Both are the kind of songwriter booking that suits a small room: alt-country, indie folk, Americana, the sort of set that a listening room serves better than a bar does.

The calendar is where anything new lands first, and the arthouse runs a newsletter for the same purpose. Upcoming Lille Aeske shows also appear on our events calendar alongside everything else happening in the valley.

First Friday, and hiring the room

Lille Aeske helped start Boulder Creek's First Friday art walk and it's still one of the anchors, opening with live music and refreshments alongside the month's art. First Friday falls on the first Friday of the month; check the calendar for the current evening's details.

The room is also available to rent by the hour. What you get is specific: a compact kitchen, a 22-piece dinner service, a redwood banquet table, seating and staging areas, the vaulted gallery, a custom redwood and steel bar, and a lounge. People use it for rehearsal dinners, off-site meetings, private parties, band practice, photo shoots, and pop-up dinners, and a host can be arranged.

Who runs it

Sarah and James Mackessy opened the arthouse in spring 2014 and built its reputation on a listening room, farm-to-table pop-up dinners with local chefs, and First Friday receptions. Their 2018 installation, Spektrum, drew people back repeatedly. They moved to Wisconsin in 2019.

It's since been run as a nonprofit. Lille Aeske Arthouse is a registered 501(c)(3), with Anil Prajapati as managing director, and it takes donations and volunteers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Lille Aeske Arthouse?

13160 Highway 9, Boulder Creek, CA 95006. Phone 408-309-0756, email arts@lilleaeske.com.

When is the gallery open?

Saturday and Sunday, 11am to 3pm. It's also open during performances and private events.

How much are concert tickets?

The shows currently listed are $30 in advance and $35 at the door, with doors at 7pm and the music at 8pm.

Is there food and drink at shows?

Yes, at events. There's no standing bar or kitchen service outside of them.

Can I rent it for a private event?

Yes, by the hour. The venue rental page lists what's included and how to ask.

Is it a business or a nonprofit?

A nonprofit. It's a registered 501(c)(3) and it accepts donations and volunteers.

How do I show my work there?

Through the submission form on its arts page. Work shown at First Friday hangs for the month.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. Show dates and gallery hours come from the arthouse's own site and calendar. Its First Friday page carries dates that have already passed, so check the calendar for the current month.

boulder-creek-farmers-market.title: The Boulder Creek Farmers Market at Junction Park
boulder-creek-farmers-market.html:
Thursday afternoon, downtown, and the lawn at Junction Park fills up with folding tables. It runs from 1:30 to 5:30, May through October, and it's small in the way a mountain town market is small.

It's easy to miss if you don't live here. The market isn't on the county's market lists, but it's there every Thursday through the season, and the rec district posts about it as the weeks come up.

The basics

  • When: Thursdays, 1:30 to 5:30 p.m.
  • Season: May through October
  • Where: Junction Park, Middleton Avenue at Railroad Avenue, Boulder Creek
  • Who runs it: the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District, 831-338-4144
  • Dogs: only certified service dogs are allowed at Junction Park during the market, per the Santa Cruz County Health Department

Thursday dates for the rest of this season are on our events calendar alongside everything else happening in town.

What a small mountain market carries

Set your expectations to the size of the town and you'll enjoy it more. This isn't the Wednesday market in downtown Santa Cruz, and it isn't trying to be. A market this size runs on a short list rather than a wide one: what's ready this week, from growers and makers who are mostly working at a scale you can see.

What that means in practice is that it rewards flexibility. Go with a fixed plan for dinner and you might come home short a vegetable. Go willing to build dinner around whatever looks good and you'll do fine. It also means the season matters more here than it does at a big market that can backfill from a hundred miles away: May is thin, high summer is the peak, and the last weeks in October are a different shop from the first ones in June.

The other thing a small market does well is that the person selling you the thing usually grew it.

I come at this market as someone who grows food a mile up the road, which means I know how much work is in every table you walk past. Buy the thing that's only there for two weeks. In this valley the season moves fast, and the best of it never makes it to a store shelf.

Getting there and parking

Junction Park sits downtown where Middleton Avenue meets Railroad Avenue, a short walk off Highway 9. It's the park with the lawn, the picnic tables, and the path down to the river, so the market shares the space with whoever's already there on a warm afternoon.

Parking is downtown parking: some on the street, some in the surrounding lots, and less of it between 1:30 and 5:30 on a Thursday than at other times. If you live close, walking is the easier call. See our roads and parking notes if you're coming in from out of the valley.

Come early in the window if you want the best of the produce, or late if you'd rather browse without a crowd.

What isn't published

Two things people ask about, and where each one stands:

EBT and CalFresh. Whether this market takes EBT isn't published anywhere we can find, and we won't guess at it. Call the recreation district at 831-338-4144 before you rely on it.

Becoming a vendor. There's no current published application or fee for a market space. The same number is the place to start.

If you get an answer from the district on either one, tell us and we'll put it on this page.

Making an afternoon of it

The market lands at a good hour for stacking errands. The downtown shops are a two-minute walk, the library is up on West Park Avenue, and dinner is easy if you'd rather not cook what you just bought. See where to eat in Boulder Creek.

The district also runs Free Food Fridays in the open lot next to Jenna Sue's Cafe, every Friday from 3 p.m. until the items are gone, moving to Junction Park if it rains. That's a separate program from the market, and it's free.

Frequently Asked Questions

What day is the Boulder Creek Farmers Market?

Thursday, from 1:30 to 5:30 p.m., at Junction Park.

What months does it run?

May through October. It doesn't run through the winter.

Where exactly is it?

Junction Park, at Middleton Avenue and Railroad Avenue in downtown Boulder Creek, a short walk off Highway 9.

Can I bring my dog?

Only certified service dogs are allowed at Junction Park during the market, under a Santa Cruz County Health Department rule that applies to markets generally.

Does the market accept EBT or CalFresh?

That isn't published anywhere. Call the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District at 831-338-4144 to check before you go.

How do I sell at the market?

There's no published application. Start with the recreation district at 831-338-4144, or its office at 13333 Middleton Avenue, open Tuesday to Friday 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

Is this a certified farmers market?

Nothing we or the organizers can point to says it is. Santa Cruz County's certified-market list doesn't include Boulder Creek, and no certification is advertised anywhere. Treat it as a community market rather than a certified one.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. Day, hours, season, and operator are confirmed locally rather than from a listings site, because no listings site carries this market. Confirm before you build a trip around it.

boulder-creek-library.title: The Boulder Creek Branch Library on West Park Avenue
boulder-creek-library.html:
The Boulder Creek branch is up on West Park Avenue, off the main run of Highway 9. On a Saturday morning there's a craft circle going, somebody's picking up a hold, and a couple of people are just sitting. All of it is free, which is most of what needs saying about why a branch matters in a town this size.

This branch was also my first job. I spent my teenage years here as a library page, and once the carts of returns were shelved, the staff would hand me projects. My favorite: painting the alphabet for the kids' reading section, twenty-six little paintings, each letter with an animal to match. I loved that job, and it's part of why this free, unhurried corner of town still feels like one of the best ones.

Hours and where it is

  • Address: 13390 West Park Avenue, Boulder Creek, CA 95006
  • Phone: 831-427-7703
  • Monday to Thursday: 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
  • Friday: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.
  • Saturday: 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
  • Sunday: closed

It's one of ten branches of Santa Cruz Public Libraries, so a card works valley-wide and holds can travel between branches.

What runs every week

Two of the branch's programs are weekly through the fall, and both are aimed squarely at the under-fives and whoever brought them.

Toddler and Preschool Storytime runs Wednesdays at 11 a.m. starting in September: stories, songs, and a simple craft, held outdoors or indoors depending on the weather.

Discovery Zone Playgroup runs Fridays, 11 a.m. to noon, also from September. It's drop-in free play for young children with an adult along, with toys for gross motor skills and a chance to practice being around other kids. Arrival and departure times are flexible, which is the detail that makes it usable with a toddler.

Community Crafters meets Saturdays, 10 a.m. to noon, and it's the one for grown-ups: learn a new craft or bring the project you've been meaning to finish and work on it alongside other people. It's been running weekly since August.

What runs monthly

The rest of the calendar follows a monthly rhythm. On the current schedule:

  • Boulder Creek Book Group, third Thursday, 11 a.m. to noon. Registration is required, and you can join in person or by Zoom.
  • Mobile Health Clinic, fourth Tuesday, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.
  • Write Now! Writing Group, last Saturday, 3 to 4 p.m.

Those patterns come from the dates currently on the calendar rather than from a standing rule, so check our events calendar for the actual date before you plan around one.

One-off events worth watching for

The branch also books talks and drop-in sessions that don't repeat. Coming up: a Quilting with Friends session on September 8, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., no registration needed, bring your own supplies. And on September 19, 1 to 2 p.m., a Firewise talk on the neighborhood program and the home ignition zone approach to hardening a house, for adults 18 and over.

That last one is worth flagging for anyone who moved here recently. See our wildfire evacuation guide and the late summer wildfire checklist for what to do in the meantime.

Everything the branch has scheduled appears on our events calendar alongside the rest of what's happening in town.

For families

Between storytime, the playgroup, and the Saturday craft circle, the library carries a real share of what there is for small children in Boulder Creek, and all of it is free. See kids' activities in and around Boulder Creek for the full picture, a day with kids in Boulder Creek for how to build a morning around it, and free resources in Boulder Creek for what else costs nothing.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the Boulder Creek library hours?

Monday to Thursday 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Friday 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., Saturday 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Closed Sunday.

Where is the Boulder Creek library?

13390 West Park Avenue, Boulder Creek, CA 95006, off Highway 9.

Is there a storytime?

Yes. Toddler and Preschool Storytime is Wednesdays at 11 a.m., starting in September, held outside or inside depending on the weather.

Does the book group meet on Zoom?

Yes, either way. It meets the third Thursday at 11 a.m., in person and by Zoom, and registration is required.

Do I need to register for the playgroup or the craft circle?

Discovery Zone Playgroup is drop-in, and you can arrive and leave when it suits you. Community Crafters is a Saturday morning drop-in too. The book group is the one that needs registering.

Can I use my card at other branches?

Yes. This is one of ten Santa Cruz Public Libraries branches, and holds move between them.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. Hours and address come from Santa Cruz Public Libraries. Program dates come from the library's own calendar and can change, so confirm before you go.

kbcz-boulder-creek-radio.title: KBCZ 89.3 FM: The Radio Station in Downtown Boulder Creek
kbcz-boulder-creek-radio.html:
At 89.3 on the dial there's a goth show, a big band show, a reggae show, and a news roundup, all of them made by people who live here. KBCZ broadcasts from a storefront studio at 13200 Highway 9, in the middle of downtown, which is a fair description of the whole thing: the radio station is right there on the street with everybody else.

How to listen

  • On the radio: 89.3 FM. Coverage runs the length of the San Lorenzo Valley, plus Scotts Valley, Lompico, and parts of Santa Cruz.
  • Online: the station runs its own web player, linked from kbcz.org. It works in a phone browser without an app store download, and it can be saved to a home screen.
  • After the fact: past shows are archived on Mixcloud.

Two pages on the station's site are worth a bookmark. The schedule shows what's on today by day of the week, and Recently Played will tell you the name of the song you just heard and missed.

What's on the air

Around thirty-eight shows a week, hosted by about twenty-six people. The station's own account of it is that the programming is entirely original and roughly 90 percent of it goes out live from the downtown studio.

The lineup is the opposite of a format. There's Americana and Irish music, goth and heavy metal, reggae, big band, doo wop, jazz, progressive rock, world music, and a drive-time rock show. There's a local news roundup and interview programming. Weekdays are the fullest, with Wednesday carrying the most; weekends are lighter.

Its tagline is "From the Skyline to the Sea," and its own summary of itself is that it's non-political and non-religious.

How the station got here

The short version is that the town went and got itself a radio license.

In 2012 an NCE, or non-commercial educational, FM license came available covering Boulder Creek. Valley residents started meeting about it, and in June 2013 the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District board voted to go after it. KBCZ was born at 90.1 FM.

Then came the years of doing it in whatever room was available: pre-recorded shows produced above Jenna Sue's coffee shop, then a move in May 2015 to a small room at the rec center that the station's own history calls, plainly, the closet. Streaming started that July. On July 15, 2016, the online programming went out over 90.1 FM for the first time.

In December 2016 the park district handed KBCZ the space at 13200 Highway 9 that it still occupies, and the doors opened to the public in February 2017. In January 2021 the FCC granted extended coverage and the frequency it has now, 89.3.

The station has since added a second room, Studio B, built largely by DJs and volunteers with paint rollers.

August 2020

The part of the station's history that matters most to people who were here is the week of the CZU fire.

On August 18, 2020, KBCZ DJs broke into regular programming and started reporting the evacuations as they came in. When the whole valley and Scotts Valley were emptied, the DJs kept an emergency broadcast schedule running from wherever they'd evacuated to, one from Watsonville, one from Santa Cruz, the station manager from Seaside. Someone attended the twice-daily press conferences and streamed them to the station's Facebook page.

Some of the people doing it had lost their own houses. The station puts that in its own history without making much of it.

For where that fire sits in the town's longer story, see six years after the CZU fire. For what to do when the next emergency comes, see wildfire evacuation and what the sirens are for.

Getting involved

The station is run by one part-time staffer and everybody else is a volunteer, which means the door is open.

It says it has both daytime and evening slots open and is actively looking for hosts, and it's explicit about the range: local history, cooking, travel, farming, gardening, homesteading, animals, cars, sports, theater. It's equally explicit about the limit: it isn't currently taking shows focused on politics or religion.

Hosting isn't the only way in. The volunteer form also takes people for technical and engineering work, events and festivals, social media, and fundraising.

Local businesses can underwrite, which on a non-commercial station is a different thing from advertising and is held to FCC guidelines about how a spot can be worded. Nonprofits and community groups can submit a public service announcement to be read on air.

Music Fest

The station's signature fundraiser is the KBCZ Music Fest, an afternoon of live bands at Garrahan Park. In 2026 it's Saturday, August 29, from 2 to 7:30 p.m., with beer and wine, food, vendors, and tickets at $15 in advance or $20 at the door for adults and $5 or $10 for children five to twelve. Under five is free.

We have a fuller guide: KBCZ Music Fest 2026, what to know before you go.

Frequently Asked Questions

What frequency is KBCZ?

89.3 FM. It was 90.1 until the FCC granted the new frequency and wider coverage in January 2021.

Where is the KBCZ studio?

13200 Highway 9, Suite A and B, in downtown Boulder Creek. The station's own site footer still lists Suite A only, which predates the second studio.

How do I listen online?

Through the web player linked from kbcz.org. No download, and it can be added to a phone's home screen.

How do I become a DJ?

Fill in the volunteer form and say what show you'd want to make. The station says it has daytime and evening slots open. It isn't taking shows focused on politics or religion.

Who runs KBCZ?

One part-time staff member plus more than thirty volunteer DJs, working under the District Manager of the Boulder Creek Recreation and Park District. The park district pursued the license and provided the space.

How do I get an announcement on the air?

Local nonprofits and community events can send a PSA through the station's form. They're aired at the station's discretion.

Can my business support the station?

Yes, through underwriting. Ask at 831-703-4420 or kbcz89.3fm@gmail.com.

boulder-creek-ioof-hall.title: The I.O.O.F. Hall on Forest Street: Boulder Creek's Odd Fellows
boulder-creek-ioof-hall.html:
There's a plaque on the building at 152 Forest Street that says 1900, and there's a hall upstairs that you can rent for a party. Both of those facts have been true of the Odd Fellows for a long time. The order was founded on the principle of a common fund for people who needed one, and a lodge hall is the physical version of that: a room the town can use.

The lodge room is the second floor. The ground floor is storefronts, currently Kitten Kornher, Boulder Creek Glass, and Geist Builders, so the building works the way lodge halls always have: the order keeps its room upstairs and the town does business below.

Boulder Creek Lodge #152 is still there, still running the hall, and still tending a cemetery in the woods.

Renting the hall

This is the practical part, and it's the reason most people arrive at this page. The lodge rents the building for events, and what's on offer is a real hall rather than a room in a restaurant: a lodge room, banquet and meeting rooms, and a kitchen that comes with china and flatware.

The published application asks for the following, and treats them as a starting point rather than a fixed price list, since it says rates depend on the type of group, the type of event, the length of the contract, and what the building has to do for you:

  • Lodge room, including the banquet and meeting rooms but not the kitchen: $350
  • Banquet and meeting rooms on their own: $50 an hour
  • Kitchen, including use of the china and flatware: $150
  • Refundable security and cleaning deposit: $300
  • Setting up the day before costs extra

The terms that catch people out are worth knowing before you fall in love with the room. You need liability insurance, at least $1,000,000 per occurrence, naming the lodge as additional insured, and you need it in writing if you're serving alcohol. The signed agreement is due 30 days before the event. Music has to be off at 11 p.m. and everyone out before 1 a.m., and amplified music may need a sound amplification permit. No candles or open flames of any kind. No smoking or vaping. You clean up, and the building has to be clean before noon the day after.

Cancel 25 or more days out and you get everything back. Closer in, you keep the deposit and part or none of the rental fee.

The rental application is a PDF on the lodge's site. Rates on that application are undated, so confirm them before you budget: call the lodge at 831-338-2531 or email BoulderCreekIOOF@gmail.com.

Boulder Creek is short on event space, and the down-valley options in our wedding venues guide mostly aren't in Boulder Creek at all. This one is, and it's walking distance from downtown.

Who the Odd Fellows are

The name is the joke that stuck. In seventeenth-century England, working people from different trades pooled part of their wages into a common fund to cover sickness, unemployment, and burial, and turned out to help each other rebuild a barn or put in a crop after a bad season. It was odd enough at the time to find people organized purely to give aid that the name got attached and never came off.

The order calls itself the Three Link Fraternity, for Friendship, Love, and Truth. It was founded in North America in Baltimore on April 26, 1819, when Thomas Wildey and four members from England instituted Washington Lodge No. 1, in a city then dealing with yellow fever and mass unemployment. The stated purpose was to visit the sick, relieve the distress, bury the dead, and educate the orphans.

It was also the first national fraternity in the country to include both men and women, when it adopted the Rebekah Degree on September 20, 1851. Boulder Creek's lodge installs its officers jointly with a Rebekah lodge.

The lodge in Boulder Creek

The Santa Cruz County Historical Trust plaque on the Forest Street building reads "1900, I.O.O.F. Hall, Built by Boulder Creek Lodge 152." And the county's Historic Resources Inventory agrees: its survey records the hall as built in 1900 for the lodge, standing on its original site, in continuous lodge use ever since, with the ground-floor storefronts part of the original design. A third line of evidence points the same way: local historian Lisa Robinson's history of the valley records a merchant opening for business on the lower floor of the IOOF building in August 1900, which only works if the building was up by then (Santa Cruz County Historic Resources Inventory, DPR 523 form for the I.O.O.F. Lodge Hall, 1980s survey with a 1994 addendum).

What is documented from further back is that the lodge was a going concern in the town's timber years. Edward Martin's 1911 History of Santa Cruz County, writing up a local man's life, notes in passing that he was a member of Boulder Creek Lodge No. 152 and had held all of its chairs (pp. 220 and 221), the sort of detail that only gets written down when a lodge is part of how a town organizes itself. That was Boulder Creek at its loudest, when the mills ran and the trains hauled lumber out of the valley. See the logging boom and our history timeline for what the town looked like around it.

Where the lodge met before the hall went up is not something we can pin down. The historic maps of downtown show more than one second-floor lodge hall within a block of the same intersection, and the records that would settle which one belonged to the Odd Fellows are the lodge's own. That's a question for the lodge, not for a map.

The cemetery

At the end of Harmon Street, a white gate marked I.O.O.F. opens onto three acres of redwoods, with graves fitted in wherever the trees allow, some perched on slopes steep enough that the stones lean into the hill. Despite the initials on the gate, it's a community cemetery. Anybody can be buried there, and the town's founding families are.

The headstone that looks oldest, dated 1862, is a promise kept. Martha S. Peery died of consumption in 1862 while she and her husband Joseph were crossing to California, and he buried her along the trail under a cottonwood headboard he carved with a jack knife. Thirty-seven years later he went back for her, and on July 25, 1899, he reinterred her here in a plot he'd prepared years before. The earliest recorded burial on the ground itself dates to 1882.

By local historian Lisa Robinson's account in the Mountain Bulletin, the cemetery came to the Odd Fellows the way a lot of things in a small town do: somebody had to take care of it. In 1909 it was offered to the Boulder Creek lodge as a free gift, along with adjoining land from J. W. Peery and Isaiah Hartman, on condition the lodge maintain it as an up-to-date cemetery, and in early 1910 the deed passed to the trustees of Lodge No. 152. That April the lodge held a cleanup day; the Mountain Echo reported nearly eighty people served lunch, schoolchildren among them. Volunteers are still doing the same work more than a century later.

A 1997 grave survey by Chris and Susan Benson, posted on the lodge's own site, counted 156 markers, three of them Civil War veterans, with the same family names recurring the way they do in a town this size: Peery, Pilger, Horstman, Hesse, Branson.

In August 2020 the CZU fire burned through the woods right up to the gates. Firefighters held the line at the cemetery by hand, stone by stone, and it came through with scorched undergrowth and singed pickets but its monuments intact, as the San Lorenzo Valley Post recorded that November.

Burying the dead was one of the four founding purposes of the order, so a lodge holding a cemetery is the original job rather than a sideline. The grave map and fee schedule pages on the lodge's site currently sit empty, so if you're researching family here or asking about a plot, the lodge office is the place to start.

Still active

The website's newest news is from 2019, which says more about who maintains websites than about who maintains the lodge. The Odd Fellows co-host the town's Winter Festival each December alongside the business association and the recreation district. See our holiday events guide.

There's also a standing fundraiser: Java Bob's donates 20 percent of proceeds to the Boulder Creek IOOF when you enter IOOF at checkout, and takes 5 percent off your order.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is the Boulder Creek IOOF Hall?

152 Forest Street, Boulder Creek, CA 95006, a short walk from downtown.

Can I rent the hall for an event?

Yes. The lodge rents the lodge room, the banquet and meeting rooms, and a kitchen, singly or together. Call 831-338-2531 or email BoulderCreekIOOF@gmail.com.

How much does it cost to rent?

The published application lists $350 for the lodge room with the banquet and meeting rooms, $50 an hour for the banquet and meeting rooms alone, $150 for the kitchen, and a $300 refundable deposit. The application is undated and says rates depend on the event, so confirm before you budget.

Do I need insurance?

Yes. The agreement requires liability cover of at least $1,000,000 per occurrence with the lodge named as additional insured, and proof of it if you're serving alcohol.

How late can an event run?

Music off at 11 p.m., everyone out before 1 a.m., per the rental agreement. Amplified music may need a sound amplification permit.

Is there a kitchen?

Yes, and it comes with china and flatware. It's priced separately from the rooms.

Where is the IOOF cemetery?

At the end of Harmon Street, behind a white gate marked I.O.O.F., on three acres of redwoods above town.

Who can be buried there?

It's a community cemetery, not a members-only one. Contact the lodge office at 831-338-2531 or BoulderCreekIOOF@gmail.com about plots; the fee schedule page on the lodge's site is not currently filled in.

How old is the building?

A Santa Cruz County Historical Trust plaque on it says 1900 and credits Boulder Creek Lodge 152 with building it. Two independent records agree: the county's Historic Resources Inventory dates it to 1900, and a merchant is recorded opening on the lower floor in August 1900. We still haven't seen a deed, but the date is well supported.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. Address, contact, and rental terms come from the lodge's own site and its published rental application, which carries no date. The 1900 building date is supported by the plaque, the county's Historic Resources Inventory, and a contemporary business opening on the ground floor that August. Cemetery history draws on local historian Lisa Robinson's Mountain Bulletin article, the Bensons' 1997 grave survey on the lodge's site, and the San Lorenzo Valley Post's 2020 reporting. Confirm rates and availability with the lodge.
