first-friday-boulder-creek.title: First Friday in Boulder Creek: The Monthly Art Walk Downtown
first-friday-boulder-creek.html:
On the first Friday of the month, downtown stays up past its bedtime. Doors that would normally be locked by six stay open until eight, makers set tables out on the sidewalk, and somebody is usually playing somewhere. It runs 5 to 8 p.m., it's free, and it's the closest thing Boulder Creek has to a standing night out.

The 2026 dates

Every one is 5 to 8 p.m. downtown, and each month has a theme:

Date Theme
Friday, August 7 Summer Carnival
Friday, September 4 Shop and Swap
Friday, October 2 Spooktacular
Friday, November 6 Giving Thanks
Friday, December 4 Ugly Sweater

These come from the Boulder Creek Business Association, which runs the event, and they're on our events calendar too.

What it is

Not a festival, and not a street fair. There's no gate and no ticket. What happens is that the businesses along Central Avenue and Highway 9 open late and put something on: art on the walls, a table of handmade things out front, a musician in a corner of a shop that isn't usually a venue. It's not just the shops, either. Vendor tables run along the sidewalks between them, selling art, candles, succulents, Stumptown shirts, whatever the month brings.

That makes it a walking event. You park once, you go up one side and down the other, and the whole thing is compact enough to do properly in two hours with time to stop and talk. The themes give each month a bit of costume and decoration, and in practice they change the mood more than the format.

If you're new to town, this is the single easiest evening to meet people. It's also the easiest way to find out what's in the shops downtown, which is not obvious from the street.

For me, First Friday is equal parts gift shopping and discovery; it's how I learned just how many talented makers live scattered through these mountains, and it's where I stock up on gifts nobody else will be giving. But my favorite memory isn't a gallery. A couple of years ago, one table belonged to a girl of maybe ten, selling books she had written and illustrated entirely on her own, set up with complete confidence among the professionals. We bought a couple as gifts for our nephew, and I still think about her. That's the real event: partly a market, and partly the town showing you who it's raising.

Who takes part

Lille Aeske Arthouse is the anchor and, by its own account, was one of the forces behind starting First Friday here. It opens for the evening with the month's art on the walls, and that art hangs for the whole month rather than the one night, so a Saturday or Sunday visit during gallery hours will still catch it.

SWAG has a room with a stage in it, and has booked live music for First Friday evenings. The shop's standing policy on music is that the entire door goes to the musicians.

Stumptown Supply sets up as a vendor. It's an online brand the rest of the month, with one rack downtown, so First Friday is the reliable way to see the shirts in person before you buy.

Boulder Creek Antiques at Mac's Place puts makers out front and keeps the doors open late.

Good Vibes takes part as well.

Plenty of the other downtown shops are open for it too. The essential shops guide and the downtown guide will tell you what else is on the street.

Practical notes

Parking. Downtown parking, on an evening when more people than usual are downtown. Arrive at five and it's easy; arrive at six thirty and it isn't. Walking or biking in from close by is the local move.

Kids. It's an early evening on a sidewalk, so it works fine with children, and the themed months in October and December work particularly well. There's also a dedicated Kid Zone behind the sheriff substation, put on by Robin Imholte of Messy Play Kits.

Dinner. Five to eight lands on either side of dinner. See where to eat in Boulder Creek, or make an evening of it with our night out guide.

Weather. Some of it is outdoors. In October and November, bring a layer for when the sun drops behind the ridge, which happens early here.

The seasonal ones

Two months get folded into something larger.

The October First Friday, Spooktacular, opens the town's Halloween stretch. See Halloween in downtown Boulder Creek for the rest of it.

The December First Friday, Ugly Sweater, sits alongside the Winter Festival and the tree lighting. See our holiday events guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is First Friday in Boulder Creek?

The first Friday of the month, 5 to 8 p.m., in downtown Boulder Creek.

Is it free?

Yes. There's no ticket and no gate. You're paying for whatever you decide to buy and nothing else.

Who organizes it?

The Boulder Creek Business Association. Its events page carries the current dates and themes.

What's the theme this month?

August is Summer Carnival, September is Shop and Swap, October is Spooktacular, November is Giving Thanks, and December is Ugly Sweater.

Can I set up a table or sell there?

BCBA doesn't publish a vendor process, though it does ask for volunteers on its events page. Contact BCBA through its site to ask.

Is it good with kids?

Yes. It's early, it's on the sidewalk, and there's a Kid Zone behind the sheriff substation run by Messy Play Kits. October and December in particular are built for it.

Where do I park?

Downtown, in the usual spots, and earlier is easier. If you're within walking distance, walk.

Last reviewed August 12, 2026. Dates, times, and themes come from the Boulder Creek Business Association. Which shops are open on a given evening varies, so treat the list above as the reliable core rather than the whole of it.

springygirl-boulder-creek.title: Springygirl: The Secondhand Boutique on Central Avenue
springygirl-boulder-creek.html:
Springygirl doesn't take your old clothes. The reason is better than the rule: the racks are bought from nonprofits, so every pass through the store sends money somewhere useful before the clothes ever reach a hanger.

What's on those racks is gently used women's clothing and accessories, hand-picked one piece at a time. Nothing arrives in a case of twelve. That's the whole proposition, and it's why regulars treat a visit as a hunt rather than an errand.

What it's like inside

Small, full, and loud in the good way. Color everywhere, racks packed close, a wall of clothing above the racks. One shopper review the shop publishes describes sizes running from small up to 4X, which isn't a given in a store this size.

Spring, who runs it, is the sort of shopkeeper who'll pull something off a rack you'd have walked past. The reviews she chooses to put on her own site all say some version of that, which tells you how the place works: you're not left alone with the racks unless you want to be.

Everything is one of a kind by definition, so the stock turns over constantly. Come back in three weeks and it's a different shop.

It's also a shop that rewards a walk rather than a trip. 13130 Central Avenue sits in the middle of the downtown block, so a Saturday afternoon here can take in the boutique, a couple of doors of antiques and glass, and lunch, without moving the car.

Hours and finding it

Springygirl is at 13130 Central Avenue, in the middle of the downtown block. It's open Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, noon to 5. Phone (831) 704-2994.

There's no online store. Everything happens in the room; the fitting room is where the shop earns its regulars.

If you join the Style Club by email, the shop sends $10 off a purchase of $20 or more, plus occasional notes about new arrivals. New stock shows up on Instagram between visits.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Springygirl?

13130 Central Avenue, Boulder Creek, CA 95006. Phone (831) 704-2994.

What are the hours?

Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, noon to 5. Closed Monday through Thursday.

Is it a thrift store?

No. It's a curated secondhand boutique. Pieces are hand-selected and sold in good condition rather than sorted by the bin.

Can I bring in clothes to sell or donate?

No. Springygirl doesn't take consignments or clothing donations. Inventory is purchased directly from nonprofit organizations.

Can I shop online?

Not currently. The shop is in-store only.

What sizes does it carry?

A shopper review published on the shop's site describes sizes from small to 4X. Stock changes constantly, so what's on the rack on any given day varies.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. Address, phone, and hours come from the shop's own site. Stock is one of a kind and turns over quickly.

herrick-games-hobbies-boulder-creek.title: Herrick Games and Hobbies: The Painting Masterclasses on Pine Street
herrick-games-hobbies-boulder-creek.html:
A hobby shop in a redwood town of a few thousand people should not be flying in Golden Demon winners. Herrick Games and Hobbies does. Its masterclass roster reads like the podium at an international painting competition, because that's what it is: World Model Expo gold medalists, Crystal Brush finalists, Monte San Savino champions, and a painter who took Golden Demon Gold at AdeptiCon this year. People drive over the hill and fly across the country to spend two days at 13111 Pine Street learning to weather a Knight Titan.

It's a family business. Brothers Skye and Christian Herrick started it with Skye's spouse Jade, first in Virginia, and it's been here since 2020. Local reporting puts the first Boulder Creek storefront above Jenna Sue's Cafe in October 2021, with the move up to Pine Street in 2024.

What's on the shelves

The core of it is Games Workshop, and the range is deeper than the square footage suggests: Warhammer 40,000, Age of Sigmar, The Old World, and Horus Heresy, plus the specialist boxes that smaller shops skip. Kill Team, Necromunda, Blood Bowl, Warcry, Warhammer Underworlds, Adeptus Titanicus, Legions Imperialis. Black Library novels and Lord of the Rings sit alongside them.

Then there's the paint wall, which is the real reason a painter drives here rather than ordering online. Citadel, Vallejo, Army Painter, Scale75, Tamiya, Kimera Kolors, AK Interactive, Abteilung 502, Coat d'Arms, Dirty Down, Colour Forge, plus brushes, glues, tools, spray, and terrain. If you paint, you already know how rare it is to see those ranges in one room.

Beyond Games Workshop, the shop stocks miniatures from Bushido, Moonstone, Perry Miniatures, Victrix, Wargames Atlantic, Relicblade, Big Child Creatives, and Star Wars, along with board games. The store describes itself as a hobby shop built around high-end products that are hard to find anywhere else, all in one place, and the shelf list backs it up.

There's a special order form on the site for anything not in stock, and the shop ships nationally at a flat $10 under $100 and free above it, going out Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays.

The painting classes

This is what makes the shop unusual for the valley. Herrick hosts multi-day masterclasses taught by competition painters, on subjects like airbrush intensives, large-scale mechanical weathering, non-metallic metal, and color composition on resin busts. One visiting artist designed the class model herself and based it on the redwoods.

The store says spaces fill fast and classes regularly sell out, and it passes 95 percent of class revenue to the teaching artist. Dates aren't posted on the artist page, so text the store to find out what's coming.

Adopt-a-Gamer

In August 2020, Skye Herrick evacuated a house he'd owned for two days, ahead of the CZU fire. He left his entire gaming collection behind, and while he was displaced, other gamers sent him models, paints, and tools so he'd have something to do with his hands.

Adopt-a-Gamer came out of that. If someone loses a collection to a fire, an illness, a job loss, the store takes an email at adoptagamer@herrickgames.com, works out quietly what was lost, and puts a replacement army together from donated product and community purchases. Anyone with unbuilt models sitting in a closet can send them in.

The shop also commits every February and September profit to charity, sponsors the NOVA Open Charitable Foundation, and has run auctions for Doctors Without Borders. For more on the fire that started this, see six years after the CZU fire.

Getting hold of them

The address is 13111 Pine Street, a short walk off Central Avenue. The store publishes the number (479)-HERRICK and says it prefers texts, so that's the way to reach them, about class dates or anything else. There's also support@herrickgames.com if you'd rather write.

Store hours aren't published anywhere on the site, so message ahead before making a special trip.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Herrick Games and Hobbies?

13111 Pine Street, Boulder Creek, CA 95006, just off Central Avenue downtown.

What are the store hours?

The shop doesn't publish hours on its website. Text (479)-HERRICK before a trip. If you know the current hours, tell us and we'll add them.

What does it sell?

Games Workshop's full range including the specialist games, hobby paints and brushes across a dozen brands, terrain, tools, board games, and miniatures from Bushido, Moonstone, Perry, Victrix, and others.

Does it run painting classes?

Yes. Multi-day masterclasses taught by international competition painters, including Golden Demon winners. Dates aren't posted online, so text the store to ask.

Is there open gaming?

The shop's own event page refers to open gaming nights, but no current schedule is published and two different patterns are in circulation, so ask before you turn up with an army.

Who owns it?

Brothers Skye and Christian Herrick, with Skye's spouse Jade.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. Address, stock, and program details come from the store's own site. It publishes no opening hours, so contact the shop before a special trip.

bowzer-baths-boulder-creek.title: Bowzer Baths: Dog Grooming on Highway 9 Since 1998
bowzer-baths-boulder-creek.html:
Read this part first: Bowzer Baths currently takes small dogs for baths and haircuts, and medium dogs for baths only. That's the shape of the business today, and it's the thing worth knowing before you call.

Beyond that, it's the town's grooming shop, at 13156 Highway 9, open Tuesday through Friday, 9 to 5, and it's been grooming mountain dogs under that name since 1998. The stated priority is a quiet room and a calm animal.

What a groom includes

The full bathing experience is more thorough than the name suggests. Flea shampoo plus a second shampoo chosen for your dog's coat, conditioner, blow dry, anal gland expression, ear cleaning, nail trim, pads shaved, and a sanitary trim.

The complete grooming experience is all of that plus a haircut of your choice.

There's also drop-in nail trimming, which is the useful one if your dog's nails have got ahead of you and you don't need the rest.

Price depends on breed size, coat, the condition the coat's in, how the dog handles the process, and the work involved, so it's quoted rather than listed. A full groom can take up to three hours.

What to expect when you drop off

Dogs are crated before and after the groom. The shop starts your dog when it arrives and calls you when it's done, and it asks for prompt pickup because it isn't a daycare. Owners don't stay during the groom, on the reasoning that most dogs stop listening to the groomer the moment a parent is in the room.

Drying is mostly done by hand. When a dog finds hand drying stressful, especially around the face, cage drying is used instead, on a low or cool setting with the dog watched throughout.

Anal glands are expressed externally only when they're full, and only if you say yes at drop-off. Teeth aren't brushed as a rule, on the sensible grounds that once every few months doesn't accomplish much. If you brush at home daily and want it done, ask at drop-off.

If your dog's coat is badly matted, expect a short cut. Small mats come out; large ones can't be brushed out without hurting the animal.

Cancellations want 24 hours' notice. Repeated no-shows or short notice get charged in full.

Puppies, older dogs, and how often

The shop suggests starting a puppy once it's had its first set of shots, around 8 to 12 weeks, with a simple bath, blow dry, and nail trim so it gets used to the noise and the handling before anything more involved. After that, most dogs go every 4, 8, or 12 weeks depending on breed and coat.

For a dog that struggles to stand or has a serious health condition, Bowzer Baths will tell you to go elsewhere: to a veterinarian who can monitor the animal, or to a mobile groomer who'll come to your house. That's the right answer and it's worth knowing they'll give it.

Booking

Phone (831) 338-0717 or email bowzerbaths@gmail.com. Appointments only, Tuesday through Friday, 9 to 5.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Bowzer Baths?

13156 Highway 9, Boulder Creek, CA 95006. Phone (831) 338-0717.

What are the hours?

Tuesday through Friday, 9 to 5.

What size dogs does it take?

Currently small dogs for baths and haircuts, and medium dogs for baths only. Call to check where your dog falls.

How much does it cost?

Prices aren't published. Cost depends on size, coat, coat condition, temperament, and services performed, so you'll get a quote.

How long does a groom take?

Up to three hours, depending on breed, size, and coat condition.

Can I stay with my dog?

No. Owners aren't allowed to stay during the groom.

Does it groom cats?

The shop's own site describes dog grooming only.

What if my dog is old or unwell?

The shop recommends grooming at a veterinarian instead, where the animal can be monitored, or using a mobile groomer who comes to you.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. Hours, services, and policies come from the shop's own site. Its current size limits are posted on the home page and may change, so call before booking.

lone-wolf-kenpo-boulder-creek.title: Lone Wolf Kenpo Academy: Karate, Kickboxing, and Tai Chi on Highway 9
lone-wolf-kenpo-boulder-creek.html:
Lone Wolf Kenpo Academy takes students from age five, which is worth knowing if you've a kid who needs somewhere to put their energy on a rainy valley evening. It's at 13089 Highway 9, at the north end of downtown, and it's open Monday through Friday, 9am to 8:45pm.

Kenpo is the house style, and it's a distinctive one. It's built on fast hand strikes thrown in quick succession, with much less kicking than most karate. Students are taught that every block is also a strike. That makes it a practical self-defense art, and it's the reason most adults walk in the door.

What's taught

Karate for children five and up, and karate for adults, are the core. Classes are graded so a beginner isn't put in with people who've been at it for years, and the school keeps class sizes limited so nobody spends the hour at the back of the room.

Cardio kickboxing runs alongside it, several days a week at a range of levels. It's a workout class built on pads and bags rather than a sparring class. It's strenuous, so it's worth talking to your doctor first if you're coming back to exercise after a long gap.

elevated-wellness-massage-boulder-creek.html:
Elevated Wellness Massage is a therapeutic practice, not a spa day. Sylvia Lynn works out of 127 Forest Street, half a block off Central Avenue, and the range she offers is Swedish, deep tissue, cranial-sacral, and polarity work, mixed to suit whoever's on the table.

It's a one-room practice a short walk from the middle of downtown, and small on purpose.

Sessions and prices

The standard hour runs $120, in either of two forms. The signature session is Swedish work with hot towels and extra attention to feet and neck. The therapeutic session blends Swedish with polarity work. Both can be extended to 90 minutes, at $140 and $150 respectively.

Massage with stretching is an hour and a half at $140, combining Swedish technique with assisted stretching.

There's a 90-minute CBD massage at $185, and a couples session at $360.

If you want one thing addressed rather than a full-body hour, the area-specific session is $60 and targets a single region.

Booking

Booking is online through the practice's own site, and the phone is (831) 345-8043. Email is elevated_wellness@yahoo.com. Sessions are by appointment.

Who runs it

Sylvia Lynn owns and runs the practice, and publishes license #96769. Before massage, she came up through martial arts: she's a fifth-degree black belt and has taught both martial arts and cardio kickboxing.

The studio also stocks a small shelf of locally made things, including candles from Bitter Bee Candle Co and soaps and lotion bars from Ladder to the Moon, some of them made for sensitive skin.

treetop-pilates-boulder-creek.title: Treetop Pilates: The Classical Studio on Forest Street
treetop-pilates-boulder-creek.html:
Treetop Pilates is the studio with the actual apparatus in it. Reformer, tower, Cadillac, chair, barrels, mats: the full classical setup, in a room on Forest Street, half a block off Central Avenue.

That matters because Pilates on a mat and Pilates on a reformer are different experiences. The springs do half the work of teaching your body where it's supposed to be, and there's no substitute for a machine when you're learning the shape of a movement.

What's offered

Three formats. Mat classes are the entry point, done without springs so the body creates its own resistance, with props like magic circles, foam rollers, and physio balls added in. Up to eight people.

Tower classes combine the tower's springs with mat work and cap at three people, which is close to private instruction with company.

Machine classes use any and all of the apparatus. You book those as a private (one student, 55 minutes), a duet, or a trio for two or three people working at similar levels with one instructor.

The studio recommends starting one-on-one. There's a $45 introductory assessment and a three-session intro package at $175, both meant to establish what you're working with before you join a group. Preregistration is required for every class, private or group.

Prices

Mat classes are $18 a session, or $150 for a ten-pack. Tower classes are $25, or $220 for ten. Private machine sessions are $80, or $750 for ten. Duets are $55 each, trios $42. There's also a flex card: spend $300 or more up front and take any class at the ten-pack rate.

Packages expire after four months, introductory offers after one, and none of them transfer to another person. Cancellations need 24 hours' notice or the session is charged. Refer a friend who buys a ten-pack and you get 10 percent off your next one.

Confirm the current figures when you book. The studio's published price list has been up a while.

Who teaches

Tammy Ogletree founded Treetop Pilates in 2017 and teaches classical Pilates. The studio's whole pitch is individual attention: small caps, one instructor, and sessions built around what a particular body can do rather than a set routine.

Booking and finding it

Treetop Pilates is at 125 Forest Street, a short walk from Central Avenue. Call (831) 419-0202 to schedule, or (831) 421-1224.

mountain-sangha-boulder-creek.title: Mountain Sangha: Hot Yoga, Pilates, and Breathwork on Highway 9
mountain-sangha-boulder-creek.html:
Sangha is a Sanskrit word for community, and the studio at 12788 Highway 9 leans into it: the mountain part is where you are, and the sangha part is the point. Mountain Sangha is Boulder Creek's hot yoga and Pilates studio, a heated room a short walk from downtown where the schedule runs from six in the morning on weekdays.

It's one of two Pilates addresses in town, and they don't overlap much. Treetop Pilates teaches classical machine work on reformers and towers; Mountain Sangha runs mat-based Hot Pilates, hot and gentle yoga, strength intervals, and a run of breathwork and sound offerings you'd otherwise be driving down the valley for.

The classes

The yoga side covers most temperatures and speeds: Hot 26 Vibes, hot flow, mixed flow, slow flow, gentle flow, yin, and restorative. The strength side is Hot Pilates, HIIT, a sculpt series, and combination classes that pair Pilates or HIIT with a yoga stretch in a longer 75-minute block. Beginners get their own on-ramp with a yoga stretch and beginner Pilates class.

Then there's the part of the schedule the studio calls Sangha Specials: breathwork sessions with Tamar Frey and Jenn Hicklin, sound baths with Sera Timms, and a women's circle. Private sessions run alongside the group schedule, including private sound healing and breathwork, and the studio rents its space for events and parties.

Space is limited and booking is online, so reserve a spot before you drive over rather than turning up on spec. The schedule and booking run through the studio's site.

Who's teaching

The studio was opened by Shanon Farney, who left a 20-year corporate career and came to teaching through a Hot Pilates class she walked into more or less by accident. She's an RYT-200 registered yoga teacher, a certified Hot Pilates teacher, and a breathwork facilitator coach.

The teaching roster around her runs deeper than a town this size has any right to expect: Charina Makovsky has practiced Ashtanga, Iyengar, yin, and restorative yoga since 2004 and has taught everyone from children to elders to postpartum mothers; Laura Manley is a Vinyasa teacher with a dance background who the studio notes is one of just a few certified Modo hot yoga teachers in Northern California; and Tamar Frey and Jenn Hicklin carry the breathwork, reiki, and ceremony side of the schedule.

Prices as published on the studio's site, worth confirming before you buy:

  • Drop-in: $25 a class
  • Wednesday drop-in: $15
  • Intro month: $100 for one month of unlimited classes, once per person
  • 15-class pass: $300, which works out to $20 a class, with no expiration date
  • Unlimited month: $165, expiring 31 days from purchase
  • 6-month unlimited auto-bill: $155 a month; 12-month: $145 a month
  • Seniors 60 and up: 10 percent off packages, passes, and drop-ins, with their own auto-bill tiers

The studio is at 12788 Highway 9, Suite 1, at the north end of the business stretch. Posted hours run 6 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. weekdays and 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. weekends, but in practice the class schedule controls access, so book rather than drop by. Phone is 831-217-3018, email hello@mountainsangha.com.

town-of-lorenzo-boulder-creek.title: Lorenzo: The Town Boulder Creek Swallowed
town-of-lorenzo-boulder-creek.html:
Boulder Creek used to have a rival, close enough to walk to. About a mile south of the village then called Boulder sat a second town with its own sawmill, its own hotel and store, and for a decade, the upper valley's lumber trade. It was called Lorenzo. Boulder Creek didn't beat it in any dramatic way. It got the railroad, and then, slowly, it got everything else.

Two villages, a mile apart

Rail historian Derek Whaley's Santa Cruz Trains: Railroads of the Santa Cruz Mountains (2015), the fullest account of how this corner of the valley sorted itself out, describes the area before unification as two rival villages: Boulder, on the north side of the creek that gave it its name, and Lorenzo, about a mile south (p. 243). They were separate places with separate ambitions, and they competed for everything, down to the post office.

The naming side of this story is covered in how Boulder Creek got its name. This article is about the town that lost.

Peery builds a town

Both villages trace back to the same man. Joseph Wilburn Peery built his sawmill north of Boulder Creek in the early 1860s, which is roughly where the settlement of Boulder began. In 1868 he moved the mill two miles south, and there, per Whaley (p. 246), he later built his town.

The town itself came in January 1875, laid out on land Peery bought mostly from Frank L. Pitt, who owned the lumber mill immediately north of the site. Local historian Lisa Robinson's The San Lorenzo Valley (Arcadia Publishing, 2012) sketches what grew there: a hotel, a store, a few dwellings, and Peery's own sawmill, known as Silver Mills (p. 19). Small, but complete. A town, not a camp.

The valley's shipping point

The timing wasn't an accident. That same year, 1875, the San Lorenzo Valley flume opened, the wooden waterway that carried sawn lumber down the valley to the railhead at Felton. And when the flume company set up its local station, it put it at Lorenzo, south of Boulder.

That decision mattered more than any other in Lorenzo's short life. The station made Lorenzo the place where the upper valley's lumber met its route to market, and for the next ten years the trade ran through the rival town down the road. Our history of the San Lorenzo Valley flume tells that whole story; in 1875, whoever held the flume held the valley's commerce.

The post office feud

The rivalry wasn't polite, and the clearest evidence is what happened to the mail.

In the mid-1870s, a storekeeper named Charles Cottrell succeeded Peery as Boulder Creek's postmaster. Cottrell's store was in Lorenzo, so he took the post office with him, moving it about a mile south to his own counter. Robinson adds the detail that made it a scandal: liquor was sold on the premises (p. 19). Residents up the road now walked a mile for their letters, to a store in the rival town, over a bar.

They didn't take it quietly. Seventy-two residents signed a petition to the postmaster general in Washington demanding the office come back, and it did, when David Hossack replaced Cottrell as postmaster. A note on the dates: Robinson puts the affair at 1874 to 1876, Whaley runs it a year or two later, so we're keeping it at "mid-1870s" until a primary postal record settles it.

The railroad picks a winner

What the flume gave Lorenzo, the railroad took away.

When the Felton & Pescadero Railroad pushed up the valley in the mid-1880s, its terminus was the prize. Whichever town got the freight yard got the future, and Lorenzo, the established shipping point, should have been the favorite. It lost for two reasons, per Whaley (p. 247). The surveyors found the site too small for the large freight yard the railroad wanted, and Lorenzo's own residents, seeing the railroad coming, raised their land prices in hopes of an easy profit. The railroad declined to pay and continued to a vacant timber tract just south of Boulder.

Then it built its own town on it. James F. Cunningham was hired to clear and stump the 160-acre redwood tract, the felled trees became railroad ties, and the railroad sold the lots beside its new yard for businesses and homes. The station took its name from the nearby Boulder Creek Hotel, and the name quickly spread to the whole community on both sides of the creek. The rival villages hadn't merged so much as been outgrown by a third thing, the one with the railhead.

Robinson's history of the flume, The San Lorenzo Valley Flume (San Lorenzo Valley Museum, 3rd edition, 2025), records the end of Lorenzo's shipping era precisely: on Thursday, May 14, 1885, the last load of lumber ran down the flume from Lorenzo to Felton, and crews began pulling that stretch apart (p. 55). Three weeks earlier, on April 26, the first train had reached Boulder Creek, a date the railroad's own published timetable confirms. A decade as the valley's shipping point ended in one spring.

The long fade

Lorenzo didn't vanish in 1885, and the "town that burned down" version you'll sometimes hear doesn't hold up either. The village kept its station and its village life for decades. It took real damage in the kitchen fire of April 1897, but insurance surveyors mapped a standing, functioning town both after the fire and again in 1908. Our name-origin article walks through that evidence.

What 1885 decided wasn't whether Lorenzo would exist. It decided which town would grow. Boulder Creek got the yard, the lots, the mills, and eventually the name for the whole district, a story our short history of Boulder Creek picks up. Lorenzo got a slow slide into being the south end of somewhere else. No original Lorenzo building is known to survive, and the surest trace is the name itself, still on the river, the valley, and the old townsite land south of downtown where the historical society places it.

For where these events sit among everything else, see the Boulder Creek history timeline.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where was Lorenzo?

About a mile south of the original village of Boulder, in what's now the southern approach to Boulder Creek. No original buildings survive, so there's no "there" to visit.

Who founded Lorenzo?

Joseph Wilburn Peery, the same sawmill man whose first mill anchored the settlement of Boulder. He moved his mill south in 1868 and laid out Lorenzo in January 1875 on land bought mostly from Frank L. Pitt.

Why did the railroad skip Lorenzo?

Two reasons, by Whaley's account: surveyors judged the site too small for a major freight yard, and Lorenzo's residents raised their land prices hoping to profit from the railroad's arrival. The railroad bought a vacant 160-acre tract near Boulder instead.

Did Lorenzo burn down in 1897?

No. The April 1897 kitchen fire did real damage, but insurance maps show the village standing afterward and still growing in 1908. Lorenzo faded over decades rather than ending in one night.

What's left of Lorenzo today?

The name, mostly, still on the river and the valley the town was named after, and on the townsite land the historical society identifies at the south end of town. If you know of a marker, a street, or a family connection to Lorenzo, we'd like to hear about it.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. The history here comes from Derek Whaley's Santa Cruz Trains: Railroads of the Santa Cruz Mountains (2015), Lisa Robinson's The San Lorenzo Valley (Arcadia Publishing, 2012), and her The San Lorenzo Valley Flume (San Lorenzo Valley Museum, 3rd edition, 2025). The two disagree on the exact years of the post office feud, so this article keeps to the decade.

For the rest of the town's past, see the short history of Boulder Creek and the history timeline. Today's town lives in the business directory. Corrections and family stories are welcome, especially anything with a date attached: tell us.

last-train-boulder-creek.title: The Day the Last Train Left Boulder Creek
last-train-boulder-creek.html:
On the morning of January 26, 1934, a Friday, a locomotive came up the San Lorenzo Valley to Boulder Creek for the last time. There wasn't much left to collect. The train gathered up the boxcars that had been sitting on the sidings, coupled on what lumber still remained, and pulled out for Santa Cruz. Demolition crews followed soon after to take up the rails. Forty-nine years of railroading in Boulder Creek ended, not with a ceremony, but with a work train hauling away the leftovers.

Two separate histories of the valley, written decades apart and working from different records, land on that exact date, January 26, 1934. When sources that don't lean on each other agree to the day, you can trust it. Most of what follows is less tidy, and this piece will say so where it matters.

The day itself

By that January there was no schedule left to cancel. The passenger trains were already gone. Freight had dwindled to occasional runs, made only when there was something worth hauling. What remained in Boulder Creek was rolling stock parked on sidings, a little lumber, and a corridor of rails and trestles that Southern Pacific had formally given up on. The line was abandoned that same month.

So the last train wasn't a goodbye excursion. It was a cleanup job. It carried out the sidetracked boxcars and the lingering lumber, and behind it came the crews who would pull up the track itself, working their way back down the valley. The railroad didn't just stop serving Boulder Creek. It was dismantled and carried away.

That's a quiet ending for something that had, within living memory of the people watching, been the reason the town existed at the scale it did.

What the railroad had been

Go back three decades and the picture inverts. Around the turn of the century, Boulder Creek was one of the busiest lumber shipping points in the United States, fifth largest in the country by one historian's account. (He gives the year as 1899 in one place and 1902 in another, which tells you something about how these records survive. The ranking itself is consistent.)

The rhythm of that era was nightly. A regularly scheduled train left Boulder Creek every evening carrying at least forty carloads of wood products down to Felton, where it was sorted and sent on around the Bay Area. Forty cars of lumber, shingles, and split stuff, every night, out of a town you can walk end to end in ten minutes. The mills up the canyons fed the yard, the yard fed the train, and the train fed the cities. San Francisco, in particular, was substantially built and then rebuilt out of these hills.

The full sweep of that story, from the first train's arrival in 1885 through the whole working life of the branch, is in our San Lorenzo Valley railroad history. The logging side of it has its own piece too, in Boulder Creek's logging history. This article is about the ending.

The slow arithmetic

The railroad didn't die in 1934. It died over about twenty years, in increments small enough that no single one of them looked like the end.

The timber gave out first. The California Timber Company mill closed in 1913, and with it went the last of the big lumber operations north of town. The extension line that had served those upper camps was pulled up during World War I and sold as scrap metal, which set the pattern for everything that followed: when a piece of the railroad stopped earning, it didn't sit idle for long. It got removed.

In September 1921 the railroad discontinued the nightly evening run, the one that had once meant forty loaded cars. After that, freight moved only on demand. A train came up when there was business, and increasingly there wasn't.

The subtractions kept coming. In May 1929, the engine house and turntable at Boulder Creek were taken out. That's the kind of removal that tells you what the railroad's own planners believed, because you don't dismantle your servicing facilities at a terminal you expect to keep busy. By late 1929 the Boulder Creek train ran only as far as Felton, and by 1931 the passenger trains were gone entirely, replaced by buses. Near the end, freight service was down to as little as a weekly run, made only as needed.

Then came January 1934, and the arithmetic finished.

What forty-nine years left behind

It's easy to read that timeline as pure loss, and for the people whose work was tied to the trains, it was. But the railroad's forty-nine years shaped the town in ways that outlasted the rails. It fixed the location of downtown, because the commercial blocks grew up around the depot and the freight yard. It brought in the people, the goods, and the money that turned a mill camp into a town with churches, lodges, hotels, and a main street. Even the town's second act, tourism, ran on the railroad first: for decades the trains carried picnickers and campers into the big trees before the automobile took that job too.

The dates and turning points of that longer story are laid out in the Boulder Creek history timeline.

What you can still trace today

There's no locomotive on display here and no depot to visit. The demolition crews of 1934 did thorough work. What survives downtown is geography.

The depot grounds sat just behind today's fire station, in the heart of the downtown blocks. Stand there and you're standing roughly where the tracks ended, on the flat ground the freight yard once covered. That flat is part of why downtown sits where it sits. The fire department connection runs deeper than shared ground, too, and it's worth reading the history of the Boulder Creek Fire Department alongside this one.

And there's a street a block off the highway still carrying the name Railroad Avenue, a label on the map that has outlived the thing it pointed to by nine decades.

That's the inventory. A name, a flat, and a site. For a town that was once among the biggest lumber shippers in the country, it's a modest set of remains, which is maybe the point. The railroad's real monument is the town itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did the last train leave Boulder Creek?

January 26, 1934. Three independent accounts agree on the exact date, and the Oakland Tribune settled any doubt the same day, reporting from Santa Cruz on January 26 that the last train had gone over the line that morning. The paper even named the crew: F. E. Page, conductor; William Bohrmeister at the throttle; A. G. Bryan firing; Jack Ryder and Al Ashley as brakemen. The Tribune closed its story with the detail that makes the whole arc: the first train ran up this line on April 26, 1885, and an Odd Fellows' excursion rode into the upper valley in its first days. Forty-nine years, almost to the season, from first celebration to last errand. The train hauled out the boxcars and lumber still in town, and demolition crews took up the rails soon after.

When did passenger train service to Boulder Creek end?

By 1931 the passenger trains were gone, replaced by buses. Sources disagree on the precise month, so we don't print one.

How long did Boulder Creek have rail service?

About 49 years, from the first train's arrival in 1885 to the last one out in January 1934.

Can you see any of the railroad today?

Downtown, only traces: the flat where the freight yard was, the depot site behind the fire station, and Railroad Avenue's name. There are no surviving structures or tracks in town.

Last reviewed August 6, 2026. The dates in this piece come from published histories of the San Lorenzo Valley; where those sources disagree, we say so rather than pick one quietly.

riding-the-flume-boulder-creek.title: Riding the Flume: The Most Dangerous Fun Boulder Creek Ever Invented
riding-the-flume-boulder-creek.html:
For ten years Boulder Creek had a water slide to Felton, and the town could not resist it.

The San Lorenzo Valley flume was built to move lumber: a V-shaped wooden trough on trestles, nine miles of moving water from a headworks two miles north of town down to the railhead at Felton. It did that job from 1875 until the mid-1880s, and our flume history tells that story. This is the other story, the one about what people did with a nine-mile ribbon of fast water running through their valley: they rode it.

The boats

Almost as soon as the flume opened, riding it in makeshift boats became a local pastime. Local historian Lisa Robinson's history of the flume for the San Lorenzo Valley Museum, The San Lorenzo Valley Flume (3rd edition, 2025), reproduces a photograph of a rider seated in one of these little craft, her companion standing on the walkway beside her in a derby hat, starched shirt, and three-piece suit. Nobody dressed down for it. A flume ride was an occasion.

The flume company itself used the water the same way. When its mill camp moved, the crew loaded tents, mattresses, bunks, and blankets into boxes and floated the whole camp downstream. Charles Brimblecom, whose 1875 diary is one of the few day-by-day records of the flume era, watched it happen that May and noted the crew got their boxes too close together, dammed up the water, and nearly stranded their own household goods. He wasn't too worried to enjoy it: "After a while the stove came down in fine style though I did not see that."

Riding wasn't simple even when it worked. At two places, road bridges crossed the flume low enough that a rider couldn't pass under them. The move, Robinson records (p. 43), was to jump out of the boat, sprint across the bridge, and jump back into the moving boat on the far side. There's no record of how often that maneuver failed, which is probably for the best.

The plank walkers

The flume's official foot traffic was the flume walkers, men employed to patrol the line with a stick and break up lumber jams. The V-shape did some of the work on its own, since water backing up behind a jam rose and lifted the boards free, but the walkers were the insurance. The walkway they patrolled was a plank about ten inches wide, sometimes running along trestlework high above the canyon floor.

In winter the walkers had company they never asked for. The valley's roads churned into knee-deep mud, and ordinary people walking between Boulder Creek and Felton found the flume's ten-inch plank preferable to the road. Brimblecom did it himself and recorded how close it came to going wrong. Crossing high trestlework one wet December Sunday in 1875, he watched his companion nearly go over the edge: "quick as a flash, Harmon's foot slipped and he went down on his knees partly on and partly off the flume," the diary reads. The man caught himself between the board and the trough. They took the road after that.

What it cost

Not everyone caught themselves. A month later Brimblecom recorded a man killed falling from the flume near Felton, whom the Sentinel identified as James Nichols, fallen between two spots the paper called "Hick's crossing" and "French John's." In March 1876 the flume lost one of its own superintendents, Thomas Lilley of San Jose, who fell ninety feet from a high section south of Ben Lomond and didn't survive it. The Santa Cruz Sentinel ran what amounts to an early workplace-safety editorial: "a walk ten inches wide, without railing or guard, over trestle-work ninety feet high, is not just the thing for its employees to be compelled to cross over daily."

The flume kept collecting close calls for as long as it stood. In 1880 a fourteen-year-old boy walking the plank with his gun as a walking stick shot himself when it slipped, and was at first reported dead before word came he might recover. In 1883 a twelve-year-old fell fifty feet and, somehow, walked away from it.

The men who knew it best

The walkers themselves are mostly anonymous, but Robinson's research names a few (p. 47). Scott Taylor served as flume foreman. Robert Cowen, a Scot who spent more than forty years as a lumberman, walked the line. And William H. Dool, Billy to the valley, went from patrolling the flume's planks to serving as a warden at Big Basin after it became California's first state park, which means at least one man spent his working life keeping people safe around both of the valley's great redwood enterprises, the one that cut the trees down and the one that saved them.

Why there's nothing left to ride

The flume's working life ended in stages. The stretch from Lorenzo down to Felton sent its last load in May 1885 and came apart as the railroad advanced up the valley. The stretch north of town kept floating lumber for the upper mills until early 1888. The redwood planks were pulled apart and reused in local construction, so the flume didn't vanish so much as dissolve into the valley's buildings. Our flume history covers the full arc, and the history timeline places it among everything else the 1880s threw at this town.

The riding, it's fair to assume, stopped when the water did.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did people really ride the lumber flume?

Yes. Riding the flume in makeshift boats became a popular pastime almost as soon as it opened in 1875, documented in photographs the San Lorenzo Valley Museum holds.

How dangerous was it?

Deadly. Contemporary records name two deaths connected to the flume in 1876 alone, one rider and one superintendent, plus serious injuries to two boys in the early 1880s.

What was a flume walker?

An employee who patrolled the flume on a ten-inch-wide plank, carrying a stick to break up lumber jams. In winter, ordinary travelers used the same planks to avoid muddy roads, which the flume company never intended.

Where did the flume run?

Nine miles, from a headworks about two miles north of Boulder Creek down the San Lorenzo Valley to the railhead at Felton, crossing the river a half dozen times on the way.

Can I see any of it today?

No section of the flume survives in place. Its lumber was reused in valley buildings after dismantling. The San Lorenzo Valley Museum keeps photographs and the research that this article draws on.

Last reviewed August 7, 2026. Drawn from Lisa Robinson's The San Lorenzo Valley Flume (San Lorenzo Valley Museum, 3rd edition, 2025), including her reproductions of Charles Brimblecom's 1875-76 diary and contemporary Santa Cruz Sentinel reporting. Billy Dool's flume-walking years and later Big Basin wardenship are independently confirmed by the county's historic-resources survey of his Boulder Creek residence.

big-basin-evacuation-czu-fire.title: The Big Basin Evacuation: Three Days in August 2020
big-basin-evacuation-czu-fire.html:
Big Basin Redwoods State Park sits thirteen miles up the road from Boulder Creek, which is the closest town to it. In the middle of August 2020 the park was doing what it always does in the middle of August: running at capacity, with all five campgrounds occupied and staff families living in the residence areas at Sky Meadow. Within three days, 97 percent of its 18,000 acres had burned. Every camper, every staff member, and every household pet in the park got out. Traci Bliss sets the account down in her park history, Big Basin Redwood Forest: California's Oldest State Park (The History Press, 2021), and it deserves telling on its own, apart from what the fire did to the town below.

A morning of lightning

The CZU Lightning Complex started on the morning of August 16, 2020, in the middle of a record heat wave. It was never one fire with one ignition: a lightning siege dropped something on the order of eleven to twelve thousand bolts across California in a matter of hours, and the complex is the name for the many fires that followed. Sources give different start times, from the small hours through mid-morning, and CAL FIRE's incident record dates it to 8:00 a.m. that day. Some of those strikes landed in the Santa Cruz Mountains, in terrain that had been drying all summer.

A lightning fire in these mountains wasn't new. Bliss records that in September 1904, somewhere between six and twenty fires burned in the Santa Cruz Mountains at once, and the forest survived largely because none of them merged before the rain came.

Then the wind changed everything

For two days the new fires burned as separate incidents. On the afternoon of August 18, a windstorm pushed three of the local fires into each other, and the merged fire expanded sharply. This was the thing 1904 had been spared, and it changed the situation at Big Basin from serious to immediate.

Much of it happened blind. Bliss notes that park staff had no information on how the fire was moving inside the park itself. The people responsible for a thousand visitors couldn't see the thing they were making decisions about.

Seven people, five campgrounds

That day, ranger Alex Tabone and a small team evacuated Big Basin's five campgrounds, along with the two staff residence areas at Sky Meadow. Everyone got out. Bliss puts the number at more than a thousand campers; we haven't found a second source for the count or for the exact size of the team, so treat those figures as hers.

It's worth sitting with the arithmetic. As late as that third day, the campgrounds were still fully occupied. Seven people cleared an 18,000-acre park holding more visitors than some nearby towns have residents, without being able to see where the fire was. There was no time to wait for certainty, and they didn't wait. The campers were moved before the fire arrived.

The lesson under the story isn't luck. It's that the evacuation started while it could still be orderly. By the time the fire's size was obvious to everyone, the park was already empty.

What the fire took, and what it didn't

The numbers from those days are stark. Across Santa Cruz and San Mateo counties, 86,509 acres burned. Big Basin's 18,000 acres were 97 percent charred within three days of the start.

The firefight itself was under-resourced from the beginning. At the 6 a.m. briefing on August 19, crews were told they had the resources for a five-thousand-acre fire and were facing a sixty-thousand-acre one. Cal Fire said publicly that it had 10 percent of what the CZU complex needed. That same day, a state parks damage assessment team driving up Highway 236 past the golf course found the historic park headquarters already gone and the famous auto tree beside it in flames. In the end, close to 180 structural resources were lost in the park. The complex took almost five weeks to be declared contained and wasn't officially extinguished until a few days before Christmas.

Against all of that, one set of numbers held. Nobody in Big Basin, staff or visitor, was killed or injured. Every domestic pet belonging to the residents inside the park survived. In a fire that consumed nearly everything built in the park's long history, the people were the thing that didn't burn.

The town was leaving too

The park's evacuation didn't happen in isolation. Bliss includes a firsthand account of the evening of August 18 in Boulder Creek: the whole town leaving at once, a constant stream of headlights heading down the valley, with law enforcement holding Highway 236 closed to everything but families getting out. The park emptied uphill of a town that was emptying too.

What that night felt like from the town's side, and what the years since have looked like, is its own story. We've told it in six years after the CZU fire. And if reading this raises the practical question, the one about your own household, our wildfire evacuation guide for Boulder Creek covers zones, alerts, and what to have ready now, in a calm season, which is when that page is most useful.

Big Basin now

The park that burned was California's first state park, and the fire took nearly every building from its long history. The forest itself is doing what redwood forests do, which is come back. Big Basin has reopened for day use, and our guide to visiting covers what's open and what to expect.

The evacuation deserves to be remembered alongside the loss. A thousand people walked, drove, and were led out of a park that was about to burn almost completely, because a small team moved early and moved everyone. Six years on, that's still the working model for this valley: know your way out, and don't wait until you can see the reason.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did the CZU fire start?

On the morning of August 16, 2020, during a record heat wave, after a lightning siege dropped something on the order of eleven to twelve thousand strikes across California. It was a complex of many fires rather than a single ignition, and reported start times vary; CAL FIRE's incident record dates it to 8:00 a.m. that day.

How many people were evacuated from Big Basin?

Everyone in the park: all five campgrounds and the two staff residence areas at Sky Meadow, on August 18, 2020, led by ranger Alex Tabone. Bliss's account puts it at more than a thousand campers and a team of six, figures we haven't been able to confirm elsewhere.

Was anyone hurt in the park?

No. Nobody in Big Basin, staff or visitor, was killed or injured, and every resident's pet survived. The wider CZU fire's toll on the surrounding communities is covered in our town-recovery article.

How much of Big Basin burned?

97 percent of the park's 18,000 acres within three days, out of 86,509 acres burned across Santa Cruz and San Mateo counties.

Is Big Basin open today?

It's open for day use. See is Big Basin open for current details before you go.

Where does this account come from?

From Traci Bliss's history of the park, Big Basin Redwood Forest (2021), which records the evacuation and the fire's first days in detail.

auto-services-boulder-creek.title: Keeping a Car Alive in Boulder Creek: Gas, Mechanics, and Parts

the-mat-laundromat-boulder-creek.title: The Mat: Boulder Creek's Laundromat, Renovated and App-Run
the-mat-laundromat-boulder-creek.html:
Every town needs a laundromat, and Boulder Creek's is The Mat, at 12890 Highway 9 in the middle of downtown. If you haven't been in since the renovation, it's not the laundromat you remember: the machines are new and they run on an app instead of quarters.

One update since our last review, straight from the business's own FAQ: The Mat is fully self-service now. There is no on-site attendant anymore; a virtual attendant is available if a machine has a problem or you need something, and the business also answers on Facebook Messenger.

How it works

Self-service. The washers and dryers are new, with touch screens, and payment runs through an app, so there's no hunting for quarters before you load up. The app also pays out cash-back rewards for regulars. The store is open 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily, which leaves room for a before-work load or an after-dinner one.

Wash-and-fold is gone. The Mat's own FAQ says the drop-off service has been shut down because it took a full staff to run. If you need laundry washed and folded for you, plan on a trip down the valley, or call 831-609-4958 to ask what they suggest.

While you wait

The Mat leans into the waiting time rather than pretending it doesn't exist. There are vending machines for detergent if you forgot yours, plus snacks and drinks, and music and TV to fill the cycle. The El Rey Leon taco truck has been known to post up on site, which turns a wash cycle into dinner; whether it's there on a given night is a truck's prerogative, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan.

A laundromat downtown is also the practical answer to comforters, sleeping bags, storm-week power outages, and the week the dryer at home gives up.

Hours and where it is

The Mat is at 12890 Highway 9, Boulder Creek, a few doors from the center of downtown. Store hours are 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily. Phone 831-609-4958, and the business also answers on Facebook Messenger. Hours can shift, so confirm before a late-night run.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is The Mat?

12890 Highway 9, Boulder Creek, CA 95006, in downtown Boulder Creek. Phone 831-609-4958.

What are the hours?

The store is open 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. every day. Confirm before you go, especially around holidays.

Do the machines take quarters?

Payment runs through an app on the new machines, so you don't need a pocket of quarters. The virtual attendant can help if you get stuck the first time.

Is there wash-and-fold service?

Not anymore. The business's own FAQ says the wash-and-fold service has been shut down, so plan on self-service.

Can I wash big items like comforters?

Large items are what a laundromat's machines are for. Check the drum sizes posted on the washers, or ask through the virtual attendant which machines fit oversized loads.

realtors-boulder-creek.title: Realtors in Boulder Creek: The Three Offices in Town
realtors-boulder-creek.html:
There are harder places to buy a house than Boulder Creek, but not many that ask more specific questions. Is the lot on septic or the CSA 7 sewer? District water or a well? Did the fire insurance quote come back at all? A realtor who works these mountains daily has answers before you think to ask, and Boulder Creek has three real estate offices that do exactly that, all within a few blocks of each other on Highway 9.

Two ground rules before the list. There are no rankings here; the offices appear in order along the strip, nothing more. And inclusion is not endorsement. These are the offices our verified directory shows in town, and choosing among them is your call.

Why a mountain realtor is its own specialty

A San Lorenzo Valley transaction carries homework a flatland deal never sees. Steep and shared driveways, septic systems with permit histories, private wells, propane tanks, and a fire insurance market that can decide a sale all by itself. Add the properties still working through recovery six years after the CZU fire, and the gap between an agent who lives this market and one who visits it gets wide fast. If you're weighing the move itself, start with moving to Boulder Creek and what it actually costs to live here.

CENTURY 21 Masters, Boulder Creek office

  • Address: 13117 Highway 9, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-338-2125
  • Website: c21masters.com
  • Hours: not published; call

The local office of CENTURY 21 Masters, a brokerage with more than fifty offices across California. The trade here is the listing reach of a big franchise network, run out of a Highway 9 storefront that works the San Lorenzo Valley and the rest of Santa Cruz County daily. For sellers who want exposure beyond the valley, the network is the argument.

Houdesheldt Traditional Team

  • Address: 13117 Highway 9, Boulder Creek (within the Century 21 Masters office)
  • Phone: 831-281-6354
  • Hours: not published; call

A named real estate team operating within the Century 21 Masters office in the same building. That's a common arrangement: a team with its own phone line and client relationships, transacting under the brokerage's license. The team serves buyers and sellers across the San Lorenzo Valley and the Santa Cruz Mountains, with listed focuses that include first-time buyers, investment properties, and relocation help. If you'd rather start with a named local team than a brokerage front desk, this is that door.

Schwarzbach Associates

  • Address: 13335 Highway 9 at West Park Avenue, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-338-2171
  • Website: schwarzbachassociatesinc.com
  • Hours: not published; call

The town's elder statesman: a family-owned Boulder Creek brokerage founded in 1955, independent by choice. Seventy years of mountain escrows is a deep well of local knowledge. Schwarzbach also covers more ground than sales alone, handling residential and commercial transactions plus property management and appraisals, with a stated service area spanning Santa Cruz, Santa Clara, San Mateo, San Benito, and Monterey counties. It's the only office on this page that advertises either service.

Questions worth asking any mountain realtor

Interview the agent the way you'd interview a contractor. A few questions that separate mountain experience from a mountain listing:

  • How many transactions have you closed in the San Lorenzo Valley in the last two years?
  • Walk me through how you'd handle a failed septic inspection mid-escrow.
  • When do you get the fire insurance quote in your timeline, and what happens to the deal if the address only qualifies for the FAIR Plan?
  • What should I know about this parcel's water source, road maintenance agreement, and defensible space obligations?
  • For sellers: what does your marketing reach beyond the valley?

And if you're shopping for the town as much as the house, spend a Saturday at something on the events calendar.

How many real estate offices are in Boulder Creek?

Three, all on Highway 9: the CENTURY 21 Masters office and the Houdesheldt Traditional Team at 13117, and Schwarzbach Associates at 13335. All serve the wider San Lorenzo Valley, not just town.

Are Century 21 Masters and the Houdesheldt Traditional Team the same office?

Same building, related but distinct. The Houdesheldt Traditional Team is a named team that operates within the Century 21 Masters office at 13117 Highway 9, with its own phone line (831-281-6354). The office's main line is 831-338-2125.

Do I need a local agent to buy in Boulder Creek?

No rule requires one, but mountain transactions involve septic, wells, private roads, and a hard fire insurance market, and an agent who handles those weekly can save you from expensive surprises.

Who handles property management or appraisals in town?

Schwarzbach Associates is the office on this page that advertises both, alongside residential and commercial sales. Call 831-338-2171 to confirm current availability.

Which office is best?

We don't rank them. The practical move is to talk to more than one, ask the mountain questions above, and pick the fit. Verify any agent's license at the California DRE's public lookup.

health-services-boulder-creek.title: Health Services in Boulder Creek: The Providers Who Practice in Town
health-services-boulder-creek.html:
Boulder Creek asks you to drive for plenty of things, but less of your health care than you'd think. The specialists, the urgent care, and the emergency room are all down the valley or over in Santa Cruz, and our healthcare guide maps every one of them. The routine appointments are a different story. A teeth cleaning, a chiropractic adjustment, a prescription refill, a facial, a yoga class: all of that happens right here in town, most of it within two blocks of the strip.

This page collects the providers who actually practice in Boulder Creek, with addresses, phones, and how to get in the door. Two ground rules, same as every guide we publish: inclusion isn't endorsement, and nothing here is medical advice. We describe who offers what; choosing a provider is your call.

The dentist: Boulder Creek Dental

  • Address: 13270 Big Basin Way, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-338-2131
  • Website: bouldercreekdental.com
  • Hours: open Monday through Thursday; closed Friday through Sunday; call for current times

The town has its own dental office, one block off Highway 9 on Big Basin Way, in a practice that describes itself as serving Santa Cruz County for over fifty years. Dr. Keith Johnson, DDS, has practiced there for more than two decades and became the owner along the way. The office handles general and family dentistry: preventive care and cleanings, crowns (single, bridge, and implant), dentures, and partials. It's accepting new patients as of this writing, with registration forms available on the site, and appointments are booked by phone or through the site's contact form. For a filling or a checkup, the days of writing off half a day to Highway 17 are optional.

The chiropractor: Kaplan Chiropractic

  • Address: 154 Forest Street, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-338-0677
  • Website: kaplanchiro.com
  • Hours: Tuesday 7 to 11 a.m.; Thursday 3 to 6 p.m.; otherwise closed

Dr. Jeffrey Kaplan's longtime chiropractic office sits just off the strip on Forest Street and practices the Gonstead system of chiropractic. The catch is the calendar: the Boulder Creek office keeps two windows a week, Tuesday mornings and Thursday afternoons, so this is an appointment stop, not a walk-in. Call rather than drop by, and if your schedule can't bend around those windows, plan ahead. The practice serves Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley.

Skin care: SuperNatural Beauty & Aesthetics

  • Address: 12615 Highway 9, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 661-889-5728
  • Website: supernatural.beauty
  • Booking: by appointment only, through its website

The newest addition to the town's health-adjacent roster is a med spa run by an aesthetic registered nurse, offering neurotoxin injections, dermal fillers, chemical peels, microneedling, red light therapy, and medical-grade skincare. Everything starts with a consultation, and booking runs online through the site or by phone. SuperNatural sits on the line between health care and spa day, so we'll cover it more fully alongside the town's spa and massage options; for now, know that this category of care no longer requires a trip to Scotts Valley.

The rest of the routine

The everyday layer is covered too. Boulder Creek Pharmacy fills prescriptions on Central Avenue and delivers free throughout the valley, which matters more up a long driveway than it ever did in a city.

For movement, Mountain Sangha runs hot yoga, Pilates, and breathwork classes on Highway 9, and Treetop Pilates teaches classical Pilates on Forest Street. Massage lives in town as well, at Elevated Wellness, also on Forest Street. It's a short list, but it's the list most households actually use in a normal month, and every entry is walkable from downtown parking.

What still means a drive down the valley

Be clear-eyed about the boundary. There's no primary care office, urgent care, or hospital in Boulder Creek itself; the nearest clinic is in Ben Lomond and the nearest ER is in Santa Cruz. When you need a physician, a specialist, or same-day walk-in care, you're leaving town, and the healthcare guide covers exactly where to go, how far it is, and who to call first. The mountain doesn't have everything, and this page doesn't pretend it does. But the recurring appointments, the ones that come around every few months, mostly don't need the drive.

Is there a dentist in Boulder Creek?

Yes. Boulder Creek Dental at 13270 Big Basin Way handles general and family dentistry, including crowns, dentures, and implant work, and is accepting new patients as of this writing. Call 831-338-2131.

Does Boulder Creek have a chiropractor?

Yes. Kaplan Chiropractic at 154 Forest Street, with published hours limited to Tuesday mornings and Thursday afternoons. Call 831-338-0677 for an appointment.

Is there a doctor's office in town?

No. Boulder Creek has no primary care office, urgent care, or hospital; the nearest clinic is in Ben Lomond and walk-in care is farther down the valley. Our healthcare guide maps all of it, including who to call in an emergency.

Where do I fill a prescription without leaving town?

Boulder Creek Pharmacy at 13081 Central Avenue, an independent with free delivery throughout the San Lorenzo Valley. Call 831-338-2144.

Kelly handles the massage and bodywork and has been practicing since 1998, with deep tissue, sports, prenatal, Swedish, and hot stone work on the list. Ashleigh Noce, a licensed esthetician and lash artist, covers facials, waxing, and lash services. The menu also includes therapeutic tub soaks and red light therapy, making this the one stop in town where a massage and a facial can happen in the same visit. Booking is by phone; there's no online scheduler, so call the main line.

Elevated Wellness Massage & Bodywork: the therapeutic option

  • Address: 127 Forest Street, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-345-8043
  • Website: elevatedwellnessmassage.com
  • Hours: by appointment

Sylvia Lynn's one-room practice sits half a block off Central Avenue, and it leans therapeutic rather than spa-day: Swedish, deep tissue, cranial-sacral, and polarity work, mixed to suit whoever's on the table, under published license #96769. Booking runs online through her site. We've covered the practice in depth, session menu and prices included, in our Elevated Wellness profile, so this is the short version: if what you want is bodywork that solves a problem, start there.

SuperNatural Beauty & Aesthetics: the med spa

  • Address: 12615 Highway 9, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 661-889-5728
  • Website: supernatural.beauty
  • Booking: by appointment only, through its website

A town this size having a med spa at all is unusual, and this one is the real article: a licensed medical practice founded and run by Brandi, a registered nurse who moved into aesthetics after years in critical care. The service list runs from chemical peels, microneedling, and medical-grade skincare through neurotoxin injections, dermal fillers, IV therapy, and red light therapy. The practice describes its aim as "subtle, natural-looking results"; this is skin care with a medical chart, not a makeover counter. Booking is online through the website, with the phone as backup. One note if you've been before: the practice is now on Big Basin Way, not at its old Highway 9 address.

Oli Nails: the Boulder Creek nail tech

  • Studio: 3101 Scotts Valley Drive, Suite 18, Scotts Valley (by appointment only)
  • Booking: direct message on Instagram, @olive__oli_nails

There's no nail salon storefront in Boulder Creek itself, and Oli Nails is the local name to know: a licensed nail tech from Boulder Creek who works by appointment from a studio at 3101 Scotts Valley Drive, Suite 18. The specialties are European manicures and dry (waterless) pedicures, and she still takes in-person concierge appointments in Boulder Creek alongside the studio. Booking runs through an Instagram direct message. We don't have hours or prices to publish, so message ahead. If you run a nail practice in the valley we should know about, tell us.

Booking a small shop

Every business on this page is an appointment operation, and most of the appointments are with the owner. Book ahead, a week or more for weekends, because a single practitioner's calendar fills in whole days. Give real notice if you need to cancel; a no-show is a meaningful slice of a one-person shop's day. And confirm details when you book rather than trusting a listing, ours included. Hours on this page mean "call first," not "walk in."

What's nearby but not spa

Haircuts and color are their own category in town, covered in our haircut guide. For yoga and movement rather than treatment, Mountain Sangha holds classes on Highway 9. If a service is booked out locally, Felton and Scotts Valley add estheticians, day spas, and nail salons; the business directory carries the ones we've verified.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get a massage in Boulder Creek without leaving town?

Yes, two ways: Redwood Mountain Spa at 12560 Highway 9 (831-703-4519) and Elevated Wellness Massage & Bodywork at 127 Forest Street (831-345-8043). Both are by appointment.

Who does facials in Boulder Creek?

Redwood Mountain Spa has a licensed esthetician for facials, waxing, and lash work, and SuperNatural Beauty & Aesthetics offers medical-grade skin care, peels, and microneedling under a registered nurse. The difference is a spa facial versus a clinical treatment; pick by what your skin needs.

Is there a nail salon in town?

Not a storefront. Oli Nails is a Boulder Creek-based nail artist who comes to your home by appointment, booked through Instagram at @olive__oli_nails. The nearest walk-in-style salons are down the valley in Felton and Scotts Valley.

Do any of these take walk-ins?

No. Everything on this page runs by appointment, and most of these are single-practitioner shops. Book ahead and call rather than dropping in.

How do I turn this into a full day?

We've already built that itinerary, coffee through dinner, in a self-care day in Boulder Creek.

money-taxes-boulder-creek.title: Taxes, Banking, and Money Help in Boulder Creek
money-taxes-boulder-creek.html:
Most money chores have quietly moved onto a screen, but the ones that haven't are the ones you feel: tax season, a cash deposit, a bookkeeping mess that needs a person who's seen one before. Boulder Creek is better set up for those than a town of five thousand has any right to be. There's an Enrolled Agent tax office on the strip, an accounting practice based in town, and a bank branch with a door and a teller behind it.

This page collects them, along with the nearest valley options for what town doesn't cover. Two ground rules, same as every guide we publish: inclusion isn't endorsement, and nothing here is financial or tax advice. We describe who does what and how to reach them; choosing is your call.

The tax office: Superior Tax Service

  • Address: 12615 Highway 9, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-338-2222
  • Hours: not published; call

Allan R. Polus, EA, runs an Enrolled Agent tax office in downtown Boulder Creek handling tax preparation, tax planning, bookkeeping, and estate and trust returns for individuals and small businesses. An EA is a tax practitioner licensed by the federal government to represent taxpayers before the IRS, a credential that matters once your return has more moving parts than a W-2. The office serves Boulder Creek and the San Lorenzo Valley, and it runs on appointments rather than walk-ins, so call to set up a time, especially once tax season gets going.

The accountant: AP Accounting & Consulting

  • Based in: Boulder Creek; by appointment
  • Phone: 408-309-0756
  • Website: apaccountingconsulting.com
  • Hours: Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; weekends by appointment

The town's other tax and numbers option is AP Accounting & Consulting, founded in 2008 by Anil Prajapati, an IRS-registered tax preparer. The practice handles individual and small-business tax preparation, bookkeeping, financial planning, and consulting, serving Boulder Creek and the greater Bay Area. There's no storefront to walk into; this is an appointment practice, so start with a call or the website. Between this office and Superior Tax, a small business in town has two local doors to knock on before anyone drives to a CPA in Scotts Valley or Santa Cruz.

The bank: Liberty Bank's Boulder Creek branch

  • Address: 13233 Highway 9, Boulder Creek
  • Phone: 831-338-6477
  • Lobby hours: Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Not many towns this size still have a bank branch, and Boulder Creek's sits right on Highway 9. Liberty Bank's branch handles personal and business banking with a weekday lobby, which is what a shop owner with a cash drawer or anyone untangling a paperwork problem actually needs. Online and mobile banking cover the everyday load between visits, and the bank is a member FDIC. A fuller write-up of the branch, including its sister branch down the valley in Felton, is coming to the site soon.

The nearest valley options

Some money help lives just down the road rather than in town. In Ben Lomond, SLV Tax is Virginia Justus, EA, preparing taxes for individuals and small businesses across the San Lorenzo Valley, currently taking new clients by referral only (slvtax.com). In Scotts Valley, Timothy Imbrie, CPA MBA, offers accounting, tax preparation, bookkeeping, financial planning, and small-business consulting at 4340 Scotts Valley Drive, Suite G (831-438-4122). Also in Scotts Valley, Cassidy Insurance Agency is a family-owned independent brokerage writing home, auto, renters, business, life, and health policies (831-438-5490); if home insurance is the money problem on your mind, our fire insurance guide covers the mountain-specific side.

What still means a drive

Be clear-eyed about the boundary. Financial advisors, most CPA firms, and insurance offices cluster in Scotts Valley and Santa Cruz, and there's no credit union or second bank in town. What Boulder Creek does keep local is the recurring layer: the annual tax appointment, the bookkeeping, the branch errand. For what the numbers on those errands look like here, see our cost of living guide, and if you've just arrived, the new resident quick start puts these stops in context.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a tax preparer in Boulder Creek?

Yes, two. Superior Tax Service, an Enrolled Agent office at 12615 Highway 9 (831-338-2222), and AP Accounting & Consulting, an appointment-based practice in town (408-309-0756).

Is there a bank in Boulder Creek?

Yes. Liberty Bank's branch at 13233 Highway 9 is open weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. for personal and business banking. Call 831-338-6477.

What's an Enrolled Agent?

A tax practitioner licensed by the federal government to represent taxpayers before the IRS. It's a meaningful credential for anything beyond a simple return.

Are these recommendations?

No. Inclusion isn't endorsement, there are no rankings here, and nothing on this page is financial or tax advice. Verify licensing and fit for your own situation.
